source: Written 2026-10-22 by Claude Sonnet from our own summaries of the NC 2026 standards, and solved blind by Claude Opus (Claude Code agents, not runAi: no ai_runs rows), code-checked by lintQuestion; "checked" questions await a platform admin.

notes.NC26.ASDS.AMD.1: 69 new questions (23 per difficulty), 35 numeric and 34 choice. Quartiles are always the medians of the lower and upper halves, with the median left out of both halves for an odd count, and the stem says so. The two standard deviation calculations (sample, n - 1; and one population) have an exact whole-number answer and an empty compute because the checker does not take square roots. No technology is needed anywhere.
notes.NC26.ASDS.AMD.2: 30 questions across linear, exponential, quadratic and logistic models (parameters and interpretation), residuals and residual plots, choosing a model, binomial and normal distributions, and z-scores. Fitting by regression or simulation is not tested; every fitted equation, residual and z-score is given or computed by hand. The logistic model is tested through its limit and starting value and its S shape.
notes.NC26.ASDS.AMD.3: 30 questions: 14 choice, 16 numeric, built to be answered by hand. Where a simulation would normally be run, the data are given: digit strings to read, tallies of simulated trials to turn into estimates, a middle-95% range or a shuffle count for the margin of error and the randomization test. One margin-of-error question gives the formula 2*sqrt(p(1-p)/n) in the stem, since the summary does not name a formula. Testing differences is limited to a randomization test of two groups (a difference in means and a count of shuffles), with no p-value formulas.
notes.NC26.ASDS.CCD.1: Concept-heavy standard: about 70 percent of the questions are choice questions about described studies, samples and surveys; numeric questions are counts, proportional allocations, random-digit selections and percent calculations. No graphs or pictures are used; random digits are written out as lists.
notes.NC26.ASDS.CCD.2: Sampling is largely conceptual, so about 60% of the questions are choice; the numeric ones cover proportional and systematic allocation, cluster counts, random-digit selection and estimating a count from a sample proportion.
notes.NC26.ASDS.CCD.3: 30 questions on the five parts of the summary: generating data, compiling and combining existing data, cleaning (duplicates, missing values, errors and outliers, units and labels), and bias and limitations. Everything is answerable by hand; no picture or software is assumed.
notes.NC26.ASDS.CCD.4: Ethics reasoning is mostly judgment, so about 40% are numeric questions built on counts, percents and shares (response and withdrawal rates, proportional samples, weighted estimates); the rest are choice questions with one defensible option about a described situation. No pictures are used.
notes.NC26.ASDS.DCC.1: Communication standard, so about half the questions are choice questions about which sentence, title or presentation is accurate and suits the audience. The numeric questions compute the figures a message would quote (percent, rate, expected count, change, interval). No slides or graphs are shown: charts are described in words.
notes.NC26.ASDS.DCC.2: First 30 questions on drawing and justifying inferences from samples, 10 per difficulty. Technology is replaced by given results: fitted equations (predictions and residuals), a stated rule of thumb (margin of error about 1 over the square root of n, always given in the stem), and described simulation outcomes (counts out of 100 or 200 simulated samples). Covers limits on generalizing (sample vs. population, experiment vs. sample, cause vs. association), sample estimates and variability, margin of error and its dependence on sample size, setting up and reading simulations, and judging predicted values (extrapolation, residuals, strength of r). Not covered: constructing a simulation from scratch or running one, and formal intervals or tests, which are not tested here.
notes.NC26.ASDS.DCC.3: Critiquing claims is mostly judgment about a described situation, so 22 of the 30 are choice; the 8 numeric ones are the quantitative critiques (absolute versus relative change, percentage points, comparing experiment groups). Statistical versus practical significance is one choice question at difficulty 3 and uses only the plain-language meaning of "statistically significant".
notes.NC26.ASDS.DV.1: Displays are described in words (data lists, five-number summaries, bar heights); no picture is referred to. Building "with technology" is tested by what a tool would output or need (bin width, axis top, fences, scale choices) and by labeling and design choices, since the tool itself cannot be used. Bin endpoints are always stated, to avoid the ambiguity pass A hit.
notes.NC26.ASDS.DV.2: 69 new questions (23 per difficulty); 21 numeric and 48 choice, because most of this standard (what a display shows, hides or exaggerates, and which revision helps) is judgment better asked as a choice with one defensible option. All graphics are described in words or by their numbers. Judging an actual image or map is not testable in text and is left out.
notes.NC26.ASDS.FSP.1: Concept-heavy standard: about two thirds are choice questions about described situations; numeric questions are counts, ranges and simple percent or rate calculations that show variability or framing. No graphs or pictures are used.

questions.skill: Tell statistical questions from non-statistical ones
questions.stem: Which of these is a statistical question?
choices: How many pets do the students in Ms. Reed's class have?
How many pets does Maya have at her house right now?
How many days are there in the month of June each year?
What time does Leo's bus pick him up at his house today?
questions.answer: How many pets do the students in Ms. Reed's class have?
questions.solution: A statistical question expects the answers to vary, so many pieces of data are needed. Different students in a class have different numbers of pets. The other questions each have one single answer.

solve.answer: How many pets do the students in Ms. Reed's class have?
solve.work: A statistical question anticipates variability in the answers. Leo's bus time today: one answer. Days in June: always 30. Maya's pets right now: one answer. Pets of the students in a class: many answers that vary, so statistical.

questions.skill: Tell statistical questions from non-statistical ones
questions.stem: Read these five questions. (A) How many minutes did Priya read last night? (B) How many minutes do the students in grade 11 read each night? (C) What is the boiling point of water at sea level in degrees Celsius? (D) Which month comes right after June? (E) How many text messages do students at our school send in a day? How many of the five are statistical questions?
questions.solution: A statistical question expects answers that vary. (B) and (E) ask about many students, and their answers will differ. (A) is about one person on one night, (C) has one fixed answer, and (D) has one fixed answer. So 2 are statistical.

solve.work: (A) one person, one night: not statistical. (B) many grade 11 students: statistical. (C) fixed fact (100): not. (D) July: not. (E) many students, varies: statistical. Count = 2.

questions.stem: Ben asks 20 classmates how many minutes they spent on homework last night. What should he expect?
choices: The answers will probably differ, because students spend different amounts of time.
The answers will all be the same, since everyone has the same homework.
The answers will differ only if some students make mistakes when they report their times.
The answers will differ only if more than 100 students are asked.
questions.answer: The answers will probably differ, because students spend different amounts of time.
questions.solution: Different students work at different speeds and have different amounts of homework, so the numbers will naturally vary. Variability is a normal part of data, not just the result of mistakes or of a large sample.

solve.answer: The answers will probably differ, because students spend different amounts of time.
solve.work: Different students spend different amounts of time on homework, so variability is expected in any group, regardless of size or reporting errors.

questions.stem: Five students report how many minutes they spent reading: 10, 25, 15, 30, 20. How many minutes are there from the shortest time to the longest time?
questions.solution: The longest time is 30 minutes and the shortest is 10 minutes. The difference, 30 - 10 = 20 minutes, shows how much the answers vary.

solve.work: Shortest 10, longest 30. Range = 30 - 10 = 20.

questions.skill: Refine a question so data can answer it
questions.stem: Lena wants to learn about students' health. Which question could she answer by collecting data?
choices: How many hours of sleep do students at our school get on a school night?
Are the students at our school as healthy as they should be for their ages?
Is a good night's sleep the best thing for students in our school?
Why do students at our school care so much about their own health?
questions.answer: How many hours of sleep do students at our school get on a school night?
questions.solution: A question that data can answer names something that can be counted or measured, for a clear group of people. Hours of sleep on a school night can be measured. "As healthy as they should be", "the best thing" and "why they care" cannot be measured.

solve.answer: How many hours of sleep do students at our school get on a school night?
solve.work: Hours of sleep is measurable by collecting data. 'As healthy as they should be', 'why they care' and 'the best thing' are vague or value judgments.

questions.skill: Refine a question for its audience and purpose
questions.stem: The student council wants to plan lunch menus that students like. Which statistical question helps the council most?
choices: Which lunch items do students at our school choose most often?
How much does the cafeteria spend on napkins and trays each month of the year?
How many students are enrolled in each grade of our school?
How many lunches does the cafeteria cook each day for the teachers?
questions.answer: Which lunch items do students at our school choose most often?
questions.solution: The council's purpose is to learn what students like to eat. Only the question about students' choices of lunch items gives that information. The others are about costs, enrollment or teachers.

solve.answer: Which lunch items do students at our school choose most often?
solve.work: Planning menus students like needs data on students' lunch choices. Enrollment, teachers' lunches and napkin costs do not address preferences.

questions.skill: Refine a question for its audience and purpose
questions.stem: A coach wants to know whether practice times fit the players' schedules. Who should be asked?
choices: Only the players who have never missed a practice
The players on the team
Students who do not play on the team
The coaches of other teams
questions.answer: The players on the team
questions.solution: The purpose is to learn about the players' schedules, so the players on the team should be asked. Asking only players who never miss a practice leaves out the very players who might be having trouble.

solve.answer: The players on the team
solve.work: Whether practice times fit the players' schedules is a question about the players, all of them, not just perfect attenders (biased) or outsiders.

questions.stem: Which question is worded to push people toward answering "yes"?
choices: Should the gym stay open until 7 p.m. on school days for all of the students?
Wouldn't you agree that our amazing new gym should obviously stay open later?
How many days a week would you use the gym if it stayed open until 7 p.m.?
Do you support or oppose keeping the gym open until 7 p.m. on school days?
questions.answer: Wouldn't you agree that our amazing new gym should obviously stay open later?
questions.solution: Words such as "wouldn't you agree", "amazing" and "obviously" lead people to a particular answer. The other three questions ask in a neutral way.

solve.answer: Wouldn't you agree that our amazing new gym should obviously stay open later?
solve.work: 'Wouldn't you agree... amazing... obviously' is a leading question pushing yes. The others are neutral.

questions.stem: Question A asks, "Did you exercise this week?" and 45 of 60 students say yes. Question B asks, "Did you exercise at least 5 days this week?" and 18 of 60 students say yes. How many more students say yes to Question A than to Question B?
questions.solution: 45 - 18 = 27. The way the question is framed changes what "yes" means, so the two answers give very different pictures of how much students exercise.

questions.skill: Refine a question so data can answer it
questions.stem: Sofia asks, "Is the school lunch good?" Numbers cannot answer this well. Which question is a better version that data can answer?
choices: Is the lunch at our school tasty or not tasty?
What score from 1 to 5 do students at our school give the lunch?
What time does lunch start at our school each day of the school week?
Should the lunch at our school cost less money than it does at present?
questions.answer: What score from 1 to 5 do students at our school give the lunch?
questions.solution: A good version names who is asked (students at our school) and what is measured (a score from 1 to 5), and the scores will differ from student to student. "Tasty or not tasty" is as vague as the original question, the start time has one answer, and "should" asks for an opinion.

solve.answer: What score from 1 to 5 do students at our school give the lunch?
solve.work: A 1-5 rating gives numeric data about lunch quality; B is unrelated, C is an opinion on policy, D yes/no vague.

questions.skill: Tell statistical questions from non-statistical ones
questions.stem: Which question can be answered only by collecting data from many students, whose answers are expected to differ?
choices: How tall is the flagpole in front of our school?
How tall are the students in grade 9 at our school?
How many inches are there in one foot?
How tall was Mia on her last birthday?
questions.answer: How tall are the students in grade 9 at our school?
questions.solution: A statistical question expects answers that vary, so many pieces of data are needed. Students in grade 9 have different heights. The other questions each have one single answer.

solve.answer: How tall are the students in grade 9 at our school?
solve.work: Heights of grade 9 students vary and need data from many students; others have a single answer.

questions.skill: Tell statistical questions from non-statistical ones
questions.stem: Read these four questions. (1) How many minutes do students in our grade spend on homework each night? (2) What day of the week comes after Tuesday? (3) How many players are on the field for one team in a soccer game? (4) How many goals do the teams in the county league score in a game? How many of the four are statistical questions?
questions.solution: A statistical question expects varying answers. Homework time (1) differs from student to student, and goals per game (4) differ from game to game. (2) and (3) each have one fixed answer. So 2 are statistical.

solve.issues: Minor: (3) assumes standard 11-a-side rules; youth soccer uses smaller sides, but the intended reading is clear.
solve.work: (1) varies by student: yes. (2) Wednesday: no. (3) fixed by the rules (11): no. (4) goals vary by team and game: yes. Total 2.

questions.skill: Tell statistical questions from non-statistical ones
questions.stem: Why is "How tall are the players on our basketball team?" a statistical question?
choices: It asks about a sport, and sports questions are always statistical.
It asks for a number, and every question with a number answer is statistical.
The players' heights are expected to differ from player to player.
Its answer is one fixed number that never changes.
questions.answer: The players' heights are expected to differ from player to player.
questions.solution: A question is statistical when its answers are expected to vary. Different players have different heights, so we need data from many players. Having a number as an answer is not enough, since "How many days are in a week?" also has a number as its answer.

solve.answer: The players' heights are expected to differ from player to player.
solve.work: Statistical because the heights vary from player to player.

questions.skill: Tell statistical questions from non-statistical ones
questions.stem: Which question has only one answer, so it is not a statistical question?
choices: How many hours do students sleep on a school night?
How many pages are in the books on the school library shelves?
How many minutes do students spend on the bus each day?
How many months are there in a year?
questions.answer: How many months are there in a year?
questions.solution: There are always 12 months in a year, so there is no variability. The other questions ask about many students or many books, and the answers will differ.

solve.answer: How many months are there in a year?
solve.work: 12 months in a year: one fixed answer.

questions.stem: Which list of data shows no variability at all?
questions.solution: There is no variability when every value is the same. Each of the other lists has at least two different values.

solve.work: All values equal: 5,5,5,5,5.

questions.stem: Mia measures the lengths of 6 leaves from one tree. What should she expect?
choices: The lengths will probably differ, because leaves are not all the same size.
The lengths will all be exactly equal, because the leaves come from one tree.
The lengths will differ only if she measures with a broken ruler.
The lengths will differ only if the leaves come from six different trees.
questions.answer: The lengths will probably differ, because leaves are not all the same size.
questions.solution: Even leaves from one tree vary in size, so measured lengths will vary. Variability is natural, not just a result of mistakes or different trees.

solve.answer: The lengths will probably differ, because leaves are not all the same size.
solve.work: Natural variability: leaves differ in size even on one tree.

questions.stem: Four runners finish a race in 12, 15, 11 and 14 minutes. How many minutes are there between the fastest time and the slowest time?
questions.solution: The fastest time is 11 minutes and the slowest is 15 minutes. The difference is 15 - 11 = 4 minutes.

solve.work: Fastest 11, slowest 15; 15 - 11 = 4.

questions.stem: If 30 different people are each asked one of these questions, which question is expected to give different answers?
choices: How many days are there in a week?
How many steps did you take today?
How many hours are there in one day?
How many letters are in the word "cat"?
questions.answer: How many steps did you take today?
questions.solution: People walk different amounts each day, so their step counts vary. The other three questions have the same answer for everyone.

solve.answer: How many steps did you take today?
solve.work: Steps today vary by person; others are fixed.

questions.skill: Refine a question so data can answer it
questions.stem: Which question is clear enough that data can answer it?
choices: Are the students at Cedar High tired at the end of the school day on most days?
Do kids in our town like going to school as much as they should?
Is homework bad for the health and the grades of students?
How many hours do 10th graders at Cedar High sleep on a school night?
questions.answer: How many hours do 10th graders at Cedar High sleep on a school night?
questions.solution: The question about 10th graders names the group, what is measured (hours of sleep) and when (a school night). The others use unclear words like "tired", "like" and "bad".

solve.answer: How many hours do 10th graders at Cedar High sleep on a school night?
solve.work: Hours of sleep of 10th graders at Cedar High on a school night is measurable with defined group; others are vague.

questions.skill: Refine a question so data can answer it
questions.stem: A student asks, "Are the students at our school healthy?" What is the main problem with this question for collecting data?
choices: The word "healthy" is not defined in a way that can be measured.
It asks about too few students to count as a statistical question.
It can be answered only with a yes or a no.
It names a single school instead of naming a whole country.
questions.answer: The word "healthy" is not defined in a way that can be measured.
questions.solution: Before collecting data, we must say how "healthy" will be measured, such as hours of exercise or number of sick days. The question as written does not do that.

solve.answer: The word "healthy" is not defined in a way that can be measured.
solve.work: "Healthy" has no measurable definition.

questions.skill: Refine a question so data can answer it
questions.stem: Which change makes "How long is the trip to school?" easier to answer with data?
choices: Asking it only one time of just a single student, whom the researcher meets in the hallway
Giving the unit, such as minutes, and naming the students at one school
Making it longer by adding many extra words and examples to the question itself
Changing it to a question that has only a yes or no answer
questions.answer: Giving the unit, such as minutes, and naming the students at one school
questions.solution: A clear question says what is measured and for whom. Giving a unit and a group makes the data consistent. The other changes do not make the question clearer.

solve.answer: Giving the unit, such as minutes, and naming the students at one school
solve.work: Specifying units and population makes it answerable with data.

questions.skill: Refine a question so data can answer it
questions.stem: Dan asks, "What do people eat?" Which refinement is best for collecting data?
choices: What does every single person in the world eat at every meal on every day of the year?
What is the best food for people to eat?
What do students in Dan's grade usually eat for lunch on school days?
Do people eat food at all?
questions.answer: What do students in Dan's grade usually eat for lunch on school days?
questions.solution: The best refinement names the group (Dan's grade), the meal (lunch) and the time (school days), so data can be collected. The others are too broad, opinion-based or not variable.

solve.answer: What do students in Dan's grade usually eat for lunch on school days?
solve.work: Defined population (students in Dan's grade) and context (lunch on school days) makes it collectible.

questions.skill: Refine a question for its audience and purpose
questions.stem: A librarian wants to buy books that children will borrow. Which question helps the most?
choices: How many books does the library already own on all of its shelves?
In what year was the library building first opened to the public?
What kinds of books do children who visit the library borrow most?
How tall are the children who visit the library on weekends?
questions.answer: What kinds of books do children who visit the library borrow most?
questions.solution: The librarian's purpose is to choose books children will borrow, so the data should be about what children borrow. The other questions do not help with that choice.

solve.answer: What kinds of books do children who visit the library borrow most?
solve.work: Kinds of books children borrow most directly informs purchasing.

questions.skill: Refine a question for its audience and purpose
questions.stem: The school nurse wants to plan flu shot clinics for the people at the school. Whom should the nurse ask?
choices: Only the students in a single class
Only the people who live far from the school
The members of a team at another school
The students and staff at the school
questions.answer: The students and staff at the school
questions.solution: The question should be asked of the group that the plan is for. Here that is the students and staff at the school.

solve.answer: The students and staff at the school
solve.work: Population of interest is the students and staff at the school.

questions.skill: Refine a question for its audience and purpose
questions.stem: A coach wants the team to practice at times that suit the players. Which question helps the coach most?
choices: Which practice times can the players on the team come to?
How tall are the players on the team?
What is the favorite color of the players on the team, when choosing a team uniform?
How many games did the team win last year, and how many of them were at home?
questions.answer: Which practice times can the players on the team come to?
questions.solution: The coach's purpose is to choose practice times, so the question should be about the players' available times. The other questions do not help with that.

solve.answer: Which practice times can the players on the team come to?
solve.work: Which practice times players can attend directly serves scheduling.

questions.stem: Which question is worded the most neutrally?
choices: How do you feel about the new school start time?
Don't you hate the awful new school start time?
Isn't the new school start time wonderful for everybody?
Do you agree that the foolish new school start time must go?
questions.answer: How do you feel about the new school start time?
questions.solution: A neutral question does not push the answer in one direction. The other questions use loaded words like "hate", "wonderful" and "foolish".

solve.answer: How do you feel about the new school start time?
solve.work: A is open and neutral; others are loaded.

questions.stem: The same 80 students were asked about a later start time using two different wordings. Wording 1 got 56 "yes" answers. Wording 2 got 40 "yes" answers. By how many percentage points do the two "yes" percents differ?
questions.solution: Wording 1: 56 / 80 = 70%. Wording 2: 40 / 80 = 50%. The difference is 70 - 50 = 20 percentage points, so the wording changed the result.

solve.work: 56/80 = 70%; 40/80 = 50%; difference 20 points.

questions.stem: A headline says, "Almost nobody likes the new lunch menu!" The survey found that 12 of 100 students like it. Which headline is more neutral?
choices: The new lunch menu is a total flop with students at school!
Twelve of the 100 students surveyed like the new menu.
Students are just crazy about the new lunch menu at school!
Nearly all of the students are hurt by the new lunch menu!
questions.answer: Twelve of the 100 students surveyed like the new menu.
questions.solution: A neutral headline reports the numbers without strong words. The other headlines use dramatic language that changes how the result feels.

solve.answer: Twelve of the 100 students surveyed like the new menu.
solve.work: A states the result plainly.

questions.stem: A club asks 50 people, "Would you try our new class?" and 40 say yes. Later it asks the same 50 people, "Would you pay 20 dollars a month for our new class?" and 10 say yes. By how many percentage points does the percent of "yes" answers drop?
questions.solution: First question: 40 / 50 = 80%. Second question: 10 / 50 = 20%. The drop is 80 - 20 = 60 percentage points. The wording (adding a cost) changed the answers.

questions.stem: A student collects data for four questions. Which set of data answers a question with the LEAST variability?
choices: Siblings of each one of 5 different students: 0, 3, 1, 2, 4
Soccer players on the field, 5 teams: 11, 11, 11, 11, 11
Minutes to run one mile for 5 students: 7, 12, 9, 15, 10
Ages of 5 people in one large family: 4, 36, 38, 9, 62
questions.answer: Soccer players on the field, 5 teams: 11, 11, 11, 11, 11
questions.solution: All five soccer teams have the same number of players on the field, so the values do not vary at all. The other three lists change from one value to the next.

solve.answer: Soccer players on the field, 5 teams: 11, 11, 11, 11, 11
solve.work: Soccer players on the field: 11, 11, 11, 11, 11 has zero spread. The other sets vary (ranges 8, 4, 58).

questions.skill: Refine a question so data can answer it
questions.stem: A student wants to refine the question "Do students like school?" so that data can answer it. Which version is best?
choices: On a scale of 1 to 5, how do students at our school rate school?
Why do students everywhere feel the way that they do about going to school?
How does a typical person feel when thinking about going to school every day?
What do students at our school think about school in general, overall?
questions.answer: On a scale of 1 to 5, how do students at our school rate school?
questions.solution: A refined question names the group (students at our school) and what will be measured (a rating from 1 to 5), so every answer can be recorded and compared. The other versions are vague, or ask about too wide a group.

solve.answer: On a scale of 1 to 5, how do students at our school rate school?
solve.work: A refined question names the population (students at our school) and a measurable response (1-5 rating). The others are vague, about 'why', or about everyone.

questions.skill: Refine a question so data can answer it
questions.stem: A well-framed statistical question names the group asked, the thing measured and the time. Look at this question: "How many minutes do the 7th graders at Park Middle School spend on homework on a school night?" Which part is the thing that is measured?
choices: the minutes of homework
the 7th graders at Park
Park Middle School itself
on a school night
questions.answer: the minutes of homework
questions.solution: The group asked is the 7th graders at Park Middle School. The time is a school night. What is measured is how long each student works, which is the minutes of homework.

solve.answer: the minutes of homework
solve.work: The group is the 7th graders at Park; the time is a school night; the thing measured is minutes of homework.

questions.skill: Tell statistical questions from non-statistical ones
questions.stem: Which question is NOT a statistical question?
choices: How do the scores of the Hawks' games this season compare?
What was the score of the final game of the Hawks' season?
What is a typical score for the Hawks in a game this season?
How much do the Hawks' scores vary from game to game?
questions.answer: What was the score of the final game of the Hawks' season?
questions.solution: The other three questions ask about all the games in a season, where the scores vary. The question about the final game has a single answer, so there is no variability to study.

solve.answer: What was the score of the final game of the Hawks' season?
solve.work: Variation from game to game, a typical score and comparing scores all involve many varying values. The score of one particular game is a single fact, so it is not statistical.

questions.skill: Tell statistical questions from non-statistical ones
questions.stem: Why is "How many sides does a hexagon have?" not a statistical question?
choices: It asks for a number of sides instead of asking for a word or a name.
It is about shapes, and shapes cannot be studied with data.
Its answer is the same every time, so there is no variability to study.
It would need a very large sample of hexagons before it could be answered.
questions.answer: Its answer is the same every time, so there is no variability to study.
questions.solution: A statistical question is one where the answers are expected to vary. Every hexagon has 6 sides, so asking many people or measuring many hexagons gives the same answer each time.

solve.answer: Its answer is the same every time, so there is no variability to study.
solve.work: A hexagon always has 6 sides; the answer never varies, so there is no variability to study. The other reasons are false.

questions.stem: A bakery owner asks, "How many loaves of bread do we sell each day?" Which is a likely source of variability in the answers?
choices: The price of one loaf of bread stays the same every day of the week.
Weekdays and weekends bring different numbers of customers.
The bakery opens at the same time every morning of the week.
The name of the bakery does not change from one day to the next.
questions.answer: Weekdays and weekends bring different numbers of customers.
questions.solution: Variability comes from things that change from day to day, like how many customers come in. Things that stay the same every day (price, opening time, name) cannot explain why the daily counts differ.

solve.answer: Weekdays and weekends bring different numbers of customers.
solve.work: A source of variability must be something that changes from day to day. Weekday vs weekend customer numbers change; price, opening time and name are constant.

questions.stem: Which group's heights would you expect to vary the most?
choices: Heights of 40 students in one first-grade class
Heights of 400 students who were all born in the same month and year
Heights of 40 students from kindergarten through grade 12
Heights of 4 students in one fifth-grade class
questions.answer: Heights of 40 students from kindergarten through grade 12
questions.solution: Heights vary most when the group covers a wide range of ages. Students from kindergarten to grade 12 range from small children to nearly full-grown teenagers. A bigger group of students of the same age still has heights that are close together.

solve.answer: Heights of 40 students from kindergarten through grade 12
solve.work: Ages 5 to 18 span a huge range of heights. One first-grade class, 4 fifth graders, or 400 children of the same age all have similar ages, so less variation. K-12 group varies most.

questions.skill: Refine a question for its audience and purpose
questions.stem: The town council is deciding whether to add bike lanes. Which statistical question is best for the council's purpose?
choices: How many bikes were sold in the whole country last year?
What is the most popular bike color among students at one school?
How many trips do residents of the town take by bike in a week?
How fast can a professional cyclist ride?
questions.answer: How many trips do residents of the town take by bike in a week?
questions.solution: The council needs to know how much residents of the town would use the lanes. Trips by bike in a week for town residents is related to that purpose and varies from person to person. The other questions are about the wrong group, an unrelated feature or a single answer.

solve.answer: How many trips do residents of the town take by bike in a week?
solve.work: The council needs local bike use: trips by town residents per week. National sales, bike colour at one school, pro speed are irrelevant.

questions.skill: Refine a question for its audience and purpose
questions.stem: A principal wants results for each of the four grades (9, 10, 11 and 12) separately, with at least 25 students surveyed in each grade. What is the least total number of students that must be surveyed?
questions.solution: Each of the 4 grades needs at least 25 students, so the smallest total is 4 x 25 = 100 students.

solve.work: At least 25 in each of 4 grades: 4 x 25 = 100.

questions.stem: A headline says, "Cases of a rare illness TRIPLED!" The cases went from 2 to 6 among 100,000 people. Which statement gives the fairest picture?
choices: Cases tripled, so most people are now at risk.
Cases rose by 600%, so the illness is now widespread.
Cases rose from 2 to 6 per 100,000 people, which is still rare.
Cases rose by only 4, so the change does not matter at all.
questions.answer: Cases rose from 2 to 6 per 100,000 people, which is still rare.
questions.solution: Going from 2 to 6 is true tripling, but the actual numbers matter: 6 in 100,000 is still rare. The best statement gives both numbers. A rise from 2 to 6 is a 200% increase, not 600%, and it is not so small that it can be ignored.

solve.answer: Cases rose from 2 to 6 per 100,000 people, which is still rare.
solve.work: 2 to 6 per 100,000 is a tripling but still rare. C wrongly says 600% (it is 200% increase); A and D overclaim.

questions.stem: A cycling club's web page asks its visitors, "Should the city build more bike lanes?" and 92% say yes. Which conclusion do the results support?
choices: Most residents of the city, even those who never ride a bike, favor more bike lanes.
Nearly everyone who uses the roads in the city favors more bike lanes.
About 92% of all of the cyclists in the whole state favor more bike lanes.
Most visitors to the cycling club's page favor more bike lanes.
questions.answer: Most visitors to the cycling club's page favor more bike lanes.
questions.solution: The answers came only from people who visit the cycling club's page, who are likely to favor bike lanes. The results describe that group. They cannot be used for all residents, all road users or all cyclists.

solve.answer: Most visitors to the cycling club's page favor more bike lanes.
solve.work: Self-selected visitors to a cycling club page only represent those visitors, not the state, road users or residents.

questions.skill: Refine a question so data can answer it
questions.stem: Original question: "Is it hot in Raleigh in summer?" Which refinement is BEST answered with data?
choices: Is Raleigh hotter in summer than most other places in the country?
Do most people who live in Raleigh feel hot during the summer months, when they are outdoors?
Is the summer weather in Raleigh too hot for outdoor activities?
What was the highest temperature, in degrees Fahrenheit, in Raleigh on each day in July?
questions.answer: What was the highest temperature, in degrees Fahrenheit, in Raleigh on each day in July?
questions.solution: The best refinement says what is measured (the highest temperature), the unit (degrees Fahrenheit), the place (Raleigh) and the time (each day in July). The other questions leave the group, the measure or the meaning of "hot" unclear, or ask for an opinion.

solve.answer: What was the highest temperature, in degrees Fahrenheit, in Raleigh on each day in July?
solve.work: Daily July high temperatures are measured data; others are subjective or vague.

questions.stem: Answers vary when different people or things give different answers. Read these five questions. (A) How many brothers and sisters does each student in our school have? (B) How many students are in Room 12 right now? (C) How tall is each tree in the park? (D) What date is the first day of school this year? (E) How many minutes does each student at our school take to eat lunch? How many of the five questions will have answers that vary?
questions.solution: Questions A, C and E ask about many different people or trees, so the answers will differ. Question B has one answer right now, and question D has one answer. So 3 questions have answers that vary.

solve.work: (A) siblings per student: varies. (B) count of students in one room now: one answer. (C) height of each tree: varies. (D) date of first day: one answer. (E) minutes each student takes to eat: varies. Three questions vary.

questions.skill: Tell statistical questions from non-statistical ones
questions.stem: Mia says, "How old is my cousin?" is a statistical question because the answer is a number. What is wrong with her reasoning?
choices: Statistical questions may never have a number as the answer.
A number as an answer is not enough; the answers must vary.
Ages cannot be measured, so no question about them counts.
The question would be statistical only if it asked about color.
questions.answer: A number as an answer is not enough; the answers must vary.
questions.solution: Her cousin has one age at a given time, so the question has one answer. A statistical question anticipates variability, such as "How old are the students in a school?"

solve.answer: A number as an answer is not enough; the answers must vary.
solve.work: One cousin's age is a single value; a number answer is not enough, the answers must vary.

questions.skill: Tell statistical questions from non-statistical ones
questions.stem: Here are six questions about the Tigers, a school team. (1) How many points did the Tigers score in their last game? (2) How many points do the Tigers score per game over a season? (3) What is the name of the Tigers' coach? (4) How tall are the Tigers' players? (5) How many players are on the Tigers' roster today? (6) How many minutes does each player spend in a game? How many are statistical questions?
questions.solution: Statistical questions expect varying answers. (2) points differ from game to game, (4) heights differ from player to player, and (6) playing time differs from player to player. (1), (3) and (5) each have one answer. So 3 are statistical.

solve.work: (1) one game: no. (2) points per game over a season vary: yes. (3) coach name: no. (4) heights vary: yes. (5) roster count today: one number: no. (6) minutes vary by player: yes. Total 3.

questions.skill: Tell statistical questions from non-statistical ones
questions.stem: Which description of a statistical question is correct?
choices: It always asks for an average of the data collected.
It can be answered only with the words "yes" or "no".
It expects varying answers and is answered with data.
It always asks about at least 100 different people.
questions.answer: It expects varying answers and is answered with data.
questions.solution: A statistical question is defined by variability and data: different individuals or occasions give different answers. It does not have to ask for an average, can have many kinds of answers, and has no required number of people.

solve.answer: It expects varying answers and is answered with data.
solve.work: A statistical question anticipates variability and is answered with data.

questions.skill: Tell statistical questions from non-statistical ones
questions.stem: Which is a statistical question whose answers are categories instead of numbers?
choices: Which season comes right after the summer season?
Which season is it today in our state of North Carolina?
How many seasons are there in one whole year?
What is the favorite season of students in our grade?
questions.answer: What is the favorite season of students in our grade?
questions.solution: Students will name different seasons, so the answers vary even though they are words. The other questions each have one correct answer.

solve.answer: What is the favorite season of students in our grade?
solve.work: Favorite season of students varies and is categorical; others are fixed facts.

questions.stem: A scientist weighs the same apple 5 times on a kitchen scale and gets 151, 150, 152, 150 and 151 grams. What is the best explanation for the small differences?
choices: The apple's true weight changes by a large amount each time it is weighed.
A different apple must have been weighed each time.
Each reading on the scale has a little measurement variability.
Any difference means the scale is broken, since an object always gives the same reading.
questions.answer: Each reading on the scale has a little measurement variability.
questions.solution: Measurements of the same thing can differ slightly because of the scale and how it is read. This is ordinary variability, not evidence of a broken scale or of a changing apple.

solve.answer: Each reading on the scale has a little measurement variability.
solve.work: Small differences when weighing the same object are measurement variability.

questions.stem: A researcher asks, "How many hours do high school students sleep each night?" Which is NOT a likely source of variability in the answers?
choices: Students going to bed and waking up at different times
Sleep being different on school nights and on weekends
Students being of different ages and having different activities
Every student being asked the same question in the same words
questions.answer: Every student being asked the same question in the same words
questions.solution: Variability comes from real differences among students and nights. Asking everyone the same question in the same way does not make the answers differ.

solve.answer: Every student being asked the same question in the same words
solve.work: Asking everyone the same wording is not a source of variability; the others are.

questions.stem: A school bus arrives at the stop at these times on five mornings, in minutes after 7:00: 41, 45, 43, 50 and 44. How many minutes are there between the earliest and the latest arrival?
questions.solution: The earliest arrival is 41 minutes after 7:00 and the latest is 50. The difference is 50 - 41 = 9 minutes.

solve.work: Earliest 41, latest 50; 50 - 41 = 9.

questions.stem: A coach says all of her runners run a mile in about the same time. The recorded times range from 6 to 14 minutes. What do the data show?
choices: The times vary a lot, so her statement is not supported by the data.
The times are almost the same, since all of them are measured in minutes.
The times are the same, because the average is the only thing that matters.
The times cannot be compared, because the runners ran on different days.
questions.answer: The times vary a lot, so her statement is not supported by the data.
questions.solution: A range from 6 to 14 minutes is a spread of 8 minutes, which is large for a mile. The data show a lot of variability, so the claim that the runners are about the same is not supported.

solve.answer: The times vary a lot, so her statement is not supported by the data.
solve.work: Range 6 to 14 minutes is large; claim not supported.

questions.stem: Two classes took a quiz and both have a mean score of 75. Class P scored 74, 76, 75 and 75. Class Q scored 60, 90, 75 and 75. How many points larger is the range of Class Q's scores than the range of Class P's scores?
questions.solution: Class P: range = 76 - 74 = 2. Class Q: range = 90 - 60 = 30. The difference is 30 - 2 = 28. The classes have the same mean but very different variability.

questions.skill: Refine a question so data can answer it
questions.stem: A student wants to learn how often teens use social media. Which refined question gives data a clear meaning for "often"?
choices: How much do the teens at our school like using social media on their phones each week?
Is social media often used by a typical teen at our school, in general, these days?
How often do all of the teens in the whole world use social media?
On how many of the last 7 days did students in grades 9 to 12 use social media?
questions.answer: On how many of the last 7 days did students in grades 9 to 12 use social media?
questions.solution: The question about the last 7 days names the group, a time period and a count, so "often" becomes the number of days. The others stay vague or cannot be answered with data.

solve.answer: On how many of the last 7 days did students in grades 9 to 12 use social media?
solve.work: Number of the last 7 days with use gives 'often' a numeric meaning.

questions.skill: Refine a question so data can answer it
questions.stem: A student wants to answer, "Do students who eat breakfast do better?" Which refinement uses measurable variables?
choices: Do students who eat breakfast on school mornings score higher on math quizzes than those who skip it?
Do students who eat breakfast on school mornings feel better about their whole day than those who skip it?
Do students who eat a good breakfast on school mornings have a better life at school than those who skip it?
Is breakfast an important part of what most students do on school mornings, compared with other things?
questions.answer: Do students who eat breakfast on school mornings score higher on math quizzes than those who skip it?
questions.solution: Breakfast on school mornings and math quiz scores can both be recorded. "Feel better", "better life" and "important" cannot be measured clearly.

solve.answer: Do students who eat breakfast on school mornings score higher on math quizzes than those who skip it?
solve.work: Math quiz scores are measurable; 'feel better', 'important', 'better life' are vague.

questions.skill: Refine a question so data can answer it
questions.stem: To answer "Do students get enough exercise?", a researcher must decide what "enough" means. What is the best way to handle that?
choices: Leave "enough" undefined so that each student can decide for themselves what counts as enough exercise.
Set a measurable standard, such as 60 minutes of activity a day, and state it in the question.
Replace "enough" with "some" and count any activity at all, however small, as meeting the standard.
Ask only the students who play on a sports team at the school, since they exercise the most.
questions.answer: Set a measurable standard, such as 60 minutes of activity a day, and state it in the question.
questions.solution: A refined question defines vague words in a way that data can measure. A set standard, such as 60 minutes a day, lets everyone's data be compared.

solve.answer: Set a measurable standard, such as 60 minutes of activity a day, and state it in the question.
solve.work: Define a measurable threshold such as 60 min/day and state it.

questions.skill: Refine a question for its audience and purpose
questions.stem: A principal is deciding whether to start school 30 minutes later. Which statistical question best fits that purpose?
choices: What time did school start in the building at the start of last year?
How many hours do the students at our school sleep on school nights?
What is the principal's favorite time of the day to work?
How many students are in the whole school this year?
questions.answer: How many hours do the students at our school sleep on school nights?
questions.solution: The decision is about students' sleep and morning schedules, so the question should measure sleep. The others do not give evidence about whether a later start would help.

solve.answer: How many hours do the students at our school sleep on school nights?
solve.work: Students' sleep on school nights is statistical and relevant to a later start.

questions.skill: Refine a question for its audience and purpose
questions.stem: A sports store wants to decide how many pairs of each shoe size to stock. Which question helps the most?
choices: What colors do the people who shop at the store like?
How many shoes did the store sell in the first year it opened?
What shoe sizes do the people who shop at the store wear?
What is the highest price of a shoe at the store?
questions.answer: What shoe sizes do the people who shop at the store wear?
questions.solution: To stock sizes, the store needs data on the sizes its shoppers wear. The other questions are not about size.

solve.answer: What shoe sizes do the people who shop at the store wear?
solve.work: Shoe sizes of customers decides stock by size.

questions.skill: Refine a question for its audience and purpose
questions.stem: Mei will report to the school board, which must decide how many buses to provide. Which question best serves the board?
choices: How many students at our school say that they like riding the bus?
What is the favorite subject of each of the students at our school, among all subjects?
How many students at our school own a bicycle of their own?
How many students at our school live more than 2 miles from the school?
questions.answer: How many students at our school live more than 2 miles from the school?
questions.solution: The board's decision about buses depends on how many students live too far to walk. Liking the bus, favorite subjects and bike ownership do not give that count.

solve.answer: How many students at our school live more than 2 miles from the school?
solve.work: Bus need depends on how many students live far from school (beyond walking distance).

questions.skill: Refine a question for its audience and purpose
questions.stem: The question "Which music do students like?" is refined for a DJ hired for the winter dance. Which refinement is best?
choices: Which songs do students at our school want to hear at the winter dance?
Which kinds of music do people in the whole country like the most in every season?
Which musical instruments do students at our school play in the band at concerts?
How many hours of music do students listen to each month?
questions.answer: Which songs do students at our school want to hear at the winter dance?
questions.solution: The DJ needs to know which songs this group wants to hear at this event. The other questions are about different groups or different information.

solve.answer: Which songs do students at our school want to hear at the winter dance?
solve.work: The DJ needs songs students at this school want at the winter dance.

questions.stem: A survey first asks students many questions about how stressful their homework is, and then asks, "How satisfied are you with school overall?" What is a concern?
choices: Surveys must always ask about satisfaction first, by a rule that all researchers follow.
The answers cannot vary from student to student, since every student sees the same questions.
The earlier questions may influence how students answer the later one.
Order matters only for questions with yes or no answers.
questions.answer: The earlier questions may influence how students answer the later one.
questions.solution: Questions that come earlier can put ideas in people's minds and shift later answers. Order can matter for any kind of question.

solve.answer: The earlier questions may influence how students answer the later one.
solve.work: Question order effect: earlier stress questions can shape the satisfaction answer.

questions.stem: Town A had 30 accidents last year and has 3,000 residents. Town B had 60 accidents and has 12,000 residents. A headline says, "Town B is twice as dangerous." What is the fairest response?
choices: Yes; Town B had twice as many accidents, so it is twice as dangerous overall.
Yes; Town B has more residents, so its accidents count for much more.
No; Town A had fewer accidents, so Town A is the less dangerous town of the two.
No; per 1,000 residents Town A had 10 accidents and Town B had 5.
questions.answer: No; per 1,000 residents Town A had 10 accidents and Town B had 5.
questions.solution: Compare rates, not counts. Town A: 30 / 3,000 = 10 per 1,000. Town B: 60 / 12,000 = 5 per 1,000. Reporting only counts frames Town B as worse when its rate is lower.

solve.answer: No; per 1,000 residents Town A had 10 accidents and Town B had 5.

questions.stem: A survey of 200 people asked about satisfaction. The answers were: very satisfied 50, somewhat satisfied 70, not very satisfied 50, not at all satisfied 30. One report shows the percent "very satisfied"; another shows the percent "at least somewhat satisfied". How many percentage points larger is the second percent than the first?
questions.solution: "Very satisfied": 50 / 200 = 25%. "At least somewhat satisfied": (50 + 70) / 200 = 60%. The difference is 60 - 25 = 35 percentage points. The choice of category changes the picture.

solve.work: Very satisfied 50/200 = 25%; at least somewhat (50+70)/200 = 60%; difference 35.

questions.stem: A bar graph's vertical axis starts at 90 instead of 0. The first bar shows 92 and the second bar shows 96, so the second bar looks about three times as tall. Why is this misleading?
choices: The bars compare 2 and 6 above the start of the axis, not 92 and 96.
The bars should always be drawn the same height, whatever the data are.
The second value is exactly three times as large as the first value.
A vertical axis may never begin at a number other than 90 in a graph.
questions.answer: The bars compare 2 and 6 above the start of the axis, not 92 and 96.
questions.solution: Above the starting point of 90, the bars measure 2 and 6, which is a ratio of 3 to 1. The real values, 92 and 96, differ by only about 4%. A start other than 0 exaggerates a small difference.

solve.answer: The bars compare 2 and 6 above the start of the axis, not 92 and 96.
solve.work: Truncated axis: bar heights show 2 and 6 above 90, not 92 and 96.

questions.skill: Refine a question so data can answer it
questions.stem: Poll 1 asks, "Do you support the new park, which will cost taxpayers 2 million dollars?" and finds 38% support. Poll 2 asks, "Do you support the new park, which will give children a safe place to play?" and finds 71% support. What is the best conclusion?
choices: Poll 2 is right, because a larger percent of the people support the new park
The true support is 54.5%, which is the average of the two poll results
Poll 1 is right, because it mentions an actual fact about the cost
The wording may have steered answers, so neither percent is a fair measure
questions.answer: The wording may have steered answers, so neither percent is a fair measure
questions.solution: Each question mentions only one side, so the framing can steer people toward yes or no. The two percents cannot be trusted as a measure of support. A better question would state the cost and the benefit neutrally.

solve.answer: The wording may have steered answers, so neither percent is a fair measure
solve.work: The two polls differ only in leading wording (cost vs benefit), and results moved from 38% to 71%. The framing shaped answers, so neither is a fair measure; averaging is not justified.

questions.skill: Refine a question for its audience and purpose
questions.stem: An organizer asks, "Is our park used?" She refines it to "How many people enter Cedar Park on a typical Saturday between 9 a.m. and 5 p.m.?" What did the refining add?
choices: A larger sample chosen with a random method
Wording that hints at the answer she wants
A countable measure, a place and a time
A comparison between Cedar Park and another park
questions.answer: A countable measure, a place and a time
questions.solution: The new question counts people (a measure data can give), names the place (Cedar Park) and gives a time (a typical Saturday, 9 a.m. to 5 p.m.). It does not mention a sample, a comparison or a hoped-for answer.

solve.answer: A countable measure, a place and a time
solve.work: The refined question adds a countable measure (number of people entering), a place (Cedar Park) and a time (typical Saturday 9-5). No sample, comparison or leading wording added.

questions.skill: Tell statistical questions from non-statistical ones
questions.stem: A pet store owner wants to learn about her customers. Which is a statistical question she could ask?
choices: How many dogs are for sale in the store today?
How many pets do the store's customers own?
What is the street address of the pet store?
What time does the store close on Saturdays?
questions.answer: How many pets do the store's customers own?
questions.solution: A statistical question is one whose answers are expected to vary, so it needs data from many people. Different customers own different numbers of pets. The other three questions each have a single fixed answer.

solve.answer: How many pets do the store's customers own?
solve.work: Closing time, today's dog count and the address each have one fixed answer. Number of pets owned varies from customer to customer, so it anticipates variability: statistical.

questions.skill: Tell statistical questions from non-statistical ones
questions.stem: The question "How many books did Sam read in May?" is not a statistical question, because it has one answer. Which change makes it a statistical question?
choices: How many books did Sam read in May and June together?
How many books did Sam read in the whole month of May, counted exactly?
How many pages are in the first book Sam read in May?
How many books did the students in Sam's class read in May?
questions.answer: How many books did the students in Sam's class read in May?
questions.solution: Asking about one person, even for a longer time or with more care, still gives a single answer. Asking about all the students in a class gives many answers that will differ, so the question becomes statistical.

solve.answer: How many books did the students in Sam's class read in May?
solve.work: Pages in one book: one answer. Sam's exact count in May: one answer. Sam's count for May and June: one answer. Books read by each student in the class: many varying answers, so statistical.

questions.skill: Tell statistical questions from non-statistical ones
questions.stem: Read these six questions. (1) What is the average number of hours teens sleep on a school night? (2) What is the capital of North Carolina? (3) How many seconds did Omar take to run the 100-meter dash at Friday's meet? (4) How do the finishing times in the 100-meter dash at Friday's meet compare? (5) How many wheels does a bicycle have? (6) How much rain falls on Charlotte on each day of a typical April? How many of the six are statistical questions?
questions.solution: Statistical questions expect varying answers from many individuals or occasions. (1) teens differ in sleep, (4) many runners have different times, and (6) rain differs from day to day. (2), (3) and (5) each have one answer. So 3 are statistical.

solve.work: (1) teens' sleep hours vary: statistical. (2) Raleigh: fact. (3) one runner, one race: single value. (4) many finishing times: statistical. (5) 2 wheels: fact. (6) rainfall on each April day varies: statistical. Count = 3.

questions.stem: Café A had these customer counts on five days: 62, 48, 75, 51, 64. Café B had these counts on five days: 58, 60, 59, 61, 57. How much larger is the range of Café A's counts than the range of Café B's counts?
questions.solution: Café A: range = 75 - 48 = 27. Café B: range = 61 - 57 = 4. The difference is 27 - 4 = 23, so Café A's counts vary much more.

solve.work: Cafe A: max 75, min 48, range 27. Cafe B: max 61, min 57, range 4. Difference 27 - 4 = 23.

questions.stem: A researcher asks, "How long do people wait at the town pharmacy?" She records six waits, all on Monday mornings. Which statement is most accurate?
choices: Waits are set by the pharmacy's rules, so all six of the recorded values will be exactly identical.
Variability only matters if the waits are measured in hours instead of minutes.
Collecting more data would make the variability in the waits disappear completely.
Waits probably differ by day and hour, so Monday mornings may hide some variability.
questions.answer: Waits probably differ by day and hour, so Monday mornings may hide some variability.
questions.solution: Waiting times change with the day, the time and how busy the pharmacy is. Six Monday-morning waits show only part of that spread. More data would show the variability more completely; it would not remove it.

solve.answer: Waits probably differ by day and hour, so Monday mornings may hide some variability.
solve.work: Waits vary by day and time; sampling only Monday mornings may miss variability. Other statements are false.

questions.skill: Refine a question so data can answer it
questions.stem: Original question: "Do people in the neighborhood exercise enough?" The words "people", "the neighborhood" and "enough" are all unclear. Which refinement fixes all three?
choices: How many minutes do people exercise during a typical day or week?
Do adults in the Maple Grove neighborhood get enough exercise each week?
How many minutes per week do adults 18 and older in Maple Grove exercise?
How many minutes per week do some of the people who live in Maple Grove exercise?
questions.answer: How many minutes per week do adults 18 and older in Maple Grove exercise?
questions.solution: The best refinement names the group (adults 18 and older), the place (Maple Grove), and a measurement with a unit and a time frame (minutes per week). The other versions still leave the group, the place or the meaning of "enough" unclear.

solve.answer: How many minutes per week do adults 18 and older in Maple Grove exercise?
solve.work: A replaces 'people' with adults 18 and older, 'the neighborhood' with Maple Grove, and 'enough' with a measure (minutes per week). B keeps 'people' and no place; C keeps 'enough'; D keeps 'some of the people'.

questions.skill: Refine a question so data can answer it
questions.stem: Omar wants to answer "What is the typical commute time for workers in Durham?" but he can only collect data from the 12 workers at his uncle's company. How should he refine the question to match the data he can collect?
choices: What is the typical commute time for workers in North Carolina?
What is the typical commute time for workers in Durham, using only these 12 workers?
What was the commute time of his uncle on one morning?
What is the typical commute time for the workers at his uncle's company?
questions.answer: What is the typical commute time for the workers at his uncle's company?
questions.solution: A question should match the group that data can really come from. Data from the 12 workers at one company can answer a question about that company. It cannot speak for all of Durham or the state, and one morning for one person would give a single value, not a statistical question.

solve.answer: What is the typical commute time for the workers at his uncle's company?
solve.work: Data from 12 workers at one company can only answer a question about that company's workers. A still claims Durham; B is wider; C is one person, not statistical.

questions.skill: Refine a question for its audience and purpose
questions.stem: A transit agency wants to plan bus routes and schedules and has data on student commute times. Which question is best refined for the agency's purpose?
choices: What is the average commute time for all students in the whole district?
Do parents of students think that the commutes to school are too long?
What is the longest commute time recorded for any one student in the school?
How long does each commute take, by neighborhood and by time of day?
questions.answer: How long does each commute take, by neighborhood and by time of day?
questions.solution: To plan routes and schedules the agency needs to see where and when commutes are long. Breaking the times down by neighborhood and time of day shows that. One district-wide average hides it, and opinions or a single value do not help.

solve.answer: How long does each commute take, by neighborhood and by time of day?
solve.work: Routes and schedules depend on where and when students travel, so commute time by neighbourhood and time of day fits. A single maximum, a district average or parent opinions do not guide routes.

questions.skill: Refine a question for its audience and purpose
questions.stem: A clinic wants to know whether its new text reminders reduce missed appointments. Which question is best refined for the clinic's purpose?
choices: Do patients with text reminders miss a lower percent of appointments than patients without them?
How many patients does the clinic see in a typical year, counting every visit made by each of them?
What percent of all the appointments at the clinic are missed in a typical year, over all patients?
Do patients who receive the text reminders say that they like getting them from the clinic?
questions.answer: Do patients with text reminders miss a lower percent of appointments than patients without them?
questions.solution: The purpose is to compare missed appointments with and without reminders. Only the question that compares the percent of appointments missed with and without reminders measures the right thing. The others do not compare, or measure something else.

solve.answer: Do patients with text reminders miss a lower percent of appointments than patients without them?
solve.work: The purpose is missed appointments with vs without reminders; A compares missed-appointment rates between the two groups.

questions.stem: Five salaries, in thousands of dollars, are 30, 30, 32, 34 and 174. One company reports the mean as the "typical" salary. Another reports the median. How many thousand dollars greater is the mean than the median?
questions.solution: Mean = (30 + 30 + 32 + 34 + 174) / 5 = 300 / 5 = 60. Median = 32 (the middle value). The difference is 60 - 32 = 28 thousand dollars. The one very high salary pulls the mean up, so the choice of summary frames the story.

questions.stem: A treatment lowers the risk of an event from 5 in 1,000 people to 3 in 1,000 people. A headline reports the relative drop in risk as a percent. What percent should the headline say?
questions.solution: The risk drops by 5 - 3 = 2 in 1,000. As a share of the original 5 in 1,000, that is 2 / 5 = 0.40, or 40%. The same change is only 2 in 1,000 in absolute terms, so the way it is framed changes how large it seems.

solve.work: Relative drop = (5 - 3)/5 = 0.4 = 40%.

questions.skill: Tell statistical questions from non-statistical ones
questions.stem: Dana wants to turn a question about one backpack into a statistical question. Which question is statistical?
choices: What is a typical weight of a backpack at Dana's school?
What does Dana's backpack weigh when it holds her math book?
How much does Dana's backpack weigh on the nurse's scale at noon today?
How much more does Dana's backpack weigh than her lunch bag?
questions.answer: What is a typical weight of a backpack at Dana's school?
questions.solution: Only the question about many students' backpacks expects different answers. The other three are about Dana's own bag at one time, so each has a single answer.

solve.answer: What is a typical weight of a backpack at Dana's school?
solve.work: Typical backpack weight at the school requires data from many backpacks that vary.

questions.skill: Tell statistical questions from non-statistical ones
questions.stem: Read these seven questions. (1) What was the high temperature in Raleigh on March 3 last year? (2) How do the high temperatures in Raleigh vary from day to day in March? (3) How many hours per week do students at Lincoln High with part-time jobs work? (4) How many hours did Carlos work last week? (5) Is 17 a prime number? (6) Do ticket prices for concerts in our city differ much? (7) How much time do students at a school spend on the bus each day? How many of the seven are statistical questions?
questions.solution: (2) asks about highs that differ from day to day, (3) covers many students with different hours, (6) asks about many prices that vary, and (7) covers many students with different times. (1) and (4) are about one day or one person, and (5) has one answer. So 4 are statistical.

solve.work: (1) single day: no. (2) yes. (3) yes. (4) one person one week: no. (5) no. (6) prices vary: yes. (7) yes. Total 4.

questions.skill: Tell statistical questions from non-statistical ones
questions.stem: Which situation describes someone asking a statistical question?
choices: A teacher asks one student on what date her birthday falls this year, expecting a single answer
A teacher asks a class how long each trip to school takes, expecting different answers.
A teacher asks the whole class for the answer to 6 times 7.
A teacher looks up how many days there are in the month of October.
questions.answer: A teacher asks a class how long each trip to school takes, expecting different answers.
questions.solution: A statistical question is one where many answers are expected to differ. Trip times differ among students. A birthday, a product and the days in October each have a single answer.

solve.answer: A teacher asks a class how long each trip to school takes, expecting different answers.
solve.issues: Minor: option D lacks the final period the other options have.
solve.work: Asking each student's trip time expecting different answers is a statistical question.

questions.skill: Tell statistical questions from non-statistical ones
questions.stem: Compare two questions. (1) How many hours per day do teenagers spend on screens? (2) How many hours did Zoe spend on screens on Sunday? Which statement is true?
choices: Only question (2) is statistical, because it is more exact.
Both questions are statistical, because both ask for hours.
Only question (1) is statistical, because teens' hours vary.
Neither question is statistical, because screen time is not measurable.
questions.answer: Only question (1) is statistical, because teens' hours vary.
questions.solution: Question (1) is about many teenagers, who will give different answers. Question (2) is about one person on one day, so it has one answer. Both ask for hours, but that does not make a question statistical.

solve.answer: Only question (1) is statistical, because teens' hours vary.
solve.work: (1) varies across teens: statistical. (2) one person one day: not.

questions.stem: Researcher 1 asks 30 teens at one school how many texts they send per day. Researcher 2 asks 30 teens from six different cities. Which statement is most reasonable?
choices: Researcher 1's answers will likely vary more, since a single school is a smaller place to ask
Researcher 2's answers will likely vary more, since teens in six cities differ more.
The answers will vary equally, since both researchers asked 30 teens.
Neither set of answers will vary, since everyone in both groups was asked the very same question.
questions.answer: Researcher 2's answers will likely vary more, since teens in six cities differ more.
questions.solution: A sample from several cities includes more kinds of teens, so it is likely to show more variability than a sample from one school. The size of the sample does not by itself decide the amount of variability.

solve.answer: Researcher 2's answers will likely vary more, since teens in six cities differ more.
solve.issues: Minor: option D lacks the final period the other options have.
solve.work: Teens from six cities are more heterogeneous, so answers likely vary more.

questions.stem: A set of daily temperatures over a week has a range of 14 degrees. The warmest day was 83 degrees. How many degrees was the coolest day?
questions.solution: Range = largest - smallest, so smallest = largest - range = 83 - 14 = 69 degrees.

solve.work: Coolest = 83 - 14 = 69.

questions.stem: Jin times his bike ride to school one time and gets 12 minutes. He says, "My ride always takes 12 minutes." What is the best response?
choices: He is right, because he timed the ride carefully.
He is right, because the distance to school does not change.
One ride cannot show how much the time varies; he should time many rides.
He should time exactly one more ride, since two rides show all the variability.
questions.answer: One ride cannot show how much the time varies; he should time many rides.
questions.solution: Variability appears only when several measurements are compared. Weather, traffic and speed change from day to day, so one ride cannot show the spread.

solve.answer: One ride cannot show how much the time varies; he should time many rides.
solve.work: One observation cannot show variability; time many rides.

questions.stem: The weights of five puppies in a litter are 4, 5, 5, 6 and 9 pounds. A sixth puppy joins the data and weighs 3 pounds. By how many pounds does the range increase?
questions.solution: Before: range = 9 - 4 = 5. After adding the 3-pound puppy: range = 9 - 3 = 6. The range increases by 6 - 5 = 1 pound.

solve.work: Original range 9 - 4 = 5; new range 9 - 3 = 6; increase 1.

questions.skill: Refine a question so data can answer it
questions.stem: Original question: "Is the new bus schedule better?" Which refinement makes "new", "better" and the group clear?
choices: Do Route 5 riders like the new schedule more than they liked the old schedule that they used?
Are the buses on the new schedule faster than the buses on the old schedule used to be in the past?
Is the mean wait for Route 5 riders shorter in the 4 weeks after the change than before it?
Do most people in the city think that the new bus schedule is better for them overall?
questions.answer: Is the mean wait for Route 5 riders shorter in the 4 weeks after the change than before it?
questions.solution: The question about mean wait names the route, the time periods and a measurable outcome (mean wait). Each of the others still uses a vague word such as "like", "faster" or "better", or an unclear group.

solve.answer: Is the mean wait for Route 5 riders shorter in the 4 weeks after the change than before it?
solve.work: Route 5 riders (group), 4 weeks after change (new), mean wait shorter (better) - all defined.

questions.skill: Refine a question so data can answer it
questions.stem: A school store keeps a log of every purchase: the item, the price and the time of the purchase. Which question can these data answer?
choices: Why do students at the school prefer some items to others?
How much money do the families of the students at the school earn?
Which students are most likely to buy healthy snacks at the store?
At what time of day does the school store make the most sales each day?
questions.answer: At what time of day does the school store make the most sales each day?
questions.solution: The log has items, prices and times, so it can show when sales are greatest. It contains no reasons, no family income and no information about individual students.

solve.answer: At what time of day does the school store make the most sales each day?
solve.work: The log has item, price, time; time of day with most sales is answerable. Others need income, reasons or student identity not recorded.

questions.skill: Refine a question so data can answer it
questions.stem: A student refines her question to "What percent of the students in grade 9 at Elm High walk to school?" She asks a random group of 50 students in grade 9, and 14 say they walk. What percent of the 50 students walk?
questions.solution: The percent is 14 out of 50, which is 14 / 50 = 0.28 = 28%.

questions.skill: Refine a question so data can answer it
questions.stem: A question asks, "How many hours do students at our school sleep?" The only data available come from exam week. Which refinement matches the data?
choices: How many hours do students at our school sleep during exam week?
How many hours do students at our school sleep during an average week?
How many hours do students in the whole state sleep in exam week?
How many hours do students at our school sleep in every week of the year?
questions.answer: How many hours do students at our school sleep during exam week?
questions.solution: The refined question must be one the data can answer. Exam-week data can answer a question about exam week at our school, but not about every week or another group.

solve.answer: How many hours do students at our school sleep during exam week?
solve.work: Data only from exam week, so restrict the question to exam week at our school.

questions.skill: Refine a question so data can answer it
questions.stem: A tutoring program wants to know "Does tutoring help?" Which refined question can be answered with data?
choices: Do students who attend tutoring sessions feel that their schoolwork has improved a lot over the year?
Do students with 4 or more fall tutoring sessions gain more on tests than students with none?
Is the tutoring program a good thing for the students who take part in it each year?
Do all the students at the school do better when a tutoring program exists?
questions.answer: Do students with 4 or more fall tutoring sessions gain more on tests than students with none?
questions.solution: The question about 4 or more fall sessions defines the treatment (at least 4 sessions), the comparison group (none), the outcome (gain in test score) and the time period. The others use unclear words.

solve.answer: Do students with 4 or more fall tutoring sessions gain more on tests than students with none?
