solve.work: Defines dose (4+ fall sessions), comparison group (none), measure (test gains).

questions.skill: Refine a question for its audience and purpose
questions.stem: A hospital wants to decide how many nurses to schedule for each hour of the day. Which question is best refined for that purpose?
choices: What is the mean wait of all of the patients for the whole day?
How do the mean waits of patients compare for each hour of the day?
What was the longest wait of any single patient last year?
How many patients came to the hospital during the whole of last year?
questions.answer: How do the mean waits of patients compare for each hour of the day?
questions.solution: Staffing by hour needs data by hour. A single daily mean, a single longest wait, or a yearly count hides the pattern the hospital needs.

solve.answer: How do the mean waits of patients compare for each hour of the day?
solve.work: Mean waits for each hour of the day matches hourly nurse scheduling.

questions.skill: Refine a question for its audience and purpose
questions.stem: A town wants to decide where to build a new playground for children under 10. Whom should a survey ask?
choices: Only the people who are already at a playground in the town on one afternoon
Every adult living in the state, wherever they live
Households with children under 10 in each neighborhood of the town
Only the members of the town council
questions.answer: Households with children under 10 in each neighborhood of the town
questions.solution: The survey should reach the families the playground is for, across every neighborhood. The other choices leave out many families or ask people the decision does not concern.

solve.answer: Households with children under 10 in each neighborhood of the town
solve.work: Households with children under 10, in each neighborhood, are the affected population and cover all locations.

questions.skill: Refine a question for its audience and purpose
questions.stem: A survey wants at least 30 responses from each of 5 neighborhoods. Only 60% of the households contacted are expected to respond. How many households should be contacted in all, so that about 30 respond in each neighborhood?
questions.solution: To get 30 responses at a 60% response rate, contact 30 / 0.6 = 50 households in a neighborhood. For 5 neighborhoods: 50 x 5 = 250 households.

solve.work: Per neighborhood 30/0.6 = 50; 5 x 50 = 250.

questions.skill: Refine a question for its audience and purpose
questions.stem: A company wants to improve a product that some customers returned. Which question is best refined for that purpose?
choices: How many customers bought the product in the first place?
What do customers who kept the product think of the company's logo?
How old is the oldest customer who bought the product?
What problems do the customers who returned the product report?
questions.answer: What problems do the customers who returned the product report?
questions.solution: To improve the product, the company needs to learn what went wrong for those who returned it. The other questions do not give that information.

solve.answer: What problems do the customers who returned the product report?
solve.work: Problems reported by customers who returned it inform improvement.

questions.stem: A restaurant says, "Of 40 diners we asked at the dessert counter, 36 loved the food." Which statement is the fairest?
choices: Nine out of every ten customers of the restaurant love the food they eat.
Of the 40 diners asked at the dessert counter, 36 loved the food; others may differ.
The food is loved by nearly every person who has ever eaten at the restaurant, past or present.
Most diners would rather eat at this restaurant than at any other place.
questions.answer: Of the 40 diners asked at the dessert counter, 36 loved the food; others may differ.
questions.solution: Diners at the dessert counter stayed through a whole meal, so they may be happier than others. The result describes only those who were asked.

solve.answer: Of the 40 diners asked at the dessert counter, 36 loved the food; others may differ.
solve.work: Only 40 diners at the dessert counter, a non-representative group; the fair statement restricts the claim to them.

questions.stem: The waiting times, in minutes, of five patients are 5, 6, 7, 8 and 64. A clinic advertises the median wait. A patient group reports the mean wait. How many minutes is the mean greater than the median?
questions.solution: Mean = (5 + 6 + 7 + 8 + 64) / 5 = 90 / 5 = 18. Median = 7. The mean is 18 - 7 = 11 minutes greater. One very long wait pulls the mean up, so each report frames the data differently.

questions.stem: Out of 2,000 people who did not take a medicine, 4 had a rare side effect. Out of 2,000 people who did take it, 12 had the side effect. A headline reports the relative increase in risk as a percent. What percent should the headline say?
questions.solution: The risk rose from 4 to 12, an increase of 8. As a share of the original 4, that is 8 / 4 = 2 = 200%. In absolute terms it is only 8 more people in 2,000, so the headline can make a small risk sound large.

questions.stem: School A reports that 9 of 10 tested students passed. School B reports that 80 of 100 tested students passed. A writer says, "School A has the higher pass rate, so it is the better school." What is the best response?
choices: School B's rate is higher, since the number 80 is larger than the number 9, so B is better.
The rates are equal, because both of the schools tested some students.
School A's rate is higher, but only 10 students were counted, so it is less certain.
School A's rate is higher, so nothing else about the two schools needs to be considered at all.
questions.answer: School A's rate is higher, but only 10 students were counted, so it is less certain.
questions.solution: School A: 9 / 10 = 90%. School B: 80 / 100 = 80%. A rate based on 10 students can change a lot if one more student fails, so a bigger sample gives more reliable information.

solve.answer: School A's rate is higher, but only 10 students were counted, so it is less certain.
solve.work: A: 90% vs B: 80%. A is higher but based on only 10 students, so less certain; 'better school' needs more.

questions.stem: A soda company pays for a survey titled "Why Teens Love Sugary Drinks." What is the most important concern about its results?
choices: Surveys that are paid for by any company are always correct.
Teens cannot give opinions about drinks that they have never bought.
The survey must be wrong, because the results of a sponsored survey can never be trusted at all.
The sponsor and title may shape the questions and how results are reported.
questions.answer: The sponsor and title may shape the questions and how results are reported.
questions.solution: Who pays for a study and how it is titled can influence the question wording and the conclusions. That is a reason to look more closely, though it does not prove the results are wrong.

solve.answer: The sponsor and title may shape the questions and how results are reported.
solve.work: Sponsor bias and a leading title may shape questions and reporting.

questions.stem: A line graph of a price has a vertical axis that runs only from 49 to 53 dollars. The price rises from 50 dollars to 52 dollars, so the line's height above the bottom of the graph looks like it triples, from 1 to 3 units. What is the actual percent increase in the price?
questions.solution: Actual increase: 52 - 50 = 2 dollars. As a share of the original 50 dollars, that is 2 / 50 = 0.04 = 4%. The graph's short axis exaggerates a small change.

questions.stem: A school has 600 students. The principal writes each student's name on a slip of paper, mixes the slips in a large box, and draws 40 slips without looking. Which sampling method is this?
choices: Stratified random sample
Simple random sample
Cluster sample
Convenience sample
questions.answer: Simple random sample
questions.solution: Every student had the same chance of being drawn, and every group of 40 students was equally likely. That is a simple random sample. Nothing was grouped first, so it is not stratified or cluster, and the draw was by chance, so it is not a convenience sample.

solve.answer: Simple random sample
solve.work: Every name is on a slip, slips are mixed and 40 drawn blind: every set of 40 students is equally likely. That is a simple random sample (no strata, no clusters, not convenience).

questions.stem: A list has 1,200 students numbered in order. A systematic sample of exactly 60 students is taken: a starting student is chosen at random from the first $k$ students on the list, and then every $k$th student after that is taken. What is $k$?
questions.solution: Taking every $k$th student from 1,200 gives 1200 / $k$ students. We want 60, so $k = 1200 \div 60 = 20$.

solve.work: Systematic sample of 60 from 1,200 taking every kth: k = 1200 / 60 = 20.

questions.stem: A radio station asks listeners to call in and vote on whether the town should build a new swimming pool. Only the people who choose to call are counted. Why might the results be biased?
choices: Small samples are always biased, whatever the method used to choose them
Random selection of the callers makes results biased, since random methods favor some people
Letting each listener vote only once would have removed the bias in the result entirely
People with strong opinions are the most likely to call in
questions.answer: People with strong opinions are the most likely to call in
questions.solution: The callers chose themselves (a voluntary response sample). People with strong feelings are more likely to call, so they are over-represented. Small samples are not automatically biased, the callers were not chosen at random, and voting once does not fix self-selection.

solve.answer: People with strong opinions are the most likely to call in
solve.work: Voluntary response: people with strong opinions are most likely to call.

questions.stem: In an experiment, subjects are assigned to the treatment groups by chance, such as by drawing names from a hat. What is the main purpose of assigning subjects at random?
choices: To make the groups alike, so results can be credited to the treatment
To make sure the sample represents the whole population of interest
To make sure every subject receives exactly the same treatment in the study
To let each subject pick the treatment that they would like best
questions.answer: To make the groups alike, so results can be credited to the treatment
questions.solution: Random assignment tends to make the groups alike in every other way (age, health, motivation). Then a difference in results is most likely due to the treatment. Representing a population is the job of random sampling, not random assignment.

solve.answer: To make the groups alike, so results can be credited to the treatment
solve.work: Random assignment balances the groups on other variables so a difference in outcome can be attributed to the treatment. Representing the population is the job of random sampling, not assignment.

questions.skill: Observational study or experiment, and what it shows
questions.stem: Researchers ask 150 students how many hours they sleep on school nights and then look up each student's grades. They do not change anything about the students' lives. What kind of study is this?
choices: A randomized experiment
A placebo-controlled experiment
An observational study
A matched-pairs experiment
questions.answer: An observational study
questions.solution: The researchers only recorded what the students already did. They did not assign any treatment, so it is an observational study, not an experiment.

solve.answer: An observational study
solve.work: No treatment is imposed; researchers just measure sleep and look up grades. Observational study.

questions.stem: Before a student joins a research study, a researcher explains what will happen and what the risks are, and the student freely agrees to take part. What is this called?
choices: Random assignment
Blinding
Informed consent
Replication
questions.answer: Informed consent
questions.solution: Telling people what the study involves and its risks, and getting their free agreement before they take part, is informed consent.

solve.answer: Informed consent
solve.work: Explaining procedures and risks and obtaining free agreement is informed consent.

questions.skill: Neutral survey questions and answer choices
questions.stem: A student council wants to know how students feel about a longer lunch period. Which survey question is worded most neutrally?
choices: Do you support or oppose making the lunch period longer?
Don't you agree that a longer lunch period would be wonderful?
Since students are hungry by noon, wouldn't you like a longer lunch period?
Most students want a longer lunch period. Do you want one too?
questions.answer: Do you support or oppose making the lunch period longer?
questions.solution: A neutral question does not suggest an answer. The other three push the reader toward yes with words like "wonderful", with a reason to agree, or by saying that most students agree.

solve.answer: Do you support or oppose making the lunch period longer?
solve.work: A, B and D are leading ("Don't you agree", bandwagon, "wouldn't you"). C offers both sides neutrally.

questions.stem: A researcher wants to learn how all students in a town spend their free time. She emails a survey link to the students and counts only the answers submitted online. Which group is most likely to be left out?
choices: Students who have two or more email addresses and receive the link more than once
Students who enjoy using computers every day
Students who check their email several times a day and reply to messages quickly
Students without a reliable internet connection
questions.answer: Students without a reliable internet connection
questions.solution: A survey that can only be answered online misses students who cannot get online. The other groups are easy to reach by email.

solve.answer: Students without a reliable internet connection
solve.work: Online-only responses exclude students without reliable internet.

questions.stem: A survey was mailed to 1,000 households, and 150 households returned it. The response rate is the percent of households that returned the survey. What is the response rate? Enter the number without the percent sign.
questions.solution: Response rate $= 150 \div 1000 \times 100 = 15$ percent. With so few replies, the households that answered may differ from the ones that did not.

questions.stem: A teacher wants to test whether a new study app raises quiz scores. She has 40 volunteers and will give the app to 20 of them. Which way of choosing the 20 is random assignment?
choices: Give the app to the 20 volunteers who signed up first
Give the app to the 20 volunteers with the highest grades
Put all 40 names in a hat and draw 20 names for the app
Let each volunteer decide whether to get the app
questions.answer: Put all 40 names in a hat and draw 20 names for the app
questions.solution: In random assignment, chance alone decides who is in each group. Drawing names from a hat does that. Choosing the first to sign up, the highest grades, or letting people decide lets some trait of the volunteers decide, which can bias the comparison.

solve.answer: Put all 40 names in a hat and draw 20 names for the app
solve.work: Random assignment means chance decides who gets the treatment. Drawing 20 names from a hat does that; first sign-ups, highest grades and self-selection are not random.

questions.stem: A researcher splits a school's students into groups by grade and then takes a simple random sample from each group. Which sampling method is this?
choices: Systematic random sample
Cluster random sample
Stratified random sample
Voluntary response sample
questions.answer: Stratified random sample
questions.solution: The population is divided into groups (strata) by grade, and a random sample is taken from every group. That is a stratified random sample.

solve.answer: Stratified random sample
solve.work: Dividing into groups by grade and SRS from each = stratified random sample.

questions.stem: Every 8th person who enters a store is asked to take a survey, starting with the 8th person. On one day, 400 people enter the store. How many people are asked to take the survey?
questions.solution: Every 8th person is asked, so the number asked is 400 / 8 = 50.

solve.work: Every 8th starting at the 8th: 8, 16, ..., 400; 400/8 = 50.

questions.stem: Which plan gives a simple random sample of 25 students from a class of 30?
choices: Take the first 25 names on the attendance list, since the list was made before the survey began
Take the 25 students who sit nearest to the door, since their seats were assigned by the teacher
Take the first 25 students who volunteer, since every student was invited to take part in it
Draw 25 of the 30 names from a hat, so every group of 25 is equally likely
questions.answer: Draw 25 of the 30 names from a hat, so every group of 25 is equally likely
questions.solution: In a simple random sample, every possible group of 25 students has the same chance. Drawing names from a hat does that. The other plans let position or choice decide.

solve.answer: Draw 25 of the 30 names from a hat, so every group of 25 is equally likely
solve.work: Drawing 25 of 30 names from a well-mixed hat gives every set of 25 equal chance = SRS.

questions.skill: Using random digits to choose a sample
questions.stem: Students are numbered 01 to 60. A researcher reads random digits two at a time: 61, 88, 27, 03. She skips any number that is not from 01 to 60. What is the number of the first student chosen?
questions.solution: 61 and 88 are not from 01 to 60, so they are skipped. The first valid number is 27.

solve.work: 61 skip, 88 skip, 27 chosen first.

questions.skill: Using random digits to choose a sample
questions.stem: Why do researchers use random digits or a random number generator to choose a sample?
choices: So that the researcher can choose the people who are the easiest to ask
So that the people with the strongest opinions are the ones chosen
So that the sample always has exactly the same results as the whole population it came from
So that every member of the population has the same chance of being chosen
questions.answer: So that every member of the population has the same chance of being chosen
questions.solution: Random choice gives each person an equal chance of selection, which prevents the researcher's preferences from biasing the sample. It does not make the sample match the population exactly.

solve.answer: So that every member of the population has the same chance of being chosen
solve.work: Random selection gives every member an equal chance, removing selector bias.

questions.skill: Using random digits to choose a sample
questions.stem: Students are numbered 1 to 9. A researcher reads the random digits 0, 7, 3, 9, 2 in order. The digit 0 is skipped because there is no student 0. What is the number of the second student chosen?
questions.solution: The first valid digit is 7, so student 7 is chosen first. The next digit is 3, so student 3 is chosen second.

solve.work: 0 skipped; 7 first; 3 second.

questions.stem: A survey about how much people exercise is given only to people who are at a gym. Why might the results be biased?
choices: People at a gym are too busy to take a survey of any length.
People at a gym cannot be counted accurately by a researcher.
People at a gym probably exercise more than most other people.
People at a gym will give answers that are all exactly the same.
questions.answer: People at a gym probably exercise more than most other people.
questions.solution: The sample leaves out people who do not go to a gym, and those people are likely to exercise less. The sample does not represent everyone, so the results are biased.

solve.answer: People at a gym probably exercise more than most other people.
solve.work: Gym-goers likely exercise more than the population: biased sample.

questions.stem: Which description of a voluntary response sample is correct?
choices: The people in the sample are chosen by a random number generator.
The people in the sample are all taken from the same neighborhood.
The people in the sample are picked by every kth name on a list.
The people in the sample choose for themselves whether to respond.
questions.answer: The people in the sample choose for themselves whether to respond.
questions.solution: In a voluntary response sample, people decide for themselves whether to answer, such as a call-in poll. People with strong opinions are more likely to respond, which makes these samples biased.

solve.answer: The people in the sample choose for themselves whether to respond.
solve.work: A voluntary response sample consists of people who choose to respond.

questions.stem: In an experiment, what is the control group?
choices: The group that is chosen by the researcher to get the best results
The group that does not get the treatment, for comparison
The group that gets a stronger treatment than the other groups
The group of people who ask the questions in the experiment
questions.answer: The group that does not get the treatment, for comparison
questions.solution: The control group is used for comparison. It gets no treatment, or a standard one, so the researcher can see what the treatment adds.

solve.answer: The group that does not get the treatment, for comparison
solve.work: Control group does not get the treatment, used for comparison.

questions.stem: Researchers give bean plants different amounts of water and measure how tall each plant grows. Which variable is the response variable?
choices: The amount of water each plant gets
The type of bean in each pot
The height of each plant
The size of each flower pot
questions.answer: The height of each plant
questions.solution: The response variable is the outcome that is measured, which here is plant height. The amount of water is the explanatory variable that the researchers change.

solve.answer: The height of each plant
solve.work: Response variable is the outcome measured: plant height.

questions.skill: Observational study or experiment, and what it shows
questions.stem: Researchers assign 50 students to study in the morning and 50 students to study in the evening, and then compare their test scores. What type of study is this?
choices: An observational study
A census
A voluntary response survey
An experiment
questions.answer: An experiment
questions.solution: The researchers assigned each student to a condition, so this is an experiment. In an observational study the researchers do not assign anything.

solve.answer: An experiment
solve.work: Researchers impose the condition (study time), so it is an experiment.

questions.skill: Observational study or experiment, and what it shows
questions.stem: Which kind of study can best show cause and effect?
choices: A randomized experiment
A call-in radio poll
A large observational study
A survey of a random sample
questions.answer: A randomized experiment
questions.solution: Random assignment makes the groups alike, so differences in the outcome can be credited to the treatment. Observational studies and polls can show only associations.

solve.answer: A randomized experiment
solve.work: Randomized experiments can establish causation.

questions.skill: Observational study or experiment, and what it shows
questions.stem: In an experiment, what is a treatment?
choices: A trait that the subjects already had before the study
A condition that the researchers assign to the subjects
An answer that a subject gives on a survey
A group of subjects who volunteer for the study
questions.answer: A condition that the researchers assign to the subjects
questions.solution: A treatment is something the researchers decide to apply to the subjects, such as an amount of fertilizer or a type of lesson.

solve.answer: A condition that the researchers assign to the subjects
solve.work: A treatment is a condition imposed/assigned by researchers.

questions.stem: When data are collected anonymously, what does that mean?
choices: Everyone in the study is told how each person answered.
The researcher keeps a list of names next to the answers.
Only people who volunteer are allowed to answer the survey.
No one can link a response to the person who gave it.
questions.answer: No one can link a response to the person who gave it.
questions.solution: Anonymous means that responses cannot be connected to individuals, which protects privacy and often encourages honest answers.

solve.answer: No one can link a response to the person who gave it.
solve.work: Anonymous: no response can be linked to the person.

questions.stem: Which statement describes a right of someone who joins a research study?
choices: The person may stop taking part at any time without a penalty.
The person must finish the study once it has begun, even if they feel unwell later
The person is not told what the study is about at all.
The person has to share private information with the researchers' sponsors if they ask
questions.answer: The person may stop taking part at any time without a penalty.
questions.solution: Participation must be voluntary. A person may leave a study at any time without being punished.

solve.answer: The person may stop taking part at any time without a penalty.
solve.issues: Minor: options A and D lack final periods while B and C have them.
solve.work: Participants may withdraw at any time without penalty.

questions.stem: A researcher gives students' names and test scores to a newspaper without their permission. Which ethical principle is broken?
choices: Random sampling
Confidentiality
Double blinding
Replication
questions.answer: Confidentiality
questions.solution: Confidentiality means keeping participants' personal information private. Sharing names with scores without permission breaks that principle.

solve.answer: Confidentiality
solve.work: Releasing names with scores without permission breaks confidentiality.

questions.skill: Neutral survey questions and answer choices
questions.stem: Which survey question is leading?
choices: How much time do you spend on homework on a typical night?
Is the amount of homework too much, too little or about right?
Don't you agree that homework takes up far too much of your time?
How would you describe the amount of homework you get?
questions.answer: Don't you agree that homework takes up far too much of your time?
questions.solution: A leading question pushes people toward one answer. The one that begins "Don't you agree" suggests that the answer should be yes, while the others are neutral.

solve.answer: Don't you agree that homework takes up far too much of your time?
solve.work: 'Don't you agree...far too much' pushes toward agreement = leading.

questions.skill: Neutral survey questions and answer choices
questions.stem: Which set of answer choices is balanced?
choices: Disagree, neutral, agree, strongly agree, completely agree
Strongly disagree, neutral, agree, strongly agree, completely agree
Neutral, agree, strongly agree, completely agree, totally agree
Strongly disagree, disagree, neutral, agree, strongly agree
questions.answer: Strongly disagree, disagree, neutral, agree, strongly agree
questions.solution: A balanced scale has the same number of choices on each side of the middle. Each of the other lists has more agreeing choices than disagreeing ones.

solve.answer: Strongly disagree, disagree, neutral, agree, strongly agree
solve.work: B has two negative, neutral, two positive: balanced.

questions.skill: Neutral survey questions and answer choices
questions.stem: A balanced answer scale has "agree" and "disagree", each with a "strongly" version, and one neutral choice. How many answer choices are there?
questions.solution: There are 2 choices on the agree side, 2 on the disagree side and 1 neutral: 2 + 2 + 1 = 5.

solve.work: Strongly disagree, disagree, neutral, agree, strongly agree = 5.

questions.stem: Which is an example of collecting data with technology?
choices: A student tallies the cars that pass the school on a sheet of paper.
A phone app records the number of steps a person takes in a day.
A teacher asks the class to raise hands to vote on a topic.
A researcher writes down the answers on a clipboard by hand.
questions.answer: A phone app records the number of steps a person takes in a day.
questions.solution: Technology records data automatically, such as an app or a sensor. Tallies and hand counts are collected by people.

solve.answer: A phone app records the number of steps a person takes in a day.
solve.work: A phone app automatically recording steps is technology-based collection.

questions.stem: A GPS device records the position of a bus every 10 seconds. What is an advantage of collecting data this way?
choices: It guarantees that the bus will always run on time every day.
It removes the need to ask any questions about the data.
It collects a large amount of data automatically and quickly.
It makes sure that every data value is exactly correct.
questions.answer: It collects a large amount of data automatically and quickly.
questions.solution: Devices can collect many measurements without a person recording each one. They do not guarantee accuracy or remove the need to think about the data.

solve.answer: It collects a large amount of data automatically and quickly.
solve.work: Automatic, frequent recording collects much data quickly.

questions.stem: A school surveys students about school lunches, but it gives the survey only to students who eat in the cafeteria. Students who bring lunch from home are never asked. What is the main source of bias?
choices: Nonresponse
Undercoverage
Voluntary response
Question wording
questions.answer: Undercoverage
questions.solution: Students who bring lunch have no chance of being in the sample, so part of the population is left out. That is undercoverage. Nonresponse would be students who were asked but did not answer.

solve.answer: Undercoverage
solve.work: Part of the population (students who bring lunch from home) is left out of the sampling frame entirely: undercoverage.

questions.stem: In an experiment, volunteers are put into the treatment group or the control group by a random number generator. What is the main benefit of this random assignment?
choices: It makes sure the results can be applied to the whole population
It evens out the groups on average so the treatment can be credited
It means the experiment can skip the control group and still be fair
It lets each volunteer pick the group that suits him or her best
questions.answer: It evens out the groups on average so the treatment can be credited
questions.solution: Random assignment tends to balance other differences between the groups, so a difference in the results can be credited to the treatment. It does not make the volunteers represent the population (that takes random sampling), it does not replace a control group, and volunteers do not choose.

solve.answer: It evens out the groups on average so the treatment can be credited
solve.work: Random assignment balances the groups on average, on known and unknown variables, so a difference in outcome can be attributed to the treatment. It does not by itself generalise to the population (that needs random sampling).

questions.stem: A school has 360 freshmen, 300 sophomores and 240 juniors. A stratified random sample of 60 students takes a simple random sample from each grade, with the number taken from each grade in proportion to the size of the grade. How many sophomores are in the sample?
questions.solution: There are $360 + 300 + 240 = 900$ students. Sophomores are $300/900 = 1/3$ of them, so they should be $1/3$ of the sample: $60 \times 300 \div 900 = 20$.

solve.work: Total 360 + 300 + 240 = 900. Sophomores: 300/900 x 60 = 20. (Check: freshmen 24, juniors 16, sum 60.)

questions.stem: A district has 40 schools with 500 students each. A researcher uses a cluster sample: she chooses 5 schools at random and surveys every student at those 5 schools. Exactly 80% of the students surveyed answer. How many answers does she receive?
questions.solution: She surveys $5 \times 500 = 2500$ students. Of these, 80% answer: $2500 \times 0.8 = 2000$.

solve.work: Surveyed: 5 schools x 500 = 2,500 students. 80% answer: 0.8 x 2500 = 2,000.

questions.skill: Using random digits to choose a sample
questions.stem: Students are numbered 01 to 80. To choose a simple random sample, a researcher reads two-digit numbers in order from a list of random digits: 41, 83, 27, 41, 05, 96, 62. She skips any number that is not from 01 to 80 and any number already chosen. What is the number of the third student chosen?
questions.solution: 41 is chosen first. 83 is skipped (more than 80). 27 is chosen second. The second 41 is skipped (already chosen). 05 is chosen third, so the student is number 5.

solve.work: 41 -> chosen (1st). 83 -> out of range, skip. 27 -> chosen (2nd). 41 -> repeat, skip. 05 -> chosen (3rd). Third student is number 05 = 5.

questions.stem: To learn about all adults in a town, a researcher chooses a random sample of homes from the town's landline telephone directory. Many adults in the town have only a cell phone and are not listed. What kind of bias does this cause?
choices: Nonresponse bias
Undercoverage bias
Voluntary response bias
Wording bias
questions.answer: Undercoverage bias
questions.solution: Adults with only a cell phone have no chance of being chosen, because they are not on the list. Leaving part of the population out of the list is undercoverage.

solve.answer: Undercoverage bias
solve.work: Part of the population (cell-only adults) has no chance of being chosen because they are not on the sampling frame: undercoverage.

questions.skill: Observational study or experiment, and what it shows
questions.stem: An observational study of 2,000 teenagers finds that those who play a musical instrument have higher math scores on average. Which conclusion is best supported by the study?
choices: Playing an instrument causes higher math scores, because the study included such a large number of teenagers
Playing an instrument goes with higher math scores, but the study does not show cause
Higher math scores cause teenagers to take up an instrument, and the study shows that direction clearly
Playing an instrument has no relationship with math scores, since the study did not assign anyone to play
questions.answer: Playing an instrument goes with higher math scores, but the study does not show cause
questions.solution: The study found an association. Because nobody was assigned to play an instrument, other differences between the groups could explain the scores, so it cannot show cause and effect in either direction.

solve.answer: Playing an instrument goes with higher math scores, but the study does not show cause
solve.work: Observational: association, not causation; large size doesn't establish cause.

questions.stem: Which statement describes a double-blind experiment?
choices: The subjects do not know their treatment, but the people measuring the results do know
The people measuring the results do not know the treatment, but the subjects do know
Every subject receives both treatments, in a random order, without being told
Neither the subjects nor the people measuring results know who got which treatment
questions.answer: Neither the subjects nor the people measuring results know who got which treatment
questions.solution: In a double-blind experiment both the subjects and the people who evaluate them are kept from knowing who got which treatment. That keeps expectations from changing the results or how they are measured.

solve.answer: Neither the subjects nor the people measuring results know who got which treatment
solve.work: Double-blind: neither subjects nor those measuring/evaluating know who got which treatment. A and B are single-blind; D is a crossover description.

questions.stem: A researcher randomly assigns 60 volunteers to a treatment group and a control group. The treatment group has twice as many volunteers as the control group. How many volunteers are in the treatment group?
questions.solution: The groups are in the ratio 2 to 1, which makes 3 equal parts. Each part has $60 \div 3 = 20$ volunteers, so the treatment group has $2 \times 20 = 40$.

questions.stem: A teacher surveys students about their study habits. Which choice best protects the students' privacy?
choices: Remove names from the answers and report only combined results
Post each student's answers beside their name on the classroom wall
Give every student's answers to their classmates to compare
Keep the names with the answers in a file shared with the whole school
questions.answer: Remove names from the answers and report only combined results
questions.solution: Keeping answers confidential means nobody can tell who said what. Removing names and reporting combined results does that. The other choices make individual answers visible to others.

solve.answer: Remove names from the answers and report only combined results
solve.work: Anonymizing answers and reporting only aggregated results protects privacy; the others expose individual answers.

questions.skill: Neutral survey questions and answer choices
questions.stem: A survey asks: "How would you rate the new city bike lanes?" The answer choices are Excellent, Very good, Good and Fair. What is the main problem with these answer choices?
choices: The scale uses words instead of numbers, so answers cannot be analyzed
The scale should offer only two choices so people can decide quickly
The scale is unbalanced, with more positive choices than negative ones
The scale is too short because it has fewer than ten choices
questions.answer: The scale is unbalanced, with more positive choices than negative ones
questions.solution: A fair scale has as many positive choices as negative ones. This one has no clearly negative choice, so it pushes ratings upward. Words can be analyzed, and four choices is a reasonable length.

solve.answer: The scale is unbalanced, with more positive choices than negative ones
solve.work: Excellent, Very good, Good are positive and Fair is at best neutral; no negative option such as Poor. The scale is unbalanced toward positive responses.

questions.stem: A fitness app records the number of steps each volunteer takes in every minute. Forty volunteers each wear the app for 2 hours. How many one-minute step counts does the app record in all?
questions.solution: Each volunteer wears the app for $2 \times 60 = 120$ minutes. For 40 volunteers that is $40 \times 120 = 4800$ step counts.

solve.work: 2 hours = 120 minutes, one count per minute per volunteer: 40 x 120 = 4,800.

questions.stem: A club has 80 juniors and 40 seniors. A stratified random sample of 30 members is taken, with the number from each group in proportion to the size of the group. How many seniors are in the sample?
questions.solution: Seniors are 40 of the 120 members, which is 1/3. One third of the 30 sampled members is 10 seniors.

solve.work: Seniors are 40/120 = 1/3 of members; 30/3 = 10.

questions.stem: A researcher picks 8 high schools in a state at random and surveys every student at those 8 schools. Which sampling method is this?
choices: Cluster sample
Stratified random sample
Systematic sample
Simple random sample
questions.answer: Cluster sample
questions.solution: Whole groups (the schools) are chosen at random, and everyone in each chosen group is surveyed. That is a cluster sample.

solve.answer: Cluster sample
solve.work: Randomly chosen whole groups (schools), everyone in them surveyed: cluster sample.

questions.stem: Why might a researcher choose a stratified random sample instead of a simple random sample?
choices: To avoid using any random choice at all when picking the people
To make sure each important group is included in proportion to its size
To let the researcher pick the people in each group who are the easiest for her to reach
To remove all of the chance variation from the final results
questions.answer: To make sure each important group is included in proportion to its size
questions.solution: Stratifying divides the population into groups and samples from each, so no important group is missed or underrepresented. Random choice is still used within each group, and some chance variation remains.

solve.answer: To make sure each important group is included in proportion to its size
solve.work: Stratification ensures each important group is represented (proportionally).

questions.skill: Using random digits to choose a sample
questions.stem: Students are numbered 001 to 250. A researcher reads random digits three at a time: 418, 092, 250, 251, 092, 137. She skips numbers outside the range and numbers already chosen. What is the number of the third student chosen?
questions.solution: 418 is out of range, so skip it. 092 is the first student and 250 is the second. 251 is out of range, and the second 092 is a repeat, so both are skipped. The third student is 137.

solve.work: 418 out; 092 first; 250 second; 251 out; 092 repeat; 137 third.

questions.skill: Using random digits to choose a sample
questions.stem: Students are numbered 01 to 60. A researcher reads the pairs 12, 45, 12, 90, 33, 05, 45, 61 in order, skipping any pair outside 01 to 60 and any pair already chosen. How many different students are chosen?
questions.solution: Valid and new: 12, 45, 33, 05. The second 12 and second 45 are repeats, and 90 and 61 are out of range. That is 4 students.

questions.skill: Using random digits to choose a sample
questions.stem: A coach numbers her 12 players 01 to 12 and wants a random sample of 3. Which method is valid?
choices: Read two-digit random numbers, skipping those outside 01 to 12 and repeats, until 3 are chosen
Roll one standard six-sided die three times and use the three numbers that come up as player numbers
Choose the first three players who walk into the gym for the practice, because arrival order is random
Pick three numbers that seem random to the coach as she looks over the list of all twelve players
questions.answer: Read two-digit random numbers, skipping those outside 01 to 12 and repeats, until 3 are chosen
questions.solution: Skipping numbers outside the range and repeats gives every player the same chance. A die has only six faces, so players 7 to 12 could never be chosen; the other methods depend on arrival or on the coach's choice.

solve.answer: Read two-digit random numbers, skipping those outside 01 to 12 and repeats, until 3 are chosen
solve.work: Reading two-digit random numbers, skipping out-of-range and repeats is valid; die only reaches 6 and may repeat.

questions.stem: A researcher surveys people at a farmers' market about how often they eat fresh vegetables. Which statement about the sample is most accurate?
choices: It leaves out many people, and market shoppers may eat more vegetables than others.
It is unbiased, because the researcher surveyed a lot of different kinds of people.
It is unbiased, because the researcher asked every single shopper the same question.
It is biased only if the researcher asks fewer than 10 shoppers.
questions.answer: It leaves out many people, and market shoppers may eat more vegetables than others.
questions.solution: People who shop at a farmers' market are likely to eat more fresh vegetables than the town as a whole. Asking everyone the same question does not fix a sample that leaves out groups.

solve.answer: It leaves out many people, and market shoppers may eat more vegetables than others.
solve.work: Convenience sample of market shoppers leaves out others, who likely eat fewer vegetables.

questions.stem: A teacher stands next to students while they answer, "In the last month, how many times did you cheat on a test?" Why might the answers be biased?
choices: Students always overstate how much they did, which is called undercoverage bias.
Students may not answer honestly with the teacher watching: response bias.
Students will not be able to count the number of times they cheated.
Students in a class can only answer with numbers that are less than 10.
questions.answer: Students may not answer honestly with the teacher watching: response bias.
questions.solution: When a question is sensitive, people often give answers that make them look good. That is response bias. It is unrelated to who was chosen for the sample.

solve.answer: Students may not answer honestly with the teacher watching: response bias.
solve.work: Teacher watching on a sensitive question leads to dishonest answers: response bias.

questions.stem: A researcher calls a random sample of landline telephone numbers at 2 p.m. on weekdays. Which group is most likely to be underrepresented?
choices: Adults who are at home during the day on a weekday and so can answer the phone
Adults who have more than one telephone
Adults who are away at work or at school during the day
Adults who answer their phone when it rings
questions.answer: Adults who are away at work or at school during the day
questions.solution: Calls at 2 p.m. on weekdays reach people who are home then, so people at work or school are missed. This is a source of bias, and the people missed may differ from those reached.

solve.answer: Adults who are away at work or at school during the day
solve.work: At 2 p.m. weekdays, people at work or school are not home to answer.

questions.stem: Why do some experiments give the control group a placebo?
choices: So the control group will always get better results than the treatment group does
So the researcher can avoid choosing people at random for the whole study
So the treatment group will not have to stay in the experiment
So subjects cannot tell which treatment they got, keeping expectations alike
questions.answer: So subjects cannot tell which treatment they got, keeping expectations alike
questions.solution: A placebo looks like the real treatment but has no active effect. Everyone expects to get a treatment, so differences between groups are more likely to come from the treatment itself.

solve.answer: So subjects cannot tell which treatment they got, keeping expectations alike
solve.work: A placebo keeps subjects blind so expectations are alike across groups.

questions.stem: A researcher randomly assigns 96 plants to 4 equal groups: a control group and three groups that each get a different fertilizer. How many plants get one of the fertilizers?
questions.solution: Each group has 96 / 4 = 24 plants. Three groups get a fertilizer: 3 x 24 = 72 plants.

solve.work: 96/4 = 24 per group; 3 fertilizer groups = 72.

questions.stem: Which method is a good way to randomly assign 20 subjects to two equal groups?
choices: Draw 10 of the 20 names from a hat for the treatment group
Let each subject pick whichever of the two groups the subject prefers
Give the first 10 subjects who arrive the treatment, and the rest not
Put the 10 oldest subjects in the treatment group and the rest in the other
questions.answer: Draw 10 of the 20 names from a hat for the treatment group
questions.solution: Drawing names gives every subject the same chance of either group. If subjects choose, arrive first or are sorted by age, the groups can differ in ways other than the treatment.

solve.answer: Draw 10 of the 20 names from a hat for the treatment group
solve.work: Drawing 10 names from a hat randomly assigns two equal groups.

questions.skill: Observational study or experiment, and what it shows
questions.stem: A town has more drownings in months when more ice cream is sold. What is the best explanation?
choices: Eating ice cream makes people more likely to drown in the town.
Drownings cause people in the town to buy more ice cream.
Hot weather leads to both more swimming and more ice cream sales.
Ice cream sales and drownings are unrelated.
questions.answer: Hot weather leads to both more swimming and more ice cream sales.
questions.solution: Hot weather is a lurking variable that raises both ice cream sales and the number of people swimming. Two things that go together do not necessarily cause one another.

solve.answer: Hot weather leads to both more swimming and more ice cream sales.
solve.work: Confounding variable: hot weather increases both swimming (drownings) and ice cream sales.

questions.skill: Observational study or experiment, and what it shows
questions.stem: One study randomly selects 500 adults in a city and surveys them. Another study randomly assigns 40 volunteers to two diets. Which statement is correct?
choices: The first can show cause and effect in the city, and the second can be generalized to the whole city.
Both can be generalized to the whole city, and neither one of them can show cause and effect.
Neither can be generalized to the whole city, and both of them can show cause and effect.
The first can be generalized to the city, and the second can support cause and effect.
questions.answer: The first can be generalized to the city, and the second can support cause and effect.
questions.solution: Random selection from a population lets us generalize to that population. Random assignment of subjects to treatments lets us credit differences to the treatment. The volunteers are not a random sample of the city.

solve.answer: The first can be generalized to the city, and the second can support cause and effect.
solve.work: Random sampling allows generalization to the city; random assignment allows cause-and-effect (for the volunteers).

questions.skill: Observational study or experiment, and what it shows
questions.stem: In an experiment, 50 plants given fertilizer grew an average of 24 cm, and 50 plants without it grew an average of 20 cm. By what percent is the average growth of the fertilized plants greater than that of the plants without it?
questions.solution: The difference is 24 - 20 = 4 cm. Compared with the 20 cm of the plants without fertilizer, that is 4 / 20 = 0.20 = 20%.

questions.stem: A 14-year-old is asked to join a research study. Which approach is the most appropriate?
choices: Only the 14-year-old's agreement is needed, because the study is voluntary
Only the school principal's permission is needed for any study
Get a parent's or guardian's permission plus the student's own agreement
No permission is needed when real names are used in the report
questions.answer: Get a parent's or guardian's permission plus the student's own agreement
questions.solution: Children cannot give full consent alone, so a parent or guardian gives permission and the student also agrees to take part.

solve.answer: Get a parent's or guardian's permission plus the student's own agreement
solve.work: For a minor: parental/guardian permission plus the minor's assent.

questions.stem: Which of these actions is unethical in research?
choices: Telling participants about a risk of the study before they join
Reporting that 8 of the 50 participants dropped out
Removing the names from the data before sharing it
Changing results so they match what the sponsor wants
questions.answer: Changing results so they match what the sponsor wants
questions.solution: Changing results is dishonest. The other actions are ethical: informing participants, reporting dropouts and protecting names.

solve.answer: Changing results so they match what the sponsor wants
solve.work: Falsifying results to please a sponsor is unethical.

questions.skill: Neutral survey questions and answer choices
questions.stem: Which question is the best rewrite of "Do you approve of the wasteful new parking fee?"
choices: Do you approve or disapprove of the new parking fee?
Do you approve of the new fee that will help to pay for parking?
Do you disapprove of the unfair new fee for parking?
Do you agree that the parking fee is a costly new burden?
questions.answer: Do you approve or disapprove of the new parking fee?
questions.solution: The neutral rewrite removes the loaded word "wasteful" and offers both sides. The other versions still push the reader toward approving or disapproving.

solve.answer: Do you approve or disapprove of the new parking fee?
solve.work: D removes the loaded word and offers both directions.

questions.skill: Neutral survey questions and answer choices
questions.stem: A researcher asks teens about a sensitive behavior. Which approach is most likely to give honest answers?
choices: Read each question aloud and have the teen answer in front of a group
Keep the survey anonymous and include a choice to skip the question
Ask the teens to write their names next to every answer on the page
Have a parent look over the teen's answers before they are handed in
questions.answer: Keep the survey anonymous and include a choice to skip the question
questions.solution: People answer sensitive questions more honestly when their answers are private. Anonymity and the option to skip protect them from embarrassment or consequences.

solve.answer: Keep the survey anonymous and include a choice to skip the question
solve.work: Anonymity and an option to skip encourage honest answers.

questions.skill: Neutral survey questions and answer choices
questions.stem: A survey asks, "What is your favorite sport? Soccer, basketball or baseball." What is the main problem with the answer choices?
choices: The sports are listed in an order that is not alphabetical in the list.
Students may not know how to play all three of the sports.
Students whose favorite is another sport have no choice that fits.
The question has too many answer choices for students.
questions.answer: Students whose favorite is another sport have no choice that fits.
questions.solution: The choices should cover all likely answers. Adding "Other" fixes the problem for students whose favorite is not listed.

solve.answer: Students whose favorite is another sport have no choice that fits.
solve.work: Choices are not exhaustive: no "other" option.

questions.stem: A study recruits volunteers who already own smartwatches and records their sleep. To which group can the results most reasonably be applied?
choices: All people in the country, whether or not they own a smartwatch
All people who have ever slept at night, in any situation
All students in the school that the researcher attended
Smartwatch owners who are willing to volunteer for a study
questions.answer: Smartwatch owners who are willing to volunteer for a study
questions.solution: The sample is volunteers who own smartwatches, so the results apply best to people like them. Other groups might sleep differently.

solve.answer: Smartwatch owners who are willing to volunteer for a study
solve.work: Results apply to volunteer smartwatch owners, the group sampled.

questions.stem: A company records which page each visitor opens on its website. Which question can those data answer?
choices: Which page do visitors open most often?
Why do visitors dislike the home page?
How much money do visitors earn each year?
What do visitors do when they are not on the website?
questions.answer: Which page do visitors open most often?
questions.solution: The data record page visits, so they show which page is opened most often. They do not show reasons, income or activity away from the site.

solve.answer: Which page do visitors open most often?
solve.work: Page-open logs answer which page is opened most.

questions.stem: A town puts traffic sensors on its busiest road and counts the cars that pass in a month. The town then uses these counts to describe the traffic on all of its roads. What is the main problem with doing so?
choices: The sensors count cars automatically, which makes any random sampling impossible
The sensors sit on only one busy road, so the counts may not represent every road
The sensors record every car, so the counts are far too large to be useful
Machines count cars with more mistakes than people do, so the counts are unreliable
questions.answer: The sensors sit on only one busy road, so the counts may not represent every road
questions.solution: Technology can collect data automatically and accurately, but the sensors were placed only where traffic is heaviest. Counts from that road are not representative of quieter roads, so they cannot describe all of the town's roads.

solve.answer: The sensors sit on only one busy road, so the counts may not represent every road
solve.work: The data come only from the busiest road, which is not representative of all roads, so generalising to every road is biased.

questions.stem: A town has 20,000 residents. A stratified random sample takes residents from each district in proportion to the district's size. The district with 3,000 residents contributes 45 people to the sample. How many people are in the whole sample?
questions.solution: The district holds $3000/20000 = 3/20$ of the town, so it supplies $3/20$ of the sample. If $3/20$ of the sample is 45, the whole sample is $45 \times 20000 \div 3000 = 300$.

solve.work: Sampling fraction = 45 / 3000 = 0.015. Whole sample = 0.015 x 20000 = 300.

questions.stem: A researcher wants to estimate the percent of all students at a large high school who walk to school. She stands at the front door and surveys the first 50 students who arrive each morning. Which statement is the best evaluation of this plan?
choices: It is a simple random sample, because the first 50 students are chosen by chance alone
It is a stratified sample, because it separates students by their arrival time
It is a convenience sample, and students who arrive first may differ from the rest
It is unbiased, because 50 students is a large enough sample to be accurate
questions.answer: It is a convenience sample, and students who arrive first may differ from the rest
questions.solution: The researcher took the students who were easiest to reach. Students who arrive first might walk (or ride a bus) more or less than the others. A larger sample does not repair bias.

solve.answer: It is a convenience sample, and students who arrive first may differ from the rest
solve.work: First 50 arrivals = convenience sample; early arrivers may differ (e.g. walkers vs bus riders).

questions.stem: A company emails a satisfaction survey to 300 customers chosen at random from its full customer list. Only 45 customers reply, and most of the replies are complaints. Which statement is the most accurate?
choices: People who reply may differ from those who do not, so the replies may be biased
Random selection guarantees that the 45 replies represent all of the customers who were chosen
The replies are biased because the 300 customers were not chosen at random
The replies are unbiased because the number of replies, 45, is more than the usual minimum of 30
questions.answer: People who reply may differ from those who do not, so the replies may be biased
questions.solution: The 300 were chosen at random, which is good, but only 45 answered. Unhappy customers may be more likely to reply, which is nonresponse bias. Random selection cannot guarantee that the people who answer are typical, and the size of 45 does not fix that.

solve.answer: People who reply may differ from those who do not, so the replies may be biased
solve.work: Nonresponse bias: 45/300 respondents may differ from non-respondents.

questions.stem: A farmer compares two fertilizers on 20 equal plots. The north half of the field has richer soil than the south half. Which plan best reduces the effect of the soil difference on the comparison?
choices: Use fertilizer A on all the north plots and fertilizer B on all the south plots
Give fertilizer A to the 10 plots that look the healthiest before the experiment starts
Use the same fertilizer on all 20 plots so that no differences can appear
Randomly assign each fertilizer to half of the plots within each half of the field
questions.answer: Randomly assign each fertilizer to half of the plots within each half of the field
questions.solution: Splitting the field into north and south blocks and randomizing within each block gives both fertilizers the same mix of soils (blocking). The other plans mix up the fertilizer with the soil, let appearance decide, or make a comparison impossible.

solve.answer: Randomly assign each fertilizer to half of the plots within each half of the field
solve.work: Block by soil: within each half (north, south) randomly assign each fertilizer to half the plots. A confounds soil with fertilizer; B is biased; D gives no comparison.

questions.stem: Ten volunteers are labeled 1 through 10. A random number generator lists the labels in this random order: 7, 3, 10, 4, 9, 1, 6, 2, 8, 5. The first five labels in the list are assigned to the treatment group. The volunteers labeled 1 through 5 are the five youngest. How many of the five youngest volunteers are in the treatment group?
questions.solution: The first five labels in the list are 7, 3, 10, 4 and 9. Of these, only 3 and 4 are from 1 to 5, so 2 of the youngest volunteers are in the treatment group. Random assignment balances the groups only on average, so an uneven split is possible.

solve.work: First five labels: 7, 3, 10, 4, 9. Of these, labels 1-5 are 3 and 4. So 2 of the youngest are in treatment.

questions.skill: Observational study or experiment, and what it shows
questions.stem: A study of 1,000 adults finds that people who drink coffee every day have more heart problems than people who do not. The study did not assign anyone to drink coffee. Coffee drinkers in the study also smoke more often. What is smoking in this study?
choices: The explanatory variable
A confounding variable
The response variable
A placebo
questions.answer: A confounding variable
questions.solution: Coffee drinking is the explanatory variable and heart problems are the response. Smoking is related to both and could explain the difference, so it is a confounding variable.

solve.answer: A confounding variable
solve.work: Smoking is associated with coffee drinking (explanatory) and with heart problems (response), so its effect is mixed with coffee's: a confounding variable.

questions.stem: A researcher plans a study of a new sleep program with student volunteers. Which plan follows ethical guidelines for research?
choices: Volunteers are told the program is completely risk-free, even though the researcher knows of one serious risk
Volunteers learn the risks beforehand, may leave at any time, and have their names kept private
Volunteers must stay until the study ends, or they lose all of the money they were promised at the start
Volunteers' names and results are shared with their teachers and parents, without asking the volunteers first
questions.answer: Volunteers learn the risks beforehand, may leave at any time, and have their names kept private
questions.solution: Ethical research gives informed consent, lets people withdraw, and protects privacy. The other plans hide a known risk, pressure people to stay, or reveal private information.

solve.answer: Volunteers learn the risks beforehand, may leave at any time, and have their names kept private
solve.work: Informed consent, freedom to withdraw, confidentiality.

questions.skill: Neutral survey questions and answer choices
questions.stem: A survey asks: "Do you support lowering the speed limit on Main Street and adding two new crosswalks?" The only answers are Yes and No. What is the main problem with this question?
choices: It uses loaded words that push people toward answering Yes
It has too many answer choices to choose from
It asks for a number instead of an opinion
It asks about two different ideas in one question
questions.answer: It asks about two different ideas in one question
questions.solution: Someone who likes the crosswalks but not the lower speed limit cannot answer honestly with Yes or No. A question should ask about one idea at a time.

solve.answer: It asks about two different ideas in one question
solve.work: Two separate proposals (speed limit, crosswalks) in one yes/no question: double-barreled.

questions.stem: A door sensor counts one visitor each time its beam is broken. When two people walk through side by side, the beam is broken only once. In one hour the sensor recorded 120 counts, and an observer found that exactly 20 of those counts were two people walking side by side. All the other counts were one person. How many people actually came through the door?
questions.solution: There were $120 - 20 = 100$ counts of one person and 20 counts of two people. The number of people is $100 + 20 \times 2 = 140$. The sensor undercounts every time, so the error does not average out.

solve.work: 20 counts were two people: 40 people. Other 120 - 20 = 100 counts were one person each: 100. Total 140.

questions.stem: An online survey is emailed to a random sample of 800 students. Fifteen percent of the emails bounce and are never delivered. Of the students who receive the survey, 40% answer it. How many students answer?
questions.solution: The emails delivered are $800 \times 0.85 = 680$. Of these, 40% answer: $680 \times 0.4 = 272$ students.

solve.work: Delivered: 85% of 800 = 680. Answer: 40% of 680 = 272.

questions.stem: A list has 1,500 names. A systematic sample takes every 12th name, starting with name number 7. What is the number of the 5th name chosen?
questions.solution: The chosen names are 7, 19, 31, 43, 55, ... Each one is 12 more than the last. The 5th is 7 + 4 x 12 = 55.

questions.stem: A school has 320 ninth graders, 280 tenth graders and 200 eleventh graders. A stratified random sample of 80 students is taken, with the number from each grade in proportion to the size of the grade. How many of the sampled students are in grades 10 and 11 together?
questions.solution: The school has 800 students, and 280 + 200 = 480 of them are in grades 10 and 11. The share is 480 / 800 = 0.6, and 0.6 x 80 = 48 students.

solve.work: Total 800; fraction 80/800 = 1/10. Grade 10: 28, grade 11: 20; together 48.

questions.stem: A researcher takes exactly 10 students from each of four grades, although the grades have very different sizes. She then pools all 40 answers to estimate the percent for the whole school. What is the problem?
choices: Taking students from every grade makes the sample no longer random, so no estimate can be made.
Pooling the answers can never give an estimate for the school.
Pooling equal numbers from unequal grades overweights the smaller grades.
Forty students is too small a sample for any survey of a whole school to be used at all.
questions.answer: Pooling equal numbers from unequal grades overweights the smaller grades.
questions.solution: A small grade is as large a part of the pooled sample as a large grade, so it counts for more than its share of the school. A proportional sample, or weighting, avoids this.

solve.answer: Pooling equal numbers from unequal grades overweights the smaller grades.
solve.work: Equal numbers from unequal grades over-represent small grades when pooled without weighting.

questions.skill: Using random digits to choose a sample
questions.stem: Classes are numbered 01 to 36. A researcher reads random pairs of digits in this order: 52, 17, 83, 09, 17, 36, 41. She skips any pair outside 01 to 36 and any pair already chosen. What is the sum of the first three class numbers chosen?
questions.solution: 52 and 83 are out of range. The first three valid new numbers are 17, 09 and 36 (the second 17 is a repeat). The sum is 17 + 9 + 36 = 62.

questions.skill: Using random digits to choose a sample
questions.stem: A researcher numbers 500 people in alphabetical order and then chooses numbers with a random number generator. Is the alphabetical order a problem?
choices: Yes; the list must first be shuffled into a random order for the sample to be truly random.
No; every number has the same chance, so the order of the list is not a problem.
Yes; people near the start of the alphabet have a better chance, because their numbers are smaller.
No, but only if the digits are read from the end of the list.
questions.answer: No; every number has the same chance, so the order of the list is not a problem.
questions.solution: The random number generator, not the list, decides who is chosen. Each of the 500 numbers is equally likely, so listing the people alphabetically does not change anyone's chance.

solve.answer: No; every number has the same chance, so the order of the list is not a problem.
solve.work: With a random number generator every number equally likely, so list order doesn't matter.

questions.stem: A survey of 300 randomly chosen customers gets only 45 replies. Which step is the best way to reduce nonresponse bias?
choices: Replace the people who did not reply with people who volunteer
Survey another 300 people in exactly the same way
Use only the 45 replies and ignore the rest of the customers
Follow up with reminders to the people who did not reply
questions.answer: Follow up with reminders to the people who did not reply
questions.solution: Nonresponse bias happens when people who do not reply differ from those who do. Following up with the chosen customers raises the response rate. Volunteers or the same method would not fix it.

solve.answer: Follow up with reminders to the people who did not reply
solve.work: Following up with nonrespondents raises the response rate and reduces nonresponse bias.

questions.stem: A website's online poll gets 10,000 votes about a new law. A writer says the large number of votes means the poll is accurate for all adults. What is the best response?
choices: A large voluntary sample can still be biased, since people choose themselves.
A sample with 10,000 people is always accurate, whoever the people in it are.
A poll is accurate only when it has fewer than 1,000 votes.
A poll on a website is accurate only if each vote is a simple yes or no.
questions.answer: A large voluntary sample can still be biased, since people choose themselves.
questions.solution: Sample size does not remove bias. In a voluntary response poll, people with strong feelings are more likely to vote, so a bigger sample just repeats the same bias.

solve.answer: A large voluntary sample can still be biased, since people choose themselves.
solve.work: Size does not fix self-selection bias in a voluntary sample.

questions.stem: A random sample of 500 people is surveyed. Only 300 respond, and 120 of the 300 say yes. Suppose that all 200 people who did not respond would have said no. What percent of all 500 people would say yes?
questions.solution: If the nonresponders would all say no, the number of yes answers is still 120 out of 500. 120 / 500 = 0.24 = 24%, which is much lower than 120 / 300 = 40% among responders.

questions.stem: Why should an experiment have many subjects in each group rather than just one?
choices: More subjects remove the need for random assignment, since the groups then balance by themselves.
More subjects reduce the effect of chance differences among people.
One subject per group lets the researcher control every factor, so chance differences cannot occur.
More subjects guarantee that the treatment will work for all.
questions.answer: More subjects reduce the effect of chance differences among people.
questions.solution: Individuals differ naturally. With many subjects per group, those individual differences tend to average out, so a real treatment effect is easier to see. Random assignment is still needed.

solve.answer: More subjects reduce the effect of chance differences among people.
solve.work: Replication reduces effect of chance variation among subjects.

questions.stem: A teacher lets students choose whether to use a new study app. The students who used the app scored higher on the test. Why can the higher scores not be credited to the app?
choices: The app group was too large for the scores to be compared with the other group.
Tests cannot be used to find out how well a study app really works.
Students who chose the app may be more motivated, so the groups were not alike.
Students who use any app will always score higher on a test.
questions.answer: Students who chose the app may be more motivated, so the groups were not alike.
questions.solution: Because students chose, the app group may have been different from the non-app group before the study began. Only random assignment makes the groups alike, so that differences can be credited to the treatment.

solve.answer: Students who chose the app may be more motivated, so the groups were not alike.
solve.work: Self-selection: motivated students may choose the app, confounding.

questions.stem: In a randomized block design, 36 younger subjects and 24 older subjects are each split at random so that half of each block gets the treatment. How many of the 60 subjects get the treatment?
questions.solution: Half of the 36 younger subjects is 18, and half of the 24 older subjects is 12. In all, 18 + 12 = 30 subjects get the treatment.

solve.work: Half of 36 = 18, half of 24 = 12; 30.

questions.skill: Observational study or experiment, and what it shows
questions.stem: An observational study finds that students who eat breakfast have higher grades. Which variable could explain the link without breakfast causing the grades?
choices: Hours of sleep, if students who sleep more eat breakfast and do better
The number of students in the study, if the sample is a large one
The name of the school, if all of the students attend one school
The year of the study, if the study was carried out in only one year for everyone
questions.answer: Hours of sleep, if students who sleep more eat breakfast and do better
questions.solution: A confounding variable is related to both the explanatory and the response variable. Sleep could lead to both breakfast and better grades, so the study cannot show that breakfast is the cause.

solve.answer: Hours of sleep, if students who sleep more eat breakfast and do better
solve.work: Sleep is a plausible confounder affecting both breakfast and grades.

questions.skill: Observational study or experiment, and what it shows
questions.stem: Which plan is best for deciding whether a new type of running shoe reduces injuries?
choices: Compare the injuries of runners who chose the new shoe with those who chose the old
Randomly assign runners to the new shoe or the old shoe and count injuries
Ask runners in an online poll whether they believe the new shoe is better
Count the injuries of only the runners who say they like the new shoe
questions.answer: Randomly assign runners to the new shoe or the old shoe and count injuries
questions.solution: Random assignment makes the two groups alike, so a difference in injuries can be credited to the shoe. If runners choose their shoes, the groups can differ in many ways.

solve.answer: Randomly assign runners to the new shoe or the old shoe and count injuries
solve.work: Random assignment to shoe type then counting injuries: a controlled experiment.

questions.skill: Observational study or experiment, and what it shows
questions.stem: Researchers want to know whether smoking causes lung disease. Why do they use observational studies instead of an experiment?
choices: Observational studies can prove cause and effect more strongly than experiments can.
Experiments cannot be used to study any disease that affects the lungs.
It would be unethical to assign people to smoke, so they observe those who do.
Random assignment is not possible when the number of people is large.
questions.answer: It would be unethical to assign people to smoke, so they observe those who do.
questions.solution: An experiment would require assigning people to a harmful behavior, which is unethical. Researchers study people who already smoke and use many studies to build the evidence.

solve.answer: It would be unethical to assign people to smoke, so they observe those who do.
solve.work: Assigning people to smoke would be unethical.

questions.stem: A company pays for a study of its new medicine. The researcher leaves out the results that show side effects. What is the main ethical problem?
choices: Selective reporting makes the results misleading to the public.
The company paid for a study, which no study is ever allowed to do.
The study included too many people, which is always unethical.
The medicine was tested, and testing a medicine is never ethical.
questions.answer: Selective reporting makes the results misleading to the public.
questions.solution: Honest research reports all the results, including unwelcome ones. Hiding side effects misleads people who rely on the study.

solve.answer: Selective reporting makes the results misleading to the public.
solve.work: Omitting side-effect results is selective reporting; misleading.

questions.stem: A study has some risk to its participants. Which step is the most important before it begins?
choices: The participants are told about the risks of the study only after it ends.
An independent review board checks that the risks are small and the plan fair.
The researcher alone decides that the risks are acceptable to all of the participants involved.
The participants are promised a reward if they do not drop out.
questions.answer: An independent review board checks that the risks are small and the plan fair.
questions.solution: Studies with risk should be reviewed by people who are not part of the study, and participants must be told the risks beforehand. A reward for staying in would pressure people not to leave.

solve.answer: An independent review board checks that the risks are small and the plan fair.
solve.work: Independent ethics/review board (IRB) approval before start.

questions.stem: A report says "only 6 of 100 volunteers had side effects." But 5 other volunteers left early because of side effects, and they were not counted among the 6. What percent of all 100 volunteers had side effects when the 5 who left are included?
questions.solution: The total with side effects is 6 + 5 = 11 out of 100 volunteers, which is 11%. Honest reporting includes the people who left early.

questions.skill: Neutral survey questions and answer choices
questions.stem: Why might a survey rotate the order of its answer choices among respondents?
choices: To make sure each respondent gets the same questions in the same order
To make the survey shorter so respondents finish it more quickly
To keep respondents from knowing what the survey is about
To reduce the effect of the order of the choices on how people answer
questions.answer: To reduce the effect of the order of the choices on how people answer
questions.solution: People are sometimes drawn to the first or last choice. Rotating the order spreads this effect evenly so that it does not bias the results.

solve.answer: To reduce the effect of the order of the choices on how people answer
solve.work: Rotation reduces order effects on choices.

questions.skill: Neutral survey questions and answer choices
questions.stem: A survey asks, "Many experts say sugary drinks harm teens. Do you support banning them from school?" What is the main problem?
choices: It cites experts first, which leads people toward answering yes.
It asks about school, which students cannot have opinions about at all.
It asks about drinks, which are not a good topic for a survey.
It lets respondents choose between yes and no to answer.
questions.answer: It cites experts first, which leads people toward answering yes.
questions.solution: Opening with an appeal to experts pushes people toward agreeing. A neutral question would state the proposal without hints about the right answer.

solve.answer: It cites experts first, which leads people toward answering yes.
solve.work: Preamble citing experts leads respondents toward yes.

questions.skill: Neutral survey questions and answer choices
