questions.stem: In a pilot test, 5 of 20 students misunderstood a survey question. After the question was rewritten, 3 of 30 students in a second pilot test misunderstood it. By how many percentage points did the percent who misunderstood decrease?
questions.solution: Before: 5 / 20 = 25%. After: 3 / 30 = 10%. The decrease is 25 - 10 = 15 percentage points.

solve.work: 5/20 = 25%; 3/30 = 10%; decrease 15 points.

questions.stem: A sensor logs 10,000 readings. Four percent of them are error codes and are removed. A researcher then examines a random 5% of the remaining readings. How many readings does she examine?
questions.solution: Removing 4% leaves 96% of 10,000, which is 9,600 readings. Five percent of 9,600 is 480 readings.

questions.stem: A researcher collects 1,000,000 public posts from a social site to study the opinions of teens. Which statement is the best evaluation?
choices: The data set is so large that it must represent all teens in the country accurately.
The data set is large, but teens who post may not represent all teens.
The data set is public, so it is not possible for the sample to be biased in any way.
The data set has posts, so it cannot be used to study opinions.
questions.answer: The data set is large, but teens who post may not represent all teens.
questions.solution: A huge data set can still be biased if it does not include everyone. Teens who post on that site may differ from teens who do not use it.

solve.answer: The data set is large, but teens who post may not represent all teens.
solve.work: Large size doesn't fix selection bias: teens who post publicly may not represent all teens.

questions.stem: A school app records the location of every student. Which practice is the most ethical?
choices: Collect all possible data about students and keep it for as long as possible
Share the location data with any company that is willing to pay for it
Collect only the location data that is needed, tell families, and protect it
Collect location data without telling students or their families about it
questions.answer: Collect only the location data that is needed, tell families, and protect it
questions.solution: Ethical data collection limits what is collected, is open about it, and keeps the data safe. Collecting everything, selling it or hiding it breaks these principles.

solve.answer: Collect only the location data that is needed, tell families, and protect it
solve.work: Collect only what is needed, inform families, protect it.

questions.skill: Identify the population and the sample
questions.stem: A company has 1,200 employees. To learn how long employees spend commuting, a manager asks 80 of them, chosen at random, how many minutes they travel to work. What is the population in this study?
choices: The 80 employees who were asked
The 80 commute times that were reported
All 1,200 employees of the company
The manager who ran the survey
questions.answer: All 1,200 employees of the company
questions.solution: The population is the whole group the manager wants to learn about: all 1,200 employees. The 80 employees who were asked are the sample.

solve.answer: All 1,200 employees of the company
solve.work: The population is the whole group the manager wants to learn about: all 1,200 employees. The 80 asked are the sample; their times are the data.

questions.stem: In a random sample of 100 students from a large school, the mean height was 165 centimeters. What is the number 165 centimeters?
choices: A statistic, because it describes a sample
A parameter, because it describes a sample
A statistic, because it describes a whole population
A parameter, because it describes a whole population
questions.answer: A statistic, because it describes a sample
questions.solution: A number that describes a sample is a statistic. A number that describes a whole population is a parameter. The 165 centimeters describes only the 100 students sampled, so it is a statistic.

solve.answer: A statistic, because it describes a sample
solve.work: 165 cm is computed from the 100 sampled students, so it describes a sample: a statistic. A parameter describes a population.

questions.skill: Identify the population and the sample
questions.stem: A club has 45 members. A reporter surveys 9 of them. What fraction of the population is in the sample? Write the fraction in simplest form.
questions.solution: The population is all 45 members and the sample is 9 of them. The fraction is 9/45, which simplifies to 1/5.

solve.work: Sample/population = 9/45 = 1/5.

questions.skill: Why we sample instead of taking a census
questions.stem: A factory wants to know how long its light bulbs last on average. Testing a bulb means leaving it on until it burns out. Why should the factory test a sample of bulbs instead of every bulb?
choices: A sample always gives exactly the same average as every bulb
Testing a sample removes all error from the estimate
Testing a few bulbs always costs more than testing all of them
Testing every bulb would use them all up, leaving none to sell
questions.answer: Testing every bulb would use them all up, leaving none to sell
questions.solution: A test that destroys what it tests cannot be done on everything. A sample lets the factory estimate the average lifetime and still have bulbs to sell. A sample does not give exactly the population value, and it does not cost more than testing all the bulbs.

solve.answer: Testing every bulb would use them all up, leaving none to sell
solve.work: Testing is destructive (the bulb burns out), so testing every bulb would leave none to sell. The other options are false statements.

questions.stem: A teacher wants a simple random sample of 5 students from her class of 30. Which method does this?
choices: Choose the first 5 students who walk into the room this morning
Write each name on a card, mix the cards well, and draw 5 cards
Choose the 5 students who sit closest to her desk in the classroom
Choose the 5 students she thinks are most typical of the class
questions.answer: Write each name on a card, mix the cards well, and draw 5 cards
questions.solution: In a simple random sample, every student and every group of 5 students has the same chance of being chosen. Drawing 5 well-mixed cards does that. The other methods let arrival time, seating or her own judgment decide.

solve.answer: Write each name on a card, mix the cards well, and draw 5 cards
solve.work: Drawing 5 well-mixed name cards gives every group of 5 the same chance: a simple random sample. The others are convenience or judgment samples.

questions.stem: A list has 200 students on it. A researcher picks every 10th student on the list, starting with student number 4. How many students are in the sample?
questions.solution: Picking every 10th student from 200 students gives 200 / 10 = 20 students (numbers 4, 14, 24, ..., 194).

questions.stem: A news website posts the question "Should the town build a new park?" and counts the votes of visitors who choose to click. What kind of sample is this?
choices: A simple random sample
A voluntary response sample
A stratified random sample
A cluster sample
questions.answer: A voluntary response sample
questions.solution: The people decided for themselves whether to be in the sample. That is a voluntary response sample, which tends to be biased because people with strong opinions are the ones who respond.

solve.answer: A voluntary response sample
solve.work: Visitors choose themselves whether to vote: a voluntary response sample.

questions.stem: In a random sample of 50 voters, 20 said they support a new library. What is the sample proportion of voters who support the library? Write it as a decimal.
questions.solution: The sample proportion is the number who support it divided by the sample size: 20 / 50 = 0.4. This is a statistic, because it comes from the sample.

questions.stem: A city wants to know how its residents feel about a new bus route. Which sample would be most likely to represent all residents?
choices: 500 people found waiting at bus stops on a weekday morning commute
500 residents who wrote to the mayor about the new route
500 residents who live within a block of the new route
500 residents chosen at random from a list of all residents
questions.answer: 500 residents chosen at random from a list of all residents
questions.solution: Random selection from a list of all residents gives every resident a chance to be chosen. The other samples include only people who ride buses, who chose to write in, or who live in one place, so they leave out or over-represent some residents.

solve.answer: 500 residents chosen at random from a list of all residents
solve.work: Only a random choice from a list of all residents gives everyone a chance; bus-stop riders, letter writers and near neighbours are each a biased subgroup.

questions.skill: Why we sample instead of taking a census
questions.stem: What is a survey called when it collects data from every individual in a population?
choices: A census
A simple random sample
A voluntary response sample
A statistic
questions.answer: A census
questions.solution: A census collects data from every individual in the population. A sample collects data from only part of it.

solve.answer: A census
solve.work: Data from every individual in the population is a census.

questions.skill: Identify the population and the sample
questions.stem: A school has 840 students. A survey about lunch is given to 60 of them. How many students in the school are not in the sample?
questions.solution: The population is all 840 students and the sample is the 60 who were surveyed. The students not in the sample are $840 - 60 = 780$.

solve.work: Not in sample = 840 - 60 = 780.

questions.skill: Identify the population and the sample
questions.stem: A researcher wants to know the mean weight of the apples picked from an orchard this week. She weighs 25 of the apples. What is the sample?
choices: All of the apples picked from the orchard this week
The 25 apples that she weighs
The mean weight of the apples
The orchard where the apples grew
questions.answer: The 25 apples that she weighs
questions.solution: The sample is the part of the population that is actually measured: the 25 apples she weighs. All of the apples picked this week are the population.

solve.answer: The 25 apples that she weighs
solve.work: The sample is the part actually measured: the 25 apples weighed. Population = all apples picked this week; mean weight is the parameter.

questions.skill: Identify the population and the sample
questions.stem: Which statement best describes the population in a statistical study?
choices: The part of the group that is actually measured
The number that is computed from the data
The whole group that the study is about
The list of questions that are asked of them
questions.answer: The whole group that the study is about
questions.solution: The population is the whole group of people or things that the study is about. The part that is actually measured is the sample, and a number computed from data is a statistic or a parameter.

solve.answer: The whole group that the study is about
solve.work: Population = the whole group the study is about; the measured part is the sample; a computed number is a statistic.

questions.stem: A principal measures the height of every one of the 400 students in her school and finds that the mean height is 160 centimeters. What is the 160 centimeters?
choices: A statistic, because it describes a whole population
A parameter, because it describes a sample
A statistic, because it describes a sample
A parameter, because every student was measured
questions.answer: A parameter, because every student was measured
questions.solution: Every student in the school was measured, so the group measured is the whole population. A number that describes a whole population is a parameter.

solve.answer: A parameter, because every student was measured
solve.work: Every student (whole population) was measured, so 160 cm is a parameter. A wrongly calls a population value a statistic; B and C call it a sample.

questions.stem: In a random sample of 80 students, 56 own a bike. What is the sample proportion of students who own a bike? Write it as a decimal.
questions.solution: The sample proportion is the part of the sample with the trait: $\frac{56}{80} = 0.7$.

questions.stem: Which of these numbers is a statistic?
choices: The mean height of 20 students chosen from a school of 900
The mean height of all 900 students in the school
The number of students enrolled, found from the school's complete roster
The percent of all 900 students who are in grade 9, found from every record
questions.answer: The mean height of 20 students chosen from a school of 900
questions.solution: A statistic is computed from a sample. Only the mean height of 20 chosen students comes from a sample. The other three numbers describe all 900 students, so they are parameters.

solve.answer: The mean height of 20 students chosen from a school of 900
solve.work: A statistic describes a sample. Only C (20 of 900 students) is from a sample; A, B, D use the whole population, so they are parameters.

questions.skill: Why we sample instead of taking a census
questions.stem: Why do polling companies usually ask a sample of people instead of everyone in a large population?
choices: A sample always gives the exact value for the population
A sample takes much less time and money than a census
A census of a large population is never possible
A sample is never affected by chance
questions.answer: A sample takes much less time and money than a census
questions.solution: Asking everyone costs far more time and money. A well-chosen sample gives a good estimate for much less effort. It does not give the exact value, and it does vary from sample to sample.

solve.answer: A sample takes much less time and money than a census
solve.work: Samples are cheaper and faster than a census. B ('never possible') is too absolute; C and D are false.

questions.skill: Why we sample instead of taking a census
questions.stem: A phone survey costs 4 dollars for each person who is called. A town has 3250 residents. How many dollars are saved by calling a sample of 250 residents instead of taking a census of all of them?
questions.solution: The sample leaves out $3250 - 250 = 3000$ residents. Each costs 4 dollars, so the savings are $3000 \times 4 = 12{,}000$ dollars.

solve.work: Census cost 3250 x 4 = 13000; sample cost 250 x 4 = 1000; saved 12000. (Equivalently 3000 x 4.)

questions.stem: A principal wants to know how all 900 students feel about a new bell schedule. Which plan is the best way to choose 90 students to ask?
choices: Ask the 90 students who are in the first class of the day
Ask the first 90 students who happen to stop by her office
Number all the students and pick 90 numbers at random
Ask the 90 students who are on the school football team
questions.answer: Number all the students and pick 90 numbers at random
questions.solution: Only a random choice from the full list gives every student a fair chance. The other plans take students who are easy to reach, which may leave out many kinds of students.

solve.answer: Number all the students and pick 90 numbers at random
solve.work: Numbering all students and picking at random gives every student an equal chance; the others are convenience/biased groups.

questions.stem: A principal wants a simple random sample of 10 students from a list of 400 students. Which method does this?
choices: Choose the first 10 students who appear on the list
Ask 10 students who are standing in the lunch line
Choose the 10 students whom she knows best from the list
Number the students 1 to 400 and pick 10 numbers at random
questions.answer: Number the students 1 to 400 and pick 10 numbers at random
questions.solution: In a simple random sample, chance alone decides who is chosen, and every student has the same chance. Numbering the list and picking numbers at random does that. The other methods let convenience or choice decide.

solve.answer: Number the students 1 to 400 and pick 10 numbers at random
solve.work: SRS: number 1-400, pick 10 at random. A, B, D are not random.

questions.stem: A simple random sample of 5 people is chosen from a group of 50 people. What is the probability that one particular person is in the sample? Write it as a fraction in simplest form.
questions.solution: Every person has the same chance of being chosen. Five of the 50 people are picked, so the chance is $\frac{5}{50} = \frac{1}{10}$.

solve.work: Each person's chance in an SRS of 5 from 50 is 5/50 = 1/10.

questions.stem: A list has 500 names. A researcher picks every 25th name on the list. How many names are in the sample?
questions.solution: Every 25th name from a list of 500 gives $500 \div 25 = 20$ names.

solve.work: 500 / 25 = 20 names (e.g. names 25, 50, ..., 500, or any start within the first 25).

questions.stem: Which description is a systematic sample?
choices: Take a random starting name, then every 8th name on the list
Split the list into age groups and pick names at random from each group
Pick a few groups at random and use every name in those groups
Use the names of the people who volunteer to answer
questions.answer: Take a random starting name, then every 8th name on the list
questions.solution: A systematic sample uses a fixed step through an ordered list after a random start. Splitting into groups first is stratified sampling, picking whole groups is cluster sampling, and volunteers make a voluntary response sample.

solve.answer: Take a random starting name, then every 8th name on the list
solve.work: Systematic: random start, then every k-th. C is stratified, D cluster, A voluntary.

questions.stem: A school has 120 girls and 80 boys. A stratified random sample takes 10 percent of the girls and 10 percent of the boys. How many girls are in the sample?
questions.solution: Ten percent of the 120 girls is $0.1 \times 120 = 12$ girls.

solve.work: 10% of 120 girls = 12.

questions.stem: A researcher wants to be sure that the sample includes both city residents and rural residents. Which plan guarantees this?
choices: Pick 100 names at random from one combined list of all residents
Sample at random from the city list, then from the rural list
Survey whoever happens to be at the town hall on one afternoon
Survey every household on one street in the middle of the city
questions.answer: Sample at random from the city list, then from the rural list
questions.solution: Sampling separately from each group makes sure both groups are in the sample. A single random sample from one combined list could happen to miss a group, and the other plans use only people who are easy to reach.

solve.answer: Sample at random from the city list, then from the rural list
solve.work: Sampling separately from the city and rural lists (stratified) guarantees both; one combined random list (D) does not guarantee it.

questions.stem: A researcher randomly selects 3 of 20 classrooms and surveys every student in those 3 classrooms. In this plan, what is each classroom called?
choices: A stratum
A census
A cluster
A parameter
questions.answer: A cluster
questions.solution: In a cluster sample the population is divided into groups, and whole groups are chosen at random. Each such group is a cluster.

solve.answer: A cluster
solve.work: Selecting whole classrooms at random and surveying everyone in them: each classroom is a cluster.

questions.stem: A town has 40 blocks. A cluster sample uses 5 of the blocks, chosen at random. What fraction of the town's blocks are in the sample? Write the fraction in simplest form.
questions.solution: Five of the 40 blocks are used, so the fraction is $\frac{5}{40} = \frac{1}{8}$.

questions.stem: A reporter surveys the first 30 people who walk out of a gym about how often people exercise. Why might the results be biased?
choices: Thirty people is always too few for any kind of survey
The reporter did not ask people enough different questions
People who go to a gym usually refuse to answer a survey
People who use a gym probably exercise more than most
questions.answer: People who use a gym probably exercise more than most
questions.solution: This is a convenience sample, taken from people who are easy to reach. People who use a gym exercise more than typical people, so the sample does not represent everyone.

solve.answer: People who use a gym probably exercise more than most
solve.work: People leaving a gym likely exercise more than average, so results overestimate exercise.

questions.stem: A radio show asks listeners to call in to vote on a question about a new stadium. Why can the results not be trusted to describe all adults in the city?
choices: Mostly people with strong opinions choose to call in
Radio shows are not allowed to ask questions to listeners
Too many adults in the city listen to the radio each day
A phone call cannot count as a real vote on a question
questions.answer: Mostly people with strong opinions choose to call in
questions.solution: Only listeners who decide to call are counted, and those who care most are the most likely to call. This is a voluntary response sample, so it does not represent all adults.

solve.answer: Mostly people with strong opinions choose to call in
solve.work: Voluntary call-in: people with strong opinions are the ones who call.

questions.stem: What is the name of the bias that happens when some members of the population have no chance of being chosen for the sample?
choices: Nonresponse
Undercoverage
Randomization
Stratification
questions.answer: Undercoverage
questions.solution: When part of the population is left out of the list or the method, those members can never be chosen. That is undercoverage. Nonresponse happens when people who were chosen do not answer.

solve.answer: Undercoverage
solve.work: Some members having no chance of being chosen is undercoverage.

questions.stem: A survey was sent to 250 people, and 175 of them answered. What percent of the people did not answer? Give the number only, without the percent sign.
questions.solution: The number who did not answer is $250 - 175 = 75$. As a percent of 250, that is $\frac{75}{250} \times 100 = 30$.

questions.stem: Which survey question is worded in a way that pushes people to answer yes?
choices: Do you think the new library is worth its cost?
How do you feel about the cost of the new library?
Wouldn't you agree that the wonderful library is worth it?
Is the cost of the new library too high, about right, or too low?
questions.answer: Wouldn't you agree that the wonderful library is worth it?
questions.solution: The first question tells the person what to think, using words such as "wonderful" and "wouldn't you agree". A fair question uses neutral words and does not lean toward one answer.

solve.answer: Wouldn't you agree that the wonderful library is worth it?
solve.work: C uses 'Wouldn't you agree' and 'wonderful', a leading question toward yes. D is a plain yes/no question.

questions.skill: Sample size, bias and validity of conclusions
questions.stem: Two random samples are taken from the same large population, one of 25 people and one of 250 people. Which sample will usually give a result closer to the true value for the population?
choices: The sample of 25, because small samples are chosen more carefully
Both are always equally close to the true value
Neither, because a sample can never be close to the truth
The sample of 250, because larger random samples vary less
questions.answer: The sample of 250, because larger random samples vary less
questions.solution: Bigger random samples usually give results that are closer to the value for the whole population and vary less from sample to sample. A sample can be close, even though it is rarely exactly right.

solve.answer: The sample of 250, because larger random samples vary less
solve.work: Larger random samples have less sampling variability, so 250 is usually closer.

questions.stem: A school has 600 students in grades 9 to 12. The principal wants a random sample that includes students from every grade. Which plan is a stratified random sample?
choices: Randomly choose 3 homerooms and survey every student in each of them
List all of the students and choose every 20th student on the list
Split the students by grade and take a random sample from each
Ask the first 30 students who arrive at school on a given morning
questions.answer: Split the students by grade and take a random sample from each
questions.solution: A stratified random sample splits the population into groups (strata), here the grades, and takes a random sample from every group. Choosing whole homerooms is a cluster sample, and choosing every 20th student is a systematic sample.

solve.answer: Split the students by grade and take a random sample from each
solve.work: Stratified: divide into strata (grades) and take a random sample within each. Every 20th = systematic; first 30 = convenience; whole homerooms = cluster.

questions.stem: A researcher randomly picks 5 of a county's 40 neighborhoods and surveys every household in those 5 neighborhoods. Which statement describes this plan?
choices: It is a stratified sample, because every neighborhood is represented
It is a systematic sample, because the neighborhoods follow a pattern
It is a simple random sample, because chance was used somewhere
It is a cluster sample, because whole groups were chosen at random
questions.answer: It is a cluster sample, because whole groups were chosen at random
questions.solution: Randomly choosing whole groups (the neighborhoods) and surveying everyone in them is a cluster sample. A stratified sample would take some households from every neighborhood.

solve.answer: It is a cluster sample, because whole groups were chosen at random
solve.work: Whole groups (neighborhoods) chosen at random and every member surveyed: cluster sample.

questions.stem: A town surveys residents by calling only the landline numbers listed in the phone book. Many young adults have only cell phones. What is the main problem with this sampling plan?
choices: Undercoverage: some residents have no chance to be chosen
Response bias: the questions push people toward an answer
Voluntary response: residents decide for themselves to join
Nonresponse: many chosen residents refuse to answer
questions.answer: Undercoverage: some residents have no chance to be chosen
questions.solution: People with only cell phones can never be called, so a whole part of the population is left out. That is undercoverage, and it can make the sample unrepresentative.

solve.answer: Undercoverage: some residents have no chance to be chosen
solve.work: Cell-only residents are not on the landline list, so they cannot be chosen: undercoverage.

questions.stem: A town council member wants to know whether residents favor a new tax for road repair. Which survey question is least likely to bias the answers?
choices: Do you favor a new tax that will finally fix our dangerous roads?
Do you agree that our terrible roads must be fixed with a new tax?
Do you favor or oppose a new tax to pay for road repairs?
Wouldn't you agree that a new road tax is a burden on families?
questions.answer: Do you favor or oppose a new tax to pay for road repairs?
questions.solution: A fair question uses neutral words and offers both sides. The other three questions use loaded words ("dangerous", "terrible", "burden") that push people toward one answer.

solve.answer: Do you favor or oppose a new tax to pay for road repairs?
solve.work: The neutral wording offers both sides ('favor or oppose') with no loaded words; the others use 'burden', 'terrible', 'dangerous', 'wouldn't you agree'.

questions.stem: A school has 1,200 students, and 480 of them are in ninth grade. A stratified random sample of 100 students is taken, with each grade represented in proportion to its size. How many ninth graders are in the sample?
questions.solution: Ninth graders are 480 / 1200 = 40% of the students, so they should be 40% of the sample: 0.40 x 100 = 40 students.

solve.work: Ninth graders are 480/1200 = 40% of the school; 40% of 100 = 40.

questions.stem: A club keeps a list of 900 members. A researcher wants a systematic sample of 45 members: after a random start, she picks every kth member on the list. What is k?
questions.solution: The list is spread over 45 picks, so she picks one member out of every 900 / 45 = 20 members.

questions.skill: Sample size, bias and validity of conclusions
questions.stem: Maya takes many random samples of 30 people from a large population and finds the mean of each sample. Jon takes many random samples of 300 people from the same population and finds the mean of each sample. What is true about the results?
choices: Maya's sample means will typically vary less from sample to sample
Jon's sample means will typically vary less from sample to sample
Both sets of sample means will equal the population mean exactly
Sample size does not change how much sample means vary
questions.answer: Jon's sample means will typically vary less from sample to sample
questions.solution: Larger random samples give sample means that are closer together, so Jon's means vary less. No random sample is guaranteed to match the population exactly.

solve.answer: Jon's sample means will typically vary less from sample to sample
solve.work: Larger samples give sample means with less variability (SD of mean = sigma/sqrt(n)). Jon's n = 300 > 30, so his means vary less.

questions.stem: A survey was mailed to 500 households, and 140 households mailed it back. What percent of the households that were sent the survey responded? Give the number only, without the percent sign.
questions.solution: The response rate is 140 / 500 = 0.28, which is 28%.

questions.stem: Only 20% of the people who were mailed a survey about a new law returned it, and most of those who did return it felt strongly about the law. What is the best conclusion about the results?
choices: They may be biased, because nonrespondents may differ from respondents
They are reliable, because those who replied felt sure of their opinions
They are reliable, because the survey was mailed to many people
They match the population exactly, because they came from a random mailing
questions.answer: They may be biased, because nonrespondents may differ from respondents
questions.solution: When most chosen people do not respond, and the ones who do respond are different (here, they feel strongly), the sample no longer represents the population. This is nonresponse bias.

solve.answer: They may be biased, because nonrespondents may differ from respondents
solve.work: 80% did not respond and respondents felt strongly, so nonresponse bias is likely: the 80% may differ.

questions.stem: The 60 students in a class are numbered 01 to 60. A teacher reads this list of random digits two digits at a time, from left to right: 47 83 15 62 09 31. She skips any number that is not from 01 to 60 and any repeat. What is the number of the third student she selects?
questions.solution: Read the numbers in order: 47 is chosen (first), 83 is skipped (too big), 15 is chosen (second), 62 is skipped (too big), 09 is chosen (third). The third student is number 9.

solve.work: 47 valid (1st), 83 skip, 15 valid (2nd), 62 skip, 09 valid (3rd). Third student = 9.

questions.skill: Identify the population and the sample
questions.stem: A researcher wants to know the opinion of all registered voters in a county. She asks 1000 voters, chosen from the county's list of registered voters. Which statement is correct?
choices: The population is all registered voters in the county; the sample is the 1000 asked
The population is the 1000 voters asked, and the sample is all registered voters in the county
The population is the list of registered voters, and the sample is the whole county
The population and the sample are both the same 1000 voters who were asked
questions.answer: The population is all registered voters in the county; the sample is the 1000 asked
questions.solution: The population is the whole group the researcher wants to learn about: all registered voters in the county. The sample is the smaller group actually asked: the 1000 voters.

solve.answer: The population is all registered voters in the county; the sample is the 1000 asked
solve.work: Population = all registered voters in the county; sample = the 1000 asked.

questions.skill: Identify the population and the sample
questions.stem: A sample of 150 people is 3 percent of the population it was taken from. How many people are in the population?
questions.solution: If 3 percent of the population is 150 people, then the population is $150 \div 0.03 = 5000$ people.

questions.stem: A baker weighs every loaf made today and finds that the mean weight is 502 grams. Another baker weighs 10 loaves picked at random from today's loaves and finds that the mean weight is 498 grams. Which statement is true?
choices: The 502 grams is a statistic, and 498 is a parameter
The 502 grams is a parameter, and 498 is a statistic
Both numbers are parameters, because both describe loaves
Both numbers are statistics, because both describe loaves
questions.answer: The 502 grams is a parameter, and 498 is a statistic
questions.solution: The first baker measured every loaf, so 502 grams describes the whole population: a parameter. The second baker measured a sample of 10 loaves, so 498 grams is a statistic.

solve.answer: The 502 grams is a parameter, and 498 is a statistic
solve.work: Every loaf weighed: 502 g is a parameter. 10 random loaves: 498 g is a statistic.

questions.stem: A random sample of 5 students has these test scores: 70, 80, 85, 90 and 95. What is the sample mean?
A researcher wants to compare the opinions of students in grades 9, 10, 11 and 12 at a school, with a good estimate for each grade. Which sampling method is best?
choices: A voluntary response survey in the school newsletter
A convenience sample of the students in one hallway
A stratified random sample, taken from each grade
A cluster sample made up of one single classroom
questions.answer: A stratified random sample, taken from each grade
questions.solution: To get a good estimate for every grade, each grade should be sampled on purpose. Taking a random sample from each grade is a stratified random sample. The other methods may leave out grades entirely.

solve.answer: A stratified random sample, taken from each grade
solve.work: To estimate each grade well, sample at random within each grade: stratified.

questions.skill: Why we sample instead of taking a census
questions.stem: For which of these populations would a census be the most practical?
choices: All of the households in the whole United States
All of the fish that live in a large lake
All of the trees in a very large national forest
The 12 members of a school's robotics team
questions.answer: The 12 members of a school's robotics team
questions.solution: A census is practical only when the population is small enough to reach everyone. Twelve team members are easy to ask. The other populations are far too large to count one by one.

solve.answer: The 12 members of a school's robotics team
solve.work: A census of a small group of 12 is practical; the others are huge or hard to count.

questions.skill: Why we sample instead of taking a census
questions.stem: Interviewing one person takes 12 minutes. A researcher interviews a sample of 300 people instead of taking a census of 1500 people. How many hours of interviewing does the sample save?
questions.solution: The sample skips $1500 - 300 = 1200$ interviews. At 12 minutes each, that is $1200 \times 12 = 14{,}400$ minutes, and $14{,}400 \div 60 = 240$ hours.

solve.work: Saved people = 1500 - 300 = 1200; 1200 x 12 = 14400 minutes = 240 hours.

questions.stem: To pick a simple random sample of 4 students from 25 numbered students, a computer gives these numbers in order: 7, 19, 7, 3, 12. A student can be chosen only once. Which students are in the sample?
choices: Students 7, 19, 3 and 12
Students 7, 19, 7 and 3
Students 19, 3 and 12 only
Students 7, 19, 3, 12 and 7
questions.answer: Students 7, 19, 3 and 12
questions.solution: A student cannot be chosen twice, so the second 7 is skipped. The first four different numbers are 7, 19, 3 and 12.

solve.answer: Students 7, 19, 3 and 12
solve.work: Take numbers in order, skipping the repeated 7: 7, 19, 3, 12 (four students).

questions.stem: The students in a class of 80 are numbered 01 to 80. A teacher reads this list of random digits two at a time, from left to right: 92 14 67 05 80 33. She skips any number that is not from 01 to 80. She adds the numbers of the first three students she chooses. What is the sum?
questions.solution: The number 92 is not from 01 to 80, so it is skipped. The first three students chosen are 14, 67 and 05. Their sum is $14 + 67 + 5 = 86$.

questions.stem: A researcher takes a systematic sample from a list of 1200 people by choosing every 15th person. How many people are in the sample?
questions.solution: Taking every 15th person from 1200 gives $1200 \div 15 = 80$ people.

questions.stem: A systematic sample starts at person number 3 on a list of 100 people and then takes every 8th person after that: numbers 3, 11, 19, and so on. What is the number of the last person chosen?
questions.solution: The chosen numbers are $3 + 8k$. The largest one that is at most 100 has $k = 12$, which gives $3 + 96 = 99$.

questions.stem: A town has 3000 adults aged 18 to 39 and 2000 adults aged 40 and older. A stratified random sample of 200 adults has each age group in proportion to its size. How many adults aged 40 and older are in the sample?
questions.solution: Adults aged 40 and older are $\frac{2000}{5000} = 0.4$ of the town. In a sample of 200, that is $0.4 \times 200 = 80$ adults.

questions.stem: A company has two offices. The downtown office has 900 workers and the other office has 100 workers. A researcher takes a stratified random sample of 50 workers with each office in proportion to its size. How many workers come from each office?
choices: 25 from the downtown office and 25 from the other office
45 from the downtown office and 5 from the other office
40 from the downtown office and 10 from the other office
49 from the downtown office and 1 from the other office
questions.answer: 45 from the downtown office and 5 from the other office
questions.solution: The downtown office has 90 percent of the workers, so it gives $0.9 \times 50 = 45$ workers. The other office gives the remaining 5.

solve.answer: 45 from the downtown office and 5 from the other office

questions.stem: A school district has 24 schools. A researcher chooses 4 schools at random and surveys every student at each of them. Each of the 4 schools has 500 students. How many students are surveyed?
questions.solution: Every student at each of the 4 chosen schools is surveyed, so the number is $4 \times 500 = 2000$.

solve.work: 4 schools x 500 = 2000 students.

questions.stem: A student government asks a question in the school newsletter and counts the replies that students email back. It receives 120 replies from a school of 1500 students. What percent of the school's students replied? Give the number only, without the percent sign.
questions.solution: The percent that replied is $\frac{120}{1500} \times 100 = 8$. Only students who chose to reply are counted, and the other 92 percent are missing, so the replies may not show what the whole school thinks.

questions.stem: A researcher stands outside a shopping mall on Saturday morning and interviews shoppers who agree to talk. She wants to learn how often all the residents of the city shop. Which description is best?
choices: A simple random sample, because shoppers differ from one another
A stratified sample, because shoppers go to different stores
A convenience sample that may not represent all residents
A census of all the shoppers in the city
questions.answer: A convenience sample that may not represent all residents
questions.solution: She is interviewing people who are easy to reach and willing to stop. Residents who do not shop at the mall on Saturday morning have no chance to be included, so the sample may not represent everyone.

solve.answer: A convenience sample that may not represent all residents
solve.work: Shoppers at one mall on Saturday who agree to talk: a convenience sample that may not represent all residents.

questions.stem: A survey about internet use is carried out only by sending emails. A town has 4000 residents, and 15 percent of them have no email address. How many residents have no chance of being chosen for the survey?
questions.solution: Residents without an email address can never receive the survey. That is $0.15 \times 4000 = 600$ residents. Leaving them out is undercoverage.

questions.stem: A mailed survey had a low response rate. Which step is the best way to reduce nonresponse bias?
choices: Count only the returned surveys and then call the sample a bigger one
Replace the people who did not respond with people who volunteer
Make the survey a lot longer so that each reply has more detail
Follow up with those who did not respond, by phone or mail
questions.answer: Follow up with those who did not respond, by phone or mail
questions.solution: Nonresponse bias comes from people who were chosen but did not answer. Following up with them brings back some of their answers. Counting only replies or adding volunteers does not fix the bias.

solve.answer: Follow up with those who did not respond, by phone or mail
solve.work: Following up with nonrespondents raises the response rate and reduces nonresponse bias; C adds voluntary bias.

questions.stem: Which survey question is worded to push people toward opposing a longer school day?
choices: Since long days harm sleep, do you oppose a longer school day?
Do you favor or oppose making the school day longer?
How do you feel about the current length of the school day?
Should the school day be longer, shorter, or stay the same length?
questions.answer: Since long days harm sleep, do you oppose a longer school day?
questions.solution: The first question adds a claim about harm before it asks, which pushes people toward "oppose". The other three questions are neutral.

solve.answer: Since long days harm sleep, do you oppose a longer school day?
solve.work: D adds a premise ('long days harm sleep') that pushes toward opposing.

questions.stem: A teacher asks teens, in person and with their parents in the room, whether they have ever skipped school. Which bias is the most likely?
choices: Undercoverage bias, because some teens have no parents at home
Response bias, because teens may not answer honestly with parents near
Nonresponse bias, because some teens would not agree to take part
Selection bias, because the teens were not chosen at random from teens
questions.answer: Response bias, because teens may not answer honestly with parents near
questions.solution: The setting gives the teens a reason to give answers that avoid trouble. That is response bias: the answers given may not be the true ones.

solve.answer: Response bias, because teens may not answer honestly with parents near
solve.work: With parents present, teens may not answer honestly: response bias.

questions.skill: Sample size, bias and validity of conclusions
questions.stem: A researcher says: "My sample of 5000 volunteers shows that 90 percent agree, so the true percent for everyone must be about 90." What is wrong with this conclusion?
choices: The sample of 5000 is too large for the result to be accurate for anyone
A percent can never be used to describe a whole population
A big sample cannot fix bias from people choosing to volunteer
The researcher should have used only the volunteers who disagree
questions.answer: A big sample cannot fix bias from people choosing to volunteer
questions.solution: Volunteers choose themselves, which creates bias. Making the sample bigger does not remove that bias. A smaller random sample could describe the population better.

solve.answer: A big sample cannot fix bias from people choosing to volunteer
solve.work: Volunteers self-select; a large sample does not remove that bias.

questions.skill: Sample size, bias and validity of conclusions
questions.stem: A random sample of 200 students from a school of 1600 students found that 35 percent ride the bus. Assuming that the sample represents the school, about how many of the 1600 students ride the bus?
questions.solution: If 35 percent of the school rides the bus, the number is $0.35 \times 1600 = 560$ students.

questions.stem: A school has 24 homerooms with about 25 students each. Which plan is a cluster sample of the students?
choices: Choose 5 students at random from each of the school's 24 homerooms and survey them
Take every 24th student from an alphabetical list of the whole school and survey them
Choose 5 homerooms at random and survey every student in those 5 homerooms
Use random numbers to pick 125 students from the school's full list and survey them
questions.answer: Choose 5 homerooms at random and survey every student in those 5 homerooms
questions.solution: In a cluster sample the population is split into groups, a few whole groups are chosen at random, and everyone in the chosen groups is surveyed. Here the groups are homerooms. Taking some students from every homeroom is stratified, every 24th name is systematic, and picking 125 names from the full list is a simple random sample.

solve.answer: Choose 5 homerooms at random and survey every student in those 5 homerooms
solve.work: A cluster sample randomly selects whole groups (homerooms) and surveys everyone in them. The other options are an SRS, a systematic sample and a stratified sample.

questions.stem: A college has 4,500 undergraduates and 500 graduate students. A researcher wants a reliable estimate of the opinions of each group separately. A simple random sample of 100 of all students would include only about 10 graduate students. Which plan solves this problem best?
choices: Randomly choose 90 undergraduates and 10 graduate students, matching the college
Randomly choose 100 undergraduates and use them to represent both groups
Randomly choose 50 undergraduates and, separately, 50 graduate students
Ask the first 100 students who walk into the student union
questions.answer: Randomly choose 50 undergraduates and, separately, 50 graduate students
questions.solution: To estimate each group well, each group needs a reasonable number of sampled students. Taking a separate random sample from each group (stratifying) does that. A sample that matches the college would still have only 10 graduate students, and the other plans ignore the graduate students or are not random.

solve.answer: Randomly choose 50 undergraduates and, separately, 50 graduate students
solve.work: To estimate each group separately, each needs an adequate sample: take random samples of 50 from each group (stratified, disproportionate). Proportional 90/10 leaves only 10 grads; the others ignore grads or are convenience.

questions.stem: At a warehouse, crates are stacked in piles of 10. The crate in the bottom corner of each pile (position 1) is the one most often crushed. An inspector checks every 10th crate in the order the crates were stacked, beginning with the first crate. What is the main problem with this plan?
choices: Every checked crate is in the safest spot, so damage would be underestimated
Every checked crate is in the crush-prone spot, so damage would be overestimated
There is no problem, because a systematic sample is always as good as a random one
A sample of only 1 crate in 10 is always too small to judge the damage
questions.answer: Every checked crate is in the crush-prone spot, so damage would be overestimated
questions.solution: Starting at the first crate and taking every 10th always picks the crate in position 1 of its pile. The pattern in the list matches the pattern in the damage, so the sample is biased toward damaged crates.

solve.answer: Every checked crate is in the crush-prone spot, so damage would be overestimated
solve.work: Crates 1, 11, 21, ... are each position 1 of a pile of 10, the crush-prone bottom corner. So every checked crate is the worst spot and damage is overestimated.

questions.skill: Sample size, bias and validity of conclusions
questions.stem: An online poll in which 20,000 visitors chose to vote found that 80% like a new park design. A separate poll of 500 residents chosen at random found that 52% like it. Which poll is more trustworthy for all residents, and why?
choices: The online poll, because a larger sample is always more trustworthy than a smaller one
The online poll, because 80% is a much stronger result than 52%
Both are equally trustworthy, because each reports a percent of the people asked
The random poll, because random selection avoids self-selection bias
questions.answer: The random poll, because random selection avoids self-selection bias
questions.solution: A very large voluntary sample can still be badly biased, because the people who choose to vote differ from the rest. Random selection gives every resident a chance to be chosen, so the poll of 500 gives a more trustworthy picture even though it is smaller.

solve.answer: The random poll, because random selection avoids self-selection bias
solve.work: The online poll is self-selected (voluntary response); size does not fix bias. The random poll of 500 is more trustworthy.

questions.stem: A restaurant manager hands each customer a satisfaction form and stands beside the table while the customer fills it in and hands it back. What is the most likely source of bias in the ratings?
choices: Undercoverage: some customers have no chance of being asked
Voluntary response: only customers with strong feelings write anything
Response bias: customers may give answers that please the manager
Nonresponse: most customers refuse to fill out the form
questions.answer: Response bias: customers may give answers that please the manager
questions.solution: Customers know the manager will see the answers, so they may say what they think the manager wants to hear. This is response bias. It is the pressure on the answers, not who was asked, that causes the problem.

solve.answer: Response bias: customers may give answers that please the manager
solve.work: Everyone is asked and hands it back, so not nonresponse/undercoverage/voluntary; the manager standing by pressures customers to give pleasing answers: response bias.

questions.stem: A researcher chooses a systematic sample from a list of 600 people. She picks person number 7, and then every 12th person after that. What is the number of the 5th person she picks?
questions.solution: The picks are 7, 19, 31, 43, 55. The 5th pick is the start plus 4 steps of 12: 7 + 4 x 12 = 55.

questions.stem: A stratified random sample takes the same percent of the students from each grade of a school. The 24 seniors chosen are 8% of all the seniors. The school has 1,500 students altogether. How many students are in the whole sample?
questions.solution: The same 8% is taken from every grade, so the whole sample is 8% of all the students: 0.08 x 1,500 = 120. (The 24 seniors are only one stratum, 8% of 300 seniors.)

solve.work: The same 8% is taken from every grade, so the sample is 8% of 1,500 = 120. (Check: 24 = 8% of 300 seniors.)

questions.stem: A district has 60 schools with about 450 students each. A researcher wants a cluster sample of about 2,700 students, made by choosing schools at random and surveying every student in each chosen school. How many schools should she choose?
questions.solution: Each chosen school adds about 450 students, so she needs 2,700 / 450 = 6 schools.

questions.stem: A group has 6 people. A simple random sample of 3 people is chosen, so every possible group of 3 is equally likely. How many different groups of 3 people can be chosen?
questions.solution: There are 6 x 5 x 4 = 120 ways to choose 3 people in order. Each group of 3 can be ordered in 3 x 2 x 1 = 6 ways, so there are 120 / 6 = 20 different groups.

questions.stem: An inspector chooses a random sample of 40 items from a shipment of 5,000 items and finds that 6 of the items are defective. If the sample represents the shipment, about how many defective items would be expected in the whole shipment?
questions.solution: The sample proportion defective is 6 / 40 = 0.15. Applying this to the shipment gives about 0.15 x 5,000 = 750 defective items.

questions.skill: Sample size, bias and validity of conclusions
questions.stem: A researcher surveys a random sample of 200 students at one high school in a large state and finds that 60% own a laptop. She reports that 60% of all teenagers in the state own a laptop. What is the best critique?
choices: The sample is too small, because 200 is never enough to estimate a percent
The sample came from one school, so it can describe only students at that school
There is no problem, because a random sample always represents every population
The researcher should survey the same 200 students again to make the result exact
questions.answer: The sample came from one school, so it can describe only students at that school
questions.solution: Random selection lets the results be generalized only to the population that was sampled from, here the students at that one school. Teenagers in the rest of the state had no chance of being chosen.

solve.answer: The sample came from one school, so it can describe only students at that school
solve.work: The sample is random only within one school, so it supports conclusions about that school's students, not all teenagers in the state.

questions.stem: A city wants to estimate the percent of its households that have a pet, and a random sample of 500 households has 58 percent with a pet. Which statement is true?
choices: Every random sample of 500 households will give exactly 58 percent
The percent for the whole city must be exactly equal to 58 percent
A different random sample would give a percent very far from 58 each time
A different random sample of 500 would likely give a different percent
questions.answer: A different random sample of 500 would likely give a different percent
questions.solution: Samples vary by chance. A different random sample of the same size would likely give a percent near, but not exactly, 58. The value for the whole city is a parameter that stays fixed but is not known exactly.

solve.answer: A different random sample of 500 would likely give a different percent
solve.work: Sampling variability: another random sample would likely give a different percent, but not a wildly different one.

questions.stem: A population has a mean of 40. A researcher takes three random samples from it, and the sample means are 38, 43 and 42. How far is the average of the three sample means from the population mean?
questions.solution: The average of the three sample means is $\frac{38 + 43 + 42}{3} = \frac{123}{3} = 41$. This is $41 - 40 = 1$ above the population mean.

questions.stem: Households in a country are spread over 100 counties, and visiting them is costly. A researcher wants to interview about 2000 households in person. Which plan is the most practical and still uses random selection?
choices: Choose 10 counties at random, then sample households within each
Choose 2000 households at random from the whole country and visit each one
Interview the volunteers who respond to a notice posted online
Interview the first 2000 people who walk into a large shopping mall
questions.answer: Choose 10 counties at random, then sample households within each
questions.solution: Choosing a few counties at random keeps the travel small, and sampling at random inside them keeps the selection fair. Picking households from the whole country is fair but costly to visit, and the other two plans are not random.

solve.answer: Choose 10 counties at random, then sample households within each
solve.work: Choosing 10 counties at random, then households within them (cluster/multistage) is practical and random. C is random but costly; A, B are not random.

questions.stem: A company has 5000 customers. About 20 percent are business accounts, which spend much more than the other customers. The company wants a good estimate of the mean spending of all customers. Which plan is the best?
choices: Run a voluntary response survey on the company's own website
Sample business accounts and other customers separately
Take a cluster sample of all the customers in just two cities
Survey 100 customers who happen to visit the store on one day
questions.answer: Sample business accounts and other customers separately
questions.solution: The two kinds of customers differ a lot in spending. A stratified random sample makes sure both are represented in the right proportion, which gives a better estimate than methods that rely on volunteers or on easy access.

solve.answer: Sample business accounts and other customers separately
solve.work: Business accounts spend much more, so sampling the two groups separately (stratified) gives a better estimate.

questions.skill: Why we sample instead of taking a census
questions.stem: A company has the age of every one of its 60 employees on file. The mean of all 60 ages, which is a parameter because nobody is left out, is 38 years. What is the sum of the 60 ages, in years?
questions.solution: The mean is the sum divided by the number of ages, so the sum is the mean times the count: $60 \times 38 = 2280$.

solve.work: Sum = mean x n = 38 x 60 = 2280.

questions.stem: A teacher wants a sample of 6 students from a class of 30 with 15 girls and 15 boys. She picks 3 girls at random and 3 boys at random. Is this a simple random sample?
choices: Yes, because every student has the same 1 in 5 chance of being chosen
Yes, because chance decides which students are picked
No, because not all groups of 6 students are equally likely
No, because 6 students is far too few for a simple random sample
questions.answer: No, because not all groups of 6 students are equally likely
questions.solution: In a simple random sample every possible group of 6 is equally likely. Here a group of 6 girls can never happen, so the groups are not equally likely, even though each student has the same chance of being picked.

solve.answer: No, because not all groups of 6 students are equally likely
solve.work: Not an SRS: a sample of, say, 6 girls can never occur, so not every group of 6 is equally likely. D's 1-in-5 chance is true but not sufficient.

questions.stem: A simple random sample of 3 people is chosen from 12 people. What is the probability that both Ana and Ben are in the sample? Write the fraction in simplest form.
questions.solution: The chance that Ana is chosen is $\frac{3}{12}$. Given that, 2 places are left among the other 11 people, so Ben is chosen with chance $\frac{2}{11}$. Together: $\frac{3}{12} \times \frac{2}{11} = \frac{6}{132} = \frac{1}{22}$.

questions.stem: A researcher takes every 15th name from a list of 400 names, starting at name number 10. How many names are in the sample?
questions.solution: The chosen numbers are $10, 25, 40, \ldots$ up to 400, which is $10 + 15k$ with $k = 0$ to $26$. The number of names is $\frac{400 - 10}{15} + 1 = 27$.

solve.work: Names 10, 25, 40, ..., 10 + 15k <= 400 gives k <= 26, so 27 names (last is 400).

questions.stem: A park ranger estimates the mean number of daily visitors by counting visitors on every 7th day of the calendar. Weekend days have many more visitors than other days. Why could this sample be misleading?
choices: Counting visitors on only some of the days is never allowed
Every 7th day of the calendar will always fall on a weekend
The ranger should have counted visitors every single day at the same hour
Every 7th day is the same weekday, so weekly patterns are missed
questions.answer: Every 7th day is the same weekday, so weekly patterns are missed
questions.solution: Stepping by 7 days always lands on the same day of the week, such as always a Tuesday or always a Saturday. The sample would then miss the difference between weekdays and weekends.

solve.answer: Every 7th day is the same weekday, so weekly patterns are missed
solve.work: Every 7th day falls on the same weekday, so it captures either all weekend or all weekday days and misses the weekly pattern. C ('always on a weekend') is false.

questions.stem: A school has 400 freshmen, 300 sophomores, 200 juniors and 100 seniors. A stratified random sample of 50 students has each grade in proportion to its size. How many juniors are in the sample?
questions.solution: Juniors are $\frac{200}{1000} = 0.2$ of the school. In a sample of 50, that is $0.2 \times 50 = 10$ juniors.

questions.stem: In a stratified sample that is proportional to size, 18 of the 45 members of group A are chosen. Group B has 70 members. How many members of group B are chosen?
questions.solution: Group A is sampled at the rate $\frac{18}{45} = 0.4$. A proportional sample uses the same rate for group B: $0.4 \times 70 = 28$.

questions.stem: A population has two groups. Group A has 600 members and a mean of 20. Group B has 400 members and a mean of 30. A stratified sample gives the correct mean for each group. What is the mean of the whole population?
questions.solution: Weight each group's mean by its size. The total is $600 \times 20 + 400 \times 30 = 12{,}000 + 12{,}000 = 24{,}000$ and there are 1000 members, so the mean is $24{,}000 \div 1000 = 24$.

questions.stem: A county has 90 farms. A cluster sample uses 12 farms chosen at random. All 35 workers at each chosen farm are surveyed, and 15 percent of the surveyed workers do not respond. How many responses are received?
questions.solution: The number of workers surveyed is $12 \times 35 = 420$. Of these, 85 percent respond: $0.85 \times 420 = 357$.

solve.work: Surveyed 12 x 35 = 420; respond 85% of 420 = 357.

questions.stem: A population is divided into 20 groups of 50 people each. A stratified sample takes 5 people at random from every group. A cluster sample picks 4 of the groups at random and uses everyone in them. How many more people are in the cluster sample than in the stratified sample?
questions.solution: The stratified sample has $20 \times 5 = 100$ people. The cluster sample has $4 \times 50 = 200$ people, since everyone in 4 whole groups is used. The difference is $200 - 100 = 100$.

solve.work: Stratified 20 x 5 = 100; cluster 4 x 50 = 200; difference 100.

questions.stem: A student estimates how many hours all students at his school sleep by asking 40 of his friends. His teacher says that asking 400 of his friends would fix the problem. Is she right?
choices: No, because a larger convenience sample has the same bias
Yes, because larger samples always remove bias
Yes, as long as the friends are asked in random order
No, because 400 friends are too many to be representative
questions.answer: No, because a larger convenience sample has the same bias
questions.solution: Asking more friends does not make the sample fairer, because his friends are still not a random sample of the school. Bias from how people are chosen is not reduced by making the sample bigger.

solve.answer: No, because a larger convenience sample has the same bias
solve.work: Friends are a convenience sample; a larger one keeps the same bias.

questions.stem: A web poll got 3200 votes, and 2400 of them were yes votes. A random sample of 400 residents found that 45 percent said yes. By how many percentage points is the web poll's percent of yes votes higher than the random sample's percent?
questions.solution: In the web poll, $\frac{2400}{3200} \times 100 = 75$ percent said yes. That is $75 - 45 = 30$ percentage points higher than in the random sample.

questions.stem: A student wants to survey 50 students about school start times. Which plan improves a survey of the first 50 students who arrive at school?
choices: Survey the first 100 students who arrive at school
Number all of the students and pick 50 at random
Survey the last 50 students who arrive at school too
Let each student decide whether to join the survey
questions.answer: Number all of the students and pick 50 at random
questions.solution: Students who arrive first differ from the rest, and asking more of them or letting students decide does not fix that. Choosing at random from the full list gives every student a fair chance.

solve.answer: Number all of the students and pick 50 at random
solve.work: Replacing the convenience sample with an SRS of all students improves it.

questions.stem: A survey was mailed to 800 randomly chosen households. Of these, 600 households replied, and 270 of the replies favored a proposal. Suppose none of the 200 households that did not reply would have favored it. What percent of all 800 households favor the proposal?
questions.solution: Only the 270 households that replied favored it, so the percent of all 800 is $\frac{270}{800} \times 100 = 33.75$. Among replies alone it was $45$ percent, so the missing households make a large difference.

questions.stem: A company invites every buyer of a product to rate it. Only 12 percent reply, and the mean rating is 4.8 stars. What is the most important concern about using 4.8 stars as the typical buyer's rating?
choices: Ratings that are given as stars cannot be averaged together
The people who replied are not actually buyers of the product
Most buyers did not reply, and the repliers may be unusual
The company asked every buyer instead of choosing a sample first
questions.answer: Most buyers did not reply, and the repliers may be unusual
questions.solution: With only 12 percent replying, nonresponse bias is a serious risk: buyers with strong feelings reply more often. Asking every buyer is not a problem in itself.

solve.answer: Most buyers did not reply, and the repliers may be unusual
solve.work: Only 12% replied; voluntary repliers may be unusually happy/unhappy: nonresponse/self-selection.

questions.stem: Which situation is an example of nonresponse rather than undercoverage?
choices: The list used to choose people leaves out those who moved in this week
The survey is drawn from a list of seniors, but the goal is to learn about all students
Only landline numbers are called, and many people have no landline
People are chosen for a survey, but 40 percent of them do not return the form
questions.answer: People are chosen for a survey, but 40 percent of them do not return the form
questions.solution: Nonresponse is when people who were chosen do not answer. In the other three situations some people could never be chosen, which is undercoverage.

solve.answer: People are chosen for a survey, but 40 percent of them do not return the form
solve.work: D: chosen people do not return the form is nonresponse; A, B, C leave people off the frame (undercoverage).

questions.stem: A survey asks, "Do you agree that traffic downtown is terrible?" Which change would fix the wording best?
choices: Ask, "Is traffic downtown light, moderate, or heavy?"
Ask, "Don't you agree that traffic downtown is awful?"
Ask, "Isn't it true that traffic downtown is heavy?"
Ask, "Do you agree that traffic is terrible downtown, yes or no?"
questions.answer: Ask, "Is traffic downtown light, moderate, or heavy?"
questions.solution: The best fix removes the loaded word and lets people choose among neutral options. The other three still push people toward agreeing that traffic is bad.

solve.answer: Ask, "Is traffic downtown light, moderate, or heavy?"
solve.work: C gives balanced, neutral choices; A still says 'terrible', B and D are leading.

questions.stem: In a survey, 85 percent of people say they "always" recycle, but a check of household trash shows that far fewer do. What is the best explanation?
choices: Undercoverage, because the survey was too short to be fair
Response bias, because people want to look good to others
The sample was too large for the answers to be accurate
The people who recycle all chose not to answer the survey
questions.answer: Response bias, because people want to look good to others
questions.solution: People often give answers that make them look good. That is response bias: the answers given differ from what is true.

solve.answer: Response bias, because people want to look good to others
solve.work: People overstate socially desirable behavior: response bias.

questions.skill: Sample size, bias and validity of conclusions
questions.stem: Survey X is a random sample of 100 people with a mean of 52. Survey Y is a voluntary poll of 10000 people with a mean of 61. The true mean for the population is 53. What best explains why Y is farther from the true value?
choices: A sample of 10000 is too large to give a reliable mean
Random samples are always exactly right about the truth
Bias from self-selection is not fixed by a bigger sample
Voluntary polls only include people who agree with the topic
questions.answer: Bias from self-selection is not fixed by a bigger sample
questions.solution: Survey Y is large, but the people chose themselves, so its mean is shifted by bias. Survey X is small, but random selection makes its mean close to the truth, though not exact.

solve.answer: Bias from self-selection is not fixed by a bigger sample
solve.work: Y is a voluntary (self-selected) poll; its bias is not fixed by size. B overstates ('only include people who agree').

questions.stem: A class list has 28 rows. Two of the rows repeat a student who is already on the list. After the repeated rows are removed, how many rows are left?
questions.solution: A repeated row is an extra copy of a row that is already there, so it is removed. Two rows are removed: $28 - 2 = 26$.

solve.work: 28 rows; 2 rows are repeats of students already listed. Removing them leaves 28 - 2 = 26.

questions.stem: In a table of student heights, one cell is empty because that student was absent on measuring day. What is an empty cell like this called in data cleaning?
choices: a missing value
an outlier
a duplicate
a categorical variable
questions.answer: a missing value
questions.solution: A cell that has no recorded value is a missing value. An outlier is a value far from the others, and a duplicate is a repeated row. Nothing is recorded in the empty cell, so it is a missing value.

solve.answer: a missing value
solve.work: An empty cell where a value should be is a missing value. Not a duplicate (repeated record), not an outlier (extreme value), not a variable type.

questions.skill: Find and fix errors and outliers
questions.stem: A teacher records quiz scores out of 20 points: 14, 17, 9, 35, 18. One of these scores cannot be right. Which score is it?
questions.solution: A quiz out of 20 points cannot have a score above 20. The score 35 is impossible, so it must be a recording error. Every other score is possible, even the lowest one, 9.

solve.work: Scores are out of 20, so no score can exceed 20. 35 > 20, impossible; 14, 17, 9, 18 are possible.

questions.stem: Mia wants to know the favorite sport of the students at her school. She asks only the members of the basketball team. What is the problem with her data?
choices: She asked so many students that the data cannot be summarized
The basketball team may not represent all the students at the school
She worded her question so that it pushes students to one answer
Several students left blanks, so some of the data are missing
questions.answer: The basketball team may not represent all the students at the school
questions.solution: The team members are only some of the students, and they are more likely to pick basketball. A sample that leaves out most of the school is biased. The other problems are not described in the question.

solve.answer: The basketball team may not represent all the students at the school
solve.work: Sampling only the basketball team is a non-representative (biased) sample of the school; they likely favor basketball. Other options (missing data, leading wording, too many) do not describe the situation.

questions.skill: Tell original from secondary data and combine sources
questions.stem: Which of these is secondary data, meaning data that someone else already collected?
choices: The number of pencils that you count in your own backpack today
Heights that you measure yourself for ten of your classmates
A table of city populations downloaded from a government website
Answers that you collect by asking your friends a survey question
questions.answer: A table of city populations downloaded from a government website
questions.solution: Secondary data were collected by someone else. The table from a government website is the only one you did not collect yourself. Counting, measuring and surveying are ways of making your own, original data.

solve.answer: A table of city populations downloaded from a government website
solve.work: Secondary data = collected by someone else. Survey, counting pencils, measuring heights are all your own (primary). A downloaded government table is secondary.

questions.stem: Class A recorded heights in centimeters. Class B recorded heights in meters. A student in class B is 1.5 meters tall. What is her height in centimeters, so that it can be combined with class A's data?
questions.solution: There are 100 centimeters in 1 meter, so multiply by 100: $1.5 \times 100 = 150$ centimeters.

questions.skill: Choose a method to generate original data
questions.stem: Which of these questions is best answered by asking people to fill out a survey?
choices: How many minutes does an ice cube take to melt in the sun?
How many cars pass the school gate in one hour?
How tall is the oak tree behind the school?
Which kind of lunch do students at our school like best?
questions.answer: Which kind of lunch do students at our school like best?
questions.solution: Food preferences live in people's heads, so you have to ask them. Melting time and tree height are measured, and cars passing the gate can be counted by watching.

solve.answer: Which kind of lunch do students at our school like best?
solve.work: Preferences (which lunch students like best) are opinions, best gathered by survey. Melting time, tree height and car counts are measured or observed.

questions.stem: A survey of 40 people asked about income. Six of them refused to answer that question. What percent of the people refused?
questions.solution: Divide the number who refused by the number of people and write it as a percent: $\frac{6}{40} = 0.15$, which is 15 percent.

questions.stem: Which source is the best choice for data on how many students are enrolled in each school of a district?
choices: The district's own published report on enrollment
A post by a stranger on a social media site
A friend's memory of how many students there are
An advertisement from a company that sells school supplies
questions.answer: The district's own published report on enrollment
questions.solution: The best source is one that is responsible for the records and publishes them: the district's own report. The other sources are guesses or have no reason to be accurate.

solve.answer: The district's own published report on enrollment
solve.work: The district's own published enrollment report is the authoritative primary source; an ad, memory or stranger's post are unreliable.

questions.stem: A survey asks: "Don't you agree that our terrible school lunch should be replaced?" What is wrong with this question?
choices: It can only be answered with a number and not with words
Its wording pushes people toward a particular answer
It asks people to remember something from many years ago
It uses words that are too hard for most of the students
questions.answer: Its wording pushes people toward a particular answer
questions.solution: Words such as "terrible" and "Don't you agree" lead the person to say yes. A leading question gives biased data. The question can be answered with yes or no, and it asks about now.

solve.answer: Its wording pushes people toward a particular answer
solve.work: "Don't you agree" and "terrible" are leading/loaded wording, pushing respondents toward agreeing.

questions.skill: Choose a method to generate original data
questions.stem: A student wants to know how long her classmates spend on the bus each morning. Which way of getting data is original data collection?
choices: Read the bus company's yearly report on its profit
Copy a table of bus times from last year's yearbook
Ask each classmate how many minutes the bus ride takes
Use an article about school buses in another state
questions.answer: Ask each classmate how many minutes the bus ride takes
questions.solution: Original data is collected by the person who will use it, for the question being asked. Asking each classmate gathers new data. The other three choices use data that someone else already collected.

solve.answer: Ask each classmate how many minutes the bus ride takes
solve.work: Original (primary) data is collected by the student herself: asking each classmate.

questions.skill: Choose a method to generate original data
questions.stem: Zoe counts the cars that pass her house each hour from 7 a.m. to 9 a.m. She changes nothing about what happens. What kind of original data collection is this?
choices: An experiment
A census of the town
A secondary source
An observation
questions.answer: An observation
questions.solution: Zoe watches and records what happens without changing anything. That is an observation. In an experiment the researcher changes something and measures the effect.

solve.answer: An observation
solve.work: Watching and counting without changing anything is an observation (an experiment imposes a treatment).

questions.skill: Choose a method to generate original data
questions.stem: A student plans a survey of 25 classmates. Each classmate will be asked 4 questions. If everyone answers every question, how many answers will she collect in all?
questions.solution: Each of the 25 classmates gives 4 answers, so she collects $25 \times 4 = 100$ answers.

solve.work: 25 x 4 = 100 answers.

questions.skill: Tell original from secondary data and combine sources
questions.stem: Which of these is original data?
choices: Heart rates that a student measures in her own gym class
A table of average heart rates by age from a health website
Heart rate data downloaded from a published study
A table of heart rates copied from a science textbook
questions.answer: Heart rates that a student measures in her own gym class
questions.solution: Original data is collected by the person using it. Measuring heart rates in her own class is original. The other three were collected by someone else, so they are secondary data.

solve.answer: Heart rates that a student measures in her own gym class
solve.work: Measuring heart rates herself is original data; the others are secondary sources.

questions.skill: Tell original from secondary data and combine sources
questions.stem: Table 1 lists 12 students in the band. Table 2 lists 15 students in the choir. No student is in both groups. The two tables are stacked into one table. How many rows does the new table have?
questions.solution: No student is on both lists, so no row is repeated. The new table has $12 + 15 = 27$ rows.

solve.work: Stacking: 12 + 15 = 27 rows (no overlaps).

questions.skill: Organize raw data into a table
questions.stem: Eight students were asked how many pets they have. The answers were 1, 0, 2, 1, 1, 3, 0 and 1. The answers are put in a frequency table. How many students have exactly 1 pet?
questions.solution: Count the answers equal to 1. The answers 1, 1, 1 and 1 appear four times, so 4 students have exactly 1 pet.
