solve.work: Answers equal to 1: 1, 1, 1, 1 (positions 1, 4, 5, 8) = 4.

questions.skill: Organize raw data into a table
questions.stem: In a data table, what should each row usually describe?
choices: One variable, such as height or age for everyone
One case, such as one student or one item
One whole data set, such as a class's results
One summary number, such as a mean or a total
questions.answer: One case, such as one student or one item
questions.solution: In a tidy table each row is one case, such as one student, and each column is one variable, such as height.

solve.answer: One case, such as one student or one item
solve.work: In a tidy table, each row is one case; columns are variables.

questions.stem: What is a duplicate record in a data set?
choices: A row with a value much larger than all the others
A cell that has nothing at all written in it
A row that repeats a record already in the data
A column with the same units as another column
questions.answer: A row that repeats a record already in the data
questions.solution: A duplicate record is the same case entered more than once. A very large value is an outlier, and an empty cell is a missing value.

solve.answer: A row that repeats a record already in the data
solve.work: A duplicate record repeats a record already in the data.

questions.stem: A list of names is Ana, Ben, Cy, Ana, Dee, Ben and Eve. Each person should be counted one time. How many different people are on the list?
questions.solution: Ana and Ben each appear twice, so those second rows are repeats. The different people are Ana, Ben, Cy, Dee and Eve: 5 people.

solve.work: Distinct: Ana, Ben, Cy, Dee, Eve = 5.

questions.stem: A data table has 60 rows. Three pairs of rows are the same record, entered twice. One row of each pair is removed. How many rows are left?
questions.solution: Each pair has one extra row, so 3 rows are removed. The table has $60 - 3 = 57$ rows left.

questions.stem: Some people skipped a question on a survey, leaving blank cells in the table. What is a good first step?
choices: Fill every blank cell with a zero so the table is full
Throw away the whole survey and collect it all again
Guess each answer by looking at the other answers
Count the blanks and note which questions they come from
questions.answer: Count the blanks and note which questions they come from
questions.solution: First find out how much is missing and where. Filling blanks with zeros or guesses can change the results, and throwing everything away wastes good data.

solve.answer: Count the blanks and note which questions they come from
solve.work: First note how many blanks and where; filling with 0 or guessing distorts the data.

questions.stem: Five students' heights in centimeters are 150, 155, (missing), 160 and 165. What is the mean of the four recorded heights?
questions.solution: Add the four recorded heights: $150 + 155 + 160 + 165 = 630$. Divide by 4: $630 \div 4 = 157.5$.

questions.stem: A survey has 40 responses. The age is blank in 6 of them. What percent of the responses include an age? Give the number only, without the percent sign.
questions.solution: The number with an age is $40 - 6 = 34$. As a percent of 40, that is $\frac{34}{40} \times 100 = 85$.

questions.skill: Find and fix errors and outliers
questions.stem: In a column of ages for a class of 10-year-olds, one entry is $-9$. What kind of problem is this entry?
choices: An impossible value, likely a typing mistake
A duplicate record that appears twice
A missing value that was left blank
A correct value that is just a bit low
questions.answer: An impossible value, likely a typing mistake
questions.solution: An age cannot be negative, so $-9$ cannot be right. It is probably a typing mistake and should be checked against the original record.

solve.answer: An impossible value, likely a typing mistake
solve.work: An age of -9 is impossible, likely a typo.

questions.skill: Find and fix errors and outliers
questions.stem: The heights in centimeters of five students are typed as 150, 148, 15, 152 and 149. The entry 15 should have been 150. What is the correct total of the five heights?

questions.skill: Find and fix errors and outliers
questions.stem: A data entry for the number of siblings is 2.5. Why is this entry an error?
choices: The number 2.5 is too large to be a real count
The number of siblings must be a whole number
Decimals are never allowed in any kind of data
Counts of siblings must always be even numbers
questions.answer: The number of siblings must be a whole number
questions.solution: A count of people must be a whole number, so 2.5 cannot be a number of siblings. Decimals are fine for measurements such as height.

solve.answer: The number of siblings must be a whole number
solve.work: Number of siblings is a count, so must be a whole number.

questions.stem: A drink's volume is listed as 2 liters, but the rest of the data set is in milliliters. How many milliliters is 2 liters?
questions.solution: There are 1000 milliliters in 1 liter, so 2 liters is $2 \times 1000 = 2000$ milliliters.

questions.stem: Some dates in a column are written like 3/4/2025 and others like 2025-03-04. What is the best way to standardize the column?
choices: Delete the dates that use the second format
Leave them alone, since computers read any format
Rewrite all of the dates in one format
Round all of the dates to the nearest year
questions.answer: Rewrite all of the dates in one format
questions.solution: Standardizing means making the same kind of entry look the same. Rewriting every date in one format keeps all of the data.

solve.answer: Rewrite all of the dates in one format
solve.work: Standardize: rewrite all dates in one format.

questions.stem: A time is recorded as 1.5 hours, but the rest of the table uses minutes. How many minutes is 1.5 hours?
questions.solution: There are 60 minutes in an hour, so 1.5 hours is $1.5 \times 60 = 90$ minutes.

solve.work: 1.5 x 60 = 90 minutes.

questions.stem: Mia wants to know the favorite sport of the 600 students at her school. She asks only the 15 members of the basketball team. What percent of the students at her school did she ask? Give the number only, without the percent sign.
questions.solution: She asked $\frac{15}{600} \times 100 = 2.5$ percent of the students. These are also not typical students, so the data may be biased.

questions.stem: Which survey question is the least biased?
choices: Don't you agree that teens sleep far too little?
Isn't it terrible that students get so little sleep?
Do you get enough sleep like all smart students do?
How many hours did you sleep last night?
questions.answer: How many hours did you sleep last night?
questions.solution: A fair question asks for a fact in neutral words. The other three push the person toward a particular answer.

solve.answer: How many hours did you sleep last night?
solve.work: B asks a neutral factual question; the others are leading.

questions.stem: Why should a data set record where its data came from?
choices: So others can check how reliable it is
So the data set looks longer and more official
Because data with a source is always correct
So that nobody else is allowed to use the data
questions.answer: So others can check how reliable it is
questions.solution: Knowing the source lets readers judge how much to trust the data and find it again. A named source does not make the data correct.

solve.answer: So others can check how reliable it is
solve.work: Recording the source lets others judge reliability.

questions.stem: A data set was collected in 2018. A student uses it in 2026. How many years old is the data?
questions.solution: The data is $2026 - 2018 = 8$ years old, which she should mention as a limitation if things may have changed.

questions.skill: Find and fix errors and outliers
questions.stem: The ages, in years, of 6 members of a school club are recorded as 15, 16, 16, 17, 160 and 16. The 160 is a typing mistake for 16. What is the mean age of the club members after the mistake is corrected?
questions.solution: Correct the list to 15, 16, 16, 17, 16, 16. The sum is $15 + 16 + 16 + 17 + 16 + 16 = 96$. The mean is $96 \div 6 = 16$ years.

questions.stem: Six students were asked how many hours they slept last night. Four answers were given: 8, 7, 9 and 6. The other two students gave no answer. What is the mean number of hours, using only the answers that were given?
questions.solution: A missing answer is not a zero and is not counted. Add the four answers: $8 + 7 + 9 + 6 = 30$. Divide by 4, the number of answers: $30 \div 4 = 7.5$ hours.

solve.work: Given answers 8, 7, 9, 6: sum 30, count 4, mean 30/4 = 7.5.

questions.stem: A store's order table has two rows with the same customer name, Sam Lee, and the same date. The rows have different order numbers and different items. What should the analyst do with these two rows?
choices: Delete one row, because the customer name is repeated
Combine them into one row and keep only the first item
Keep both rows, because they are two different orders
Delete both rows, because they conflict with each other
questions.answer: Keep both rows, because they are two different orders
questions.solution: A duplicate is a row that repeats the same record. These rows have different order numbers and items, so they record two real orders by one customer. Removing either would lose real data.

solve.answer: Keep both rows, because they are two different orders
solve.work: Different order numbers and different items mean these are two distinct orders, not duplicates. Keep both.

questions.stem: A weather data set is in degrees Celsius, but one temperature is recorded as 68 degrees Fahrenheit. Use $C = \frac{5}{9}(F - 32)$ to convert it. What is the temperature in degrees Celsius?
questions.solution: Substitute $F = 68$: $C = \frac{5}{9}(68 - 32) = \frac{5}{9} \times 36 = 20$ degrees Celsius.

questions.skill: Tell original from secondary data and combine sources
questions.stem: Two lists of students are combined into one table, and each student should appear only once. List A has 24 students and list B has 27 students. Five students are on both lists. How many rows will the combined table have?
questions.solution: Adding $24 + 27 = 51$ counts the five students who are on both lists twice. Take away the extra copies: $51 - 5 = 46$ rows.

solve.work: Union of the lists: 24 + 27 - 5 = 46 distinct students, so 46 rows.

questions.stem: A researcher wants to know how many hours students typically spend on homework. She posts a survey link on a website where students ask for help with their homework. What is the main problem with the data?
choices: A survey posted on a website always has a sample that is too small to use
Students may type their answers with spelling mistakes that cannot be fixed
Hours of homework are too hard to measure, so no survey can find them
Students on that website probably do more homework than typical students
questions.answer: Students on that website probably do more homework than typical students
questions.solution: Only students who already look for homework help will see the link, and they may do more homework than other students. The sample is not typical of all students, so the data are biased.

solve.answer: Students on that website probably do more homework than typical students
solve.work: Posting on a homework-help site gives a self-selected sample of students engaged with homework (likely spending more time than typical), so estimates are biased. Other options are false generalizations or irrelevant.

questions.skill: Choose a method to generate original data
questions.stem: A student wants to find out whether a new plant food makes bean plants grow taller. Which plan generates the best original data?
choices: Grow two similar groups of plants, feed one group only, and measure them all
Ask the people shopping at a garden store whether they like the plant food
Measure only the tallest bean plants in a friend's garden and report them
Give plant food to all of the bean plants and measure them one time only
questions.answer: Grow two similar groups of plants, feed one group only, and measure them all
questions.solution: To see an effect, you need a comparison group. One group gets the plant food and the other does not, and everything else is kept the same. The other plans ask opinions, pick only some plants, or have nothing to compare with.

solve.answer: Grow two similar groups of plants, feed one group only, and measure them all
solve.work: A controlled comparison: two similar groups, one receives plant food (treatment), one does not (control), measure all. Others lack a control or measure opinions/biased subsets.

questions.skill: Find and fix errors and outliers
questions.stem: A data set has $Q_1 = 20$ and $Q_3 = 30$. The $1.5 \times \text{IQR}$ rule marks a value as an outlier if it is above $Q_3 + 1.5 \times \text{IQR}$ or below $Q_1 - 1.5 \times \text{IQR}$. What is the upper fence, $Q_3 + 1.5 \times \text{IQR}$?
questions.solution: The IQR is $30 - 20 = 10$. Then $1.5 \times 10 = 15$, so the upper fence is $30 + 15 = 45$. A value above 45 would be flagged.

questions.stem: A student uses a published data set in a project. What should the student record about its source?
choices: Only the number of rows and the number of columns in the data table
Who published the data, where it was found, and when it was collected
Only the name of the computer program used to open the data file
Nothing, because published data never needs a source to be listed
questions.answer: Who published the data, where it was found, and when it was collected
questions.solution: A reader needs to know where secondary data came from and when, to judge whether to trust them. Recording who published the data, where it was found and its date lets others check it.

solve.answer: Who published the data, where it was found, and when it was collected
solve.work: Proper source documentation: who published it, where it was found, when it was collected.

questions.stem: A column called State has these entries for the same state: NC, N.C., North Carolina and nc. A student wants to count how many records there are for the state. What should be done first?
choices: Count each different spelling as if it were a separate state
Delete all the rows except those that say exactly NC
Recode every entry to one consistent label, such as NC
Delete the whole State column from the data set
questions.answer: Recode every entry to one consistent label, such as NC
questions.solution: The four entries mean the same thing, but a computer sees four different labels. Recoding them to one label keeps all the records and lets them be counted together.

solve.answer: Recode every entry to one consistent label, such as NC
solve.work: Inconsistent labels for the same category must be standardized (recoded) to one label before counting.

questions.skill: Choose a method to generate original data
questions.stem: Which question can be answered best by observing what happens, rather than by giving a survey?
choices: How do students feel about the school dress code?
How many cars are parked in the school lot at 8 a.m.?
How many hours of sleep do students say they get?
What do parents think of the school lunch menu?
questions.answer: How many cars are parked in the school lot at 8 a.m.?
questions.solution: Counting cars is something that can be seen directly. The other three questions are about opinions or self-reports, which need people to be asked.

solve.answer: How many cars are parked in the school lot at 8 a.m.?
solve.work: Counting parked cars is an observation; the others ask opinions or self-reports.

questions.skill: Choose a method to generate original data
questions.stem: An experiment compares 3 brands of battery. Each brand is tested in 5 flashlights, and each flashlight is tested at 2 temperatures. How many measurements are collected?
questions.solution: Each of the $3 \times 5 = 15$ flashlights is tested at 2 temperatures, so there are $15 \times 2 = 30$ measurements.

solve.work: 3 brands x 5 flashlights x 2 temperatures = 30 measurements.

questions.skill: Choose a method to generate original data
questions.stem: Why does an experiment include a control group?
choices: To make sure that every subject receives the treatment
To make the group that gets the treatment larger
To have a group that gets no treatment to compare with
To remove all of the chance variation from the data
questions.answer: To have a group that gets no treatment to compare with
questions.solution: The control group does not receive the treatment. Comparing it with the treatment group shows what the treatment did.

solve.answer: To have a group that gets no treatment to compare with
solve.work: A control group (no treatment or placebo) gives a baseline for comparison.

questions.skill: Tell original from secondary data and combine sources
questions.stem: A student has two data sets of city temperatures. One lists each day's high temperature and the other lists each day's average temperature. What should she do before combining them?
choices: Average the two columns together to make one column of temperatures
Combine them right away because both are columns of temperatures
Keep only the data set that has more rows and drop the other
Check that they measure the same thing; a high is not an average
questions.answer: Check that they measure the same thing; a high is not an average
questions.solution: A daily high and a daily average are different variables. Combining them as if they were the same would mix up two different measurements.

solve.answer: Check that they measure the same thing; a high is not an average
solve.work: Daily highs and daily averages measure different things; check before combining.

questions.skill: Tell original from secondary data and combine sources
questions.stem: A club roster has 90 students and a sign-in sheet has 70 students. Of these, 55 students are on both. The two lists are merged so that each student has one row. How many rows does the merged table have?
questions.solution: Adding the lists counts the 55 students twice. The number of different students is $90 + 70 - 55 = 105$.

questions.skill: Organize raw data into a table
questions.stem: A frequency table of 40 responses has categories A, B, C and D. A has 12 responses, B has 15 and C has 9. How many responses are in category D?
questions.solution: The categories add up to 40. D has $40 - 12 - 15 - 9 = 4$ responses.

questions.skill: Organize raw data into a table
questions.stem: A table has one row per student and the columns Name, Test 1, Test 2 and Test 3. It is rewritten with one row for each score, using the columns Name, Test and Score. There are 5 students and every score is present. How many rows does the new table have?
questions.solution: Each student has 3 scores, and each score gets its own row, so the new table has $5 \times 3 = 15$ rows.

solve.work: Long format: 5 students x 3 tests = 15 rows.

questions.stem: Which is the best evidence that two rows are duplicates of the same record?
choices: They match in the unique ID and in every other column
They have the same first name in the name column
They are next to each other in the table
They show the same grade level for each person
questions.answer: They match in the unique ID and in every other column
questions.solution: A matching unique ID plus matching values everywhere else shows the same record was entered twice. Matching names or grades alone can be different people.

solve.answer: They match in the unique ID and in every other column
solve.work: Matching unique ID and every column is the best evidence of a duplicate.

questions.stem: A data file has 300 rows. Of these, 24 are duplicates and are removed, and 6 more rows are removed because of missing values. What percent of the original 300 rows are left? Give the number only, without the percent sign.
questions.solution: The rows left are $300 - 24 - 6 = 270$. As a percent of 300, that is $\frac{270}{300} \times 100 = 90$.

questions.stem: An analyst removes every row that has a missing value. What is a possible drawback?
choices: The remaining data can no longer be used for averages
Fewer rows remain, and they may differ from those removed
New duplicate rows are created in the remaining data
The units of the remaining values are changed unexpectedly
questions.answer: Fewer rows remain, and they may differ from those removed
questions.solution: Deleting rows shrinks the data, and the people with missing values may be different from those who answered. That can make the rest of the data unrepresentative.

solve.answer: Fewer rows remain, and they may differ from those removed
solve.work: Dropping rows reduces the sample, and removed rows may differ systematically (bias).

questions.stem: A missing value is replaced with the mean of the five recorded values 10, 12, 14, 18 and 16. What value is filled in?
questions.solution: The recorded values add up to 70. The mean is $70 \div 5 = 14$, so 14 is filled in.

questions.stem: In a survey, many people with high incomes refuse to give their income. What is the effect on the mean of the incomes that were given?
choices: The mean will probably be higher than the true mean
The mean will be exactly the true mean of everyone
The mean will probably be lower than the true mean
The mean cannot be found, since values are missing
questions.answer: The mean will probably be lower than the true mean
questions.solution: The high incomes are the ones left out, so the incomes that remain are lower on average. The mean of the given incomes will probably be too low.

solve.answer: The mean will probably be lower than the true mean
solve.work: High incomes missing, so the mean of given incomes is probably lower than the true mean.

questions.skill: Find and fix errors and outliers
questions.stem: Four scores out of 100 are recorded as 88, 92, 105 and 90. The score 105 is impossible, so it is removed. What is the mean of the three remaining scores?
questions.solution: The remaining scores add up to $88 + 92 + 90 = 270$. The mean is $270 \div 3 = 90$.

questions.skill: Find and fix errors and outliers
questions.stem: The daily temperatures for a city in degrees Celsius are recorded as 21, 23, 22, 230 and 24. What is the best thing to do about the 230?
choices: Delete the whole column of temperatures from the table
Change all of the temperatures to 230 to match it
Leave it alone, since no value may ever be changed
Check the original record and fix 230 if it was a typo
questions.answer: Check the original record and fix 230 if it was a typo
questions.solution: A temperature of 230 degrees Celsius is not possible for a city, so it is probably a typing mistake. The best step is to check the original record and fix it if it was a mistake.

solve.answer: Check the original record and fix 230 if it was a typo
solve.work: 230 is likely a typo for 23; check the original record and fix.

questions.skill: Find and fix errors and outliers
questions.stem: A data set has $Q_1 = 30$ and $Q_3 = 46$. A value is a possible outlier if it is below $Q_1 - 1.5 \times \text{IQR}$. What is the lowest value that is not flagged as an outlier by this rule?
questions.solution: The IQR is $46 - 30 = 16$, and $1.5 \times 16 = 24$. The lower limit is $30 - 24 = 6$. Values below 6 are flagged, so 6 itself is not flagged.

solve.work: IQR = 46 - 30 = 16; lower fence = 30 - 1.5 x 16 = 30 - 24 = 6. Values below 6 are flagged, so 6 itself is the lowest value not flagged.

questions.skill: Find and fix errors and outliers
questions.stem: A data set of player heights includes one very tall player of 231 centimeters, who was measured correctly. What should the analyst do with this value?
choices: Keep it, since it is real, and note that it is unusual
Delete it, because every outlier must be removed
Change it to the mean so it matches the others
Keep it only if it makes the mean look larger
questions.answer: Keep it, since it is real, and note that it is unusual
questions.solution: An outlier that is a real, correct measurement belongs in the data. The analyst should keep it and mention that it is unusual.

solve.answer: Keep it, since it is real, and note that it is unusual
solve.work: A real, correctly measured extreme value should be kept and noted.

questions.stem: A weight is recorded as 55 pounds. The rest of the data set is in kilograms. Use 1 kilogram = 2.2 pounds. What is the weight in kilograms?
questions.solution: Divide the pounds by 2.2: $55 \div 2.2 = 25$ kilograms.

questions.stem: A column has these 7 entries: yes, Yes, Y, no, N, NO and No. All entries are recoded into just two labels, Yes and No. How many entries become Yes?
questions.solution: The entries yes, Yes and Y all mean Yes. The other four entries mean No. So 3 entries become Yes.

solve.work: Yes group: yes, Yes, Y = 3; No group: no, N, NO, No = 4.

questions.stem: A column of heights has entries such as 66 inches, 170 cm and 1.65 m. What is the best way to prepare the column for analysis?
choices: Sort the entries in alphabetical order and then leave them
Convert every height to the same unit, such as centimeters
Delete the entries that have units written next to them
Keep only the first digit of every one of the entries
questions.answer: Convert every height to the same unit, such as centimeters
questions.solution: Heights in different units cannot be compared as they are. Converting them all to one unit lets the values be compared and averaged.

solve.answer: Convert every height to the same unit, such as centimeters
solve.work: Convert all heights to one unit, e.g. centimeters.

questions.stem: A data set of grades was collected only from students who volunteered to share their grades. Why might these grades not represent all students?
choices: Grades can only be collected from students who are absent
Students who volunteer always report their grades wrongly
The volunteers choose themselves, so they are not typical
Grades do not describe anything about students at school
questions.answer: The volunteers choose themselves, so they are not typical
questions.solution: Volunteers choose themselves, so they may differ from the other students. The data may not represent all students.

solve.answer: The volunteers choose themselves, so they are not typical
solve.work: Volunteers self-select (e.g. those with good grades), so they may not be typical.

questions.stem: A thermometer reads 2 degrees too high in every record. The mean of the recorded temperatures is 21.4 degrees. What is the true mean temperature?
questions.solution: Every record is 2 degrees too high, so the mean is also 2 degrees too high. The true mean is $21.4 - 2 = 19.4$ degrees.

solve.work: Every reading 2 too high: true mean = 21.4 - 2 = 19.4.

questions.stem: A student finds a bar chart on a website that does not say who made it or where its data came from. What should she do before using it?
choices: Use it, since a chart on a website must be right
Use it, but remove the title so nobody can ask about it
Use the chart only if it looks professional and neat
Look for the original source before using the chart
questions.answer: Look for the original source before using the chart
questions.solution: Without a source she cannot tell how reliable the data are. She should find the original source first, and not use the chart if she cannot.

solve.answer: Look for the original source before using the chart
solve.work: Find the original source to judge reliability before use.

questions.stem: A data set about home prices was collected in 2008. A student uses it to describe today's home prices. What is the main limitation?
choices: The data are old and may not show today's prices
The data are too accurate to be of any use
Home prices never change from one year to another
Data from 2008 can never be used for anything
questions.answer: The data are old and may not show today's prices
questions.solution: Home prices change over time, so data from 2008 may not describe today's prices. It can still be useful for describing 2008.

solve.answer: The data are old and may not show today's prices
solve.work: Data from 2008 may not reflect today's prices.

questions.stem: A raw data file has 500 rows. Forty of the rows are exact repeats of other rows and are removed. Then 5 percent of the remaining rows are removed because they have a missing value. How many rows are left?
questions.solution: After the repeats are removed, $500 - 40 = 460$ rows remain. Five percent of 460 is $0.05 \times 460 = 23$. Removing those gives $460 - 23 = 437$ rows.

questions.stem: The mean of the 10 test scores in a table is 70. Two of the 10 scores are 0, typed in for students who were absent, so those two scores are really missing. What is the mean of the 8 real scores?
questions.solution: The 10 scores add up to $10 \times 70 = 700$. The two zeros add nothing, so the 8 real scores also add up to 700. Their mean is $700 \div 8 = 87.5$.

solve.work: Sum of 10 scores = 10 * 70 = 700. The two zeros add 0, so the 8 real scores sum to 700. Mean = 700/8 = 87.5.

questions.skill: Find and fix errors and outliers
questions.stem: Five quiz scores were typed in as 72, 80, 90, 85 and 68. Checking the paper quizzes shows that the 90 should have been 50. By how many points does the mean decrease when the typing error is corrected?
questions.solution: Correcting the error lowers the total by $90 - 50 = 40$ points. The mean is a total divided by 5, so it falls by $40 \div 5 = 8$ points. Check: the means are $395 \div 5 = 79$ and $355 \div 5 = 71$.

solve.work: Correcting 90 to 50 lowers the sum by 40; mean drops by 40/5 = 8. (Means: 395/5 = 79 to 355/5 = 71.)

questions.stem: A table lists the lengths of three trails in kilometers: 8, 12.8 and 4.8. The rest of the data set uses miles, so these lengths must be converted. Use 1 mile = 1.6 kilometers. What is the total length of the three trails in miles?
questions.solution: The total in kilometers is $8 + 12.8 + 4.8 = 25.6$. Each 1.6 kilometers is 1 mile, so divide by 1.6: $25.6 \div 1.6 = 16$ miles.

questions.skill: Tell original from secondary data and combine sources
questions.stem: Table 1 lists each student's student ID, name and grade. Table 2 lists each student's student ID, name and club. The rows are not in the same order, and two different students are both named Jamie Cruz. Which column should be used to match the rows of the two tables?
choices: Name, because both tables include it
First name, because it is short and easy to match
Row number, because both tables list the students
Student ID, because no two students share one
questions.answer: Student ID, because no two students share one
questions.solution: To match rows you need a column that identifies one student and no other. Names can repeat, as the two students called Jamie Cruz show. The rows are in different orders, so row numbers would match the wrong students. A student ID is different for each student.

solve.answer: Student ID, because no two students share one
solve.work: Names are not unique (two Jamie Cruz), rows are in different orders, so match on the unique key, Student ID.

questions.stem: A researcher phones households at 2 p.m. on weekdays to ask about weekly commute time. Which best describes the main source of bias?
choices: People who work during the day are not home, so they are left out
The question may be worded so that it leads people toward one answer
People who volunteer to answer are different from those who do not
People may not remember the details of a commute from long ago
questions.answer: People who work during the day are not home, so they are left out
questions.solution: Many people who commute are at work at 2 p.m. on a weekday, so they will not answer the phone. The sample leaves out the very group being studied. This is undercoverage.

solve.answer: People who work during the day are not home, so they are left out
solve.work: Calling at 2 p.m. on weekdays misses people at work, who are exactly the commuters; undercoverage/nonresponse of daytime workers is the main bias.

questions.stem: A survey asks: "Do you eat healthy food and exercise every day?" Students may answer yes or no. Why is it hard to use the answers?
choices: The question has too many possible answers to be counted up
It asks about two things at once, so a "no" could mean either
Only students who exercise are able to see and answer the question
Answers of yes and no cannot be recorded in a data table
questions.answer: It asks about two things at once, so a "no" could mean either
questions.solution: A student who eats healthy food but does not exercise cannot answer honestly. A "no" might mean no to eating, no to exercise, or both. A question should ask about one thing at a time.

solve.answer: It asks about two things at once, so a "no" could mean either
solve.work: Double-barreled question: asks about healthy eating and daily exercise together, so a no is ambiguous.

questions.skill: Choose a method to generate original data
questions.stem: A group needs 120 completed surveys to analyze. From earlier work, only 40 percent of the people who are sent a survey send it back completed. How many surveys should the group send so that they expect 120 back?
questions.solution: If 40 percent of the surveys sent are returned, then $0.4 \times (\text{number sent}) = 120$. So the number sent is $120 \div 0.4 = 300$. Check: 40 percent of 300 is 120.

solve.work: Expected returns = 0.4 * n = 120, so n = 120 / 0.4 = 300.

questions.skill: Find and fix errors and outliers
questions.stem: A data set has $Q_1 = 40$ and $Q_3 = 52$. An analyst flags a value as a possible outlier if it is more than $1.5 \times \text{IQR}$ below $Q_1$ or more than $1.5 \times \text{IQR}$ above $Q_3$. Which value would be flagged?
questions.solution: The IQR is $52 - 40 = 12$, and $1.5 \times 12 = 18$. The lower fence is $40 - 18 = 22$ and the upper fence is $52 + 18 = 70$. A value is flagged only if it is below 22 or above 70. Of the four, only 73 is above 70; 22 is exactly on the lower fence and is not more than 18 below $Q_1$.

solve.work: IQR = 52 - 40 = 12; 1.5 * IQR = 18. Lower fence 40 - 18 = 22, upper fence 52 + 18 = 70. 22 is exactly 18 below (not MORE than), not flagged; 25 and 68 inside; 73 > 70 flagged.

questions.skill: Cleaning and combining data from different sources
questions.stem: A student combines the heights of students from two sources into one data set. One source recorded heights in meters, so its rows read 1.62, 1.58 and 1.71. The other recorded heights in centimeters, so its rows read 165, 172 and 159. What should she do before she analyzes the data?
choices: Delete the rows in meters, since they are too small to be heights
Leave the rows as they are, because the mean will balance the two units
Multiply every height by 100 so that all the numbers are larger
Put all the heights in the same unit before combining them
questions.answer: Put all the heights in the same unit before combining them
questions.solution: A data set must use one unit for one variable. The rows in meters can be turned into centimeters (1.62 m = 162 cm) or all rows can be turned into meters. Deleting the rows throws away good data, leaving the mixed units makes any mean meaningless, and multiplying everything by 100 would make the centimeter rows 100 times too large.

solve.answer: Put all the heights in the same unit before combining them
solve.work: Mixed units must be converted to one unit (e.g. 1.62 m = 162 cm) before combining. Leaving them, deleting valid rows, or multiplying all by 100 (makes cm values wrong) are incorrect.

questions.skill: Choose a method to generate original data
questions.stem: A researcher needs 63 usable surveys. Of the surveys that people complete, 90 percent are usable, and 70 percent of the people who are sent a survey complete it. How many surveys should she send?
questions.solution: Of every survey sent, $0.7 \times 0.9 = 0.63$ is expected to be completed and usable. To get 63 usable surveys she should send $63 \div 0.63 = 100$ surveys.

solve.work: Completed needed = 63/0.9 = 70; sent = 70/0.7 = 100.

questions.skill: Choose a method to generate original data
questions.stem: A teacher randomly assigns 40 students to two groups to test a new study method. Why is the assignment made at random?
choices: It makes sure every student gets the treatment
It makes the groups alike on average before treatment
It lets the teacher put the best students in one group
It guarantees the two groups end up with equal scores
questions.answer: It makes the groups alike on average before treatment
questions.solution: Random assignment makes the groups similar on average before the treatment starts, so a difference afterward is more likely due to the treatment. It does not guarantee equal scores.

solve.answer: It makes the groups alike on average before treatment
solve.work: Random assignment makes the groups alike on average before treatment; it does not guarantee equal scores.

questions.skill: Tell original from secondary data and combine sources
questions.stem: Table A lists each student's ID and grade. Table B lists each student's ID and club, but some students in table A are not in table B. The tables are joined by ID, keeping every student from table A. What will the club column show for a student who is not in table B?
choices: The student's grade, copied into the club cell
Nothing, since the student is removed from the table
An empty cell, meaning the club is missing
A second copy of the whole row for that student
questions.answer: An empty cell, meaning the club is missing
questions.solution: The join keeps every student of table A. A student with no row in table B has no club recorded, so that cell is empty, a missing value.

solve.answer: An empty cell, meaning the club is missing
solve.work: Left join keeping all of table A: unmatched club cells are empty (missing).

questions.skill: Tell original from secondary data and combine sources
questions.stem: A town's population was 4200 in a census. A later estimate from another source says 4410. By what percent did the estimate grow over the census figure? Give the number only, without the percent sign.
questions.solution: The growth is $4410 - 4200 = 210$. As a percent of 4200: $\frac{210}{4200} \times 100 = 5$.

questions.skill: Tell original from secondary data and combine sources
questions.stem: Two secondary data sets are about air quality in a city. One gives particle levels in micrograms per cubic meter and the other gives an index from 0 to 500. Can the two columns be combined directly?
choices: Yes, since both are about the air quality of a city
Yes, by averaging the two numbers for each day
No, because secondary data sets can never be combined
No, because they use different scales for the measure
questions.answer: No, because they use different scales for the measure
questions.solution: The two columns measure air quality on different scales, so a value in one is not comparable with a value in the other. They would need to be converted to a common scale first.

solve.answer: No, because they use different scales for the measure
solve.work: Different scales (concentration vs an index) cannot be combined directly.

questions.skill: Organize raw data into a table
questions.stem: A raw file stores each survey answer on its own line, with the student ID, the question number and the answer. Thirty students were each asked 8 questions, and 12 of the answers are missing entirely, with no line for them. How many lines are in the file?
questions.solution: If every answer were present there would be $30 \times 8 = 240$ lines. Twelve have no line, so the file has $240 - 12 = 228$ lines.

questions.skill: Organize raw data into a table
questions.stem: A column called Name and Grade holds entries such as Jo, 9. Why is it better to split it into a Name column and a Grade column?
choices: Each column then holds one variable and can be sorted
Splitting a column always makes the file smaller
Each student's name will then appear one single time
The table will then have fewer rows than students
questions.answer: Each column then holds one variable and can be sorted
questions.solution: Each column should hold one variable. Then the grades can be sorted, counted and averaged on their own.

solve.answer: Each column then holds one variable and can be sorted
solve.work: One variable per column lets each be sorted and analyzed.

questions.stem: A file has 800 rows. Exact duplicates make up 5 percent of the rows and are removed. Then 10 percent of the rows that are left are removed for missing values. What percent of the original 800 rows remain? Give the number only, without the percent sign.
questions.solution: After removing 5 percent, 95 percent remain: 760 rows. Removing 10 percent of those leaves 90 percent of them: $0.95 \times 0.9 = 0.855$, which is 85.5 percent of the original rows.

solve.work: After duplicates: 800 x 0.95 = 760; after missing: 760 x 0.9 = 684; 684/800 = 85.5%.

questions.stem: A table of clinic visits has three rows for the same patient. Each row has a different date and a different reason for the visit. An analyst calls two of them duplicates and deletes them. What is wrong with this?
choices: Nothing; any patient with several rows has duplicates
The rows differ, so they are three separate visits
Only the row with the latest date should have been deleted
The analyst should have deleted all three of the rows
questions.answer: The rows differ, so they are three separate visits
questions.solution: Duplicates are the same record entered more than once. Rows with different dates and reasons are different visits and should all be kept.

solve.answer: The rows differ, so they are three separate visits
solve.work: Different dates and reasons mean three separate visits, not duplicates.

questions.stem: A column has 20 values, but 4 are missing. The 16 recorded values add up to 96. Each missing value is filled in with the mean of the 16 recorded values. What is the sum of all 20 values?
questions.solution: The mean of the recorded values is $96 \div 16 = 6$. The 4 filled-in values are 6 each, so the sum is $96 + 4 \times 6 = 120$.

questions.stem: A column for the number of absences is left blank for students who had no absences. An analyst treats the blanks as missing and ignores them. What is the effect on the mean number of absences?
choices: The mean will be too low, because the blanks add zeros
The mean will be right, because blanks carry no information
The mean will be too high, because the zeros are left out
The mean cannot be found, because the column has blanks
questions.answer: The mean will be too high, because the zeros are left out
questions.solution: The blanks really mean zero absences. Ignoring them removes the smallest values, so the mean of the remaining values is too high.

solve.answer: The mean will be too high, because the zeros are left out
solve.work: Blanks are really zeros; ignoring them leaves out zeros, so the mean is too high.

questions.skill: Find and fix errors and outliers
questions.stem: The mean of six recorded weights is 62 kilograms. One weight was typed as 94 but is really 49. What is the correct mean of the six weights, in kilograms?
questions.solution: The typed total is $62 \times 6 = 372$. Correcting 94 to 49 lowers it by 45, to 327. The correct mean is $327 \div 6 = 54.5$.

questions.skill: Find and fix errors and outliers
questions.stem: In a data set $Q_1 = 30$ and $Q_3 = 40$. A value is a suspected outlier if it is more than $1.5 \times \text{IQR}$ below $Q_1$ or above $Q_3$. Which of these values is a suspected outlier?
questions.solution: The IQR is $40 - 30 = 10$, and $1.5 \times 10 = 15$. The limits are $30 - 15 = 15$ and $40 + 15 = 55$. Only 56 is above 55. The values 54, 16 and 45 are all inside the limits.

solve.work: IQR = 10; fences 30 - 15 = 15 and 40 + 15 = 55. 45, 16 and 54 are inside; 56 > 55 is a suspected outlier.

questions.skill: Find and fix errors and outliers
questions.stem: A set of 7 values has a mean of 20. One value, 62, is an outlier caused by an instrument error and is removed. What is the mean of the remaining 6 values?
questions.solution: The total of the 7 values is $20 \times 7 = 140$. Without 62 the total is 78, and the mean of 6 values is $78 \div 6 = 13$.

questions.stem: The masses of four packages are listed in grams as 450, 1200, 850 and 500. Another table lists masses in kilograms, so these must be converted before the tables are combined. What is the total mass of the four packages, in kilograms?
questions.solution: The total in grams is $450 + 1200 + 850 + 500 = 3000$. There are 1000 grams in a kilogram, so the total is 3 kilograms.

questions.stem: A column of incomes has the entries 45K, 52000 dollars and 38000. What is the best way to standardize the column?
choices: Convert them all to plain numbers, such as 45000
Remove the letters and keep only 45 for the first entry
Delete the entry 45K because it contains a letter
Turn all three entries into text and leave them alone
questions.answer: Convert them all to plain numbers, such as 45000
questions.solution: The entry 45K means 45 thousand, so it should become 45000. Each entry should be a plain number of dollars so they can be compared.

solve.answer: Convert them all to plain numbers, such as 45000
solve.work: Convert all to plain numbers in dollars (45K = 45000).

questions.stem: A survey asks people, "How many times did you exercise during the past year?" What is the main problem with the answers?
choices: People who exercise a lot will refuse to answer it
People cannot recall exactly, so their answers may be off
A question about the past year is not allowed in surveys
Every person asked will give exactly the same answer
questions.answer: People cannot recall exactly, so their answers may be off
questions.solution: It is hard to remember a whole year of exercise accurately, so answers may be rough guesses. This is called recall bias.

solve.answer: People cannot recall exactly, so their answers may be off
solve.work: Recall over a whole year is inexact: recall (response) error.

questions.stem: A researcher studies only the businesses that are still open today to learn what makes a business succeed. What is the main problem with this data?
choices: Businesses that are open are always the largest ones
Too many businesses are included, so it takes too long
Closed businesses are left out, so failures are missing
Open businesses refuse to answer questions about success
questions.answer: Closed businesses are left out, so failures are missing
questions.solution: Businesses that failed are not in the data, so the researcher sees only the survivors. This can make the reasons for success look stronger than they are.

solve.answer: Closed businesses are left out, so failures are missing
solve.work: Studying only survivors leaves out failures: survivorship bias.

questions.stem: A student uses emergency room visits from one hospital during one summer to describe visits at all hospitals in the state during the whole year. What is the biggest limitation?
choices: Counts of visits can never be added up across hospitals
The data should have come from winter rather than summer
The student should not have used any real hospital data
The data come from one place and one season only
questions.answer: The data come from one place and one season only
questions.solution: Visits at one hospital in one summer may differ from visits in other places and other seasons, so the data may not describe the whole state all year.

solve.answer: The data come from one place and one season only
solve.work: One hospital and one season cannot represent all hospitals for the year.

questions.stem: A town's population is 60 percent women. A data set of 200 people from the town has 150 women. How many more women are in the data set than would be expected if it matched the town?
questions.solution: If the data matched the town, there would be $0.6 \times 200 = 120$ women. The data set has 150, which is $150 - 120 = 30$ more, so it does not match the town.

questions.stem: Which note about limitations is the most useful to the readers of a report?
choices: Only students with email were reached, so others are left out
The survey was fairly long, and it took a lot of time to write
The data are stored on a computer in one spreadsheet file
Many students enjoyed being asked questions in the survey
questions.answer: Only students with email were reached, so others are left out
questions.solution: A limitation says how the data may not represent the group of interest. Leaving out students without email affects what the results mean. The other notes do not.

solve.answer: Only students with email were reached, so others are left out
solve.work: The useful limitation states who was left out (no email, undercoverage).

questions.stem: Two sources report different numbers for the same quantity. What is the best thing to do?
choices: Average the two numbers and report just the average
Check how each source defined and collected the data
Choose the larger number, since it is the bigger one
Choose the number that agrees with the hypothesis best
questions.answer: Check how each source defined and collected the data
questions.solution: Different definitions or collection methods can explain different numbers. Checking them tells which number fits the question, and the choice should be explained in the report.

solve.answer: Check how each source defined and collected the data
solve.work: Check each source's definitions and methods before choosing or reconciling.

questions.stem: A note on a data set says that 15 percent of its 2400 rows came from one county that holds only 5 percent of the state's people. How many more rows come from that county than a proportional share (5 percent of 2400) would give?
questions.solution: The county has $0.15 \times 2400 = 360$ rows. A proportional share is $0.05 \times 2400 = 120$ rows. It has $360 - 120 = 240$ more rows, so it is over-represented, which is a limitation.

solve.work: County rows 0.15 x 2400 = 360; proportional 0.05 x 2400 = 120; difference 240.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes informed consent in a research study?
choices: A person agrees to take part, and the purpose is explained only after all the data have been collected.
A person is told the study is required for everyone, so there is no chance to say no and no explanation.
A person agrees to take part after being told what the study is for, what they will do and what the risks are.
A person signs a form whose pages are all blank, trusting the researcher to fill in the details later.
questions.answer: A person agrees to take part after being told what the study is for, what they will do and what the risks are.
questions.solution: Informed consent means a person freely agrees after being told the purpose, what taking part involves and the risks. Agreeing before knowing these things, or having no choice, is not informed consent.

solve.answer: A person agrees to take part after being told what the study is for, what they will do and what the risks are.
solve.work: Informed consent means agreeing after being told the purpose, the tasks and the risks. A explains only afterwards, B is a blank form, D gives no choice and no explanation. Only C fits.

questions.stem: Partway through a survey, a participant says they want to stop. What should the researcher do?
choices: Ask the participant to finish, since they already agreed to take part.
Let the participant stop, but tell them they will be blocked from other studies.
Let the participant stop, with no penalty for leaving.
Tell the participant they must give a reason that the researcher accepts.
questions.answer: Let the participant stop, with no penalty for leaving.
questions.solution: Participants may leave a study at any time, for any reason, without penalty. The researcher should not pressure them, punish them or make them justify leaving.

solve.answer: Let the participant stop, with no penalty for leaving.
solve.work: Participants have the right to withdraw at any time without penalty or reason. A.

questions.stem: A school wants to know what all of its students think about lunch. Which plan gives every student a fair chance of being asked?
choices: Ask only the students who are first in line at the cafeteria.
Choose students at random from a list of every student in the school.
Ask only the students who are members of the student council.
Ask only the students who stop to answer in the hallway.
questions.answer: Choose students at random from a list of every student in the school.
questions.solution: A random choice from a list of all students gives each student the same chance. The other plans reach only certain groups of students and leave the rest out.

solve.answer: Choose students at random from a list of every student in the school.
solve.work: Only a random selection from a complete list of students gives every student an equal chance. A, B, C are convenience/restricted samples. D.

questions.stem: A club has 60 members: 36 are juniors and 24 are seniors. A committee of 10 members is to reflect the club, with the same share of juniors as the club has. How many juniors should be on the committee?
questions.solution: Juniors are $\frac{36}{60} = \frac{3}{5}$ of the club. $\frac{3}{5}$ of 10 members is 6, so 6 juniors should be on the committee.

solve.work: Juniors share = 36/60 = 0.6. 0.6 x 10 = 6 juniors.

questions.stem: A survey of 100 people found that 52 of them agreed with a statement. Which report of this result is a misrepresentation?
choices: "52 of the 100 people surveyed agreed with the statement."
"A little over half of the people surveyed agreed with the statement."
"52% of the 100 people asked agreed with the statement."
"Nearly everyone who was surveyed agreed with the statement."
questions.answer: "Nearly everyone who was surveyed agreed with the statement."
questions.solution: 52 out of 100 is a little over half, not nearly everyone. Saying "nearly everyone" makes the result sound much stronger than the data show.

solve.answer: "Nearly everyone who was surveyed agreed with the statement."
solve.work: 52% is a little over half. 'Nearly everyone' greatly overstates 52%. A, C, D are accurate. B.

questions.stem: A report compares two companies' customer ratings of 94 and 96 out of 100. Its bar graph starts the vertical axis at 93 instead of 0, so the second bar looks three times as tall as the first. Why is this graph misleading?
choices: It makes the two ratings look equal.
It makes a small difference look like a large one.
It makes both ratings look lower than they really are.
It makes the first company look better rated than the second.
questions.answer: It makes a small difference look like a large one.
questions.solution: The bars show only the part above 93: heights 1 and 3. The ratings differ by just 2 points out of 100, but the bars make the difference look three times over. Starting the axis at 0 would show the true size.

solve.answer: It makes a small difference look like a large one.
solve.work: Axis from 93: bars have heights 1 and 3, so a 2-point difference (about 2%) looks like a threefold difference. A.

questions.stem: A survey for a school project needs to know only each student's grade level (6, 7 or 8). Which plan for the survey form is the most ethical?
choices: Ask for name and home address too, in case they are useful later.
Ask only for grade level, because the project needs nothing more personal.
Ask for name as well, so each answer can be linked to a student.
Ask for grade level and phone number, to be able to ask follow-up questions.
questions.answer: Ask only for grade level, because the project needs nothing more personal.
questions.solution: Collect only the information the project needs. Extra personal details such as names, addresses or phone numbers add risk to the participants and no benefit to the project.

solve.answer: Ask only for grade level, because the project needs nothing more personal.
solve.work: Data minimisation: collect only what is needed, i.e. grade level only. B.

questions.stem: A researcher collects paper forms with students' answers about their sleep habits. Which is the most ethical way to store the forms?
choices: On a classroom desk where anyone can read them.
On the school bulletin board, so students can see the results.
In a locked cabinet that only the research team can open.
In a shared folder that anyone at the school can open.
questions.answer: In a locked cabinet that only the research team can open.
questions.solution: Answers should be kept private. A locked cabinet limits who can read them to the research team, while the other places let many people see them.

solve.answer: In a locked cabinet that only the research team can open.
solve.work: Confidential data should be stored securely with access limited to the research team. C.

questions.stem: A teacher wants to use her students' quiz scores in a research study. Which action respects informed consent?
choices: Use the scores of all her students, because the quizzes were already graded
Explain the study and how the scores will be used, and let each student choose whether to join
Tell the students about the study only after their scores have been collected
Explain the study only to the students who earned the highest scores
questions.answer: Explain the study and how the scores will be used, and let each student choose whether to join
questions.solution: Informed consent means people are told what the study is and how their information will be used, before it is collected, and they freely choose whether to take part. The other actions skip the explanation, give it too late, or leave out most of the students.

solve.answer: Explain the study and how the scores will be used, and let each student choose whether to join
solve.work: Informed consent means participants are told about the study and how their data are used, before use, and choose freely whether to take part. Only option C does that.

questions.stem: Halfway through a study, a volunteer says she wants to stop taking part. What should the researcher do?
choices: Let her stop, without pressuring her to continue or punishing her
Remind her that she signed the form, so she must finish the study
Let her stop only if she finds another volunteer to take her place
Let her stop, but give her a lower grade in the class
questions.answer: Let her stop, without pressuring her to continue or punishing her
questions.solution: Taking part in a study is voluntary, and a participant may withdraw at any time. The researcher may not force, pressure or penalize her for stopping.

solve.answer: Let her stop, without pressuring her to continue or punishing her
solve.work: Participants have the right to withdraw at any time without pressure or penalty. Only B respects that.

questions.stem: Which of these must a consent form tell people before they agree to join a study?
choices: What they will do and how their answers will be used
Which answers the researcher hopes that they will give
Which other people have already agreed to join the study
How much money the researcher expects to earn from it
questions.answer: What they will do and how their answers will be used
questions.solution: Informed consent means people know what they are agreeing to. They need to know what will happen to them and how their answers will be used. The researcher's hopes, who else joined, and earnings are not what a person needs to decide.

solve.answer: What they will do and how their answers will be used
solve.work: Informed consent requires telling people what they will do and how their data will be used. The other options are irrelevant or would bias the study.

questions.stem: Maya is asked to join a study. Which statement shows that her consent is voluntary?
choices: She is told that her friends will be upset if she says no.
She is told she may say no and nothing will happen to her.
She is told that her grade will drop if she says no.
She is told that she must decide before she leaves the room.
questions.answer: She is told she may say no and nothing will happen to her.
questions.solution: Voluntary means free of pressure. Being told she can say no without any penalty is the only choice with no pressure. Upsetting friends, a lower grade or a rushed decision are all pressure.

solve.answer: She is told she may say no and nothing will happen to her.
solve.work: Voluntary means free of pressure or penalty: being told she may say no with no consequence. B, C, D add pressure.

questions.stem: A researcher hands out a form that only says "Sign here to join." Why is this not informed consent?
choices: The researcher, not the participants, should be the one to sign the form.
The form should be handed out only after all of the data are collected.
People are not told what the study involves, so cannot choose knowingly.
Forms are needed only when participants are paid money for joining.
questions.answer: People are not told what the study involves, so cannot choose knowingly.
questions.solution: Informed consent requires that people understand what they are agreeing to. A form with no information gives them nothing to base a decision on.

solve.answer: People are not told what the study involves, so cannot choose knowingly.
solve.work: "Informed" means participants know what the study involves; a bare "Sign here" tells them nothing.

questions.stem: A teacher invites 30 students to a survey. 21 say yes, 4 say no, and the rest give no answer at all. Only students who clearly said yes may take part. How many students may take part?
questions.solution: Consent has to be given, not assumed. Only the 21 who said yes may take part. A student who gave no answer has not agreed, so those students are left out, just like the ones who said no.

solve.work: Only clear yes answers count: 21. (4 no, 5 no answer are excluded.)

questions.stem: A participant in a study says, "I want to leave now." When may a participant stop being in a study?
choices: Only after the last question of the study has been answered
At any time, for any reason, without being punished
Only if the researcher agrees that the person may leave
Only if the person gives a reason that the researcher accepts
questions.answer: At any time, for any reason, without being punished
questions.solution: The right to withdraw means a person may stop whenever they choose, without giving a reason and without penalty.

solve.answer: At any time, for any reason, without being punished
solve.work: Right to withdraw: at any time, for any reason, without penalty.

questions.stem: Which sentence should a consent form include about leaving the study?
choices: You may stop only if you tell us a good reason for stopping.
You may not stop once you have signed this form.
You may stop at any time, and you will not be penalized.
You may stop, but only during the first day of the study.
questions.answer: You may stop at any time, and you will not be penalized.
questions.solution: A fair form says participants may stop at any time without penalty. The other sentences limit or cancel that right.

solve.answer: You may stop at any time, and you will not be penalized.
solve.work: A consent form should say participants may stop at any time without penalty.

questions.stem: A survey of 60 people is stopped for 3 of them, who ask to withdraw halfway through. What percent of the 60 people withdrew?
questions.solution: 3 out of 60 is 1/20, which is 5%.

questions.stem: A researcher says, "You already signed the form, so you have to finish the study." Is this ethical?
choices: Yes, because a signed form is a promise that cannot be broken.
Yes, because quitting would waste the researcher's time.
No, but only if the participant is under 18.
No, because signing does not take away the right to stop.
questions.answer: No, because signing does not take away the right to stop.
questions.solution: The right to withdraw applies to everyone, even after signing. Wasted time is not a reason to force someone to continue.

solve.answer: No, because signing does not take away the right to stop.
solve.work: Signing consent does not remove the right to withdraw; not ethical.

questions.stem: The consent form for a quiz study promises that if a volunteer withdraws, all of their answers are deleted. Each volunteer answers 10 questions. Three volunteers each withdraw after answering 6 questions. How many answers are deleted in all?
questions.solution: Each of the 3 volunteers has 6 answers, so 3 x 6 = 18 answers are deleted.

solve.work: All answers of each withdrawing volunteer are deleted: 3*6 = 18.

questions.stem: A principal wants to know how all 400 students feel about a new bell schedule. Which sample is the most representative?
choices: The 40 students sitting in the front row of the first class
40 students picked at random from the full list of students
The 40 students who stay after school for clubs
The first 40 students to answer a message posted on the school website
questions.answer: 40 students picked at random from the full list of students
questions.solution: A random pick from the full list gives every student an equal chance. Front-row students, club members and early volunteers are special groups.

solve.answer: 40 students picked at random from the full list of students
solve.work: A simple random sample from the full list is most representative; the others are convenience/voluntary samples.

questions.stem: A school has 300 students: 120 in grade 7 and 180 in grade 8. A survey of 50 students is to have the same share from each grade as the school. How many grade 7 students are in the survey?
questions.solution: Grade 7 is 120 of 300, or 2/5, of the school. 2/5 of 50 is 20.

questions.stem: A survey is done only by phone calls to landline telephones during working hours. Why might it be unfair?
choices: It costs far more than a survey done by mail, which makes it unfair.
It can ask only very short questions, so it gives little information.
It leaves out people without a landline and people at work.
It reaches only the people who happen to be good at math or reading.
questions.answer: It leaves out people without a landline and people at work.
questions.solution: Fair collection gives every group a chance to be included. Calling landlines at work hours leaves out many people.

solve.answer: It leaves out people without a landline and people at work.
solve.work: Landline calls in working hours miss people without landlines and people at work: undercoverage.

questions.stem: The same data are graphed twice. One graph's vertical axis runs from 0 to 100, and the other's from 90 to 100. Which graph can make small differences look big?
choices: The graph whose axis starts at 0
The graph whose axis starts at 90
Neither graph, because the axis never affects how data look
Both graphs look exactly the same
questions.answer: The graph whose axis starts at 90
questions.solution: A shortened axis stretches the bars, so small differences seem large. Starting at 0 shows sizes honestly.

solve.answer: The graph whose axis starts at 90
solve.work: A truncated axis from 90 to 100 exaggerates small differences.

questions.stem: A shop owner says, "Nine out of ten customers love our cookies," after asking only ten of her friends who work in the shop. What makes this misleading?
choices: Nine is too small a number to be reported at all.
The result should have been written as a fraction.
Her friends are not a fair sample of customers.
Cookies cannot be rated by customers.
questions.answer: Her friends are not a fair sample of customers.
questions.solution: The people asked are biased in favor of the shop, so the result does not describe customers.

solve.answer: Her friends are not a fair sample of customers.
solve.work: Ten friends who work in the shop are a biased sample, not representative of customers.

questions.stem: A survey of 5 people finds that 3 of them prefer cats. Which report is the least misleading?
choices: Most people probably prefer cats over dogs.
The public prefers cats to dogs by 3 to 1.
Everyone agrees that cats are better than dogs.
In our survey of 5 people, 3 preferred cats.
questions.answer: In our survey of 5 people, 3 preferred cats.
questions.solution: The honest report says who was asked and how many. The others claim more than 5 people can support.

solve.answer: In our survey of 5 people, 3 preferred cats.
solve.work: Stating the actual sample size and count is least misleading.

questions.stem: A bar graph shows two values, 40 and 80, but the bar for 80 is drawn 4 times as tall as the bar for 40. The taller bar should be how many times as tall as the shorter one?
questions.solution: 80 is 2 times 40, so the bar should be 2 times as tall. Drawing it 4 times as tall exaggerates the difference.

solve.work: 80/40 = 2, so the taller bar should be 2 times as tall.

questions.stem: Why should a researcher replace names with ID codes before sharing data?
choices: To make the data easier to sort in alphabetical order
To make the sample of people larger
To stop people from being able to withdraw from the study
To protect privacy while the data can still be studied
questions.answer: To protect privacy while the data can still be studied
questions.solution: Codes keep data usable while hiding who the people are.

solve.answer: To protect privacy while the data can still be studied
solve.work: ID codes protect privacy while preserving the data for analysis.

questions.stem: A researcher collected 6 pieces of information from each of 80 students but needs only 2 of them. How many unneeded pieces of information were collected in all?
questions.solution: Each student has 6 - 2 = 4 unneeded pieces. For 80 students that is 4 x 80 = 320. Collecting less would have been more ethical.

solve.work: Unneeded per student 6 - 2 = 4; 4*80 = 320.

questions.stem: A survey collects no names. Which sentence on the form is both truthful and protective?
choices: Your answers are anonymous, and we cannot tell who gave which answer.
Your answers are anonymous, but your teacher will see each one with your name.
Your answers will be shared with your parents.
We will not tell you how your answers will be used.
questions.answer: Your answers are anonymous, and we cannot tell who gave which answer.
questions.solution: A truthful promise matches what is actually done. Because no names are collected, the first sentence is true and protects privacy.

solve.answer: Your answers are anonymous, and we cannot tell who gave which answer.
solve.work: With no names collected, saying answers are anonymous and untraceable is truthful and protective.

questions.stem: A study invites senior citizens, some of whom read very little English, to answer questions about their health. Which plan respects informed consent?
choices: Give the form only in English since that is the language of the study
Explain the study in each person's own language and ask for a decision
Ask a relative to sign the form without telling the person about the study
Tell each person only the benefits so that the person feels at ease joining
questions.answer: Explain the study in each person's own language and ask for a decision
questions.solution: Informed consent means people understand what the study involves, including its risks, before they agree. Explaining it in the person's own language makes the choice informed and voluntary. The other plans leave out the person or hide information.

solve.answer: Explain the study in each person's own language and ask for a decision
solve.work: Informed consent requires that the person understands the study (risks and benefits) and decides freely; explaining in the person's own language and asking for their decision does that. The others hide risks, exclude understanding, or bypass the person.

questions.stem: A researcher studies how people sleep, but recruits volunteers only through an ad in one gym's newsletter. Which concern about representation does this raise most directly?
choices: Volunteers who answer an ad are unable to give informed consent to a study at all
A study of sleep needs fewer volunteers, because a big sample is always unfair to some
Gym members may sleep differently from others, so the results may not fit all
Sleep habits cannot be measured, so any results about them are invalid
questions.answer: Gym members may sleep differently from others, so the results may not fit all
questions.solution: The volunteers come from one narrow group. Gym members may not be typical of the whole population, so the results may not represent everyone. Answering an ad is a normal way to volunteer and does not by itself spoil consent.

solve.answer: Gym members may sleep differently from others, so the results may not fit all
solve.work: Recruiting only from one gym's newsletter gives a non-representative sample (gym members may have different sleep habits). The other options are false claims about consent, sample size or measurability.

questions.stem: A headline says "Accidents tripled on Oak Road!" because the road had 1 accident last year and 3 this year. Which added fact would best keep readers from being misled?
choices: The counts, 1 accident last year and 3 this year
The opinion of the mayor about how safe the road is
A brighter color for the headline so it stands out more
The total number of cars in the whole country this year
questions.answer: The counts, 1 accident last year and 3 this year
questions.solution: "Tripled" sounds alarming, but the counts are tiny. Giving the actual numbers lets readers judge the size of the change. The other facts do not show how big the change really is.

solve.answer: The counts, 1 accident last year and 3 this year
solve.work: 'Tripled' sounds alarming, but going from 1 to 3 is a change of 2 accidents. Reporting the raw counts shows how small the numbers are. Colour, national car totals and the mayor's opinion do not address the misleading ratio.

questions.stem: A library surveys visitors only about whether longer opening hours would help them. Which item should the survey leave out?
choices: Whether the current hours fit the visitor's schedule
Which days the visitor would use the library more
Whether the visitor would come more on weekends
Each visitor's household income
questions.answer: Each visitor's household income
questions.solution: An ethical survey collects only what it needs. Household income has nothing to do with opening hours, so it should be left out. The other three items each help decide which hours to offer.

solve.answer: Each visitor's household income
solve.work: Data minimisation: collect only what the purpose needs. Weekend visits, fit of current hours and which days are all relevant to opening hours; household income is sensitive and not needed.

questions.stem: A researcher wants to survey 14-year-old students at school about their sleep. Which is the most appropriate way to get consent?
choices: Get permission from each student's parent or guardian, and ask each student whether they agree to take part.
Get permission from the school principal only, since the survey will take place at the school during class.
Get agreement from each student only, since they are the ones who will answer the questions in the survey.
Skip consent, since a short survey about sleep cannot harm any of the students.
questions.answer: Get permission from each student's parent or guardian, and ask each student whether they agree to take part.
questions.solution: For students under 18, researchers need permission from a parent or guardian and also the student's own agreement. A principal cannot agree for every family, the student alone is not enough, and even a short survey needs consent.

solve.answer: Get permission from each student's parent or guardian, and ask each student whether they agree to take part.
solve.work: 14-year-olds are minors: the standard is parental/guardian permission plus the student's own assent. A omits parents, C skips consent, D uses only the principal. B.

questions.stem: Which situation shows a problem with informed consent?
choices: Participants read a form that explains the risks, ask the researcher questions and then choose whether to sign.
Participants are told before they begin what they will be asked to do and that they may skip any question.
Participants get a copy of the form with the researcher's phone number, in case they have questions later.
Participants sign a form written in a language they cannot read, and nobody explains what it says to them.
questions.answer: Participants sign a form written in a language they cannot read, and nobody explains what it says to them.
questions.solution: Consent is informed only if people can understand what they are agreeing to. Signing a form they cannot read, with no explanation, is not informed. In the other situations people are told what to expect and may ask questions.

solve.answer: Participants sign a form written in a language they cannot read, and nobody explains what it says to them.
solve.work: A, B and C are all good consent practice. D: signing a form in a language one cannot read, with no explanation, means consent is not informed. D.

questions.stem: Before any data were analyzed, a participant asked the researcher to remove their answers from the study. The consent form had said participants could withdraw at any time. What should the researcher do?
choices: Remove the participant's answers from the data set before analyzing it.
Keep the answers, because removing them would change the results.
Keep the answers, because the participant already gave them freely.
Keep the answers, but replace the participant's name with a number.
questions.answer: Remove the participant's answers from the data set before analyzing it.
questions.solution: The right to withdraw includes having one's data removed when that is still possible, as it is before analysis. Changing the results, or a past agreement, is not a reason to keep data the participant asked to be removed.

solve.answer: Remove the participant's answers from the data set before analyzing it.
solve.work: The consent form promised withdrawal at any time and no analysis has happened yet, so the answers must be removed. Anonymising (A) does not honour withdrawal. C.

questions.stem: A study plans to analyze the data from all 200 students who joined. Before the analysis, 8% of the students withdraw and ask that their data be removed. How many students' data will be analyzed?
questions.solution: 8% of 200 is 16 students, so $200 - 16 = 184$ students' data will be analyzed. Equivalently, $200 \times 0.92 = 184$.

questions.stem: A city posts an online-only survey to learn how all of its residents feel about its public Wi-Fi. Which statement about this plan is true?
choices: The plan is fair, because every resident has the same chance to answer the survey.
The plan is fair, because residents who skip the survey do not affect the results.
Residents without internet access cannot answer, so their views are left out.
The plan is fair as long as at least 100 residents take part in the survey.
questions.answer: Residents without internet access cannot answer, so their views are left out.
questions.solution: An online-only survey cannot reach people who have no internet, and they may feel differently from those who do. Leaving them out is a fairness problem. The number of responses does not fix it.

solve.answer: Residents without internet access cannot answer, so their views are left out.
