solve.work: An online-only survey excludes residents without internet access, so it is not representative of all residents. A, B, C are false claims of fairness. D.

questions.stem: A town has 800 residents aged 18 to 34, 1,200 aged 35 to 54, and 1,000 aged 55 and over. A survey of 150 residents is to reflect these age groups in proportion. How many of the 150 should be aged 35 to 54?
questions.solution: The town has $800 + 1200 + 1000 = 3000$ residents. Those aged 35 to 54 are $\frac{1200}{3000} = 0.4$ of the town, and $0.4 \times 150 = 60$.

questions.stem: A company tests a new battery 10 times. In 3 tests it lasts a long time, and in 7 tests it does not. An advertisement reports only the 3 long-lasting tests. What is the ethical problem?
choices: There is none, because each of the 3 tests that was reported really did happen.
The company ran only 10 tests, and any report based on fewer than 100 tests is dishonest.
Leaving out the other 7 tests gives a false picture of how the battery usually works.
The company should have reported only the 7 tests in which the battery did not last.
questions.answer: Leaving out the other 7 tests gives a false picture of how the battery usually works.
questions.solution: Choosing only the favorable results hides most of the evidence. An honest report would include all 10 tests. True individual results can still add up to a misleading story.

solve.answer: Leaving out the other 7 tests gives a false picture of how the battery usually works.
solve.work: Reporting only the 3 favourable results out of 10 is selective reporting; the battery usually (7 of 10) does not last long. D.

questions.stem: A group of 200 people was surveyed in each of two years. Two years ago, 2 of them supported a new park. This year, 4 of them did. A headline says "Support for the park doubled!" By how many percentage points did the percent of people who support the park actually change?
questions.solution: 2 of 200 is 1%, and 4 of 200 is 2%. The change is 2% - 1% = 1 percentage point. "Doubled" is true of the counts but makes a tiny change sound huge.

solve.work: 2/200 = 1%; 4/200 = 2%. Change = 2% - 1% = 1 percentage point (the 'doubling' is only 1 point).

questions.stem: A health researcher plans to ask 16-year-olds sensitive questions about their habits. Which plan best protects the participants?
choices: Collect the answers without names, and let students skip any question they choose.
Collect names with the answers and give each student's answers to the student's school.
Read each question aloud in front of the whole class and ask for a show of hands.
Make every question required, so that no answers are missing.
questions.answer: Collect the answers without names, and let students skip any question they choose.
questions.solution: Collecting no names keeps answers private, and letting students skip questions respects their choices. The other plans expose the students or pressure them to answer.

solve.answer: Collect the answers without names, and let students skip any question they choose.
solve.work: Anonymous answers and the right to skip questions protect participants answering sensitive questions. A forces answers, B exposes them publicly, C breaks confidentiality. D.

questions.stem: A researcher collected records from 500 participants. A privacy check finds that 8% of the records contain a home address that the study does not need. The researcher will delete the address from each of those records. How many records need this change?
questions.solution: 8% of 500 is $500 \times 0.08 = 40$ records.

solve.work: 8% of 500 = 40 records.

questions.stem: A teacher tells her class that students who do not join her survey will lose 5 points of participation credit. Why is the consent of the students not truly voluntary?
choices: A teacher is never allowed to ask students questions in class.
The survey is too short for students to be able to give consent to it.
Students under 18 cannot give consent to anything at all.
A penalty pressures students, so saying no is not a free choice.
questions.answer: A penalty pressures students, so saying no is not a free choice.
questions.solution: Voluntary consent needs a real freedom to say no. Losing credit for refusing is a penalty, so students are pushed to say yes.

solve.answer: A penalty pressures students, so saying no is not a free choice.
solve.work: Losing credit is a penalty, so refusing has a cost: consent is coerced, not free.

questions.stem: Which consent form is best for a study of 11-year-olds?
choices: It describes in plain words what will happen and the risks, and asks both a parent and the child.
It explains the methods in technical words, and is signed only by the researcher in charge of the study.
It briefly says the study is safe, and is signed by a teacher on behalf of every child.
It uses plain words to explain what will happen, but does not mention any possible risks.
questions.answer: It describes in plain words what will happen and the risks, and asks both a parent and the child.
questions.solution: Children need information they can understand, including the risks, and both a parent's permission and their own willingness. The other forms are hard to read, omit risks, or let someone else decide for the child.

solve.answer: It describes in plain words what will happen and the risks, and asks both a parent and the child.
solve.work: Children need plain language, disclosure of risks, parental permission and the child's own assent: D.

questions.stem: A researcher will record interviews on video. The consent form only says, "Your answers will be used for research." What should the form add?
choices: The names of all the other people who will be interviewed
That the interview is recorded and who may watch it
A promise that the video will be shown on a public website
The results that the researcher expects to find in the study
questions.answer: That the interview is recorded and who may watch it
questions.solution: People need to know what is collected about them and who will see it. Recording and who may watch are central. Other people's names, a public showing and expected results are not what consent requires.

solve.answer: That the interview is recorded and who may watch it
solve.work: Video recording is identifiable; the form must say it is recorded and who may watch it.

questions.stem: An online survey begins with a box that is already checked: "I agree that my answers may be shared with other companies." Why is this a problem for consent?
choices: Computers cannot read answers from surveys that use checked boxes.
Answers can be shared only after the survey has closed to new people.
Agreement should be an active choice, not a default people may miss.
The box should be checked in advance only for people under 18.
questions.answer: Agreement should be an active choice, not a default people may miss.
questions.solution: Consent has to be given on purpose. A box that is already checked makes agreement the automatic result of doing nothing, which people may not notice.

solve.answer: Agreement should be an active choice, not a default people may miss.
solve.work: A pre-checked box is a default people may not notice; consent should be an active opt-in.

questions.stem: A school sends consent forms to 180 families. 45% return a yes, 20% return a no, and the rest return nothing. Only students whose families returned a yes may take part. How many students may take part?
questions.solution: 45% of 180 is 81. Families who said no or sent nothing have not agreed, so only these 81 students may take part.

questions.stem: A volunteer in a three-week diet study withdraws in week 2 because of a health worry. The researcher would like complete data. Which response respects the volunteer's rights?
choices: Accept the withdrawal and stop collecting data from the volunteer.
Ask the volunteer to stay until week 3 so that the data are complete.
Keep collecting the volunteer's data without telling them.
Tell the volunteer that leaving early will be noted in their school record.
questions.answer: Accept the withdrawal and stop collecting data from the volunteer.
questions.solution: Participants may leave at any time, so the researcher must stop collecting data. Pressure, secrecy or threats violate the right to withdraw.

solve.answer: Accept the withdrawal and stop collecting data from the volunteer.
solve.work: The volunteer's withdrawal must be accepted and data collection stopped.

questions.stem: Which is the best way to make the right to withdraw real in an online survey?
choices: A note on the last page says that people could have quit earlier.
A visible button on every page lets people quit at once.
A rule says people may quit only after answering every required question.
A message says quitting is allowed if people email the research director.
questions.answer: A visible button on every page lets people quit at once.
questions.solution: The right to withdraw is real only when quitting is easy at any time. Hiding it, delaying it or adding hurdles takes it away.

solve.answer: A visible button on every page lets people quit at once.
solve.work: A visible quit button on every page makes withdrawal immediate and easy.

questions.stem: A study pays each teen 4 dollars for every session attended, up to 10 sessions. The form says a teen who withdraws keeps the pay for the sessions already attended. A teen withdraws after attending 6 sessions. How many dollars does the teen keep?
questions.solution: The teen attended 6 sessions and is paid 4 dollars for each, so keeps 6 x 4 = 24 dollars. Leaving does not take away pay already earned.

solve.work: 6 sessions * 4 dollars = 24.

questions.stem: After 5% of the people recruited for a study withdrew, exactly 171 remained. How many people were recruited?
questions.solution: 171 is 95% of the people recruited. Dividing, 171 / 0.95 = 180.

questions.stem: A researcher studies how much teens sleep by surveying only students on the school's varsity teams. What is the problem?
choices: Varsity teams are too small for any survey to be done on their members.
Students on varsity teams are not able to give consent to any survey.
The amount of sleep cannot be measured by a survey of any kind at all.
Athletes may sleep differently, so results may not describe all teens.
questions.answer: Athletes may sleep differently, so results may not describe all teens.
questions.solution: The sample should reflect the whole group of teens. Athletes are a particular subgroup, which can bias the results.

solve.answer: Athletes may sleep differently, so results may not describe all teens.
solve.work: Varsity athletes are not representative of all teens; their sleep may differ.

questions.stem: A city has 5,000 renters and 15,000 homeowners. A fair survey of 400 residents is to match these two groups in proportion. How many renters should be surveyed?
questions.solution: Renters are 5,000 of 20,000 residents, which is 1/4. One fourth of 400 is 100.

questions.stem: A medicine study enrolls 200 adults, all between ages 20 and 30. The medicine will be sold to people of all ages. What is the ethical concern?
choices: Safety for older adults and children is unknown, since they were left out.
Adults between 20 and 30 are too healthy to be included in any study.
Two hundred people is always too small a number for any ethical study.
The medicine should first have been tested on one person at a time.
questions.answer: Safety for older adults and children is unknown, since they were left out.
questions.solution: A study should include the groups that the results will be applied to. Leaving others out means the results may not be safe or useful for them.

solve.answer: Safety for older adults and children is unknown, since they were left out.
solve.work: Leaving out older adults and children means the medicine's safety for them is unknown: a representation/fairness concern.

questions.stem: A survey of 240 people took equal numbers from 4 neighborhoods, which have 1,000, 2,000, 3,000 and 4,000 residents. To match the neighborhoods in proportion, how many of the 240 should come from the neighborhood with 3,000 residents?
questions.solution: The neighborhoods have 10,000 residents in all. The 3,000 neighborhood is 3/10 of them, and 3/10 of 240 is 72.

questions.stem: A survey asks, "Do you agree that the wonderful new library should be built?" Why is this a fairness problem?
choices: Questions about libraries should always ask for a number.
The loaded word "wonderful" pushes people toward agreeing.
The question should have asked about the old library instead.
Questions with only a yes or a no are never allowed.
questions.answer: The loaded word "wonderful" pushes people toward agreeing.
questions.solution: A fair question uses neutral words. Calling the library "wonderful" nudges people to agree.

solve.answer: The loaded word "wonderful" pushes people toward agreeing.
solve.work: "Wonderful" is a loaded word that pushes respondents to agree.

questions.stem: A graph uses a drawing of a dog to show the number of homes with dogs. For a count twice as large, the drawing is made twice as wide and twice as tall. Why is this misleading?
choices: Doubling width and height makes the area 4 times as big, which looks like 4 times.
Pictures of dogs cannot be used in any graph that shows counts of homes.
Doubling the height alone would have made the graph more misleading than this.
The drawing should have been made 3 times as wide and 3 times as tall.
questions.answer: Doubling width and height makes the area 4 times as big, which looks like 4 times.
questions.solution: People judge the size by area. Doubling both dimensions multiplies the area by 2 x 2 = 4, so the picture exaggerates.

solve.answer: Doubling width and height makes the area 4 times as big, which looks like 4 times.
solve.work: Scaling both dimensions by 2 scales area by 4, so the picture looks 4 times as large.

questions.stem: An ad says, "Our firm pays an average salary of 50 thousand dollars." The five employees earn 30, 30, 30, 30 and 130 thousand dollars. What is the median salary, in thousands of dollars?
questions.solution: The mean is (30+30+30+30+130)/5 = 50, which the ad uses. The median is the middle of the ordered values, 30. The mean is pulled up by one large salary and is misleading.

solve.work: Sorted 30,30,30,30,130: median 30 (mean 50 is pulled up by the outlier).

questions.stem: Classes using a reading app scored 6 points higher than classes that did not. The report does not say that the app classes were picked because they already had the highest scores. What is the problem?
choices: Six points is too small a difference to be reported in a school study.
The groups differed before the app, so the gap may not be due to the app.
The other classes should have been given a different app to try instead.
Test scores in a report should always be reported as percents, not points.
questions.answer: The groups differed before the app, so the gap may not be due to the app.
questions.solution: If the groups were already different, the gap cannot be credited to the app. Hiding how the classes were chosen misleads readers.

solve.answer: The groups differed before the app, so the gap may not be due to the app.
solve.work: App classes already scored highest: selection/confounding, so the gap may not be due to the app.

questions.stem: A headline says "100% of people who tried our product loved it!" Only 3 people tried it. What detail makes the headline misleading?
choices: It uses a percent where it should have used a fraction or a count.
It says "loved" where a more careful word like "liked" would be better.
It hides that only 3 people tried it, too few to show what most think.
It should have said that 100% of the people is the same as the number 3.
questions.answer: It hides that only 3 people tried it, too few to show what most think.
questions.solution: A percent from a tiny sample sounds strong but means little. An honest report gives the number of people.

solve.answer: It hides that only 3 people tried it, too few to show what most think.
solve.work: The headline hides the tiny sample of 3.

questions.stem: A news story says a drug "cuts the risk of a side effect by half." Without the drug, 2 people in 1,000 have the side effect, and with the drug 1 in 1,000 does. By how many people per 1,000 does the drug reduce the number with the side effect?
questions.solution: The change is from 2 per 1,000 to 1 per 1,000, a drop of 1 per 1,000. "Half" is true in relative terms but makes the benefit sound far larger than it is.

solve.work: 2 - 1 = 1 per 1,000 (absolute reduction, vs 50% relative).

questions.stem: A school counselor wants to study student stress using the counseling office's files. Which plan is the most ethical?
choices: Use the files with names because the counselor already has access to them.
Ask for consent, remove names, and share only summary results.
Post each student's results on the bulletin board.
Ask only the teachers for permission to use the files.
questions.answer: Ask for consent, remove names, and share only summary results.
questions.solution: The students' information is theirs. Consent, removing names and sharing only summaries respect their privacy.

solve.answer: Ask for consent, remove names, and share only summary results.
solve.work: Consent, de-identification and summary-only reporting is the ethical plan.

questions.stem: A researcher's records for 2,400 participants may be kept for 3 years, as the consent form promised. 15% of the records are older than 3 years. How many records must be deleted?
questions.solution: 15% of 2,400 is 360. These records are past the promised time and must be deleted.

questions.stem: A report on 5 students in a small town gives each student's exact age, grade and town. Readers could work out who they are. Which fix is best?
choices: Add each student's full name next to the details for clarity.
Remove the results and publish only the town's name.
Group details into broader categories, such as "ages 12 to 14".
Keep the details, but call the students "participants".
questions.answer: Group details into broader categories, such as "ages 12 to 14".
questions.solution: Broader groups make it harder to identify a person. Names or unchanged details do not.

solve.answer: Group details into broader categories, such as "ages 12 to 14".
solve.work: Coarsening details (age ranges) reduces re-identification while keeping results.

questions.stem: A study team has 24 members. The privacy plan lets only 25% of them see participants' names, and the rest see only ID codes. How many team members see only ID codes?
questions.solution: 25% of 24 is 6 people who can see names. The other 24 - 6 = 18 see only ID codes.

solve.work: 25% of 24 = 6 see names; 24 - 6 = 18 see only ID codes.

questions.stem: Participants in a sleep study agreed that their data would be used only to study sleep. A researcher now wants to use the same data to study screen time. What must the researcher do first?
choices: Nothing, because the participants already agreed to be in the study and gave their data.
Ask the participants for permission to use their data for the new purpose of studying screen time.
Replace the names with numbers, which means that no permission is needed for the new purpose.
Look at the data first, and ask for permission only if the results turn out to be interesting.
questions.answer: Ask the participants for permission to use their data for the new purpose of studying screen time.
questions.solution: People consented to one use of their data. A new purpose needs new consent. Removing names does not replace permission, and asking after looking at the data is too late.

solve.answer: Ask the participants for permission to use their data for the new purpose of studying screen time.
solve.work: Consent was given for sleep research only; a new purpose needs new consent. A ignores the limit, B wrongly claims anonymising removes the need, D is cherry-picking. C.

questions.stem: A school sends a consent form to the family of each of 250 students. A student can take part only if the family returns the form with a yes. 60% of the families return the form, and 10% of the returned forms say no. How many students can take part?
questions.solution: 60% of 250 is 150 returned forms. 10% of those say no, so 90% say yes: $150 \times 0.9 = 135$. So 135 students can take part.

solve.work: Returned: 60% of 250 = 150. No: 10% of 150 = 15. Yes: 150 - 15 = 135. Unreturned forms count as no consent, so 135 can take part.

questions.stem: A parent gave permission for their 9-year-old to try a reading game for a study. Partway through, the child says, "I don't want to do this anymore." What should the researcher do?
choices: Continue, because the parent's permission is all that is needed to keep going.
Continue, because the child can decide to stop only after finishing one game.
Ask the parent to tell the child to keep going, since the parent gave permission.
Stop, because the child can decide to withdraw even though a parent gave permission.
questions.answer: Stop, because the child can decide to withdraw even though a parent gave permission.
questions.solution: A parent's permission does not take away a child's own right to stop. When the child says they do not want to continue, the researcher stops and does not pressure the child or the parent.

solve.answer: Stop, because the child can decide to withdraw even though a parent gave permission.
solve.work: A child's assent matters even with parental permission; the child may withdraw. A.

questions.stem: A study begins with 120 volunteers. In week 1, 25% of them withdraw. In week 2, 10 more withdraw. In week 3, one-eighth of the volunteers still in the study withdraw. How many volunteers are left after week 3?
questions.solution: Week 1: 25% of 120 is 30, so 90 are left. Week 2: $90 - 10 = 80$. Week 3: one-eighth of 80 is 10, so $80 - 10 = 70$ volunteers are left.

solve.work: Start 120. Week 1: 25% of 120 = 30 leave, 90 left. Week 2: 10 leave, 80 left. Week 3: 1/8 of 80 = 10 leave, 70 left.

questions.stem: A trial of a new medicine for a condition that affects men and women equally enrolled 400 people: 360 men and 40 women. The researchers want to add only women until half of all the participants are women. How many women must they add?
questions.solution: No men are added, so there are still 360 men. For half to be women, there must be 360 women. They have 40, so they must add $360 - 40 = 320$ women.

solve.work: Men stay at 360. For women to be half, women = men = 360. Add 360 - 40 = 320 women (total 720).

questions.stem: A company trains a face-recognition tool on photos in which 85% of the faces belong to one group. The tool is much less accurate for people in the other groups. Which change in how the photos are collected best addresses this fairness problem?
choices: Add photos, with permission, of people from the groups that are underrepresented.
Add many more photos of people from the group that already makes up 85% of the photos.
Remove the photos of the other groups so that all of the training photos look alike.
Collect new photos only from the volunteers who are easiest to reach, to save time.
questions.answer: Add photos, with permission, of people from the groups that are underrepresented.
questions.solution: The tool is less accurate for groups it saw few times, so the data need more people from those groups, collected with their permission. Adding more of the largest group or removing the small groups makes it worse, and easy-to-reach volunteers may be just as unrepresentative.

solve.answer: Add photos, with permission, of people from the groups that are underrepresented.
solve.work: The problem is underrepresentation of other groups in the training data; the fix is to collect more photos (with permission) of those groups. A worsens the imbalance, B is convenience sampling, C removes groups. D.

questions.stem: A poll of 1,000 people reports Candidate A at 51% and Candidate B at 49%, with a margin of error of 3 percentage points. A headline says "A leads B." Which statement is the most honest description of the result?
choices: The race is too close to call, because the 2-point gap is within the margin of error.
A is ahead, because 51% is greater than 49% and the poll asked 1,000 people.
B is ahead, because the margin of error always favors the candidate with the lower percent.
A will win by exactly 2 points, because the poll asked 1,000 people.
questions.answer: The race is too close to call, because the 2-point gap is within the margin of error.
questions.solution: With a margin of error of 3 points, each candidate's true support could be a few points higher or lower. A 2-point gap is smaller than that, so the poll cannot show who is ahead.

solve.answer: The race is too close to call, because the 2-point gap is within the margin of error.
solve.work: Gap 51 - 49 = 2 points, smaller than the 3-point margin of error, so the poll cannot say who leads. A, B, C overclaim. D.

questions.stem: A study found that students who eat breakfast have higher test scores. The students chose for themselves whether to eat breakfast. A headline says "Eating breakfast raises your test score." What is the main problem with the headline?
choices: It is fine, because breakfast eaters really did score higher on the tests.
It should say that doing well on tests makes students more likely to eat breakfast.
It is wrong, because the test scores of different students cannot be compared at all.
It claims breakfast causes higher scores, but the study shows only that the two go together.
questions.answer: It claims breakfast causes higher scores, but the study shows only that the two go together.
questions.solution: Students chose their own habits, so other things (sleep, family, motivation) could explain the difference. The study shows an association, not cause and effect. The reverse claim is just as unsupported.

solve.answer: It claims breakfast causes higher scores, but the study shows only that the two go together.
solve.work: Observational study (students self-selected), so it shows association, not causation. B asserts the reverse causation without evidence. D.

questions.stem: A researcher believes that telling participants a study is about how often they check their phones would change how they behave. Which plan is the most ethical way to handle this?
choices: Say nothing about the study to anyone, so participants cannot refuse or change their behavior.
Give a false description of the study, and never explain the real purpose to participants afterward.
Give a false description of the risks, so that more people agree to take part in the study.
Describe the study in general terms, get consent, then explain the purpose and offer to delete their data.
questions.answer: Describe the study in general terms, get consent, then explain the purpose and offer to delete their data.
questions.solution: Participants must still be told what they will do and the risks, and must agree freely. Holding back only the narrow purpose, then explaining it afterward and letting people withdraw their data, respects them. Hiding the study, lying about risks or never explaining do not.

solve.answer: Describe the study in general terms, get consent, then explain the purpose and offer to delete their data.
solve.work: Ethical partial disclosure: describe in general terms (no lies about risks), obtain consent, then debrief with the true purpose and offer withdrawal of data. B, C lie and C never debriefs, D has no consent. A.

questions.stem: A district compares two plans to study how study habits relate to grades. Plan 1 uses school records with student names and tells no one. Plan 2 asks for consent, replaces names with ID codes, keeps the code list separately and reports only group results. Which statement best justifies choosing Plan 2?
choices: It guarantees that every participant's grades will improve after the study is finished.
It respects choice and protects identity, and the study can still answer its question.
It lets the district see which student gave which answer without needing to ask the students.
It needs no consent at all, because the names are replaced by ID codes in the records.
questions.answer: It respects choice and protects identity, and the study can still answer its question.
questions.solution: Plan 2 asks permission, hides identities and shares only group results, yet still gives the district the data to study habits and grades. It does not change grades, and it does ask for consent.

solve.answer: It respects choice and protects identity, and the study can still answer its question.
solve.work: Plan 2 uses consent, pseudonymisation, separate key storage and group-level reporting: it respects autonomy and privacy while still answering the question. A is false, B describes Plan 1's flaw, C is wrong (Plan 2 does ask consent). D.

questions.stem: A researcher wants 7-year-olds to try a new math game for a study. Which is the best way to get agreement?
choices: Get only the child's agreement, because the child is the one who will be playing the game, not the parent.
Get only a parent's permission, then tell the child to play whether or not they want to.
Ask the teacher to pick children who will not object, and skip the permission step.
Get a parent's permission, then explain the game simply and ask the child if they are willing.
questions.answer: Get a parent's permission, then explain the game simply and ask the child if they are willing.
questions.solution: A young child cannot give full consent, so a parent gives permission. The child should still be told in simple words and may decline. Skipping the parent, ignoring the child, or having a teacher choose silently all fail.

solve.answer: Get a parent's permission, then explain the game simply and ask the child if they are willing.
solve.work: For young children: parental permission plus the child's own assent explained simply.

questions.stem: A consent form says, "You will complete a short online survey." The survey really has 20 questions about family income and health. What is the problem?
choices: The form leaves out what the survey asks about, so people cannot judge risks.
A survey done on the internet is never allowed to ask people about their family income.
Health questions must always be placed before income questions.
The form should state exactly how many people will answer the survey.
questions.answer: The form leaves out what the survey asks about, so people cannot judge risks.
questions.solution: Informed consent requires telling people about the content that matters to their decision. Sensitive health and income questions matter, and the form hides them.

solve.answer: The form leaves out what the survey asks about, so people cannot judge risks.
solve.work: The form hides that the survey asks sensitive income and health questions, so people cannot weigh the risks.

questions.stem: In a pilot test, 12 of 80 people did not understand a consent form and needed it explained. The full study will invite 500 people, and the same share of them is expected to need an explanation. How many of the 500 people are expected to need one?
questions.solution: 12 out of 80 is 15%. 15% of 500 is 75 people. The team should plan time for explaining the form to about that many.

questions.stem: A survey has this rule: a student under 18 needs a parent's permission AND their own agreement, while a student 18 or older needs only their own agreement. Of 400 students, 250 are under 18. 90% of their parents give permission, and 80% of the students whose parents gave permission also agree. Of the 150 students who are 18 or older, 70% agree. How many students can take part?
questions.solution: Under 18: 250 x 0.9 = 225 have permission, and 80% of 225 is 180 who also agree. 18 or older: 70% of 150 is 105. Together, 180 + 105 = 285.

questions.stem: A researcher has combined survey answers from 300 people into one file that has no names and no ID codes. One person then asks to have their answers removed. What is the real difficulty?
choices: Answers that were once collected can never be changed under any circumstances.
The person gave up the right to withdraw by answering the questions at all.
No one can tell which answers are theirs, which the form should have said.
Removing one answer would make all of the other answers in the file invalid.
questions.answer: No one can tell which answers are theirs, which the form should have said.
questions.solution: When data can no longer be linked to a person, withdrawal is impossible afterwards. An ethical form says so before people agree. The other statements are not true.

solve.answer: No one can tell which answers are theirs, which the form should have said.
solve.work: With no names or IDs, the person's answers cannot be identified to remove; the form should have warned of this limit on withdrawal.

questions.stem: In a study, 25% of the volunteers withdrew in week 1. Then 20 more withdrew in week 2. At the end, 70 volunteers remained. How many volunteers started the study?
questions.solution: Before week 2 there were 70 + 20 = 90 volunteers. These 90 were the 75% left after week 1, so the start was 90 / 0.75 = 120.

questions.stem: A study follows students for four years. Which plan best respects the right to withdraw?
choices: Rely on the consent signed in year 1 and never ask the students again.
Ask again each year, but treat any "no" as a form that must be re-sent.
Remind only the parents each year, since the students were minors in year 1.
Remind participants each year that they may stop, and ask if they still agree.
questions.answer: Remind participants each year that they may stop, and ask if they still agree.
questions.solution: Over years, people change their minds and grow up. Reminders and fresh agreement keep the right real. Ignoring a "no" or the student defeats it.

solve.answer: Remind participants each year that they may stop, and ask if they still agree.
solve.work: In a long study, periodic reminders of the right to stop and renewed agreement respect withdrawal, especially as minors grow up.

questions.stem: An app's terms say: "Once you install the app, you cannot ever remove your data." Why does this conflict with ethical data collection?
choices: It removes the user's right to withdraw consent and have data deleted.
Apps are never allowed to collect any usage data about their own users.
Terms of use must always be shorter than one page to be considered fair.
Data about use must be deleted automatically from every phone each day.
questions.answer: It removes the user's right to withdraw consent and have data deleted.
questions.solution: Ethical collection lets people withdraw, including having their data removed. The terms cancel this right in advance.

solve.answer: It removes the user's right to withdraw consent and have data deleted.
solve.work: Permanently refusing data removal takes away the right to withdraw consent and have data deleted.

questions.stem: A study assigns 120 volunteers to a treatment group and 120 to a control group. In the treatment group 18 withdraw, and in the control group 6 withdraw. What percent of all 240 volunteers withdrew?
questions.solution: In total 18 + 6 = 24 volunteers withdrew. 24 out of 240 is 10%.

questions.stem: A survey has 300 responses: 200 from urban residents and 100 from rural residents. In truth, the population is 40% urban and 60% rural. 70% of urban respondents and 40% of rural respondents support a plan. If each group is weighted by its true share of the population, what percent of the population is estimated to support the plan?
questions.solution: Weighted support: 0.40 x 70% + 0.60 x 40% = 28% + 24% = 52%. The unweighted result, 180 of 300 or 60%, would overstate the urban share.

questions.stem: A researcher says, "My sample of 5,000 volunteers from an online forum is so large that it must be representative." What is the best reply?
choices: Correct: any sample larger than 1,000 is automatically representative of everyone.
Incorrect: samples of volunteers are always too small to use for a survey.
A large sample can still be biased if the way people were chosen leaves groups out.
Incorrect: a representative sample must always have fewer than 100 people.
questions.answer: A large sample can still be biased if the way people were chosen leaves groups out.
questions.solution: Representativeness depends on how people were selected, not on size alone. Volunteers from one forum may differ from everyone else.

solve.answer: A large sample can still be biased if the way people were chosen leaves groups out.
solve.work: Size does not fix selection bias; a large volunteer sample from one forum can still leave groups out.

questions.stem: A study will enroll 800 people, with 25% from each of four age groups. So far 200, 180, 150 and 120 people have enrolled in the four groups. How many more people are needed in the group that is furthest below its target?
questions.solution: Each group has a target of 25% of 800, which is 200. The shortfalls are 0, 20, 50 and 80. The biggest is 80.

solve.work: Target 25% of 800 = 200 per group. Shortfalls: 0, 20, 50, 80. Furthest below is the group with 120: needs 80.

questions.stem: A survey of drivers has answers from 90% men, but drivers are about half men and half women. What is the most ethical way to report the results?
choices: Report the results as if they describe all drivers equally.
Hide the gender breakdown so that readers do not question the sample.
Report only the answers from the women who replied.
State that men are over-represented and say who the results cover.
questions.answer: State that men are over-represented and say who the results cover.
questions.solution: Honest reporting shows the sample's limits. Hiding the imbalance or pretending it does not matter misleads readers.

solve.answer: State that men are over-represented and say who the results cover.
solve.work: Ethical reporting discloses the over-representation of men and states who the results cover.

questions.stem: A health survey is sent to 1,000 randomly chosen households, and 300 reply, mostly retired people. What is the best way to improve fairness?
choices: Follow up with non-responders by phone or visit to reach those missed.
Send the survey to 1,000 more retired people, who tend to reply.
Report that 300 replies is a large enough sample to describe everyone.
Count each household that did not reply as having answered no to everything.
questions.answer: Follow up with non-responders by phone or visit to reach those missed.
questions.solution: Non-response bias comes from who answers. Following up with those who did not reply makes the sample more representative. The other options make the imbalance worse or invent data.

solve.answer: Follow up with non-responders by phone or visit to reach those missed.
solve.work: Following up non-responders reduces nonresponse bias; the others worsen or ignore it.

questions.stem: A fund reports that "the companies we invested in earned great returns." It counted only companies that are still in business after 10 years. What is wrong?
choices: Only the companies that failed should have been counted in the average.
Ten years is too short a time for any returns to be counted at all.
Returns should have been reported as whole numbers of percent only.
Failed companies were left out, so the returns look better than they were.
questions.answer: Failed companies were left out, so the returns look better than they were.
questions.solution: Counting only survivors hides the failures, so the results are too good. This is called survivorship bias.

solve.answer: Failed companies were left out, so the returns look better than they were.
solve.work: Survivorship bias: failed companies were excluded, inflating returns.

questions.stem: A company says its customers' average rating is 4.5. It found this by averaging 5 (the mean of 10 ratings from its fan club) and 4 (the mean of 40 ratings from other customers). What is the actual mean of all 50 ratings?
questions.solution: The ratings total 10 x 5 + 40 x 4 = 50 + 160 = 210. Dividing by 50 gives 4.2. Averaging the two means gives 4.5, which ignores the group sizes.

questions.stem: A news chart shows crimes in a city rising from 800 to 900 over ten years, but the city's population doubled in that time. What is a fairer comparison?
choices: Compare the crime rate per 1,000 residents each year.
Compare only the count in the final year.
Compare only the years with the highest crime counts.
Compare the counts, but start the vertical axis at 700.
questions.answer: Compare the crime rate per 1,000 residents each year.
questions.solution: A rate adjusts for the size of the population. Here the number of crimes per resident fell. Raw counts and shortened axes mislead.

solve.answer: Compare the crime rate per 1,000 residents each year.
solve.work: With population doubling, compare rates per 1,000 residents.

questions.stem: A researcher runs 20 separate tests on unrelated traits, finds one "significant" result that arose by chance, and publishes only that one. Why is this unethical?
choices: Running 20 tests on one data set is never allowed by researchers.
Hiding the other 19 tests makes a chance result look real.
Only studies with significant results should be published.
A significant result can never happen by chance in a data set.
questions.answer: Hiding the other 19 tests makes a chance result look real.
questions.solution: With many tests, some will look significant by chance. Reporting only that one conceals how it was found and misleads readers.

solve.answer: Hiding the other 19 tests makes a chance result look real.
solve.work: Selective reporting of one chance result among 20 tests (p-hacking) misleads.

questions.stem: A researcher collects phone locations to study traffic and plans to record only the zone of the city, not the exact position. Which justification is best?
choices: Exact positions use up more storage space than zones do on a server.
Zone data are always more accurate than the exact positions of phones.
People always prefer researchers to know as little about them as possible.
The zone answers the question, and exact positions could show where people live.
questions.answer: The zone answers the question, and exact positions could show where people live.
questions.solution: Collect only what is needed and avoid what could identify people. The zone is enough, and exact positions are risky.

solve.answer: The zone answers the question, and exact positions could show where people live.
solve.work: Data minimisation: the zone suffices for the traffic question and exact positions could reveal homes.

questions.stem: A researcher collects names, birth dates and zip codes for a study that only needs age groups and regions. Which change best protects participants?
choices: Keep only age group and region, since nothing more is needed.
Keep all the details, but hide them in a long file name.
Keep all the details, because more data are always better.
Keep the names and drop the ages, because ages are not needed.
questions.answer: Keep only age group and region, since nothing more is needed.
questions.solution: Data minimization means collecting only what the study needs. Dropping names, birth dates and zip codes reduces the risk.

solve.answer: Keep only age group and region, since nothing more is needed.
solve.work: Keep only what is needed: age group and region.

questions.stem: A dataset is released with only age group and zip code. A rule says any group with fewer than 5 people must be merged with the others of its kind. In one zip code the groups have 12, 3, 2 and 8 people. The groups with fewer than 5 people are merged into one. How many people are in the merged group?
questions.solution: The groups with fewer than 5 people are the groups of 3 and 2. Merging them gives 3 + 2 = 5 people, which meets the minimum.

solve.work: Groups under 5: 3 and 2; merged 3 + 2 = 5.

questions.stem: Which storage plan best protects identifiable survey data from 300 people?
choices: Keep names and answers together on a shared drive that every staff member can open.
Keep names apart from answers, locked, open to few people, and delete them when done.
Email the file to every team member and to the sponsor so each has a copy.
Keep the file with names forever in case it turns out to be useful someday.
questions.answer: Keep names apart from answers, locked, open to few people, and delete them when done.
questions.solution: Separating identity from answers, limiting access and deleting data on time reduce risk. The others spread or keep the data without need.

solve.answer: Keep names apart from answers, locked, open to few people, and delete them when done.
solve.work: Separate identifiers, restrict access, lock, and delete when done.

questions.stem: A study needs 64 participants. Past studies show that 20% of the people recruited will withdraw. Recruiting more than needed exposes extra people to risk, so the researchers recruit the fewest people so that at least 64 remain. How many people do they recruit?
questions.solution: If 20% withdraw, 80% remain. So 0.8 x (number recruited) must be 64, and 64 / 0.8 = 80.

solve.work: 80% remain: 0.8N >= 64, N >= 80; fewest is 80.

questions.skill: Choose a display that fits the data and the purpose
questions.stem: Ms. Lopez records how many students joined each of 5 clubs. Which display is best for comparing the sizes of the clubs?
choices: A bar graph with a separate bar for each club
A box plot made from the five club sizes
A scatterplot with the club names along one axis
A line graph joining the clubs in the order they were listed
questions.answer: A bar graph with a separate bar for each club
questions.solution: The clubs are categories and each has one count, so a bar graph with one bar per club makes the sizes easy to compare. A box plot, a scatterplot or a line joining unrelated categories does not.

solve.answer: A bar graph with a separate bar for each club
solve.work: Counts for 5 categories: a bar graph with one bar per club compares sizes directly. Scatterplot, line graph and box plot do not suit categories.

questions.skill: Choose a display that fits the data and the purpose
questions.stem: A town's population was recorded every year from 2010 to 2020. Which display best shows how the population changed over time?
choices: A pie chart with one slice for each of the eleven years
A line graph with the years along the horizontal axis
A box plot made from the eleven population values
A histogram made from the eleven years
questions.answer: A line graph with the years along the horizontal axis
questions.solution: Data recorded over time are best shown with a line graph, because the line shows whether the values rise or fall from year to year. The other displays lose the order of the years.

solve.answer: A line graph with the years along the horizontal axis
solve.work: Change over time: line graph with years on the horizontal axis.

questions.skill: Read the key features of a display
questions.stem: A histogram of quiz scores has four bars. The bar for scores 0 to 4 has height 2, the bar for 5 to 9 has height 6, the bar for 10 to 14 has height 9, and the bar for 15 to 19 has height 3. The heights are numbers of students. How many students took the quiz?
questions.solution: Add the heights of all the bars: 2 + 6 + 9 + 3 = 20 students.

solve.work: 2 + 6 + 9 + 3 = 20 students.

questions.skill: Read the key features of a display
questions.stem: In a histogram of the ages of the people at a playground, the tallest bar is the one for ages 5 to 9. What does that tell you?
choices: Everyone at the playground is aged 5 to 9, and nobody is older.
Exactly 9 people at the playground are aged 5 to 9.
More people are aged 5 to 9 than in any other group shown.
The oldest person at the playground is 9 years old, as shown.
questions.answer: More people are aged 5 to 9 than in any other group shown.
questions.solution: The height of a bar is the number of people in that age group. The tallest bar means that group has the most people. It does not mean that everyone is in the group, or that its height is the age.

solve.answer: More people are aged 5 to 9 than in any other group shown.
solve.work: Tallest bar = most frequent interval: more people aged 5-9 than any other group. It does not say everyone, the max age, or the count 9.

questions.stem: The values in group X run from 20 to 70. The values in group Y run from 35 to 60. How much larger is the range of group X than the range of group Y?
questions.solution: Range of X = 70 - 20 = 50. Range of Y = 60 - 35 = 25. The difference is 50 - 25 = 25.

solve.work: Range X = 70 - 20 = 50; range Y = 60 - 35 = 25. Difference 25.

questions.stem: Two classes took the same test. Class P: minimum 50, first quartile 60, median 70, third quartile 80, maximum 90. Class Q: minimum 65, first quartile 68, median 70, third quartile 72, maximum 75. Which statement is true?
choices: Class Q has the higher median, and its scores are more spread out.
The classes have the same median, but class P is more spread out.
Class P's scores are less spread out than class Q's scores are.
Class Q has the highest score of all the students in the two classes.
questions.answer: The classes have the same median, but class P is more spread out.
questions.solution: Both medians are 70. Class P ranges from 50 to 90 and has an interquartile range of 20, while class Q ranges from 65 to 75 and has an interquartile range of 4. So class P is far more spread out, and its maximum of 90 is the highest.

solve.answer: The classes have the same median, but class P is more spread out.
solve.work: Both medians are 70. P: range 40, IQR 20; Q: range 10, IQR 4. So same median, P more spread. Highest score is P's 90, not Q's.

questions.stem: A scatterplot shows the age (x) and the resale value (y) of 30 used cars. The value tends to go down as the age goes up. How is this association described?
choices: Negative: as age increases, value tends to decrease.
Positive: as age increases, value tends to decrease.
Negative: as age increases, value tends to increase.
None: age and value are not related at all.
questions.answer: Negative: as age increases, value tends to decrease.
questions.solution: When y tends to go down as x goes up, the association is negative. A positive association means y tends to go up as x goes up.

solve.answer: Negative: as age increases, value tends to decrease.
solve.work: Value decreases as age increases: negative association, correctly described as 'as age increases, value tends to decrease'.

questions.skill: Build and label a display with technology
questions.stem: Which item is most important to include so that a reader can understand a scatterplot of height, in inches, and shoe size?
choices: Axis labels that name each variable and give its units
A three-dimensional effect added to every point on the plot
A bright background color placed behind the whole plot
A photograph of a shoe placed behind all of the points
questions.answer: Axis labels that name each variable and give its units
questions.solution: A reader needs to know what each axis shows and in what units. Decorations such as 3-D effects, bright backgrounds and pictures do not help, and can make the plot harder to read.

solve.answer: Axis labels that name each variable and give its units
solve.work: A reader needs to know what each axis is and its units. The other items are decoration that hinder reading.

questions.stem: A dot plot shows the number of pets owned by each of 20 students. The dots are: 0 pets, 4 dots; 1 pet, 7 dots; 2 pets, 5 dots; 3 pets, 3 dots; 4 pets, 1 dot. What percent of the students own exactly 1 pet?
questions.solution: Check that the dots add up: $4 + 7 + 5 + 3 + 1 = 20$. The column for 1 pet has 7 dots, so $7 \div 20 = 0.35$, which is 35 percent.

solve.work: Dots: 4+7+5+3+1 = 20, matching 20 students. Exactly 1 pet: 7 of 20 = 0.35 = 35%.

questions.skill: Build and label a display with technology
questions.stem: A teacher has quiz scores that are whole numbers from 0 to 99. She asks a spreadsheet for a histogram with bins 0 to 19, 20 to 39, and so on, each 20 scores wide. How many bins does the histogram have?
questions.solution: The scores 0 to 99 are 100 different whole numbers. Each bin holds 20 of them: 0 to 19, 20 to 39, 40 to 59, 60 to 79 and 80 to 99. That is $100 \div 20 = 5$ bins.

solve.work: Bins: 0-19, 20-39, 40-59, 60-79, 80-99. That covers 0 to 99 with 5 bins of 20.

questions.skill: Choose a display that fits the data and the purpose
questions.stem: A coach records the favorite sport of each of 40 students: soccer, tennis, swimming or track. Which display shows how many students chose each sport?
choices: A scatterplot with the sports on both axes
A bar graph with one bar for each sport
A line graph that joins the sports in order
A box plot of the sport names
questions.answer: A bar graph with one bar for each sport
questions.solution: The sports are categories, and we want a count for each. A bar graph with one bar per category does this.

solve.answer: A bar graph with one bar for each sport
solve.work: Counts of a categorical variable: a bar graph with one bar per sport.

questions.skill: Choose a display that fits the data and the purpose
questions.stem: Which display is best for showing what share of a 1,000 dollar monthly budget goes to each of 4 spending categories?
choices: A scatterplot of the four categories
A line graph of the four categories over time
A pie chart with one slice for each category
A histogram with one bin for each dollar
questions.answer: A pie chart with one slice for each category
questions.solution: The categories are parts of one whole, which is what a pie chart shows. The other displays are for relationships, trends or distributions.

solve.answer: A pie chart with one slice for each category
solve.work: Parts of a whole with 4 categories: a pie chart.

questions.skill: Choose a display that fits the data and the purpose
questions.stem: A histogram of 60 ages uses bins of width 10 that cover 0 to 9, 10 to 19, and so on, up to 50 to 59. How many bins does it have?
questions.solution: The bins start at 0, 10, 20, 30, 40 and 50. That is 6 bins.

questions.skill: Choose a display that fits the data and the purpose
questions.stem: A student records the noon temperature on each of 30 days in a row. Which display is best for showing how it changed from day to day?
choices: A pie chart with one slice for each of the 30 days
A bar graph with the days listed in a random order
A box plot of the day numbers
A line graph with the days in order along the axis
questions.answer: A line graph with the days in order along the axis
questions.solution: The data follow time, so a line graph with days in order shows the rise and fall. The other displays hide the order or are for parts of a whole.

solve.answer: A line graph with the days in order along the axis
solve.work: Change over time: a line graph with days in order.

questions.skill: Choose a display that fits the data and the purpose
questions.stem: Which data would you show in a histogram?
choices: The weights of 50 apples, in grams
The color of each of 50 cars
The favorite snack of each of 50 students
The name of each of 50 pets
questions.answer: The weights of 50 apples, in grams
questions.solution: A histogram groups numbers measured on a scale into bins. Colors, snacks and names are categories, which belong in a bar graph.

solve.answer: The weights of 50 apples, in grams
solve.work: A histogram needs numeric data: weights in grams.

questions.skill: Read the key features of a display
questions.stem: In a dot plot of the shoe sizes of 15 students, the tallest stack of dots is above size 7. What does this show?
choices: More students wear size 7 than any other.
The mean shoe size must be exactly 7.
Size 7 is the largest shoe size in the group.
Exactly 7 students have the same shoe size.
questions.answer: More students wear size 7 than any other.
questions.solution: The tallest stack marks the most common value, called the mode. It does not tell the mean or the largest value, or by itself how many students are in the stack.

solve.answer: More students wear size 7 than any other.
solve.work: The tallest stack is the mode: more students wear size 7 than any other size.

questions.skill: Read the key features of a display
questions.stem: A histogram of 25 plant heights has four bars. The first three bars have heights 5, 11 and 7. How tall is the fourth bar?
questions.solution: The bar heights add to 25. The first three add to 23, so the fourth is 25 - 23 = 2.

questions.skill: Read the key features of a display
questions.stem: The line in the middle of the box in a box plot shows which summary?
choices: The mean
The median
The mode
The range
questions.answer: The median
questions.solution: The line inside the box marks the median, the middle of the ordered values.

solve.answer: The median
solve.work: The line inside the box is the median.

questions.skill: Read the key features of a display
questions.stem: A line graph shows a plant's height each week: 4 cm in week 1, 7 cm in week 2, 11 cm in week 3 and 14 cm in week 4. How many centimeters did the plant grow from week 1 to week 4?
questions.solution: The height went from 4 cm to 14 cm, so the plant grew 10 cm.

questions.stem: Class A's quiz scores range from 4 to 10. Class B's scores range from 1 to 10. Which class has the larger range?
choices: Class A, with a range of 6
Class A, with a range of 10
Neither, since they have the same highest score
Class B, with a range of 9
questions.answer: Class B, with a range of 9
questions.solution: Range = highest - lowest. Class A: 10 - 4 = 6. Class B: 10 - 1 = 9. Class B has the larger range.

solve.answer: Class B, with a range of 9
solve.work: A: 10 - 4 = 6; B: 10 - 1 = 9. Class B, range 9.

questions.stem: Two groups of plants have the same mean height. Group P's heights are all between 20 and 22 cm. Group Q's heights are between 10 and 32 cm. Which statement is true?
choices: Group Q's heights are more spread out than group P's heights.
Group P's heights are more spread out than group Q's heights.
The two groups have the same spread, since the means match.
Group Q's tallest plant is shorter than group P's tallest plant.
questions.answer: Group Q's heights are more spread out than group P's heights.
questions.solution: Group P's heights span 2 cm and group Q's span 22 cm, so Q is more spread out. The same mean does not mean the same spread.

solve.answer: Group Q's heights are more spread out than group P's heights.
solve.work: Q spans 22 cm vs P 2 cm: Q is more spread out.

questions.stem: Which statistic is used to compare the centers of two distributions?
choices: The range
The median
The interquartile range
The standard deviation
questions.answer: The median
questions.solution: The median (and the mean) describe the center. The range, interquartile range and standard deviation describe spread.

solve.answer: The median
solve.work: The median measures center; the others measure spread.

questions.stem: In a scatterplot, the points slope upward from left to right. What does this tell you about the two variables?
choices: As one variable goes up, the other tends to go up too.
As one variable increases, the other tends to decrease.
The two variables are not related at all.
One variable always causes the other to change.
questions.answer: As one variable goes up, the other tends to go up too.
questions.solution: An upward slope is a positive association. A scatterplot shows association, not cause.

solve.answer: As one variable goes up, the other tends to go up too.
solve.work: Upward slope: positive association, both tend to rise together (not causation).

questions.stem: A data set records 4 variables for each of 50 students: height, weight, age and grade. How many data values are recorded in all?
questions.solution: Each student has 4 values, so 50 x 4 = 200.

questions.stem: The points in a scatterplot are scattered all over with no pattern. Which correlation is most likely?
questions.solution: No pattern means a correlation close to 0. The value 1.5 is impossible, because r is always between -1 and 1.

solve.work: No pattern: r near 0, i.e. 0.05 (1.5 is impossible).

questions.stem: A shop owner wants to use the temperature to predict the number of coats sold. Which variable is usually placed on the vertical axis of the scatterplot?
choices: The temperature
Both variables, one on top of the other
The number of coats sold
Neither, because scatterplots have only one axis
questions.answer: The number of coats sold
questions.solution: The variable being predicted goes on the vertical axis. Temperature is the explanatory variable and goes on the horizontal axis.

solve.answer: The number of coats sold
solve.work: Response variable (coats sold) goes on the vertical axis.

questions.stem: The points of a data set are (1, 2), (2, 4), (3, 6), (4, 20) and (5, 10). Which point does not fit the pattern of the others?
questions.solution: Except for (4, 20), each y is twice x: 2, 4, 6, 10. At x = 4 the pattern gives 8, but the point is at 20, so it is an outlier.

solve.work: Pattern y = 2x; (4, 20) breaks it (expected 8).

questions.skill: Build and label a display with technology
questions.stem: Which of these should every graph include so that it can be understood?
choices: Bright colors and a three-dimensional look
A title and labels on the axes, with units
The name of the person who made each bar
A different scale on the two axes of each graph
questions.answer: A title and labels on the axes, with units
questions.solution: Readers need to know what the graph shows and how it is measured. A title, axis labels and units do that.

solve.answer: A title and labels on the axes, with units
solve.work: A title and labeled axes with units.

questions.skill: Build and label a display with technology
questions.stem: A data table has 12 rows (people) and 5 columns (variables). A scatterplot uses 2 of the columns. How many columns are not shown in the scatterplot?
questions.solution: 5 - 2 = 3 columns are left out.

solve.work: 5 - 2 = 3 columns.

questions.skill: Build and label a display with technology
questions.stem: A spreadsheet makes a bar graph of the average temperature in each month, and its title is "Chart 1." What is the best next step?
choices: Keep the title because the tool chose it as the default.
Delete the title so that the graph has more room on the page.
Replace it with a title such as "Average Temperature by Month".
Change the title to the name of the spreadsheet program.
questions.answer: Replace it with a title such as "Average Temperature by Month".
questions.solution: A good title says what the graph shows. A default title tells the reader nothing.

solve.answer: Replace it with a title such as "Average Temperature by Month".
solve.work: Replace the default title with a descriptive one.

questions.skill: Build and label a display with technology
questions.stem: A line graph's vertical axis runs from 0 to 100 with a gridline every 20. Counting the gridlines at 0 and at 100, how many gridlines are there?
questions.solution: The gridlines are at 0, 20, 40, 60, 80 and 100. That is 6.

questions.skill: Read the key features of a display
questions.stem: A histogram of the commute times of 300 workers has a long tail stretching to the right. A few commutes are over 60 minutes, and most are under 20. Which statement describes it?
choices: It is skewed right, and its mean is probably below its median
It is skewed right, and its mean is probably above its median
It is skewed left, and its mean is probably below its median
It is symmetric, and its mean is probably about equal to its median
questions.answer: It is skewed right, and its mean is probably above its median
questions.solution: The long tail points to the right, so the distribution is skewed right. The few very long commutes pull the mean up more than the median, so the mean is greater than the median.

solve.answer: It is skewed right, and its mean is probably above its median
solve.work: A long right tail means skewed right; the few large values pull the mean up above the median.

questions.stem: Two box plots show the scores of Group A and Group B, and both have a median of 50. The box of Group A, from the first quartile to the third quartile, is short. The box of Group B is long. Which statement is correct?
choices: The middle half of Group A's scores is more spread out than that of Group B
Group B has the higher typical score, because its box is longer than the other
Group A has the lower typical score, because its box is shorter than the other
The middle half of Group B's scores is more spread out than that of Group A
questions.answer: The middle half of Group B's scores is more spread out than that of Group A
questions.solution: The box covers the middle half of the scores, so a longer box means a larger interquartile range and more spread. The medians are equal, so neither group has the higher typical score.

solve.answer: The middle half of Group B's scores is more spread out than that of Group A
solve.work: Box length is the IQR, the spread of the middle half. Longer box for B means B's middle half is more spread out. Medians are equal, so the 'typical score' options are wrong.

questions.skill: Choose a display that fits the data and the purpose
questions.stem: For 40 students you know the hours each one studied and the score each one got on a test. You want to see whether more studying goes with higher scores. Which display is best?
choices: A pie chart that splits the total hours studied into slices
A histogram that shows the test scores alone
A scatterplot of hours studied against test score
A bar graph with one bar for each student's name
questions.answer: A scatterplot of hours studied against test score
questions.solution: To see how two numerical variables are related, plot each student as a point with one value on each axis. The other displays show only one of the variables or do not show a relationship.

solve.answer: A scatterplot of hours studied against test score
solve.work: Two numerical variables per student, looking for association: scatterplot of hours vs score.

questions.skill: Choose a display that fits the data and the purpose
questions.stem: Which statement correctly says when to use a histogram instead of a bar graph?
choices: Use a histogram for categories like favorite colors, with a gap between the bars.
Use a histogram to show how two numerical variables are related.
Use a histogram when the parts of the data must add up to 100% of a whole.
Use a histogram for numbers grouped into intervals, such as test scores.
questions.answer: Use a histogram for numbers grouped into intervals, such as test scores.
questions.solution: A histogram shows how numerical data are distributed across intervals, so its bars touch. A bar graph is for categories. A scatterplot shows how two numerical variables are related, and a pie chart shows parts of a whole.

solve.answer: Use a histogram for numbers grouped into intervals, such as test scores.
solve.work: Histograms show numerical data grouped into intervals (no gaps). Categories use bar graphs, parts of a whole use pie charts, two variables use scatterplots.

questions.skill: Read the key features of a display
questions.stem: A box plot of delivery times, in minutes, shows these values: minimum 12, first quartile 20, median 26, third quartile 34, maximum 60. What is the interquartile range, in minutes?
questions.solution: The interquartile range is the third quartile minus the first quartile: 34 - 20 = 14 minutes.

questions.skill: Read the key features of a display
questions.stem: A histogram of household incomes has its tallest bars at the left and a long tail that stretches far to the right. Which description is correct?
choices: The shape is skewed right, and the mean is smaller than the median.
The shape is skewed left, and the mean is greater than the median.
The shape is symmetric, and the mean is equal to the median.
The shape is skewed right, and the mean is greater than the median.
questions.answer: The shape is skewed right, and the mean is greater than the median.
questions.solution: A long tail to the right is called skewed right. The few very high incomes in the tail pull the mean up more than the median, so the mean is greater than the median.

solve.answer: The shape is skewed right, and the mean is greater than the median.
solve.work: Bulk on the left with a long right tail is skewed right; the tail pulls the mean above the median.

questions.stem: Trip times in minutes. By bus: minimum 8, first quartile 12, median 15, third quartile 20, maximum 35. By walking: minimum 5, first quartile 7, median 9, third quartile 11, maximum 15. How many minutes larger is the interquartile range of the bus times than that of the walking times?
questions.solution: Bus IQR = 20 - 12 = 8. Walking IQR = 11 - 7 = 4. The difference is 8 - 4 = 4 minutes.

solve.work: Bus IQR = 20 - 12 = 8. Walking IQR = 11 - 7 = 4. 8 - 4 = 4.

questions.stem: Group 1 has mean 48, median 48 and standard deviation 5. Group 2 has mean 55, median 40 and standard deviation 25. Which statement is best supported by these numbers?
choices: Group 2 is less variable than group 1, because its mean is larger.
Group 1 is more variable than group 2, because its standard deviation is smaller.
Group 2 is probably skewed right, because its mean is far above its median.
Group 1 must be skewed, because its mean and its median are equal.
questions.answer: Group 2 is probably skewed right, because its mean is far above its median.
questions.solution: When the mean is far above the median, a few high values are pulling the mean up, which is the sign of a right-skewed distribution. A larger standard deviation means more variability, so group 2 varies more. A mean equal to the median suggests symmetry.

solve.answer: Group 2 is probably skewed right, because its mean is far above its median.
solve.work: Group 2's mean (55) is well above its median (40) with a large SD: likely right skew. A and B confuse variability with mean or invert SD; C is false (equal mean and median suggests symmetry).

questions.stem: Which value of the correlation $r$ describes the strongest negative linear association?
questions.solution: A negative association has a negative $r$, and the closer $r$ is to $-1$, the stronger it is. Of the negative values, $-0.92$ is closest to $-1$. The value 0.95 is strong but positive.

solve.work: Strongest negative: the negative r with the largest magnitude, -0.92.

questions.stem: A scatterplot shows price (y) against size (x) for houses, with points colored by neighborhood, A or B. In both colors the points rise as size increases, and the B points sit higher on the graph than the A points. What does this suggest?
choices: Size does not affect the price of homes in either neighborhood.
For homes of the same size, those in neighborhood A tend to cost more than those in B.
For homes of the same size, those in neighborhood B tend to cost more than those in A.
Every home in neighborhood B is larger than every home in neighborhood A.
questions.answer: For homes of the same size, those in neighborhood B tend to cost more than those in A.
questions.solution: Both groups rise with size, so larger homes cost more in both. At any given size the B points are higher, so B homes tend to cost more. The graph says nothing about every home being larger.

solve.answer: For homes of the same size, those in neighborhood B tend to cost more than those in A.
solve.work: Both groups rise with size; B points are higher at comparable sizes, so B homes cost more for the same size.

questions.skill: Build and label a display with technology
questions.stem: A tool counts 40 values into four groups: 6, 14, 12 and 8. A pie chart is drawn from these counts. What angle, in degrees, should the slice for the group of 14 have?
questions.solution: The group of 14 is 14 / 40 of all the values, and the full circle is 360 degrees, so the angle is 14 / 40 x 360 = 126 degrees.

questions.skill: Build and label a display with technology
questions.stem: A bar graph shows sales of 410, 420, 415 and 425 units in four weeks. Its vertical axis starts at 400, so the bars look very different in height. What is the best fix?
choices: Make the bars much thicker and add gridlines so the differences are easier to see.
Start the vertical axis at 0 so that the bar heights are proportional to the values.
Remove the axis labels completely so the reader focuses on the bar heights alone.
Change the display to a pie chart in which all four slices have exactly equal size.
questions.answer: Start the vertical axis at 0 so that the bar heights are proportional to the values.
questions.solution: The height of a bar should be proportional to the value it stands for. An axis that starts at 400 exaggerates small differences. Starting at 0 shows that the four weeks are really quite similar.

solve.answer: Start the vertical axis at 0 so that the bar heights are proportional to the values.
solve.work: A truncated axis exaggerates small differences; starting at 0 makes bar heights proportional to the values.

questions.skill: Choose a display that fits the data and the purpose
questions.stem: A teacher has the number of books read last month by each of 12 students, all between 0 and 8. Which display shows each student's value and the shape of such a small data set?
choices: A pie chart with 12 slices, one for each student
A dot plot with one dot per student at that value
A line graph that joins the students in alphabetical order
A histogram with a single bin that runs from 0 to 8
questions.answer: A dot plot with one dot per student at that value
questions.solution: For a small set of numbers, a dot plot shows every value and the shape. A pie chart or a line in alphabetical order is meaningless, and one bin hides the shape.

solve.answer: A dot plot with one dot per student at that value
solve.work: Small numeric data set: a dot plot shows each value and the shape.

questions.skill: Choose a display that fits the data and the purpose
questions.stem: A school asks 120 students in grades 6, 7 and 8 which of 3 lunch choices they prefer. Which display best compares the lunch preferences across the three grades?
choices: A scatterplot of grade against lunch choice
A histogram that shows only the grades
A bar graph with three bars for each grade
A line graph of the lunch choices over time
questions.answer: A bar graph with three bars for each grade
questions.solution: Both variables are categories, so grouped bars compare the choices within each grade side by side.

solve.answer: A bar graph with three bars for each grade
solve.work: Two categorical variables: a grouped bar graph, three bars per grade.

questions.skill: Choose a display that fits the data and the purpose
questions.stem: A store records its monthly sales of coats and of sandals for 24 months. Which display best shows how both products' sales changed over time?
choices: A pie chart with one slice for each of the months
A histogram of all the sales values of both products together
A bar graph of the total sales for each product
A line graph with a line for coats and a line for sandals
questions.answer: A line graph with a line for coats and a line for sandals
questions.solution: Two time series are shown together by two lines on the same axes. The other displays lose the time order.

solve.answer: A line graph with a line for coats and a line for sandals
solve.work: Two time series: a line graph with a line per product.

questions.skill: Choose a display that fits the data and the purpose
questions.stem: A group of 20 people, a group of 50 people and a group of 80 people each choose between several options. To compare the groups fairly, a display shows the percent of each group choosing each option instead of the counts. In the group of 50, 15 people chose option X. What percent of the group chose option X?
questions.solution: 15 out of 50 is 0.3, which is 30%. Percents make groups of different sizes comparable; counts do not.

questions.skill: Choose a display that fits the data and the purpose
questions.stem: A pie chart is drawn for a survey with 12 answer choices. Why is a pie chart a poor display here?
choices: Many slices are small and hard to compare, so a bar graph is better.
A pie chart can show only data that are numbers measured on a scale.
A pie chart needs exactly 12 slices of equal size.
A pie chart can be used only if the answers are in order of time.
questions.answer: Many slices are small and hard to compare, so a bar graph is better.
questions.solution: With many categories the slices get tiny and are hard to compare. A bar graph lets us compare the lengths easily.

solve.answer: Many slices are small and hard to compare, so a bar graph is better.
solve.work: With 12 categories many slices are thin and hard to compare; a bar graph is better.

questions.skill: Read the key features of a display
questions.stem: In a box plot of 80 test scores, a quarter of the scores lie from the minimum up to the first quartile. How many scores is that?
questions.solution: One quarter of 80 is 20 scores.

solve.work: A quarter of 80 = 20.

questions.skill: Read the key features of a display
questions.stem: A histogram of scores on an easy quiz has most scores near the top, between 8 and 10 out of 10, and a few low scores. Which description is correct?
choices: It is skewed left, and the mean is greater than the median.
It is skewed right, and the mean is less than the median.
It is skewed left, and the mean is less than the median.
It is symmetric, and the mean equals the median.
questions.answer: It is skewed left, and the mean is less than the median.
questions.solution: A tail toward the low values means skewed left. The few low scores pull the mean below the median.

solve.answer: It is skewed left, and the mean is less than the median.
solve.work: Tail toward low scores: skewed left; the low values pull the mean below the median.

questions.skill: Read the key features of a display
questions.stem: A histogram of 20 values has four bars with heights 3, 8, 6 and 3. What percent of the values are in the first two bars?
questions.solution: The first two bars hold 3 + 8 = 11 values. 11 out of 20 is 55%.

questions.skill: Read the key features of a display
questions.stem: In a box plot made by a computer, a single dot appears far above the end of the upper whisker. What does the dot represent?
choices: The mean of the data, shown above the whisker
The most common value, shown above the whisker
The largest value that is not an outlier
A possible outlier, a value far above the rest
questions.answer: A possible outlier, a value far above the rest
questions.solution: Computer box plots mark values beyond the fences as separate dots. The whisker ends at the largest value that is not an outlier.

solve.answer: A possible outlier, a value far above the rest
solve.work: A separate dot beyond the whisker marks a possible outlier.

questions.stem: Group A has first quartile 20 and third quartile 35. Group B has first quartile 28 and third quartile 34. How many times as large is the interquartile range of A as that of B?
questions.solution: IQR of A = 35 - 20 = 15. IQR of B = 34 - 28 = 6. The ratio is 15 / 6 = 2.5.
