questions.stem: A simulation using random samples of 100 people gets a margin of error of about $0.08$. If the simulation uses random samples of 400 people instead, about what will the margin of error be?
questions.solution: Quadrupling the sample size cuts the margin of error to about half, because it shrinks with the square root of the sample size: $0.08 \div 2 = 0.04$. It does not fall to a quarter, and it does not stay the same or grow.

solve.work: Margin of error is proportional to 1/sqrt(n). n x 4 -> margin / 2 = 0.08/2 = 0.04. D.

questions.skill: Testing a difference between groups by randomization
questions.stem: In a randomization test, the scores were shuffled 1,000 times. A difference in means as large as the one actually observed happened in 36 of the shuffles. What proportion of the shuffles gave a difference that large? Give the answer as a decimal.
questions.solution: The proportion is $\frac{36}{1000} = 0.036$.

questions.skill: Testing a difference between groups by randomization
questions.stem: In a randomization test comparing two study methods, the scores were shuffled 1,000 times, and 410 of the shuffles gave a difference at least as large as the one observed. Using 0.05 as the cutoff, what is the conclusion?
choices: The difference is convincing, because 410 is a large number of shuffles in the test.
The difference is not convincing, because one this large happens by chance about 41% of the time.
The difference is convincing, because the observed difference between the means is not 0.
The difference is not convincing, because the two methods differ by 41% in their scores.
questions.answer: The difference is not convincing, because one this large happens by chance about 41% of the time.
questions.solution: The proportion of shuffles at least this extreme is $\frac{410}{1000} = 0.41$, which is much larger than 0.05. A difference this big often happens by chance alone, so it is not convincing evidence that the methods differ.

solve.answer: The difference is not convincing, because one this large happens by chance about 41% of the time.
solve.work: 410/1000 = 0.41 > 0.05, so a difference this large is common by chance; not convincing. D misreads 41% as a score difference. A.

questions.skill: Designing and running a simulation with random digits
questions.stem: A basketball player makes 35% of her shots. A student simulates one shot by picking a two-digit number from 00 to 99, each equally likely. Which rule matches the 35% chance of a made shot?
choices: 00 to 34 is a made shot, and 35 to 99 is a miss
00 to 35 is a made shot, and 36 to 99 is a miss
35 to 99 is a made shot, and 00 to 34 is a miss
00 to 49 is a made shot, and 50 to 99 is a miss
questions.answer: 00 to 34 is a made shot, and 35 to 99 is a miss
questions.solution: There are 100 two-digit numbers from 00 to 99. A 35% chance means 35 of them should be a made shot. The numbers 00 to 34 are exactly 35 numbers. 00 to 35 is 36 numbers (36%), 35 to 99 is 65 numbers (65%), and 00 to 49 is 50 numbers (50%).

solve.answer: 00 to 34 is a made shot, and 35 to 99 is a miss
solve.work: 00 to 99 is 100 equally likely numbers. 00 to 34 is 35 numbers = 35%. Option B is 65 numbers, C is 36 numbers, D is 50 numbers. So A.

questions.skill: Role of probability in modeling random processes
questions.stem: A student flips a coin and records the proportion of heads after 10, 100, 1,000 and 10,000 flips. Which pattern is most likely?
choices: The proportion varies a lot at first, and then settles close to 0.5
The proportion becomes exactly 0.5 after 10,000 flips and stays exactly there
The numbers of heads and tails become exactly equal by 10,000 flips
The proportion moves farther from 0.5 as the number of flips grows
questions.answer: The proportion varies a lot at first, and then settles close to 0.5
questions.solution: With few flips the proportion can be far from 0.5. As the number of flips grows, the proportion tends to settle near 0.5 (the law of large numbers), though it need not be exactly 0.5.

solve.answer: The proportion varies a lot at first, and then settles close to 0.5
solve.work: Law of large numbers: varies early, settles near 0.5.

questions.skill: Role of probability in modeling random processes
questions.stem: A fair six-sided die is rolled 600 times. About how many times is the number rolled expected to be greater than 4?
questions.solution: A number greater than 4 is a 5 or a 6, so the probability is $\frac{2}{6}$. The expected count is $600 \times \frac{2}{6} = 200$.

questions.skill: Role of probability in modeling random processes
questions.stem: In a school, 40 percent of the students have a pet and 25 percent play an instrument. Assume that having a pet and playing an instrument are independent. What is the probability that a randomly chosen student has a pet and plays an instrument? Give the answer as a decimal.
questions.solution: For independent events, multiply: $0.4 \times 0.25 = 0.1$.

questions.skill: Role of probability in modeling random processes
questions.stem: Why do statisticians simulate a chance situation instead of always calculating its probability?
choices: A simulation always gives the exact probability, while a calculation can only ever give an estimate
A simulation needs no random numbers at all, because the computer already knows the answer to give
Some situations are too complicated to calculate exactly, but many random trials give an estimate
A calculation cannot be used for coins or dice, which can only ever be studied by using a simulation
questions.answer: Some situations are too complicated to calculate exactly, but many random trials give an estimate
questions.solution: For complicated situations, working out the exact probability can be very hard. Repeating the random process many times and counting gives an estimate that gets better with more trials.

solve.answer: Some situations are too complicated to calculate exactly, but many random trials give an estimate
solve.work: Simulation estimates probabilities too complex to compute.

questions.skill: Role of probability in modeling random processes
questions.stem: Of 200 students, 80 play a sport, 50 play music and 20 do both. One student is chosen at random. What is the probability that the student does neither? Give the answer as a decimal.
questions.solution: Students who do at least one: $80 + 50 - 20 = 110$. Students who do neither: $200 - 110 = 90$. The probability is $\frac{90}{200} = 0.45$.

solve.work: Sport or music: 80+50-20=110; neither 90/200=0.45.

questions.skill: Designing and running a simulation with random digits
questions.stem: A student uses two-digit numbers from 00 to 99, each equally likely, to simulate an event with probability 0.35. Which assignment is correct?

questions.skill: Designing and running a simulation with random digits
questions.stem: Three outcomes A, B and C are equally likely. A student has random digits 0 to 9, each equally likely. Which plan simulates one outcome correctly?

Digits 0, 1, 2 mean A; 3, 4, 5 mean B; 6, 7, 8, 9 mean C; every digit that comes up is used
Digits 0 to 3 mean A; 4 to 6 mean B; 7 to 9 mean C; every digit that comes up is used
Digits 1 to 3 mean A; 4 to 6 mean B; 7 to 9 mean C; a 0 always means B

questions.skill: Designing and running a simulation with random digits

questions.stem: A spinner has three sectors with probabilities $\frac{1}{2}$, $\frac{1}{4}$ and $\frac{1}{4}$. A student uses random two-digit numbers from 00 to 99, each equally likely, giving the sectors the numbers in that order. Which assignment is correct?

00 to 49 for the first sector, 50 to 79 for the second, and 80 to 99 for the third

questions.skill: Estimating a probability or mean from simulated trials
questions.stem: A simulation of 20 trials recorded the number of successes in each trial: 0 successes in 6 trials, 1 success in 9 trials and 2 successes in 5 trials. Estimate the mean number of successes per trial. Give the answer as a decimal.
questions.solution: The total number of successes is $0(6) + 1(9) + 2(5) = 19$ over 20 trials. The mean is $19 \div 20 = 0.95$.

questions.skill: Estimating a probability or mean from simulated trials
questions.stem: A student's simulation of 50 trials estimated a probability of 0.30. Which change most likely makes the estimate closer to the true probability?
choices: Run the same 50 trials again and keep whichever of the two estimates is larger
Run many more trials, such as 5,000, and use the proportion from all of them
Use fewer trials, so that the digits are easier to count without making errors
Change the rule so that the event is more likely to occur on each trial
questions.answer: Run many more trials, such as 5,000, and use the proportion from all of them
questions.solution: Estimates from more trials vary less from the true probability. Keeping the larger of two estimates is biased, fewer trials are less accurate, and changing the rule changes the situation being modeled.

solve.answer: Run many more trials, such as 5,000, and use the proportion from all of them
solve.work: More trials reduce sampling variability.

questions.skill: Estimating a probability or mean from simulated trials
questions.stem: In a simulation of 25 trials, the estimated probability of an event was 0.32. In how many trials did the event happen?
questions.solution: The estimate is successes divided by trials, so successes $= 0.32 \times 25 = 8$.

questions.skill: Estimating a probability or mean from simulated trials
questions.stem: A student simulates flipping a fair coin 3 times in each of 12 trials and records the number of heads: 3, 1, 2, 0, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3, 2, 1, 3. Estimate the probability of getting at least one tail in 3 flips.
questions.solution: At least one tail means fewer than 3 heads. The number 3 appears 4 times, so the other $12 - 4 = 8$ trials had at least one tail. The estimate is $\frac{8}{12} = \frac{2}{3}$.

solve.work: At least one tail = fewer than 3 heads. Four trials had 3 heads; 8 of 12 = 2/3.

questions.skill: Margin of error of a simulation-based estimate
questions.stem: A poll of 1,000 residents of a city finds that 45 percent support a plan, with a margin of error of 3 percentage points. The city has 20,000 residents. Using the margin of error, what is the largest plausible number of residents who support the plan?
questions.solution: The largest plausible percent is $45 + 3 = 48$ percent. Then $0.48 \times 20000 = 9600$ residents.

solve.work: Upper plausible 48%; 0.48*20000=9600.

questions.skill: Margin of error of a simulation-based estimate
questions.stem: A simulation-based margin of error from random samples of 100 people is 0.09. By what should the sample size be multiplied to cut the margin of error to 0.03?
choices: Multiply it by 9
Multiply it by 3
Multiply it by 6
Multiply it by 27
questions.answer: Multiply it by 9
questions.solution: The margin of error is proportional to $\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}$. To cut it to one third, $\sqrt{n}$ must triple, so $n$ must be multiplied by $3^2 = 9$.

solve.answer: Multiply it by 9
solve.work: MOE ~ 1/sqrt(n); divide MOE by 3 needs n times 9.

questions.skill: Margin of error of a simulation-based estimate
questions.stem: A random sample of 2,500 people finds that 50 percent favor a plan, so $p = 0.5$. Use the formula margin of error $= 2\sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}}$ with $n = 2500$. What is the margin of error? Give the answer as a decimal.

questions.skill: Margin of error of a simulation-based estimate
questions.stem: A school claims that 60 percent of its seniors go on to college. A random-sample poll of seniors finds 55 percent, with a margin of error of 6 percentage points. Which statement is best?
choices: The claim is false, since the sample result of 55 percent is not equal to 60 percent
The claim is proven, since 60 percent is inside the interval from 49 to 61 percent
The claim is false, since the margin of error of 6 points is more than the 5-point gap
The claim is plausible, since 60 percent is inside the interval of 49 to 61 percent
questions.answer: The claim is plausible, since 60 percent is inside the interval of 49 to 61 percent
questions.solution: The interval of plausible values is $55 \pm 6$, which is 49 to 61 percent. The claimed 60 percent is inside it, so the data are consistent with the claim, although they do not prove it.

solve.answer: The claim is plausible, since 60 percent is inside the interval of 49 to 61 percent
solve.work: Interval 49-61 contains 60: claim plausible, not proven.

questions.skill: Margin of error of a simulation-based estimate
questions.stem: The sample proportion from a simulation is 0.58, and the lower end of its interval of plausible values is 0.52. The interval is centered on the sample proportion. What is the upper end of the interval? Give the answer as a decimal.
questions.solution: The margin of error is $0.58 - 0.52 = 0.06$, so the upper end is $0.58 + 0.06 = 0.64$.

questions.skill: Testing a difference between groups by randomization
questions.stem: In a randomization test, 2 percent of the shuffles gave a difference at least as large as the one observed. Using a cutoff of 5 percent, what is the best conclusion?
choices: The difference is likely to be due to chance alone, so there is no evidence that the groups differ
The difference is certain to be real, because only 2 percent of the shuffles were as large
The difference is unlikely to be due to chance alone, so there is evidence that the groups differ
The groups are the same, because the shuffles rarely gave exactly the observed difference
questions.answer: The difference is unlikely to be due to chance alone, so there is evidence that the groups differ
questions.solution: 2 percent is below the 5 percent cutoff, so a difference this large would be unusual by chance alone. That is evidence of a real difference, though not certainty.

solve.answer: The difference is unlikely to be due to chance alone, so there is evidence that the groups differ
solve.work: 2% < 5%: evidence that groups differ.

questions.skill: Testing a difference between groups by randomization
questions.stem: In a randomization test, the observed difference in means is 3. Ten shuffles gave these differences in means: $-1$, 4, 0, 3.5, $-2$, 5, 1, $-3$, 2 and 3. How many of the ten shuffles gave a difference of 3 or more?
questions.solution: The differences that are 3 or more are 4, 3.5, 5 and 3. That is 4 shuffles.

solve.work: At least 3: 4, 3.5, 5, 3 = 4 shuffles.

questions.skill: Testing a difference between groups by randomization
questions.stem: Eight scores are 4, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 12 and 14. In one shuffle, group X gets the scores 4, 6, 12 and 14, and group Y gets the other four scores. What is the difference between the means, X minus Y? Give the answer as a decimal.
questions.solution: Group X: $\frac{4 + 6 + 12 + 14}{4} = 9$. Group Y has 7, 8, 9 and 10: $\frac{34}{4} = 8.5$. The difference is $9 - 8.5 = 0.5$.

questions.skill: Testing a difference between groups by randomization
questions.stem: Four randomization tests each used 1,000 shuffles. Which test gives the strongest evidence that its two groups differ?
choices: The test in which 40 of the 1,000 shuffles gave a difference at least as large as the observed one
The test in which 200 of the 1,000 shuffles gave a difference at least as large as the observed one
The test in which 3 of the 1,000 shuffles gave a difference at least as large as the observed one
The test in which 500 of the 1,000 shuffles gave a difference at least as large as the observed one
questions.answer: The test in which 3 of the 1,000 shuffles gave a difference at least as large as the observed one
questions.solution: The fewer shuffles that give a difference as large as the observed one, the harder it is to explain the difference by chance alone. 3 of 1,000 is the smallest.

solve.answer: The test in which 3 of the 1,000 shuffles gave a difference at least as large as the observed one
solve.work: Smallest proportion 3/1000 is strongest evidence.

questions.skill: Role of probability in modeling random processes
questions.stem: Two students each simulate the same chance situation 100 times, using the same fair rules. One student's estimate of the probability is $0.46$ and the other's is $0.52$. What best explains the difference?
choices: Random processes vary from one set of trials to the next, even when the rules are the same.
One student must have made an arithmetic mistake, since the same rules always give the same result.
The true probability changed between the two simulations because the trials were done at different times.
The simulation with the larger estimate is always the more accurate one.
questions.answer: Random processes vary from one set of trials to the next, even when the rules are the same.
questions.solution: Each simulation is a different random sample of outcomes, so estimates differ by chance. Neither need be wrong, the true probability has not changed, and a larger estimate is not automatically better.

solve.answer: Random processes vary from one set of trials to the next, even when the rules are the same.
solve.work: Simulations are random, so two runs of 100 trials naturally give different estimates (sampling variability). B.

questions.skill: Role of probability in modeling random processes
questions.stem: Each seed independently sprouts with probability $0.8$. A gardener plants 3 seeds. What is the probability that at least one seed sprouts? Give the answer as a decimal.
questions.solution: "At least one" is the opposite of "none". Each seed fails with probability $0.2$, so none sprout with probability $0.2^3 = 0.008$. Then $1 - 0.008 = 0.992$.

solve.work: P(none sprout) = 0.2^3 = 0.008. P(at least one) = 1 - 0.008 = 0.992.

questions.skill: Designing and running a simulation with random digits
questions.stem: A basketball player makes 80% of her free throws, each shot independent of the others. A student wants to estimate the probability that she makes at least 3 of her next 4 shots, using random digits from 0 to 9. Which simulation plan is correct?
choices: Digits 0 to 7 mean a make and 8 and 9 mean a miss; use 1 digit per trial and count trials that are makes
Digits 0 to 3 mean a make and 4 to 9 mean a miss; use 4 digits per trial and count trials with at least 3 makes
Digits 0 to 7 mean a make and 8 and 9 mean a miss; use 4 digits per trial and count trials with all 4 makes
Digits 0 to 7 mean a make and 8 and 9 mean a miss; use 4 digits per trial and count trials with at least 3 makes
questions.answer: Digits 0 to 7 mean a make and 8 and 9 mean a miss; use 4 digits per trial and count trials with at least 3 makes
questions.solution: Eight of the ten digits (0 to 7) give an 80% chance of a make. One trial is 4 shots, so it needs 4 digits, and the event is at least 3 makes. Dividing the number of such trials by the total number of trials gives the estimate. The other plans use the wrong chance, a single shot or the wrong event.

solve.answer: Digits 0 to 7 mean a make and 8 and 9 mean a miss; use 4 digits per trial and count trials with at least 3 makes
solve.work: Make probability 0.8 needs 8 of 10 digits (0-7 make), 4 digits per trial for 4 shots, count trials with at least 3 makes. B counts only 4 makes, C uses 1 digit, D uses 0.4. A.

questions.skill: Designing and running a simulation with random digits
questions.stem: Each seed sprouts with probability $0.3$. A student simulates planting 5 seeds with 5 random digits: 0, 1 and 2 mean a seed sprouts, and 3 through 9 mean it does not. Four trials used these digits. Trial 1: 8 5 0 7 4. Trial 2: 2 1 9 6 3. Trial 3: 7 8 9 4 5. Trial 4: 1 0 2 8 6. In how many of the four trials did at least 2 seeds sprout?
questions.solution: Count the digits 0, 1 or 2 in each trial. Trial 1: one (the 0). Trial 2: two (2 and 1). Trial 3: none. Trial 4: three (1, 0 and 2). Trials 2 and 4 have at least 2 sprouts, so the answer is 2.

solve.work: Sprout digits 0,1,2. T1: 8 5 0 7 4 -> 1 sprout. T2: 2 1 9 6 3 -> 2 sprouts. T3: 7 8 9 4 5 -> 0. T4: 1 0 2 8 6 -> 3 sprouts. Trials with at least 2: T2, T4 = 2.

questions.skill: Estimating a probability or mean from simulated trials
questions.stem: A student simulated a situation 40 times and recorded the number of successes each time. There were 0 successes in 6 trials, 1 success in 14 trials, 2 successes in 12 trials and 3 successes in 8 trials. Estimate the mean number of successes per trial. Give the answer as a decimal.
questions.solution: The total number of successes is $0 \times 6 + 1 \times 14 + 2 \times 12 + 3 \times 8 = 0 + 14 + 24 + 24 = 62$. Divide by the 40 trials: $\frac{62}{40} = 1.55$.

questions.skill: Estimating a probability or mean from simulated trials
questions.stem: A student simulated flipping a fair coin 5 times and recorded the number of heads, 250 times. The results: 0 heads in 8 trials, 1 head in 42, 2 heads in 80, 3 heads in 70, 4 heads in 40 and 5 heads in 10. Estimate the probability of getting at least 4 heads in 5 flips. Give the answer as a decimal.
questions.solution: "At least 4 heads" means 4 heads or 5 heads: $40 + 10 = 50$ trials out of 250. The estimate is $\frac{50}{250} = 0.2$.

questions.skill: Margin of error of a simulation-based estimate
questions.stem: A random sample of 400 voters finds that 20% of them favor a plan, so $p = 0.2$. Use the formula margin of error $= 2\sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}}$ with $n = 400$. What is the margin of error? Give the answer as a decimal.
questions.solution: First $p(1-p) = 0.2 \times 0.8 = 0.16$. Then $\frac{0.16}{400} = 0.0004$, and $\sqrt{0.0004} = 0.02$. The margin of error is $2 \times 0.02 = 0.04$.

questions.skill: Margin of error of a simulation-based estimate
questions.stem: A simulation-based estimate says the mean wait at a clinic is $14.2$ minutes, with a margin of error of $1.1$ minutes. The clinic claims the true mean wait is $16$ minutes. What can be said?
choices: The estimate does not support the claim, because 16 is outside the interval from 13.1 to 15.3 minutes.
The estimate supports the claim, because 16 minutes is within 2 minutes of the estimate of 14.2 minutes.
The estimate supports the claim, because a margin of error of 1.1 minutes is small enough to ignore.
The estimate does not support the claim, because the claim of 16 is not equal to the estimate of 14.2.
questions.answer: The estimate does not support the claim, because 16 is outside the interval from 13.1 to 15.3 minutes.
questions.solution: The plausible values are $14.2 \pm 1.1$, from 13.1 to 15.3 minutes. The claimed 16 minutes lies outside this interval, so the data do not support it. Being close, or being merely different from the sample mean, is not the test.

solve.answer: The estimate does not support the claim, because 16 is outside the interval from 13.1 to 15.3 minutes.
solve.work: Interval 14.2 +/- 1.1 = 13.1 to 15.3. 16 lies outside it, so the claim is not plausible given the estimate. C gives the wrong reason (not equal is insufficient). A.

questions.skill: Testing a difference between groups by randomization
questions.stem: A randomization test compared a new study method with the usual one, using the difference in means (new minus usual). The observed difference was 5 points. In 2,000 shuffles, 90 shuffles gave a difference of 5 or more and 110 shuffles gave a difference of $-5$ or less. What proportion of the shuffles gave a difference at least as extreme as the observed one, in either direction? Give the answer as a decimal.
questions.solution: Differences at least as extreme in either direction are those of 5 or more and those of $-5$ or less: $90 + 110 = 200$ shuffles. The proportion is $\frac{200}{2000} = 0.1$.

questions.skill: Testing a difference between groups by randomization
questions.stem: A school randomly assigns 60 students to use a tutoring app or not. A randomization test finds that a difference in mean scores as large as the one observed would happen by chance in only 1% of shuffles. Which conclusion is best supported?
choices: The app will raise the scores of all students in every school, since the test result was so strong.
There is only a 1% chance that the app has any effect on the scores of the students.
The app has no effect on scores, because the observed difference could have happened by chance.
The app very likely caused the higher scores here, because students were assigned at random.
questions.answer: The app very likely caused the higher scores here, because students were assigned at random.
questions.solution: A difference this large is rare when the app does nothing, and random assignment means the groups were alike to begin with, so the app is the likely cause here. This says nothing about all students everywhere, 1% is not the chance that the app works, and the result argues against "no effect".

solve.answer: The app very likely caused the higher scores here, because students were assigned at random.
solve.work: 1% is small, so chance alone is an unlikely explanation; random assignment allows a causal conclusion for these students. A misreads the p-value, B over-generalises, C contradicts the evidence. D.

questions.skill: Role of probability in modeling random processes
questions.stem: A coin is flipped 20 times and lands heads 14 times. A student says that a fair coin could not do that. Which response is best?
choices: That is impossible for a fair coin, because a fair coin always gives 10 heads in 20 flips
That proves the coin is unfair, because the proportion of heads in any set of flips must equal the probability
That is unlikely but possible for a fair coin; simulating many sets of 20 flips shows how often it happens
That is certain for any fair coin, because results of random processes only vary a little
questions.answer: That is unlikely but possible for a fair coin; simulating many sets of 20 flips shows how often it happens
questions.solution: A fair coin can give 14 or more heads in 20 flips (about 6 percent of the time). The way to judge how unusual it is would be to simulate many sets of 20 fair flips and count how often it happens.

solve.answer: That is unlikely but possible for a fair coin; simulating many sets of 20 flips shows how often it happens
solve.work: 14 of 20 is unlikely but possible for a fair coin; simulation shows how often.

questions.skill: Role of probability in modeling random processes
questions.stem: A fair six-sided die is rolled 4 times. What is the probability of getting at least one 6?
questions.solution: The probability of no 6 in 4 rolls is $\left(\frac{5}{6}\right)^4 = \frac{625}{1296}$. So the probability of at least one 6 is $1 - \frac{625}{1296} = \frac{671}{1296}$.

questions.skill: Role of probability in modeling random processes
questions.stem: Events A and B are independent, with $P(A) = 0.6$ and $P(B) = 0.5$. What is the probability that A or B (or both) happens? Give the answer as a decimal.

questions.skill: Role of probability in modeling random processes
questions.stem: On 100 days when a forecaster said there was a 30 percent chance of rain, it rained on 28 of the days. Which conclusion is best?
choices: This is consistent with the forecasts, since about 30 rainy days are expected and chance varies
The forecaster was wrong, because it should have rained on exactly 30 of those 100 days with the forecast
The forecaster was right on the 28 days that had rain and wrong on the other 72 days that did not have rain
The forecaster was wrong, because every forecast should have been either 0 percent or 100 percent
questions.answer: This is consistent with the forecasts, since about 30 rainy days are expected and chance varies
questions.solution: With a 30 percent chance on each of 100 days, about 30 rainy days are expected, and 28 is a normal amount of variation. A probability forecast is not wrong just because it did not give 0 or 100 percent.

solve.answer: This is consistent with the forecasts, since about 30 rainy days are expected and chance varies
solve.work: 28 is close to the expected 30; consistent with chance variation.

questions.skill: Role of probability in modeling random processes
questions.stem: In a game, a player pays 2 points to spin a spinner. The spinner gives a prize of 10 points with probability 0.1, a prize of 4 points with probability 0.3, and nothing otherwise. What is the expected net gain per spin, in points, after paying the 2 points?
questions.solution: The expected prize is $10(0.1) + 4(0.3) + 0(0.6) = 1 + 1.2 = 2.2$ points. After paying 2 points, the expected net gain is $2.2 - 2 = 0.2$ points per spin.

solve.work: Expected prize 10(0.1)+4(0.3)=2.2; minus 2 = 0.2.

questions.skill: Designing and running a simulation with random digits
questions.stem: The bus arrives on time with probability 0.7 and the train arrives on time with probability 0.9, independently. A student estimates the probability that both are on time, using random digits 0 to 9. Which plan is correct?
choices: Use 1 digit per trial: digits 0 to 6 are a bus on time, digits 0 to 8 are a train on time; count both on time
Use 2 digits per trial: first digit 0 to 7 is a bus on time, second digit 0 to 9 is a train on time; count both on time
Use 2 digits per trial: first digit 0 to 6 is a bus on time, second digit 0 to 8 is a train on time; count both on time
Use 2 digits per trial: first digit 0 to 6 is a bus on time, second 0 to 8 is a train on time; count either one on time
questions.answer: Use 2 digits per trial: first digit 0 to 6 is a bus on time, second digit 0 to 8 is a train on time; count both on time
questions.solution: Each vehicle needs its own digit, since they are independent. The bus is on time 7 of 10 digits (0 to 6) and the train 9 of 10 digits (0 to 8). We want both on time, so we count those trials.

solve.answer: Use 2 digits per trial: first digit 0 to 6 is a bus on time, second digit 0 to 8 is a train on time; count both on time
solve.work: Separate digits: 0-6 is 0.7, 0-8 is 0.9; count both.

questions.skill: Designing and running a simulation with random digits
questions.stem: A simulation uses two-digit numbers from 00 to 99, each equally likely. Four outcomes A, B, C and D have probabilities 0.12, 0.30, 0.25 and 0.33. The numbers are assigned in that order starting at 00, so A gets the first numbers. What is the smallest number assigned to D?
questions.solution: A gets 12 numbers (00 to 11), B gets 30 numbers (12 to 41), C gets 25 numbers (42 to 66). So D starts at $12 + 30 + 25 = 67$.

questions.skill: Designing and running a simulation with random digits
questions.stem: A student simulates rolls of a fair six-sided die using random digits 0 to 9, each equally likely. A digit from 1 to 6 gives that roll, and the digits 0, 7, 8 and 9 are skipped. On average, how many random digits are needed to simulate 60 rolls?
questions.solution: Each digit is used with probability $\frac{6}{10}$, so about $0.6$ rolls come from each digit. To get 60 rolls, about $60 \div 0.6 = 100$ digits are needed.

solve.work: 6 of 10 digits used; 60/0.6=100.

questions.skill: Designing and running a simulation with random digits
questions.stem: A basketball player makes 75 percent of her shots. A student uses one random digit per shot: the digits 0 to 7 mean a make and 8 and 9 mean a miss. What is wrong with this plan?
choices: The digits 0 to 7 are 8 of the 10 digits, which models 80 percent, not 75 percent
Nothing is wrong, because 8 of 10 digits is close enough to 75 percent to count as exact
The digits 0 to 7 are 7 of the 10 digits, which models 70 percent, not 75 percent
Random digits cannot be used to model shooting, because the shots of a player are not random
questions.answer: The digits 0 to 7 are 8 of the 10 digits, which models 80 percent, not 75 percent
questions.solution: The digits 0 to 7 are eight digits, so the plan gives a 0.8 chance of a make, not 0.75. Using two-digit numbers, with 00 to 74 meaning a make, gives exactly 0.75.

solve.answer: The digits 0 to 7 are 8 of the 10 digits, which models 80 percent, not 75 percent
solve.work: 0-7 is 8 digits = 80%, not 75%.

questions.skill: Estimating a probability or mean from simulated trials
questions.stem: A student simulated a game 60 times and recorded the points scored each time: 0 points in 6 games, 2 points in 15 games, 3 points in 27 games and 5 points in 12 games. Estimate the mean number of points per game. Give the answer as a decimal.

questions.skill: Estimating a probability or mean from simulated trials
questions.stem: A student simulated a situation 200 times and recorded the number of successes each time: 0 successes in 14 trials, 1 in 56, 2 in 70, 3 in 44 and 4 in 16. Estimate the probability of having 1 or 2 successes. Give the answer as a decimal.
questions.solution: The trials with 1 or 2 successes number $56 + 70 = 126$. The estimate is $\frac{126}{200} = 0.63$.

questions.skill: Estimating a probability or mean from simulated trials
questions.stem: The true probability of an event is 0.2. A student's simulation of 40 trials finds the event in 6 trials, an estimate of 0.15, and the student says the simulation must be broken. What is the best response?
choices: It is broken, because a correct simulation of 40 trials must find the event in exactly 8 trials every time it is run
It is not necessarily broken: with only 40 trials an estimate can be this far off by chance; more trials would help
It is broken, because a correct simulation of any size always gives an estimate larger than the true value
It is not broken, but running more trials would not help, because an estimate cannot get any closer to the truth
questions.answer: It is not necessarily broken: with only 40 trials an estimate can be this far off by chance; more trials would help
questions.solution: In 40 trials the expected number of successes is 8, and getting 6 is within normal chance variation. Estimates from more trials tend to be closer to the true probability.

solve.answer: It is not necessarily broken: with only 40 trials an estimate can be this far off by chance; more trials would help
solve.work: 40 trials has notable chance variation; more trials help.

questions.skill: Estimating a probability or mean from simulated trials
questions.stem: Run A of a simulation had 40 trials with a mean of 2.5 successes per trial. Run B had 60 trials with a mean of 3.0 successes per trial. Using both runs together, estimate the mean number of successes per trial. Give the answer as a decimal.
questions.solution: Run A had $40 \times 2.5 = 100$ successes and Run B had $60 \times 3.0 = 180$ successes. Together: $\frac{100 + 180}{100} = 2.8$. (This is not the plain average of 2.5 and 3.0, because the runs have different numbers of trials.)

questions.skill: Estimating a probability or mean from simulated trials
questions.stem: A simulation of 100 trials is run five times to estimate a mean. The five estimates are 3.1, 2.8, 3.4, 3.0 and 2.7. Which is the best single estimate of the mean?
choices: The first estimate, 3.1, because it was the first run that was completed
The largest estimate, 3.4, because it shows the most that could happen
The smallest estimate, 2.7, because it is the one that is the most cautious
The mean of the five estimates, 3.0, because it uses all 500 trials
questions.answer: The mean of the five estimates, 3.0, because it uses all 500 trials
questions.solution: The mean of the five estimates is $\frac{3.1 + 2.8 + 3.4 + 3.0 + 2.7}{5} = \frac{15}{5} = 3.0$. It combines all 500 trials, so it varies less than any single run.

solve.answer: The mean of the five estimates, 3.0, because it uses all 500 trials

questions.skill: Margin of error of a simulation-based estimate
questions.stem: Two random polls of the same population are compared. Poll A asked 1,000 people and has a margin of error of 3 percentage points. Poll B has a margin of error of 6 percentage points. About how many people did poll B ask?
choices: About 500 people, since doubling the margin of error means a sample half as large
About 250 people, since doubling the margin of error means a sample one quarter as large
About 2,000 people, since a larger margin of error means a larger sample
About 4,000 people, since doubling the margin of error means a sample four times as large
questions.answer: About 250 people, since doubling the margin of error means a sample one quarter as large
questions.solution: The margin of error is proportional to $\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}$. Doubling it means $\sqrt{n}$ is halved, so $n$ is divided by 4: $1000 \div 4 = 250$ people.

solve.answer: About 250 people, since doubling the margin of error means a sample one quarter as large
solve.work: MOE ~ 1/sqrt(n): double MOE means n/4 = 250.

questions.skill: Margin of error of a simulation-based estimate
questions.stem: For a random sample of $n$ people, a simple formula for the margin of error of a proportion is $\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}$. How many people must be sampled to get a margin of error of 0.05?
questions.solution: Solve $\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} = 0.05$. Then $\sqrt{n} = \frac{1}{0.05} = 20$, so $n = 20^2 = 400$ people.

questions.skill: Margin of error of a simulation-based estimate
questions.stem: A poll reports a margin of error. Which kind of error does the margin of error account for?
choices: Any error at all, including bias from a sample made only of volunteers
Chance variation from random sampling, but not bias from a poorly designed sample
Only the mistakes made when the answers were written down or entered
Bias from a poorly designed sample, but not chance variation from random sampling
questions.answer: Chance variation from random sampling, but not bias from a poorly designed sample
questions.solution: The margin of error describes how much a random sample's result is likely to vary just by chance. It does not correct for bias, such as a sample of volunteers.

solve.answer: Chance variation from random sampling, but not bias from a poorly designed sample
solve.work: MOE covers random sampling variation only, not bias.

questions.skill: Margin of error of a simulation-based estimate
questions.stem: Poll A finds a proportion of 0.52 with a margin of error of 0.04. Poll B finds a proportion of 0.42 with a margin of error of 0.03. The two intervals of plausible values do not overlap. What is the size of the gap between the top of poll B's interval and the bottom of poll A's interval? Give the answer as a decimal.
questions.solution: Poll A's interval is 0.48 to 0.56. Poll B's interval is 0.39 to 0.45. The gap is $0.48 - 0.45 = 0.03$.

solve.work: A bottom 0.48; B top 0.45; gap 0.03.

questions.skill: Testing a difference between groups by randomization
questions.stem: A researcher compares the test scores of students who chose to join a study club with those who did not. A randomization test finds that a difference as large as the observed one would happen in only 0.2 percent of shuffles. Which conclusion is best?
choices: The difference is unlikely to be just chance, but it does not show the club caused it, since students chose to join
The club caused the higher scores, because the randomization test showed the difference is very unlikely
There is no real difference, because students chose to join and the groups were not randomly assigned
The difference is unlikely to be just chance, and it shows that the club caused it, since the test itself was random
questions.answer: The difference is unlikely to be just chance, but it does not show the club caused it, since students chose to join
questions.solution: The shuffles show that chance alone rarely produces such a difference. But the students were not randomly assigned, so another factor, such as motivation, could explain it. Only random assignment supports a cause-and-effect conclusion.

solve.answer: The difference is unlikely to be just chance, but it does not show the club caused it, since students chose to join
solve.work: Significant, but self-selected groups: no causation.

questions.skill: Testing a difference between groups by randomization
questions.stem: In a randomization test, the shuffled differences in means have a mean of about 0 and a standard deviation of 2.5 points. The observed difference between the groups is 6 points. How many standard deviations from 0 is the observed difference? Give the answer as a decimal.
questions.solution: $\frac{6 - 0}{2.5} = 2.4$ standard deviations. A value that far out is unusual among the shuffled differences.

questions.skill: Testing a difference between groups by randomization
questions.stem: In a randomization test where the groups truly do not differ, near what value are the shuffled differences in means centered?
choices: The observed difference, because the shuffles copy the original groups of scores exactly
The overall mean of all the scores, because every shuffle uses the same scores each time
Half of the observed difference, because each shuffle moves half of the scores to the other group
Zero, because any difference arises only from the random way the scores were split
questions.answer: Zero, because any difference arises only from the random way the scores were split
questions.solution: With no real difference, shuffling sends high and low scores to each group by chance, so the difference in means is sometimes positive and sometimes negative, and averages about 0.

solve.answer: Zero, because any difference arises only from the random way the scores were split
solve.work: Under no difference shuffled differences center at 0.

questions.skill: Testing a difference between groups by randomization
questions.stem: A tiny randomization test uses six scores: 2, 4, 5, 6, 9 and 10. In the actual data, group A has 5, 9 and 10 (mean 8) and group B has 2, 4 and 6 (mean 4), so the difference A minus B is 4. All 20 ways to choose which 3 of the 6 scores go to group A are considered. In how many of the 20 ways is the mean of A minus the mean of B at least 4?
questions.solution: The six scores total 36. If A has total $s$, then B has $36 - s$, and A minus B is $\frac{s - (36 - s)}{3} = \frac{2s - 36}{3}$. This is at least 4 when $s \ge 24$. Triples with a total of 24 or more: 10, 9, 6 (total 25) and 10, 9, 5 (total 24). Any other triple has a total of at most 23. So there are 2 ways.

questions.skill: Testing a difference between groups by randomization
questions.stem: Two randomization tests use the same observed difference in means. In the first, each group has 5 students and the proportion of shuffles at least as extreme is 0.12. In the second, each group has 50 students and the proportion is 0.002. What best explains the difference?
choices: Larger groups always have larger observed differences, so the shuffles also give much larger differences
Larger groups have less variation in their means, so the same difference is much less likely by chance
Smaller groups are always more accurate, so their shuffles give more extreme differences in means
The number of shuffles must have been different, since the observed difference was the same in both
questions.answer: Larger groups have less variation in their means, so the same difference is much less likely by chance
questions.solution: The mean of a larger group varies less from shuffle to shuffle, so the shuffled differences are more tightly clustered near 0. The same observed difference then lies farther out among them, and is rarer.

solve.answer: Larger groups have less variation in their means, so the same difference is much less likely by chance
solve.work: Larger groups: less variability in means, same difference less likely by chance.

questions.skill: Pair a visual with a narrative that matches the data
questions.stem: A bar graph shows the number of books a club read each month: January 12, February 18, March 25, April 30. Which headline matches the graph?
choices: The number of books read rose every month from January to April
The number of books read fell every month from January to April
The number of books read stayed the same from January to April
The greatest number of books was read in January, not in April
questions.answer: The number of books read rose every month from January to April
questions.solution: The values 12, 18, 25 and 30 go up each month, so the headline must say the number rose every month. The other headlines say the opposite or something the graph does not show.

solve.answer: The number of books read rose every month from January to April
solve.work: 12, 18, 25, 30 increases each month, so 'rose every month' matches.

questions.skill: Pair a visual with a narrative that matches the data
questions.stem: A slide's headline says, "Weekly sales doubled." Last week's sales were 140 units. According to the headline, how many units were sold this week?
questions.solution: Doubled means multiplied by 2: 2 x 140 = 280 units.

solve.work: Doubled from 140: 2 x 140 = 280.

questions.stem: A weather report says there is a 90% chance of rain tomorrow. Which statement describes this best?
choices: Rain is very likely, but it is not certain to happen.
It will certainly rain tomorrow, with no doubt at all.
It will rain during 90% of the hours of the day.
Rain is unlikely, so people should not expect any.
questions.answer: Rain is very likely, but it is not certain to happen.
questions.solution: A 90% chance means that rain is very likely but not guaranteed. It does not say that rain will fall for 90% of the day.

solve.answer: Rain is very likely, but it is not certain to happen.
solve.work: 90% chance means very likely but not certain. It is not the share of hours with rain.

questions.skill: Adapt the message to the audience
questions.stem: A scientist explains her results to a class of fifth graders. Which wording is best for this audience?
choices: The mean difference in height was statistically significant, with $p = 0.02$ in this study.
A one-way analysis of variance indicated heterogeneity among the treatment means.
The null hypothesis was rejected at the 0.05 level of significance in this experiment.
Most plants that got more light grew taller than the plants that got less light did.
questions.answer: Most plants that got more light grew taller than the plants that got less light did.
questions.solution: Fifth graders need plain words and a clear idea. The first sentence says what happened without technical terms. The others use terms such as significance, analysis of variance and null hypothesis.

solve.answer: Most plants that got more light grew taller than the plants that got less light did.
solve.work: Fifth graders need plain everyday words; B states the finding simply. The others use technical jargon (ANOVA, p-value, null hypothesis).

questions.skill: Adapt the message to the audience
questions.stem: Which detail should be in a technical report for statisticians, even though a short summary for the general public might leave it out?
choices: How the sample was chosen and how many people were in it
A one-line headline in everyday words
A short story about one person in the study
A call to action addressed to all of the readers of the report
questions.answer: How the sample was chosen and how many people were in it
questions.solution: Experts need to judge whether the results can be trusted, and that depends on how the sample was chosen and its size. A headline, a story and a call to action help ordinary readers but do not let experts check the study.

solve.answer: How the sample was chosen and how many people were in it
solve.work: Statisticians need the methods: how the sample was chosen and its size. The others are general-public features.

questions.skill: Avoid claims the data do not support
questions.stem: A survey asked 10 students in one class whether they like pizza, and 8 said yes. Which statement goes beyond what the data show?
choices: 8 of the 10 students surveyed like pizza.
Most of the students who were surveyed like pizza.
More of the surveyed students like pizza than do not.
Most of the students in the whole state like pizza.
questions.answer: Most of the students in the whole state like pizza.
questions.solution: The data come from 10 students in one class. They can describe those students, but they say nothing reliable about all the students in the state.

solve.answer: Most of the students in the whole state like pizza.
solve.work: A sample of 10 in one class cannot support a claim about all students in the state. The other three statements describe only the surveyed students.

questions.skill: Avoid claims the data do not support
questions.stem: A study finds that students who eat breakfast tend to have higher grades. Which sentence presents this carefully?
choices: Students who eat breakfast tend to have higher grades, but breakfast may not be the cause of that.
Eating breakfast every morning is exactly what raises students' grades at school, as the study shows.
Skipping breakfast ruins students' grades, so everyone should eat breakfast every single day of the year.
Breakfast and grades have nothing to do with each other, so the study found no pattern in the data.
questions.answer: Students who eat breakfast tend to have higher grades, but breakfast may not be the cause of that.
questions.solution: The study found an association, not proof of cause. Other things, such as sleep or family routines, might explain both breakfast and grades. The careful sentence reports the pattern and says what it cannot show.

solve.answer: Students who eat breakfast tend to have higher grades, but breakfast may not be the cause of that.
solve.work: An observational association: report the tendency without claiming causation. A and C claim cause, D denies the pattern found.

questions.skill: Work out the numbers a message quotes
questions.stem: 6 of the 20 students in a class walk to school. What percent should a slide quote?

questions.skill: Work out the numbers a message quotes
questions.stem: A town of 5,000 people had 20 flu cases. How many cases per 1,000 people should the report quote?
questions.solution: There are 5,000 / 1,000 = 5 groups of 1,000 people. The 20 cases divided by 5 groups give 4 cases per 1,000 people.

solve.work: 20 cases / 5000 people = 4 per 1000.

questions.stem: A report says an event has a probability of 0.02. Which sentence describes this correctly for a general audience?
choices: It is impossible, so people can ignore it
It will happen in 2 out of every 10 tries
It is unlikely, but it can still happen
It is certain to happen at least once in 100 tries
questions.answer: It is unlikely, but it can still happen
questions.solution: A probability of 0.02 means a 2% chance, which is small but not zero, so it is unlikely but possible. It is not impossible. It is 2 in 100, not 2 in 10. And in 100 tries it is not certain to happen, since each try is still only a 2% chance.

solve.answer: It is unlikely, but it can still happen
solve.work: 0.02 = 2%: unlikely but possible. Not impossible (A), not 2 in 10 (B is 0.2), not certain in 100 tries (D).

questions.skill: Pair a visual with a narrative that matches the data
questions.stem: A slide pairs a scatterplot of 8 students with the headline, "Students who slept more scored higher." The two students with the least sleep scored 62 and 66. The two with the most sleep scored 85 and 91. How many points higher is the mean score of the two who slept most than the mean score of the two who slept least?
questions.solution: The mean of 85 and 91 is 88. The mean of 62 and 66 is 64. The difference is 88 - 64 = 24 points.

questions.stem: A coach says, "Our team has a 1 in 4 chance of winning on Saturday." Which statement describes this best?
choices: The team will win on one of the next four Saturdays for sure
The team will certainly lose on Saturday, but only by a little
The team is very likely to win, because 1 is a small number of losses
The team will probably not win, but winning is possible
questions.answer: The team will probably not win, but winning is possible
questions.solution: A 1 in 4 chance is 25%. Winning is possible but less likely than not, and nothing is certain.

solve.answer: The team will probably not win, but winning is possible
solve.work: 1 in 4 = 25%: unlikely but possible. D.

questions.stem: A report says an event has a probability of 0.2. A presenter wants to say it as "1 in ?". What number replaces the ?
questions.solution: A probability of 0.2 is 1/5, so the event happens about 1 time in 5.

questions.stem: Which phrase best describes an event with a probability of 0.98?
choices: Almost certain to happen, though not guaranteed
Equally likely to happen or not to happen
Unlikely to happen, though it could still occur
Certain to happen every single time it is tried
questions.answer: Almost certain to happen, though not guaranteed
questions.solution: A probability of 0.98 is very close to 1 but not equal to it, so the event is almost certain but not guaranteed.

solve.answer: Almost certain to happen, though not guaranteed
solve.work: 0.98 is near 1 but not 1: almost certain. A.

questions.stem: A weather app says there is a 40% chance of rain. On 100 days that each have this same forecast, about how many days should you expect rain?
questions.solution: A 40% chance means rain on about 40 out of every 100 such days.

questions.stem: A presenter says, "The coin has landed heads 5 times in a row, so tails is due." What is wrong with this statement?
choices: Five heads in a row is impossible for a fair coin, so the coin must be unfair and heads is certain
Each flip is independent, so earlier flips do not change the chance of the next flip
The chance of tails shrinks with every head that has landed, so heads is now the more likely result
Tails becomes due only after exactly ten heads in a row have landed, and not after only five
questions.answer: Each flip is independent, so earlier flips do not change the chance of the next flip
questions.solution: For a fair coin each flip has the same chance of tails, whatever happened before. A streak does not make tails "due".

solve.answer: Each flip is independent, so earlier flips do not change the chance of the next flip
solve.work: Flips are independent; gambler's fallacy. B.

questions.skill: Adapt the message to the audience
questions.stem: A city planner shares traffic results with neighbors at a community meeting. Which opening is best for this audience?
choices: Mean daily vehicle counts showed a 20% reduction (two-tailed test, significant) after the change
Things are a lot better on Oak Street now, and we hope you can all see it too
Traffic on Oak Street dropped by about one car in every five after the new light went in
Here are 365 rows of raw counts, and we will read through the numbers one by one
questions.answer: Traffic on Oak Street dropped by about one car in every five after the new light went in
questions.solution: Neighbors need a plain, specific finding. Jargon, a vague claim, or a pile of raw numbers will not tell them what changed.

solve.answer: Traffic on Oak Street dropped by about one car in every five after the new light went in
solve.work: Plain-language 20% drop = one in five. A suits neighbors.

questions.skill: Adapt the message to the audience
questions.stem: At a talk, which audience would most need the term "standard deviation" explained in plain words?
choices: A team of data analysts at the company
A panel of professors who teach statistics
Reviewers for a journal of statistics
Neighbors at a community meeting
questions.answer: Neighbors at a community meeting
questions.solution: Analysts, professors and journal reviewers use the term every day. People at a community meeting probably do not, so it must be explained.

solve.answer: Neighbors at a community meeting
solve.work: Lay audience needs the term explained: neighbors. A.

questions.skill: Adapt the message to the audience
questions.stem: A technical table lists a rate of 0.03 for students who miss more than 10 days. A newsletter for families says, "About ? out of every 1,000 students miss more than 10 days." What number replaces the ?
questions.solution: A rate of 0.03 means 3 in 100, which is 0.03 x 1,000 = 30 in 1,000.

questions.skill: Adapt the message to the audience
questions.stem: A student has five minutes to share the results of a lunch survey with a class of ninth graders. Which plan is best?
choices: Lead with the main finding, show one simple chart and then invite questions
Read every survey question and every answer aloud, in the order they were asked
Show all twelve charts at once and let the class decide which ones matter
Start with the formulas used to compute the results and give the findings last
questions.answer: Lead with the main finding, show one simple chart and then invite questions
questions.solution: In five minutes the class needs the main point first, with one clear visual. A long reading, a crowd of charts or formulas first would lose the audience.

solve.answer: Lead with the main finding, show one simple chart and then invite questions
solve.work: Short talk to peers: lead with main finding, one chart, questions. D.

questions.skill: Adapt the message to the audience
questions.stem: A summary written for experts says that 2,400 of 8,000 patients improved. A patient brochure should say, "About ? in every 10 patients improved." What number replaces the ?
questions.solution: 2,400 out of 8,000 is 0.3, which is 3 in every 10.

questions.skill: Avoid claims the data do not support
questions.stem: A survey of 30 members of a hiking club finds that 24 of them own hiking boots. Which claim cannot be supported by this survey?
choices: 24 of the 30 surveyed club members own hiking boots
Most people in the country own hiking boots
Four out of every five surveyed members own hiking boots
Fewer than 10 of the surveyed members do not own hiking boots
questions.answer: Most people in the country own hiking boots
questions.solution: The survey covers only 30 club members. Statements about those members are supported (24 of 30 is 4 in 5, and 6 do not own boots), but a claim about the whole country goes beyond the data.

solve.answer: Most people in the country own hiking boots
solve.work: Club sample cannot support claim about the whole country. D.

questions.skill: Avoid claims the data do not support
questions.stem: Ice cream sales and sunburn cases are both higher in summer months. A slide claims that ice cream causes sunburn. What should the presenter mention instead?
choices: Sunburn makes people want to buy more ice cream than they otherwise would
People who buy ice cream are careless about using sunscreen on their skin
Hot, sunny weather leads to both more ice cream sales and more sunburn
Ice cream sales rise only after sunburn cases have already gone up first
questions.answer: Hot, sunny weather leads to both more ice cream sales and more sunburn
questions.solution: A third factor, sunny weather, explains why both rise together. The data do not show that one causes the other.

solve.answer: Hot, sunny weather leads to both more ice cream sales and more sunburn
solve.work: Confounder: hot sunny weather. C.

questions.skill: Avoid claims the data do not support
questions.stem: A slide claims, "Our new method doubled the number of volunteers." The number of volunteers was 12 before and 18 after. By what percent did the number of volunteers increase?
questions.solution: The increase is 18 - 12 = 6, and 6/12 = 0.5, which is 50%. "Doubled" would mean 100%.

questions.skill: Avoid claims the data do not support
questions.stem: A trend line fitted to a school's enrollment from 2015 to 2020 shows enrollment rising. A student writes, "Enrollment will keep rising forever." Which revision is best?
choices: Enrollment will rise every year through 2050, because the trend line shows it
Enrollment will fall soon, because every trend ends after about five years
Enrollment rose in 2015 and 2020, and nothing can be said about the years between
Enrollment rose from 2015 to 2020; whether it keeps rising is uncertain
questions.answer: Enrollment rose from 2015 to 2020; whether it keeps rising is uncertain
questions.solution: The data cover 2015 to 2020, so we can describe that period. A forecast far beyond it is uncertain.

solve.answer: Enrollment rose from 2015 to 2020; whether it keeps rising is uncertain
solve.work: Extrapolation is uncertain; A states observed trend and uncertainty.

questions.skill: Work out the numbers a message quotes
questions.stem: 35 of the 140 students in a grade ride the bus. What percent of the students should a slide quote?

questions.skill: Work out the numbers a message quotes
questions.stem: A county of 40,000 people had 120 bicycle accidents last year. How many accidents per 10,000 people should a report quote?
questions.solution: There are 4 groups of 10,000 people, so 120 / 4 = 30 accidents per 10,000.

questions.skill: Work out the numbers a message quotes
questions.stem: A slide reports the mean of five quiz scores: 7, 9, 8, 10 and 6. What mean should it quote?

questions.skill: Work out the numbers a message quotes
questions.stem: A poll reports that 48% of voters favor a plan, with a margin of error of 3 percentage points. A slide quotes the interval as "from ?% to 51%." What number replaces the ?
questions.solution: The interval is 48 - 3 = 45 up to 48 + 3 = 51.

questions.skill: Work out the numbers a message quotes
questions.stem: A pie chart has three labels. One slice is 45% and another is 35%. The last slice is labeled "other." What percent should the "other" label read?
questions.solution: The slices must total 100%, so other = 100 - 45 - 35 = 20%.

questions.skill: Adapt the message to the audience
questions.stem: A student must present the results of a survey to a room of classmates who have not studied statistics. Which approach best fits that audience?
choices: Show every row of the raw data and the formula for each statistic
Show one clear chart and state the main finding in plain words
Use technical terms such as "confidence interval" without explaining them
Read the whole data file aloud so that nothing is left out
questions.answer: Show one clear chart and state the main finding in plain words
questions.solution: A general audience needs a simple visual and a plain-language message about the main finding. Raw tables, unexplained jargon and a full reading of the data bury the point.

solve.answer: Show one clear chart and state the main finding in plain words
solve.work: A non-statistical audience needs a simple visual and a plain-language main finding. Reading raw data or unexplained jargon does not fit.

questions.stem: A poll reports that 52% of voters support a plan, with a margin of error of 4 percentage points. Which sentence tells a general audience what this means?
choices: Support is likely between 48% and 56%, so the race is too close to call
Support is exactly 52% among all voters, so the plan has a clear majority here
Support is only 4%, because the margin of error is the size of the support itself
Support is above 50%, so we can be certain that most voters want the plan
questions.answer: Support is likely between 48% and 56%, so the race is too close to call
questions.solution: A margin of error of 4 points puts support at about 52 - 4 = 48% to 52 + 4 = 56%. That range includes values below 50%, so the poll cannot say who is ahead. The other sentences claim exactness or certainty that the poll does not have.

solve.answer: Support is likely between 48% and 56%, so the race is too close to call
solve.work: 52% +/- 4 points gives a plausible range 48% to 56%, which includes values below 50%, so a majority is not established.

questions.skill: Pair a visual with a narrative that matches the data
questions.stem: A line graph shows a company's yearly profit. The line rises every year, but each year's rise is smaller than the year before. Which caption matches the graph?
choices: Profit keeps growing, and at a faster pace each year
Profit is dropping, a little more each year than before
Profit keeps growing, by the same amount every year
Profit keeps growing, but at a slower pace each year
questions.answer: Profit keeps growing, but at a slower pace each year
questions.solution: A line that rises every year means profit grows. Rises that get smaller mean the growth slows down, but profit does not fall. The caption must say both.

solve.answer: Profit keeps growing, but at a slower pace each year
solve.work: Rising every year means profit grows; each rise smaller than the last means the growth is slowing.

questions.skill: Pair a visual with a narrative that matches the data
questions.stem: Which title for a line graph of monthly rainfall states the main finding rather than just naming the data?
choices: Monthly rainfall in Raleigh for each month of the year 2025
Rainfall peaked in July at 6 inches and was lowest in October
A line graph of the rainfall in inches measured month by month
Chart 1: the rainfall data collected by the weather station
questions.answer: Rainfall peaked in July at 6 inches and was lowest in October
questions.solution: A good title tells the audience what to notice. Only the first title states a finding (when rainfall peaked and when it was lowest). The others only say what the graph is about.

solve.answer: Rainfall peaked in July at 6 inches and was lowest in October
solve.work: A finding-stating title says what the data show: the July peak and October low. The others only name the data or the chart.

questions.skill: Pair a visual with a narrative that matches the data
questions.stem: A callout on a chart says, "The median wait fell from 20 minutes to 15 minutes." By what percent did the median wait fall?
questions.solution: The wait fell by 20 - 15 = 5 minutes. As a share of the original 20 minutes, that is 5 / 20 = 0.25, or 25%.

questions.stem: A poll finds that 52% of voters favor a plan, with a margin of error of 3 percentage points. Which statement uses probabilistic language correctly?
choices: Exactly 52% of all voters support the plan, with no error.
The true level of support is probably between 49% and 55%.
The true level of support is certainly between 49% and 55%.
The plan definitely has majority support, because 52% is above 50%.
questions.answer: The true level of support is probably between 49% and 55%.
questions.solution: A poll gives an interval, not an exact value, and we are never completely certain. The interval is 52 - 3 = 49% to 52 + 3 = 55%, and it includes values below 50%, so a majority is not certain.

solve.answer: The true level of support is probably between 49% and 55%.
solve.work: 52 +/- 3 gives 49% to 55%; the margin of error makes this a likely, not certain, range, and 49% means majority is not definite.

questions.stem: The chance that a customer returns an item is 15%. Out of 400 customers, about how many returns should the store expect?
questions.solution: The expected number of returns is 15% of 400: 0.15 x 400 = 60.

solve.work: 0.15 x 400 = 60 expected returns.

questions.skill: Adapt the message to the audience
questions.stem: A hospital report gives an infection rate of 0.004 per patient. For patients, the hospital wants to say, "About 1 in every ? patients gets an infection." What number replaces the ?
questions.solution: A rate of 0.004 is 4 in 1,000, which is the same as 1 in 250. Check: 1 / 250 = 0.004.

solve.work: 0.004 = 1/250, so about 1 in every 250 patients.

questions.skill: Adapt the message to the audience
questions.stem: A manager has two minutes to decide whether to approve a project. Which way of presenting the survey results is best?
choices: All 40 charts from the survey, shown one after another in order
One slide with the main result, a supporting chart and a recommendation
A table listing every one of the 600 individual responses to the whole survey
A detailed description of the software used to make all of the charts
questions.answer: One slide with the main result, a supporting chart and a recommendation
questions.solution: A busy decision maker needs the main result, the evidence for it and what to do next. Showing everything, or details of the software, would bury the message.

solve.answer: One slide with the main result, a supporting chart and a recommendation
solve.work: A decision-maker with two minutes needs the key result, one supporting chart and a recommendation.

questions.skill: Avoid claims the data do not support
questions.stem: A line fitted to a tree's height at ages 2 to 8 years predicts that the tree will be 75 meters tall at age 100. What is the main flaw in this prediction?
choices: The line should have been fitted with several more decimal places in its numbers, to be exact and precise.
The line was fitted only to ages 2 to 8, so using it at age 100 goes far beyond the data it covers.
Predictions are never allowed from a fitted line, whatever the ages or the data involved.
Heights of trees cannot be given in meters, only in feet or in inches, so the claim is invalid.
questions.answer: The line was fitted only to ages 2 to 8, so using it at age 100 goes far beyond the data it covers.
questions.solution: Predicting far outside the range of the data is extrapolation. The growth pattern of ages 2 to 8 need not continue until age 100, so the prediction is not supported.

solve.answer: The line was fitted only to ages 2 to 8, so using it at age 100 goes far beyond the data it covers.
solve.work: Extrapolating from ages 2-8 to age 100 goes far outside the data; tree growth is not linear over a century.

questions.skill: Avoid claims the data do not support
questions.stem: Sales were 50 units in year 1, 60 units in year 2 and 90 units in year 3. A slide claims, "Sales grew 50% in each of the last two years." By what percent did sales actually grow from year 1 to year 2?
questions.solution: From year 1 to year 2, sales grew by 10 units, which is 10 / 50 = 0.20, or 20%. (From year 2 to year 3 the growth was 30 / 60 = 50%.) So the slide's claim is true only for the second year.

questions.skill: Work out the numbers a message quotes
questions.stem: A poll finds that 540 of 900 voters favor a plan, and it reports a margin of error of 4 percentage points. What is the upper end of the interval, in percent?
questions.solution: 540 / 900 = 0.60, which is 60%. Adding the margin of error gives 60 + 4 = 64%.

questions.skill: Work out the numbers a message quotes
questions.stem: The number of absences in a month fell from 80 to 62. By what percent did the number of absences fall?
questions.solution: The number fell by 80 - 62 = 18. As a share of the original 80, that is 18 / 80 = 0.225, or 22.5%.

questions.skill: Pair a visual with a narrative that matches the data
questions.stem: A line graph shows a store's monthly profit, in thousands of dollars: January 20, February 24, March 22, April 30, May 33. Which headline fits the graph best?
choices: Profit grew overall from January to May, with one dip in March
Profit rose every month from January to May without a single dip
Profit fell in March and stayed lower than January for the rest of the period
Profit doubled between January and May, from 20 to 40 thousand dollars
questions.answer: Profit grew overall from January to May, with one dip in March
questions.solution: Profit went from 20 to 33 with one drop, from 24 to 22 in March. It did not rise every month, and it did not double.

solve.answer: Profit grew overall from January to May, with one dip in March
solve.work: 20->24 up, 24->22 dip, 22->30->33 up. Overall growth with one dip in March: C. D wrong (33 not 40).

questions.skill: Pair a visual with a narrative that matches the data
questions.stem: A bar graph shows a town's recycling rate rising from 32% in 2019 to 44% in 2023. A caption says, "The recycling rate rose by ?% from 2019 to 2023," measuring the change against the 2019 rate. What number replaces the ?
questions.solution: The rate rose by 12 percentage points. Compared with 32, that is 12/32 = 0.375, or 37.5%.

questions.skill: Pair a visual with a narrative that matches the data
questions.stem: A scatterplot of 40 cities shows points rising from lower left to upper right, with a correlation of 0.85 between average income and house price. Which caption is best?
choices: Higher incomes in a city are what cause its house prices to rise
Cities with higher average incomes tend to have higher house prices
Every city that has a higher average income has a higher house price than every other city
Average income and house price have a strong and negative association with each other
questions.answer: Cities with higher average incomes tend to have higher house prices
questions.solution: A correlation of 0.85 is a strong positive association. It describes a tendency, not a cause and not a rule for every city.

solve.answer: Cities with higher average incomes tend to have higher house prices
solve.work: r=0.85, positive strong association, no causation, not every city. C.

questions.skill: Pair a visual with a narrative that matches the data
questions.stem: A pie chart splits a 1,200 dollar budget into rent 600, food 300, travel 180 and other 120. Which statement is true of the chart?
choices: Food is a third of the budget, and travel is a quarter of it
Rent is two thirds of the budget, and other is a tenth of it
Rent is half of the budget, and food is a quarter of it
Travel is a fifth of the budget, and other is a quarter of it
questions.answer: Rent is half of the budget, and food is a quarter of it
questions.solution: Rent is 600/1,200 = 1/2 and food is 300/1,200 = 1/4. Travel is 15% and other is 10%, so the other statements are wrong.

solve.answer: Rent is half of the budget, and food is a quarter of it
solve.work: Rent 600/1200=1/2, food 300/1200=1/4. A true. B: rent not 2/3. C: food not 1/3. D: travel 0.15.

questions.skill: Pair a visual with a narrative that matches the data
questions.stem: A table shows the commute times of 100 workers: under 20 minutes, 30 workers; 20 to under 30 minutes, 42; 30 to under 40, 16; 40 to under 60, 8; 60 to 90, 4. Which narrative matches it?
choices: Commute times are spread evenly, with about the same number of workers in every group
Most workers (72 of 100) commute an hour or more, and only 4 commute under 30 minutes
Every worker commutes under 30 minutes, with 42 of them taking 20 minutes or longer
Most workers (72 of 100) commute under 30 minutes, and only 4 commute an hour or more
questions.answer: Most workers (72 of 100) commute under 30 minutes, and only 4 commute an hour or more
questions.solution: 30 + 42 = 72 workers commute under 30 minutes, and 4 commute 60 minutes or more. The counts are not equal, and some commute longer than 30 minutes.

solve.answer: Most workers (72 of 100) commute under 30 minutes, and only 4 commute an hour or more
solve.work: Under 30: 30+42=72; 60-90: 4 (an hour or more). C.

questions.stem: A news site reports, "There is a 70% chance that Candidate X wins the election." What does the 70% describe?
choices: If the election could be held many times in the same way, X would win about 7 of every 10
X will receive 70% of all of the votes that are cast in the election, a clear majority
70% of all of the voters have already made up their minds to vote for Candidate X
X will win the election by a margin of exactly 70 votes, or by more than 70 votes
questions.answer: If the election could be held many times in the same way, X would win about 7 of every 10
questions.solution: A chance of 70% is about how often X would win in many repeats of the same situation. It is not a share of the votes or a margin.

solve.answer: If the election could be held many times in the same way, X would win about 7 of every 10
solve.work: A probability forecast: in many repetitions X wins about 7 of 10. D.

questions.stem: A machine makes a faulty part 2% of the time. A presenter says, "In a run of 1,500 parts, we expect about ? faulty parts." What number replaces the ?
A forecaster said, "There is a 30% chance of rain," on 10 different days. It rained on 3 of those 10 days. What does this show?
choices: Her forecasts were wrong, since it did not rain on 7 of those 10 days
Her forecasts were consistent with her stated chances, since about 30% of such days had rain
Her forecasts were wrong, since she should have said 100% on the days it rained
Her forecasts cannot be checked at all, since a chance can never be compared with real weather
questions.answer: Her forecasts were consistent with her stated chances, since about 30% of such days had rain
questions.solution: If 30% is the right chance, we expect rain on about 3 of 10 such days. That is what happened, so the forecasts were consistent.

solve.answer: Her forecasts were consistent with her stated chances, since about 30% of such days had rain
solve.work: Rain on 3/10 = 30% of such days, consistent with forecasts. D.

questions.stem: A presenter says, "The odds are 3 to 1 in favor of finishing on time," meaning that for every 3 times it finishes on time, it is late once. What percent chance of finishing on time does this give?
questions.solution: Out of every 3 + 1 = 4 tries, 3 are on time. That is 3/4 = 75%.

solve.work: Odds 3:1 in favor: 3/(3+1) = 75%.

questions.stem: A drug study finds that the treatment group improved more than the control group, by an amount that would be unlikely to happen by chance alone. Which sentence in a press release is accurate?
choices: The difference proves that the drug works for every patient who takes it
There is a 95% chance that the drug works for each individual patient
The difference was larger than chance alone would probably produce
Chance played no role at all in the difference between the groups
questions.answer: The difference was larger than chance alone would probably produce
questions.solution: Studies speak about groups and about what chance would probably produce. They do not prove an effect for every person, and chance is never ruled out completely.

solve.answer: The difference was larger than chance alone would probably produce
solve.work: Statistically significant: larger than chance would probably produce. A.

questions.skill: Adapt the message to the audience
questions.stem: A data scientist reports a model's accuracy to company executives who must decide whether to launch it. Which summary is best?
choices: The model scores 0.93 on the area under the curve across ten folds of cross-validation
The model's accuracy is high, so launching it is a wise choice for the company
Here are the accuracy, precision, recall and four other measures for all 12 model versions we tried
The model is right about 9 times in 10, so we recommend launching it, with a review in three months
questions.answer: The model is right about 9 times in 10, so we recommend launching it, with a review in three months
questions.solution: Executives need a plain figure, a recommendation and a next step. Jargon, a vague claim or a long list of measures would not help them decide.

solve.answer: The model is right about 9 times in 10, so we recommend launching it, with a review in three months
solve.work: Executives: plain accuracy + recommendation + review plan. D.

questions.skill: Adapt the message to the audience
questions.stem: A report says, "The 95% confidence interval for the mean wait is 12 to 18 minutes." Which rewording for a customer notice is accurate and simple?
choices: The average wait is probably between 12 and 18 minutes
Every customer waits between 12 and 18 minutes
The average wait is exactly 15 minutes for all customers
The average wait is 95% of 18 minutes for most customers
questions.answer: The average wait is probably between 12 and 18 minutes
questions.solution: An interval estimates the average, not each customer's wait, and the average is not known exactly.
