solve.answer: The average wait is probably between 12 and 18 minutes
solve.work: CI describes plausible range of the mean wait: D.

questions.skill: Adapt the message to the audience
questions.stem: A report gives the risk of an accident as 0.0125 per trip. To explain it to drivers, a writer says, "About 1 in ? trips ends in an accident." What number replaces the ?
questions.solution: A risk of 0.0125 is 1/80, so about 1 trip in 80.

questions.skill: Adapt the message to the audience
questions.stem: A school nurse reports the same survey about vaccination to the school board and to a group of sixth graders. Which description of how the two talks should differ is most appropriate?
choices: The board gets a simple example with no numbers; the sixth graders get all costs and technical tables
The board gets key numbers and costs; the sixth graders get the main health message and an example
Both audiences get exactly the same slides, so nobody can say they were told different things
The board gets the main health message only; the sixth graders must choose among the costs
questions.answer: The board gets key numbers and costs; the sixth graders get the main health message and an example
questions.solution: The message should be fitted to the audience: decision makers need numbers and costs, and young students need a clear idea and an example.

solve.answer: The board gets key numbers and costs; the sixth graders get the main health message and an example
solve.work: Board: key numbers and costs; sixth graders: main message and example. B.

questions.skill: Adapt the message to the audience
questions.stem: A bar chart will be shown on a projector in a large room. Which design choice will help the audience most?
choices: Small labels in a crowded legend, so that all the details fit on one slide
One bright color for each of the 15 categories, so they stand out
Large labels, only a few colors and a title that states the finding
A title that names the data but leaves the audience to find the main point
questions.answer: Large labels, only a few colors and a title that states the finding
questions.solution: People at the back of a room need large text, few colors and a title that tells them what to notice.

solve.answer: Large labels, only a few colors and a title that states the finding
solve.work: Large labels, few colors, title states finding. D.

questions.skill: Avoid claims the data do not support
questions.stem: A study of 60 teenagers in one city found that a 20-minute nap improved their quiz scores. A headline says, "Naps boost memory in people of all ages." Which revision is best?
choices: Naps boost memory in all teenagers everywhere, although other ages were not studied at all
Naps do not boost memory at all, because only 60 people in one city were studied
Naps boosted memory for everyone in the city, though other ages were not studied
A 20-minute nap improved quiz scores for 60 teenagers in one city; other ages were not studied
questions.answer: A 20-minute nap improved quiz scores for 60 teenagers in one city; other ages were not studied
questions.solution: The study covers 60 teenagers in one city. The revision should say that and not extend the result to everyone.

solve.answer: A 20-minute nap improved quiz scores for 60 teenagers in one city; other ages were not studied
solve.work: Restrict claim to the population and conditions studied. C.

questions.skill: Avoid claims the data do not support
questions.stem: A headline says, "Cases up 400%." The number of cases rose from 5 to 20. By what percent did the number of cases actually rise?
questions.solution: The rise is 20 - 5 = 15, and 15/5 = 3, which is 300%. A 400% rise would mean 25 cases.

questions.skill: Avoid claims the data do not support
questions.stem: A study finds that people who own more books live longer, on average. Which concern should be raised about the claim "Buy books to live longer"?
choices: Owning many books may go along with income or education, which also affect how long people live
The study should have asked everyone to read more books before measuring anything about their health
A claim about averages can never be applied to any one individual person, even a little
People who own fewer books have no chance of living a long life, as the data show
questions.answer: Owning many books may go along with income or education, which also affect how long people live
questions.solution: The study shows an association. Other factors, such as income or education, could explain both book ownership and long life.

solve.answer: Owning many books may go along with income or education, which also affect how long people live
solve.work: Confounding by income/education. D.

questions.skill: Avoid claims the data do not support
questions.stem: A report on 5 classrooms says, "Our reading program raised scores in all schools in the district." Which concern is most important?
choices: The report used scores, which can never show whether a program has any effect
Only 5 classrooms were studied, so the district's other schools are not covered
The program should have been tried in the schools outside of the district as well
Scores that went up must have gone up in every classroom by the same amount
questions.answer: Only 5 classrooms were studied, so the district's other schools are not covered
questions.solution: The claim is about every school in the district, but the data come from 5 classrooms.

solve.answer: Only 5 classrooms were studied, so the district's other schools are not covered
solve.work: Only 5 classrooms; cannot generalize to all district schools. B.

questions.skill: Work out the numbers a message quotes
questions.stem: In a poll of 600 voters, 330 favor a plan. The poll's margin of error is 4 percentage points. A slide says, "Between ?% and 59% of voters favor the plan." What number replaces the ?
questions.solution: 330/600 = 55%. The interval runs from 55 - 4 = 51 to 55 + 4 = 59.

questions.skill: Work out the numbers a message quotes
questions.stem: A school's enrollment was 1,250 students in 2020 and 1,000 students in 2024. By what percent did enrollment fall? A slide should quote this percent.
questions.solution: The drop is 250, and 250/1,250 = 0.2, which is 20%.

questions.skill: Work out the numbers a message quotes
questions.stem: The yearly salaries of 7 employees, in thousands of dollars, are 40, 42, 45, 48, 50, 52 and 95. A slide quotes the median salary. What number of thousands should it quote?
questions.solution: With 7 values in order, the median is the 4th value, 48. The large value 95 does not move it.

questions.skill: Work out the numbers a message quotes
questions.stem: A press release says a drug "cuts the risk of a stroke by 50%." Without the drug, the risk is 4 in 1,000. With it, the risk is 2 in 1,000. Out of 10,000 people who take the drug, how many fewer strokes are expected than if they had not taken it?
questions.solution: Without the drug, 4/1000 of 10,000 people is 40 strokes. With it, 2/1000 of 10,000 is 20 strokes. That is 20 fewer. The "50%" is a relative change, and quoting the actual numbers shows how small the change is for each person.

solve.work: Without drug: 4/1000 x 10,000 = 40 strokes. With drug: 2/1000 x 10,000 = 20 strokes. Difference 40 - 20 = 20.

questions.skill: Pair a visual with a narrative that matches the data
questions.stem: A line graph shows monthly users: January 100, February 140, March 190, April 120, May 110, June 105. Which sentence should the presenter use to tell the story honestly?
choices: Users have grown steadily every month since January, with no drop at all.
Users peaked at 120 in April and have fallen every month since then.
Users peaked at 190 in March and have fallen every month since then.
Users fell in February and have risen every single month after that.
questions.answer: Users peaked at 190 in March and have fallen every month since then.
questions.solution: The values rise from 100 to a peak of 190 in March, then go down: 120, 110, 105. So users peaked in March and have fallen each month since. The other sentences describe a different pattern than the data.

solve.answer: Users peaked at 190 in March and have fallen every month since then.
solve.work: Values rise to 190 in March, then 120, 110, 105: fell every month after March. A false (drop), C false (Feb rose), D false (peak was March).

questions.skill: Pair a visual with a narrative that matches the data
questions.stem: A slide shows that the share of customers under 25 rose from 20% in 2020 to 35% in 2025, while no other age group's share changed by more than 4 points. Which sentence interprets this for the audience instead of just reading out numbers?
choices: The graph shows the share of customers in each age group in both 2020 and 2025.
In 2025, 35% of our customers were under 25 years old, according to the figures we have.
Customers under 25 are better customers for our business than older customers are, clearly.
The biggest change in our customers is the rise in those under 25, up 15 points since 2020.
questions.answer: The biggest change in our customers is the rise in those under 25, up 15 points since 2020.
questions.solution: An interpretation says what the numbers mean: the under-25 group changed the most, by 35 - 20 = 15 points. The other sentences only describe the graph or repeat a number, or make a judgment the data do not support.

solve.answer: The biggest change in our customers is the rise in those under 25, up 15 points since 2020.
solve.work: Interpretation highlights the meaning: the biggest change is the under-25 rise, 35 - 20 = 15 points. C and D just read the chart; A claims something the data do not show.

questions.stem: A study of a new medicine reports: "If the medicine had no effect, results this strong would happen only about 3% of the time." Which plain-language statement is correct?
choices: There is only a 3% chance that the medicine really works for people who take it.
The medicine works for 97% of the people who take it, as the study clearly shows.
Results this strong would be unusual if the medicine did nothing, so it may help.
There is a 97% chance that the medicine does nothing at all for the people who take it.
questions.answer: Results this strong would be unusual if the medicine did nothing, so it may help.
questions.solution: The 3% is the chance of results this strong if the medicine had no effect. Because that is small, the results are evidence that the medicine may help. It is not the chance that the medicine works, and it is not the share of people helped.

solve.answer: Results this strong would be unusual if the medicine did nothing, so it may help.
solve.work: A p-value of 0.03 means such results are unusual if the medicine had no effect, suggesting it may help. It is not the probability the medicine works or doesn't, nor a 97% success rate.

questions.skill: Adapt the message to the audience
questions.stem: A study finds that grade 10 students take about 900 more steps a day than grade 9 students, with a margin of error of 300 steps. Which sentence is best for a student audience while staying accurate?
choices: The difference between the two sample means is 900, with a margin of error of 300 steps.
Grade 10 students walk way, way more than grade 9 students every single day.
Grade 10 students take about 900 more steps a day than grade 9 students, give or take 300.
Grade 9 students and grade 10 students take the same number of steps a day, on average, in the study.
questions.answer: Grade 10 students take about 900 more steps a day than grade 9 students, give or take 300.
questions.solution: The best sentence uses everyday words, keeps the size of the difference (900) and the uncertainty (give or take 300). The technical version is hard for students to read, the third sentence exaggerates, and the last one contradicts the data.

solve.answer: Grade 10 students take about 900 more steps a day than grade 9 students, give or take 300.
solve.work: A keeps the numbers and uncertainty in plain words ('give or take 300'). B exaggerates, C is technical, D is false.

questions.skill: Adapt the message to the audience
questions.stem: A technical report says the relative risk of a problem with treatment is 0.75. Without treatment, 8 in every 100 people have the problem. For the public, the report says, "With the treatment, about ? in every 100 people have the problem." What number replaces the ?
questions.solution: A relative risk of 0.75 means the risk is 0.75 times as large: 8 x 0.75 = 6. So about 6 in every 100 people have the problem with the treatment.

solve.work: Risk with treatment = 0.75 x 8/100 = 6/100: about 6 in every 100.

questions.skill: Avoid claims the data do not support
questions.stem: A company's chart shows its stock price only from March to May, when the price rose, although over the whole year from January to December the price fell. Which revision is best?
choices: Keep only March to May, but draw the line much bolder so that it really stands out to readers.
Keep only March to May and remove the axis labels so that the chart looks cleaner.
Show all twelve months and say that the price rose in spring but fell over the year.
Show only the single highest month of the year, so that the point is very clear.
questions.answer: Show all twelve months and say that the price rose in spring but fell over the year.
questions.solution: Choosing only the favorable stretch of time leaves out data and gives a misleading story. An honest chart shows the whole year and describes both the rise and the overall fall.

solve.answer: Show all twelve months and say that the price rose in spring but fell over the year.
solve.work: Cherry-picked window misleads; showing the whole year and explaining the spring rise and yearly fall is honest.

questions.skill: Avoid claims the data do not support
questions.stem: A radio host says, "The city supports building a new stadium," because 15 of the 25 people who phoned in (60%) were in favor. Which correction is best?
choices: Say that 60% of the whole city is in favor of the stadium, because 60% is a majority.
Say that exactly 15 people in the whole city are in favor of building the stadium.
Say nothing at all, because 25 callers is too few to report any number or percent.
Say that 15 of the 25 callers favored it, and that callers may not represent the city.
questions.answer: Say that 15 of the 25 callers favored it, and that callers may not represent the city.
questions.solution: The callers chose themselves, so they may differ from the city as a whole. The honest report gives the count for the callers and says that it may not describe everyone. Claiming the whole city, or claiming nothing can be said, would both be wrong.

solve.answer: Say that 15 of the 25 callers favored it, and that callers may not represent the city.
solve.work: Report the actual result (15 of 25 callers) and note that self-selected callers may not represent the city.

questions.skill: Work out the numbers a message quotes
questions.stem: Of 200 adults surveyed, 120 are women and 80 are men. 70% of the women and 45% of the men favor a plan. What percent of all 200 adults favor the plan?
questions.solution: Women in favor: 0.70 x 120 = 84. Men in favor: 0.45 x 80 = 36. Together 84 + 36 = 120 of the 200 adults, which is 120 / 200 = 0.60, or 60%.

solve.work: Women in favor: 0.70 x 120 = 84. Men in favor: 0.45 x 80 = 36. Total 120 of 200 = 60%.

questions.skill: Work out the numbers a message quotes
questions.stem: A rough margin of error for a poll is 1 divided by the square root of the sample size, written as a decimal. A poll of 625 people finds that 56% are in favor. Using this rough margin of error, what is the lower end of the interval, in percent?
questions.solution: The square root of 625 is 25, so the margin of error is 1 / 25 = 0.04, or 4 percentage points. The lower end of the interval is 56 - 4 = 52%.

solve.work: sqrt(625) = 25; 1/25 = 0.04 = 4 percentage points. Lower end 56 - 4 = 52%.

questions.stem: A report says a river has a 1% chance of flooding in any given year. After a flood, a presenter tells residents, "You are safe for the next 99 years." Which correction is best?
choices: The chance rises every year after a flood, until it reaches 100% at year 100
Each year has about a 1% chance of a flood, no matter when the last flood was
The river must flood again after exactly 100 years, so the next flood is certain then
A 1% chance means the river cannot flood in the next 10 years
questions.answer: Each year has about a 1% chance of a flood, no matter when the last flood was
questions.solution: Years are independent, so a flood last year does not change the chance this year. Each year is still about 1%. A 1% yearly chance is not a schedule, and it does not rule out a flood next year.

solve.answer: Each year has about a 1% chance of a flood, no matter when the last flood was
solve.work: A 1% annual chance applies each year independently of the last flood (the 100-year flood misconception). B is the correct correction; A, C, D are wrong.

questions.skill: Pair a visual with a narrative that matches the data
questions.stem: A line graph of monthly sales, in thousands of units, shows January 50, February 52, March 51, April 53, May 52 and June 54. The vertical axis runs only from 50 to 54, so the line looks steep. Which narrative is the most honest?
choices: Sales soared, climbing steeply and steadily in every month of the half year
Sales climbed in every month from January to June, with no month lower than the last
Sales were nearly flat, rising only from 50 to 54 thousand units over six months
Sales dropped sharply in March and again in May before they recovered
questions.answer: Sales were nearly flat, rising only from 50 to 54 thousand units over six months
questions.solution: The change is 4 thousand units out of 50, a small rise, and sales dipped slightly in March and May. A short axis makes a small change look large.

solve.answer: Sales were nearly flat, rising only from 50 to 54 thousand units over six months
solve.work: 50,52,51,53,52,54: small changes; nearly flat from 50 to 54. D. B false (March and May dips).

questions.skill: Pair a visual with a narrative that matches the data
questions.stem: A scatterplot of 30 students shows a clear upward trend between study hours and score, except for one student who studied 10 hours and scored 40. Which narrative is best?
choices: Study time has no link with scores, because one student studied 10 hours and still scored 40 points on it
Every student who studies more scores higher, so the data for the student who scored 40 must be wrong
The student who studied 10 hours should be removed from the data and never mentioned in the talk
More study generally goes with higher scores; one student who studied a lot but scored low is worth a look
questions.answer: More study generally goes with higher scores; one student who studied a lot but scored low is worth a look
questions.solution: The overall pattern is upward, so the narrative should say so and also mention the unusual student, who may deserve a closer look.

solve.answer: More study generally goes with higher scores; one student who studied a lot but scored low is worth a look
solve.work: Overall positive trend, note the outlier. C.

questions.skill: Pair a visual with a narrative that matches the data
questions.stem: A bar graph of a survey has bars for Agree (180 people), Neutral (60 people) and Disagree (60 people). A caption says, "People who agree outnumber people who disagree by ? to 1." What number replaces the ?
questions.solution: 180 / 60 = 3, so Agree outnumbers Disagree 3 to 1.

questions.skill: Pair a visual with a narrative that matches the data
questions.stem: A slide says, "Hospital A has a higher survival rate (90%) than Hospital B (85%)." Hospital A treats mostly mild cases and Hospital B mostly severe cases. Which narrative is most accurate?
choices: The overall rates are not a fair comparison, because the hospitals treat patients with different severity
Hospital A is clearly the better hospital for every kind of patient, since 90% is higher than 85%
Hospital B is clearly the better hospital, since it treats harder cases overall than Hospital A does
The survival rates cannot be compared at all, because percentages can never be compared across places
questions.answer: The overall rates are not a fair comparison, because the hospitals treat patients with different severity
questions.solution: The hospitals treat different kinds of patients, so the overall rates do not show which gives better care. A fair comparison compares similar patients.

solve.answer: The overall rates are not a fair comparison, because the hospitals treat patients with different severity
solve.work: Case mix (severity) confounds; not a fair comparison. C.

questions.stem: A forecaster says there is a 20% chance of rain in each of two towns, and rain in one town does not affect the other. A presenter says, "The chance of rain in both towns is 40%." What is the right correction?
choices: The chance of rain in both towns is 40%, found by adding 20 and 20
The chance of rain in both towns is 4%, found by multiplying 0.2 by 0.2
The chance of rain in both towns is 20%, the same as for one town
The chance of rain in both towns is 0.4%, found by multiplying 0.2 by 0.02
questions.answer: The chance of rain in both towns is 4%, found by multiplying 0.2 by 0.2
questions.solution: For independent events we multiply the chances: 0.2 x 0.2 = 0.04, which is 4%.

solve.answer: The chance of rain in both towns is 4%, found by multiplying 0.2 by 0.2
solve.work: Independent: 0.2*0.2 = 0.04 = 4%. C.

questions.stem: A report says, "The 95% interval for the mean is 20 to 24." Which statement correctly describes what "95%" refers to?
choices: About 95% of all of the individual values in the sample lie between 20 and 24 exactly
There is a 95% chance that the mean of the next sample that is taken falls between 20 and 24
Intervals made this way capture the true mean in about 95% of repeated samples
The true mean of the population lies 95% of the way along the interval from 20 up to 24
questions.answer: Intervals made this way capture the true mean in about 95% of repeated samples
questions.solution: The 95% describes how often the method captures the true mean over many samples. It is not about individual values or the next sample.

solve.answer: Intervals made this way capture the true mean in about 95% of repeated samples
solve.work: Confidence level refers to the method: about 95% of such intervals capture the true mean. A.

questions.stem: A lab tested 20 different foods for a link with headaches. One food showed a link that would appear by chance only about 4% of the time for a single food. Which statement is the most careful?
choices: Because chance would produce it only 4% of the time, the food certainly causes headaches
Because 20 foods were tested, every one of them probably causes headaches
Because 4% is small, the chance that the link is false is exactly 4%
Testing 20 foods makes some chance link likely, so this finding needs to be confirmed
questions.answer: Testing 20 foods makes some chance link likely, so this finding needs to be confirmed
questions.solution: With 20 tests, one unusual result is easy to find by chance alone. A careful report says it needs confirming.

solve.answer: Testing 20 foods makes some chance link likely, so this finding needs to be confirmed
solve.work: Multiple comparisons: with 20 tests a chance hit is likely; needs confirmation. B.

questions.stem: A report must quote, as a percent, the chance that at least one of 3 independent backup generators fails during a storm. Each generator fails with a chance of 10%. What percent should it quote?
questions.solution: The chance none fails is 0.9 x 0.9 x 0.9 = 0.729. So at least one fails with chance 1 - 0.729 = 0.271, or 27.1%.

solve.work: P(none fail) = 0.9^3 = 0.729; P(at least one) = 0.271 = 27.1%.

questions.skill: Adapt the message to the audience
questions.stem: A dietitian studied 400 adults on a diet. The mean weight loss was 3.2 kilograms, with a 95% interval of 2.1 to 4.3 kilograms. Which sentence is best in a newsletter for the general public?
choices: People on this diet lost about 3 kilograms on average; the true average is probably between 2 and 4 kilograms
People on this diet lost exactly 3.2 kilograms on average, so you will lose exactly 3.2 kilograms too
The mean loss was 3.2 kg with a 95% confidence interval of [2.1, 4.3] for the sample of 400 adults
The diet works, and everyone who tries it will lose weight in the same way and by the same amount
questions.answer: People on this diet lost about 3 kilograms on average; the true average is probably between 2 and 4 kilograms
questions.solution: The public needs a plain statement of the typical result and the uncertainty. It should not promise the same result for everyone or use technical notation.

solve.answer: People on this diet lost about 3 kilograms on average; the true average is probably between 2 and 4 kilograms
solve.work: Public: rounded mean and plain-language interval. C.

questions.skill: Adapt the message to the audience
questions.stem: An analyst sends the same finding to a CEO in one email and to the engineers who built the model in a technical appendix. Which statement correctly describes how the two should differ?
choices: The CEO's email gives every assumption and every detail; the appendix just states the decision made
The CEO's email leads with the decision and its risk; the appendix gives the methods, data and assumptions
Both should be identical, word for word, so that nobody can say they were told different things
The CEO's email should leave out any mention of uncertainty; the appendix should include it fully
questions.answer: The CEO's email leads with the decision and its risk; the appendix gives the methods, data and assumptions
questions.solution: The same facts must appear in both, but the CEO needs the decision and the risk first, while engineers need the details to check the work.

solve.answer: The CEO's email leads with the decision and its risk; the appendix gives the methods, data and assumptions
solve.work: CEO: decision and risk; appendix: methods, data, assumptions. B.

questions.skill: Adapt the message to the audience
questions.stem: A technical report gives a daily dose of 0.5 milligrams per kilogram of body weight. A leaflet for the parent of a 24 kilogram child should say, "Give ? milligrams per day." What number replaces the ?
questions.solution: The dose is 0.5 x 24 = 12 milligrams per day.

questions.skill: Adapt the message to the audience
questions.stem: A student gives a talk to 10th graders on a survey in which 62% of students sleep fewer than 8 hours a night. Which slide title is best for this audience?
choices: Distribution of nightly sleep duration in hours by respondent, with a sample size of 480
Sleep: a complex topic with many factors that are worth thinking about
Most of you are not getting enough sleep: about 6 in 10 students sleep under 8 hours
Students' sleep is a problem that the school administration should solve at once
questions.answer: Most of you are not getting enough sleep: about 6 in 10 students sleep under 8 hours
questions.solution: A good title for students states the finding in plain words with a number they can picture. The others are technical, vague or give a recommendation the data do not state.

solve.answer: Most of you are not getting enough sleep: about 6 in 10 students sleep under 8 hours
solve.work: Peers: direct, relatable title with plain number (62% ~ 6 in 10). B.

questions.skill: Adapt the message to the audience
questions.stem: A report says that a treatment lowers the chance of a bad outcome from 12% to 9%, a relative reduction of 25%. A clinic wants to describe this to patients without overstating the benefit. Which sentence is best?
choices: The treatment cuts the chance of a bad outcome by 25 people in every 100
The treatment makes a bad outcome 25 times less likely than before
The treatment prevents a bad outcome for one person in every four
For every 100 people treated, about 3 fewer have a bad outcome
questions.answer: For every 100 people treated, about 3 fewer have a bad outcome
questions.solution: The chance falls from 12 in 100 to 9 in 100, which is 3 fewer in 100. The relative figure of 25% is easy to misread as 25 in 100.

solve.answer: For every 100 people treated, about 3 fewer have a bad outcome
solve.work: Absolute reduction 12%-9% = 3 per 100. D. A, B, C overstate.

questions.skill: Avoid claims the data do not support
questions.stem: A hospital reports that patients who took Vitamin Z recovered faster than those who did not. Patients chose for themselves whether to take it. Which sentence should the communicator use?
choices: Patients who chose Vitamin Z recovered faster, but they may differ in other ways, so it may not be the cause
Vitamin Z caused faster recovery, because the patients who took it recovered faster than the rest
Vitamin Z had no effect, because the patients chose to take it for themselves, not by chance
Vitamin Z speeds recovery for all people, because the patients who took it did better than others
questions.answer: Patients who chose Vitamin Z recovered faster, but they may differ in other ways, so it may not be the cause
questions.solution: Without random assignment, the groups may differ in other ways. The data show an association and do not prove a cause.

solve.answer: Patients who chose Vitamin Z recovered faster, but they may differ in other ways, so it may not be the cause
solve.work: Self-selected (observational): association may be confounded. C.

questions.skill: Avoid claims the data do not support
questions.stem: A news story says, "City A had 4,000 robberies and City B had 800, so City A is more dangerous." City A has 2,000,000 people and City B has 200,000. What is the flaw in the claim?
choices: The counts are too large to compare, so only percentages of the cities' areas can ever be used
The counts ignore population size: City A has 2 robberies per 1,000 people and City B has 4
The counts ignore the weather: City A has 2 robberies per day and City B has 4 per day
The counts are right: a city with more robberies always has the higher rate of robberies
questions.answer: The counts ignore population size: City A has 2 robberies per 1,000 people and City B has 4
questions.solution: Rates matter more than counts. City A: 4,000/2,000,000 is 2 per 1,000. City B: 800/200,000 is 4 per 1,000, a higher rate.

solve.answer: The counts ignore population size: City A has 2 robberies per 1,000 people and City B has 4

questions.skill: Avoid claims the data do not support
questions.stem: A press release says, "Our tutoring raised grades by 30%." The average grade was 70 before and 77 after. By what percent did the average grade actually rise?
questions.solution: The rise is 7 points, and 7/70 = 0.1, which is 10%.

questions.skill: Avoid claims the data do not support
questions.stem: A study of 5,000 students finds a correlation of -0.15 between hours of screen time and test scores. A press release says, "Screen time is strongly linked to lower scores." Which revision is best?
choices: There is a strong negative association between the two, because 5,000 students were studied
There is no association at all, because the correlation is not exactly equal to -1 in value
There is a weak negative association: more screen time goes with slightly lower scores, which does not prove a cause
There is a weak positive association, because the correlation is small in size and so positive
questions.answer: There is a weak negative association: more screen time goes with slightly lower scores, which does not prove a cause
questions.solution: A correlation of -0.15 is weak and negative. A large sample does not make the link strong, and correlation alone does not show cause.

solve.answer: There is a weak negative association: more screen time goes with slightly lower scores, which does not prove a cause
solve.work: r = -0.15 is a weak negative association; no causation. B.

questions.skill: Avoid claims the data do not support
questions.stem: A mailed survey sent to 5,000 customers got 400 replies, and 85% of the replies were happy. A report says, "85% of our customers are happy." Which sentence should replace it?
choices: Of the 5,000 customers, 85% were happy, since replies always represent every customer fairly
Of the 400 customers who replied, 85% were happy, so 85% of the other 4,600 were also happy too
Nothing at all can be said, since 400 replies is fewer than 10% of 5,000 customers
Of the 400 customers who replied, 85% were happy; those who did not reply may feel differently
questions.answer: Of the 400 customers who replied, 85% were happy; those who did not reply may feel differently
questions.solution: Only 400 of 5,000 replied, and people who reply may differ from those who do not. The report can state what the repliers said and name that limit.

solve.answer: Of the 400 customers who replied, 85% were happy; those who did not reply may feel differently
solve.work: Nonresponse bias; restrict claim to responders. D.

questions.skill: Work out the numbers a message quotes
questions.stem: Class A has 20 students with a mean score of 80. Class B has 30 students with a mean score of 70. A slide quotes the mean score of all 50 students together. What mean should it quote?
questions.solution: The totals are 1,600 and 2,100, which makes 3,700 points for 50 students: 3,700/50 = 74.

questions.skill: Work out the numbers a message quotes
questions.stem: A poll of 1,600 people finds that 52% are in favor. Use a margin of error of 1 divided by the square root of the sample size. What is the lower end of the interval, in percent?
questions.solution: The margin of error is 1/40 = 0.025, which is 2.5 percentage points. The lower end is 52 - 2.5 = 49.5%.

questions.skill: Work out the numbers a message quotes
questions.stem: A savings balance grows by 10% in the first year and by another 10% of the new balance in the second year. A slide wants to quote the total percent growth over the two years. What percent should it quote?
questions.solution: Each year multiplies the balance by 1.1, so after two years it is 1.1 x 1.1 = 1.21 times the start: growth of 21%, not 20%.

questions.stem: In a screening of 1,000 people, 40 are sick. The test is positive for 32 of the sick people and for 48 of the 960 healthy people. Which sentence correctly tells a general audience what a positive result means?
choices: Of every 10 people with a positive test, about 8 are sick
Of every 10 people with a positive test, about 6 are sick
Of every 10 people with a positive test, about 4 are sick
Of every 10 people with a positive test, about 9 are sick
questions.answer: Of every 10 people with a positive test, about 4 are sick
questions.solution: In all 32 + 48 = 80 people test positive, and 32 of them are sick: 32/80 = 40%, or about 4 in 10. The 8 comes from 32 of 40 sick people testing positive, which answers a different question. The others misread the counts.

solve.answer: Of every 10 people with a positive test, about 4 are sick
solve.work: Positives = 32 (sick) + 48 (healthy) = 80. Fraction sick among positives = 32/80 = 0.4, i.e. about 4 of every 10.

questions.stem: A forecast says there is a 30% chance of rain on Saturday and a 30% chance of rain on Sunday, and the two days are independent. What percent chance should a presenter quote for rain on at least one of the two days?
questions.solution: The chance of no rain on a day is 70%. No rain on both days is 0.7 x 0.7 = 0.49, or 49%. So rain on at least one day is 100% - 49% = 51%. It is not 30% + 30% = 60%.

solve.work: P(no rain both days) = 0.7 x 0.7 = 0.49. P(rain at least one day) = 1 - 0.49 = 0.51 = 51%.

questions.skill: Limits on generalizing from a sample or an experiment
questions.stem: A random sample of 100 students from Lincoln High School finds that 60 of them walk to school. To which group can the school fairly apply this result?
choices: All high school students in the whole state
All of the students at Lincoln High School
All students at the elementary schools nearby
All adults who live near Lincoln High School
questions.answer: All of the students at Lincoln High School
questions.solution: A random sample supports conclusions about the population it was drawn from, which here is the students at Lincoln High School. It says nothing reliable about students elsewhere or about adults.

solve.answer: All of the students at Lincoln High School
solve.work: A random sample from Lincoln High generalizes to the population it was drawn from: all Lincoln High students only.

questions.skill: Estimating a population value from a sample
questions.stem: In a random sample of 200 voters, 90 say they will vote yes on a proposal. What is the sample proportion that say yes? Give your answer as a decimal.
questions.solution: The sample proportion is $90 \div 200 = 0.45$.

questions.skill: Margin of error and what it means
questions.stem: A poll estimates that 52% of voters support a plan, with a margin of error of 3 percentage points. What is the lowest percent of voters that the poll's interval allows? Enter the number without the percent sign.
questions.solution: The interval runs from the estimate minus the margin of error to the estimate plus it: from $52 - 3 = 49$ to $52 + 3 = 55$ percent. The lowest value is 49.

solve.work: Interval 52 +/- 3 = 49% to 55%. Lowest = 49.

questions.skill: Margin of error and what it means
questions.stem: Which choice best describes the margin of error in a poll?
choices: The percent of the people chosen who refused to answer the poll
The chance that the wording of the poll's questions was biased
The total number of people who were included in the poll sample
How far the poll result may be from the truth because of chance
questions.answer: How far the poll result may be from the truth because of chance
questions.solution: The margin of error describes how far a sample result may be from the true population value just because of the luck of the draw. It is not the nonresponse rate, a measure of wording bias, or the sample size.

solve.answer: How far the poll result may be from the truth because of chance
solve.work: Margin of error measures how far the sample estimate may plausibly be from the population value due to random sampling variation. Not sample size, nonresponse or wording bias.

questions.stem: Two different random samples of 50 students from the same school give mean sleep times of 7.2 hours and 7.8 hours. What does this show?
choices: Sample means vary from sample to sample just by chance
At least one of the two samples must have been biased
The true mean sleep time for the school must be 7.5 hours
The school's students slept more on the day of the second sample
questions.answer: Sample means vary from sample to sample just by chance
questions.solution: Different random samples give different results even from the same population. Such differences do not mean that a sample was biased, and they do not pin the true mean at the middle of the two sample means.

solve.answer: Sample means vary from sample to sample just by chance
solve.work: Different random samples give different means purely through sampling variability; it does not pin the true mean at 7.5 or imply bias.

questions.stem: Why do statisticians repeat a simulation many times instead of running it once?
choices: To make the result of the first run more accurate
To avoid the need for any random numbers at all
To see how much the results vary just by chance
To prove that the original sample was truly random
questions.answer: To see how much the results vary just by chance
questions.solution: One run is only one possible outcome. Many runs show the whole range of results that chance alone can produce, which is what we compare an observed result against.

solve.answer: To see how much the results vary just by chance
solve.work: Repeating a simulation many times reveals the distribution of outcomes, i.e. how much results vary by chance. It does not change the first run or prove randomness.

questions.stem: A line fitted to data about hours studied (x) and test score has the equation predicted score $= 50 + 5x$. What score does the line predict for a student who studies 4 hours?
questions.solution: Put $x = 4$ into the equation: $50 + 5 \times 4 = 50 + 20 = 70$.

questions.skill: When to trust a predicted value
questions.stem: A line for predicting height from age was fitted to data from children aged 10 to 15. Which prediction should be trusted most?
choices: The height of a child who is 3 years old
The height of an adult who is 40 years old
The height of a child who is 12 years old
The height of an adult who is 70 years old
questions.answer: The height of a child who is 12 years old
questions.solution: A prediction is reliable inside the range of the data used to build the line. An age of 12 is inside 10 to 15. The other ages are far outside it, and growth does not follow the same line there.

solve.answer: The height of a child who is 12 years old
solve.work: Age 12 lies inside the data range 10-15 (interpolation); 3, 40 and 70 are extrapolations.

questions.skill: Margin of error and what it means
questions.stem: A poll reports that 60% of voters like a plan, with a margin of error of 2 percentage points. How many percentage points wide is the interval from the lowest to the highest plausible value?
questions.solution: The interval runs from $60 - 2 = 58$ to $60 + 2 = 62$ percent, which is $62 - 58 = 4$ percentage points wide.

solve.work: Interval 58% to 62%: width 62 - 58 = 4 points.

questions.skill: Informal inference: sample size and reliability
questions.stem: Two students each take one random sample from a very large bag of candies to estimate the proportion that are red. Ana's sample has 20 candies and Ben's sample has 200 candies. Which statement is best?
choices: Ana's estimate is likely closer, because a small sample is easier to count correctly
Both estimates are equally reliable, because both samples are random
Neither estimate is useful, because the bag is too large to sample
Ben's estimate is likely closer to the true proportion, because larger random samples vary less
questions.answer: Ben's estimate is likely closer to the true proportion, because larger random samples vary less
questions.solution: Estimates from larger random samples tend to be closer to the true proportion, because they vary less from sample to sample. Random selection removes bias but does not make a small sample as reliable as a large one. A random sample can describe a large bag.

solve.answer: Ben's estimate is likely closer to the true proportion, because larger random samples vary less
solve.work: Sampling variability of a sample proportion decreases with sample size (SE ~ sqrt(p(1-p)/n)), so the 200-candy random sample is likely closer. A.

questions.skill: Limits on generalizing from a sample or an experiment
questions.stem: A researcher surveys 150 students chosen at random from the band, orchestra and choir of one high school. They practice 5 hours a week on average. To which group does the result fairly apply?
choices: All high school students across the whole state
All students in the band, orchestra and choir at that school
All students at that school, including those who do not play
All musicians of any age who live in the same town
questions.answer: All students in the band, orchestra and choir at that school
questions.solution: A random sample describes the group it was drawn from, which here is the students in the school's music groups.

solve.answer: All students in the band, orchestra and choir at that school
solve.work: Sample drawn at random from band, orchestra and choir students of one school: applies to that group. C.

questions.skill: Limits on generalizing from a sample or an experiment
questions.stem: A principal asks the first 20 students to arrive each morning whether the school day should start later. Why is it risky to use their answers for all students?
choices: Twenty students is always too few for any survey to be used by a principal
Students who arrive early always give answers that are more thoughtful than others
Early arrivals may feel differently about the start time from other students
A survey can be given only after school and never before the school day has begun
questions.answer: Early arrivals may feel differently about the start time from other students
questions.solution: The 20 early arrivals were not chosen at random and may differ from other students in how they feel about the start time.

solve.answer: Early arrivals may feel differently about the start time from other students
solve.work: Convenience sample of early arrivals may differ on start time. B.

questions.skill: Limits on generalizing from a sample or an experiment
questions.stem: A drug trial randomly assigns 200 adult volunteers with high blood pressure to a new pill or a placebo. The pill group improves more. To whom is the conclusion most reasonable to apply?
choices: Children who have high blood pressure of any kind
All people, whether or not their blood pressure is high
Only the exact 200 volunteers and nobody else
Adults with high blood pressure like the volunteers
questions.answer: Adults with high blood pressure like the volunteers
questions.solution: The volunteers were adults with high blood pressure, so the result reaches people like them. Children and people with normal blood pressure were not studied.

solve.answer: Adults with high blood pressure like the volunteers
solve.work: Random assignment among adults with high BP: generalize to similar adults. D.

questions.skill: Estimating a population value from a sample
questions.stem: A random sample of 60 apples from an orchard has a mean mass of 180 grams. Based on the sample, estimate the total mass, in kilograms, of 2,000 apples from the orchard.
questions.solution: The sample mean is the best estimate of the mean mass of all apples. 180 x 2,000 = 360,000 grams, which is 360 kilograms.

questions.skill: Estimating a population value from a sample
questions.stem: A random sample of 80 bolts from a shipment of 4,000 bolts contains 2 defective bolts. Based on the sample, about what percent of the shipment is defective?
questions.solution: 2/80 = 0.025, which is 2.5%. We use the sample percent as the estimate for the whole shipment.

questions.skill: Margin of error and what it means
questions.stem: A poll of 800 adults finds that 42% prefer brand X, with a margin of error of 4 percentage points. Which interval does the poll give for the percent of all adults who prefer brand X?
questions.solution: The interval is 42 - 4 = 38 up to 42 + 4 = 46.

questions.skill: Margin of error and what it means
questions.stem: A candidate needs more than 50% of the votes. A poll reports 58% support with a margin of error of 3 percentage points. By how many percentage points is the lowest value in the poll's interval above 50%?
questions.solution: The lowest value is 58 - 3 = 55%, which is 5 points above 50%.

questions.skill: Margin of error and what it means
questions.stem: A poll reports a margin of error of 3 points. A friend says, "That means 3% of the people surveyed gave wrong answers." What is wrong with this?
choices: The margin of error is really the percent of people who refused to answer
It describes chance in choosing the sample, not wrong answers
The margin of error is the number of people who gave wrong answers, not a percent
The margin of error shows that the poll was done by a poor method of sampling
questions.answer: It describes chance in choosing the sample, not wrong answers
questions.solution: The margin of error shows how far the sample result may be from the true value because a random sample varies by chance.

solve.answer: It describes chance in choosing the sample, not wrong answers
solve.work: MOE is about sampling variability, not wrong answers. C.

questions.skill: Sample size and margin of error
questions.stem: A pollster wants a smaller margin of error and can change only one thing. What should she do?
choices: Take a smaller random sample, since fewer answers are easier to check
Ask the same people the same question a second time to double the data
Take a larger random sample of the population she is studying
Ask only people who answer the phone quickly, so the poll is finished faster
questions.answer: Take a larger random sample of the population she is studying
questions.solution: A larger random sample varies less from sample to sample, so the margin of error is smaller. The other choices do not help.

solve.answer: Take a larger random sample of the population she is studying
solve.work: Larger random sample reduces MOE. B.

questions.skill: Sample size and margin of error
questions.stem: A pollster uses the rule that the margin of error, in percentage points, is about 100 divided by the square root of the sample size. What is the margin of error, in percentage points, for a sample of 2,500 people?
questions.solution: The square root of 2,500 is 50, and 100 / 50 = 2 percentage points.

questions.stem: A class draws many random samples of 25 marbles from the same jar and records the percent that are red each time: 36%, 44%, 40%, 32% and 48%. What does this show?
choices: The percent of red marbles in the jar changes each time marbles are drawn
At least four of the samples must have been chosen in a careless way
A sample of 25 marbles can never say anything about the whole jar
Sample percents of the same jar differ from each other by chance
questions.answer: Sample percents of the same jar differ from each other by chance
questions.solution: The jar stays the same, but each random sample is different, so the sample percents vary.

solve.answer: Sample percents of the same jar differ from each other by chance
solve.work: Sampling variability. B.

questions.stem: Five random samples of 40 students each have mean heights of 150, 154, 152, 148 and 156 centimeters. What is the range of these five sample means, in centimeters?
questions.solution: The largest sample mean is 156 and the smallest is 148, so the range is 156 - 148 = 8 centimeters.

questions.skill: Informal inference by simulation: setting up
questions.stem: A student uses random digits 0 to 9, each equally likely, to simulate flipping a fair coin. Which rule works?
choices: Even digits mean heads and odd digits mean tails
Digits 0, 1 and 2 mean heads and digits 3 to 9 mean tails
Digit 0 means heads and every other digit means tails
Digits 5 and 6 mean heads and every other digit means tails
questions.answer: Even digits mean heads and odd digits mean tails
questions.solution: There are 5 even digits and 5 odd digits, so each result has a chance of 5/10, as for a fair coin.

solve.answer: Even digits mean heads and odd digits mean tails

questions.skill: Informal inference by simulation: setting up
questions.stem: A basketball player makes 70% of her free throws. A student uses random digits 0 to 9, each equally likely, to simulate one free throw. Which rule is correct?
choices: Digits 0 to 7 mean she makes it and digits 8 and 9 mean she misses it
Digits 0 to 6 mean she makes it and digits 7 to 9 mean she misses it
Digit 7 means she makes it and every other digit means she misses it
Digits 0 to 6 mean she misses it and digits 7 to 9 mean she makes it
questions.answer: Digits 0 to 6 mean she makes it and digits 7 to 9 mean she misses it
questions.solution: Seven of the ten digits (0 to 6) give a 7/10 = 70% chance of a make.

solve.answer: Digits 0 to 6 mean she makes it and digits 7 to 9 mean she misses it
solve.work: Need 7 of 10 digits for make: 0-6 make, 7-9 miss. D. C gives 0.8.

questions.skill: Informal inference by simulation: setting up
questions.stem: A student simulates one random sample of 10 people, where each person is a fan with a chance of 40%. She uses one random digit for each person. She wants to simulate 50 samples. How many random digits does she need in all?
questions.solution: Each sample needs 10 digits, so 50 samples need 10 x 50 = 500 digits.

solve.work: 10 digits per sample * 50 = 500.

questions.skill: Informal inference by simulation: reading the results
questions.stem: A simulation of a company's claim produced a result as extreme as the one actually observed in 48 of 100 runs. What is the best statement?
choices: The result is very rare if the claim is true, so the claim must be a false one
The result proves the claim is true, because it happened in 48 of the 100 runs
The result is common if the claim is true, so it is weak evidence against the claim
The result cannot be compared with the simulation, because it came from real data
questions.answer: The result is common if the claim is true, so it is weak evidence against the claim
questions.solution: A result that turns up in nearly half of the runs is not unusual under the claim.

solve.answer: The result is common if the claim is true, so it is weak evidence against the claim
solve.work: 48% of runs as extreme: common under claim, little evidence against it. A is the best option.

questions.skill: Informal inference by simulation: reading the results
questions.stem: A simulation of 100 sets of 10 flips of a fair coin gave these numbers of sets by heads: 8 heads, 5 sets; 9 heads, 2 sets; 10 heads, 0 sets. Fewer than 8 heads occurred in all other sets. How many of the 100 sets had 8 or more heads?
questions.solution: 5 + 2 + 0 = 7 sets had 8 or more heads.

solve.work: 8 heads: 5, 9 heads: 2, 10 heads: 0; total 7.

questions.stem: A line fitted to a plant's growth predicts height from days of growth: $y = 4 + 1.5x$, where y is the height in centimeters and x is the number of days. What height does the line predict after 10 days?
questions.solution: Replace x with 10: 4 + 1.5 x 10 = 4 + 15 = 19 centimeters.

questions.stem: A fitted line for predicting y from x is $y = 12 + 3x$. What does the 3 tell you?
choices: When x is 3 units, the line predicts that y is 12 units
Each increase of 1 unit in y goes with a predicted increase of 3 units in x
The line predicts that y is always exactly 3 times as large as x is
Each increase of 1 unit in x goes with a predicted increase of 3 units in y
questions.answer: Each increase of 1 unit in x goes with a predicted increase of 3 units in y
questions.solution: The slope is the predicted change in y for each 1 unit increase in x.

solve.answer: Each increase of 1 unit in x goes with a predicted increase of 3 units in y
solve.work: Slope: +1 in x -> +3 in y. C.

questions.stem: A line predicts a student's test score from the hours studied: $y = 40 + 6x$. A student who studied 5 hours scored 65. What is the residual, the actual score minus the predicted score?
questions.solution: The predicted score is 40 + 6 x 5 = 70. The residual is 65 - 70 = -5.

solve.work: Predicted 40+6*5 = 70; residual 65-70 = -5.

questions.stem: The residual for one data point is negative. What does that say about the point?
choices: The actual value of the point is below the value the line predicts
The actual value of the point is above the value the line predicts
The point is an error and should not be included in the data
The slope of the fitted line must be negative for such a point
questions.answer: The actual value of the point is below the value the line predicts
questions.solution: A residual is the actual value minus the predicted value. If it is negative, the actual value is smaller than the prediction.

solve.answer: The actual value of the point is below the value the line predicts
solve.work: Negative residual: actual below predicted. C.

questions.skill: When to trust a predicted value
questions.stem: Which situation gives the most reason to trust a prediction from a fitted line?
choices: The line was drawn on a large, colorful graph with a clear title and labels
The points hug the line and the new x-value lies inside the range of the data
The new x-value is far larger than any in the data, so the pattern will surely go on
The line was found with a computer, so it fits every possible new x-value
questions.answer: The points hug the line and the new x-value lies inside the range of the data
questions.solution: A prediction is trusted when the points follow the line closely and the new x-value is inside the range that the data cover.

solve.answer: The points hug the line and the new x-value lies inside the range of the data
solve.work: Strong fit and interpolation. C.

questions.skill: When to trust a predicted value
questions.stem: A line is fitted to data in which the points are scattered widely around the line, with a correlation of only 0.2. How reliable are predictions from it?
choices: Very reliable, since any fitted line always fits the data quite well
Perfectly reliable for any x-value that lies inside the range of the data
Not very reliable, since the line explains little of the variation in y
Reliable only when the x-value is exactly equal to 0 or is a whole number
questions.answer: Not very reliable, since the line explains little of the variation in y
questions.solution: A weak correlation means that individual values are often far from the line, so predictions are rough.

solve.answer: Not very reliable, since the line explains little of the variation in y
solve.work: r=0.2 weak; predictions not reliable. D.

questions.skill: Limits on generalizing from a sample or an experiment
questions.stem: A study recruited 80 volunteers aged 18 to 25 from one college. They were randomly assigned to a new study technique or the usual one, and the new-technique group scored higher. Which conclusion is best supported?
choices: The technique probably helped volunteers like these, but other ages need more evidence
The technique works for people of every age, because the subjects were randomly assigned
No conclusion about cause is possible, because the volunteers were not a random sample
The technique helped every single volunteer in the group that used the technique
questions.answer: The technique probably helped volunteers like these, but other ages need more evidence
questions.solution: Random assignment supports a cause-and-effect conclusion for subjects like these volunteers. Because they were not a random sample of everyone, the result cannot safely be applied to other ages. A group average also does not mean every person improved.

solve.answer: The technique probably helped volunteers like these, but other ages need more evidence
solve.work: Random assignment supports a causal conclusion for these subjects; lack of random sampling (one college, ages 18-25) limits generalizing to other people. A is overclaiming, B wrong (assignment does not give generalization), C wrong (cause can be concluded for subjects).

questions.skill: Sample size and margin of error
questions.stem: A pollster uses the rule of thumb that the margin of error for a sample proportion is about 1 divided by the square root of the sample size. What is the margin of error, as a decimal, for a sample of 400 people?
questions.solution: The square root of 400 is 20, so the margin of error is about $1 \div 20 = 0.05$, or 5 percentage points.

questions.skill: Margin of error and what it means
questions.stem: A poll of 1,000 adults finds that 55% favor a proposal, with a margin of error of 3 percentage points. Which is a reasonable conclusion?
choices: Exactly 55% of all adults in the population favor the proposal
Between 52% and 58% of the 1,000 adults who were surveyed favor it
The poll gave a wrong answer for 3% of the people who were asked
The percent of all adults who favor it is probably 52% to 58%
questions.answer: The percent of all adults who favor it is probably 52% to 58%
questions.solution: The margin of error describes the population value, not the sample. The interval is $55 \pm 3$, from 52 to 58 percent. In the sample, exactly 55% (550 of 1,000) said they favor it.

solve.answer: The percent of all adults who favor it is probably 52% to 58%
solve.work: The interval 52% to 58% is a plausible range for the population percent. The sample percent is exactly 55%, so B is wrong; A and D misinterpret.

questions.skill: Sample size and margin of error
questions.stem: A poll of 400 people has a margin of error of about 5 percentage points. About how many people must be polled to cut the margin of error in half, to 2.5 percentage points?
questions.solution: The margin of error shrinks with the square root of the sample size, so halving it takes 4 times as many people: $400 \times 4 = 1600$. (Check: $1/\sqrt{1600} = 1/40 = 0.025$.)

solve.work: Margin ~ 1/sqrt(n). Halving it requires sqrt(n) to double, so n x 4 = 1,600. Check: 1/sqrt(1600) = 0.025.

questions.skill: Informal inference by simulation: reading the results
questions.stem: A coin maker says her coins land heads 50% of the time. A tester flips one coin 20 times and gets 15 heads. A computer simulates 100 sets of 20 flips of a fair coin, and only 2 of the 100 sets give 15 or more heads. What is the best conclusion?
choices: A fair coin can never give 15 or more heads, so the coin is certainly unfair
15 or more heads is rare for a fair coin, so it is evidence of unfairness
15 or more heads is typical for a fair coin, so the coin is probably fair
The simulation proves that this particular coin lands heads 75% of the time
questions.answer: 15 or more heads is rare for a fair coin, so it is evidence of unfairness
questions.solution: Only 2 of 100 fair-coin sets did as well as the tester's coin, so the result would be unusual if the coin were fair. That is evidence against fairness, not proof. The simulation shows a fair coin can give 15 heads, just rarely, and it cannot tell us the coin's true heads rate.

solve.answer: 15 or more heads is rare for a fair coin, so it is evidence of unfairness
solve.work: Only 2% of simulated fair-coin sets gave 15+ heads, so the observed result is unusual under the claim: evidence (not proof) the coin is unfair. B and C overclaim; D contradicts the simulation.

questions.skill: Informal inference by simulation: reading the results
questions.stem: In a simulation of 200 random samples taken under a claim, 14 of the samples gave a result at least as extreme as the one actually observed. What proportion of the simulated samples is this? Give your answer as a decimal.
questions.solution: The proportion is $14 \div 200 = 0.07$. A result that happens in 7% of simulated samples is fairly uncommon but not extremely rare.

questions.stem: A line fitted to data from used cars predicts the price y (in thousands of dollars) from the age x (in years): $y = 24 - 2x$. A 3-year-old car actually sold for 20 thousand dollars. What is the residual, the actual price minus the predicted price, in thousands of dollars?
questions.solution: The predicted price at $x = 3$ is $24 - 2 \times 3 = 18$. The residual is $20 - 18 = 2$ thousand dollars: the car sold for 2 thousand more than the line predicts.

solve.work: Predicted y = 24 - 2(3) = 18. Residual = 20 - 18 = 2.

questions.skill: When to trust a predicted value
questions.stem: A line fitted to the first 10 weeks of a plant's growth predicts its height y (in centimeters) from its age x (in weeks): $y = 3 + 4x$. A student uses it to predict the height at 80 weeks and gets 323 centimeters. What is the best comment?
choices: The line was calculated incorrectly and should be thrown away completely
Age 80 weeks is far outside the data, so the prediction is unreliable
The prediction is reliable, because the line fits the first 10 weeks well
The prediction is reliable if it is rounded to the nearest centimeter
questions.answer: Age 80 weeks is far outside the data, so the prediction is unreliable
questions.solution: The line was built from ages 0 to 10 weeks. Predicting at 80 weeks is extrapolation, and plants do not keep growing at the same rate forever. The arithmetic ($3 + 4 \times 80 = 323$) is correct, but the prediction is not trustworthy.

solve.answer: Age 80 weeks is far outside the data, so the prediction is unreliable
solve.work: 3 + 4(80) = 323, arithmetic right, but 80 weeks is far beyond the 10 weeks of data: extrapolation, unreliable (plants stop growing linearly).

questions.skill: Estimating a population value from a sample
questions.stem: A random sample of 150 residents of a town finds that 60 of them recycle. The town has 9,000 residents. About how many residents of the town recycle, based on the sample proportion?
questions.solution: The sample proportion is $60/150 = 0.4$. Applying it to the town gives about $0.4 \times 9000 = 3600$ residents.

solve.work: Sample proportion 60/150 = 0.4. Estimate 0.4 x 9000 = 3,600.

questions.skill: Limits on generalizing from a sample or an experiment
questions.stem: A city wants to estimate the opinions of all its adult residents. Which sample would let it generalize most safely?
choices: 300 shoppers surveyed at one mall on a Saturday afternoon
300 people who chose to answer an advertisement online
300 members of the largest fitness club in the city
300 adults chosen at random from a list of all residents
questions.answer: 300 adults chosen at random from a list of all residents
questions.solution: Only random selection from the whole population lets us generalize to it. The other samples reach only shoppers, volunteers or gym members, who may differ from the city as a whole.

solve.answer: 300 adults chosen at random from a list of all residents
solve.work: A random sample from a list of all residents represents the population; the others are convenience or voluntary-response samples.

questions.skill: Limits on generalizing from a sample or an experiment
questions.stem: A researcher studies how teens use social media. She recruits 500 teens from the sign-up page of a website and finds that 80% use social media daily. What limits the conclusion?
choices: Five hundred is too few teens for any percent of them to be reported at all
Teens do not use social media as often as the adults of the same state do
A website can never be used to collect any kind of data from anyone at all
Teens who visit that website may use social media more than other teens do
questions.answer: Teens who visit that website may use social media more than other teens do
questions.solution: The teens were not chosen at random from all teens, and those who visit the website may be different from the rest.

solve.answer: Teens who visit that website may use social media more than other teens do
solve.work: Website recruits are self-selected, may use social media more. D.

questions.skill: Limits on generalizing from a sample or an experiment
questions.stem: In an experiment, 40 mice are assigned at random to a new diet or the usual diet, and the mice on the new diet live longer. Which statement is best supported?
choices: The new diet probably helped mice like these; humans would need a separate study
The new diet will lengthen life for humans too, since mice are animals as well
The new diet had no effect, since only 40 mice were used in the whole study
The new diet lengthens life for every animal, since the assignment was made at random
questions.answer: The new diet probably helped mice like these; humans would need a separate study
questions.solution: Random assignment supports a cause for these mice. It does not show that the same holds for humans.

solve.answer: The new diet probably helped mice like these; humans would need a separate study
solve.work: Randomized on mice: causal for similar mice; humans need study. D.

questions.skill: Limits on generalizing from a sample or an experiment
questions.stem: A random sample of 200 customers from a store's loyalty list finds that 70% like the new layout. To which group may the store apply this result?
choices: All shoppers in the city, since the sample of 200 customers was chosen at random
Customers on the loyalty list; shoppers not on the list may feel differently
Every customer of the store, since a sample of 200 customers is large enough
Only the 200 customers who were asked, and nobody else who is on the loyalty list
questions.answer: Customers on the loyalty list; shoppers not on the list may feel differently
questions.solution: The sample was drawn from the loyalty list, so it speaks for people on that list.

solve.answer: Customers on the loyalty list; shoppers not on the list may feel differently
solve.work: Sampling frame is loyalty list. B.

questions.skill: Estimating a population value from a sample
questions.stem: A random sample of 400 households in a city of 50,000 households finds that 120 of them have a pet. About how many households in the city have a pet?
questions.solution: The sample proportion is 120/400 = 0.3. Then 0.3 x 50,000 = 15,000 households.

questions.skill: Estimating a population value from a sample
questions.stem: A random sample of 36 students from a school of 1,200 students had a mean of 3.5 hours of screen time a day. Estimate the total number of hours of screen time in one day for all 1,200 students.
questions.solution: Use the sample mean as the estimate for every student: 3.5 x 1,200 = 4,200 hours.

questions.skill: Margin of error and what it means
questions.stem: A poll of 1,000 voters finds Candidate A at 48% and Candidate B at 45%, with a margin of error of 3 percentage points. Which statement is best?
choices: A is certain to win, since 48% is greater than 45%
The poll proves that the two candidates are exactly tied
A leads in the sample, but the poll cannot rule out B being ahead
B is ahead, since the margin of error is taken away from A's total
questions.answer: A leads in the sample, but the poll cannot rule out B being ahead
questions.solution: A's plausible range is 45% to 51% and B's is 42% to 48%. They overlap, so the lead is not certain.

solve.answer: A leads in the sample, but the poll cannot rule out B being ahead
solve.work: A: 45-51, B: 42-48 overlap; B could be ahead. A.

questions.skill: Margin of error and what it means
questions.stem: A poll reports that between 41% and 49% of voters favor a proposal. What is the poll's margin of error, in percentage points?
questions.solution: The interval is centered at 45%. The distance from 45 to 49 is 4, so the margin of error is 4 points.

questions.skill: Margin of error and what it means
questions.stem: A poll of 1,000 voters has a margin of error of 3 points. A reporter says the same margin of error applies to the 80 voters in the poll who are aged 18 to 20. What is wrong?
choices: A group of 80 voters is a much smaller sample, so its margin of error is much smaller
A group of 80 voters always has a margin of error of exactly 3 points as well
A group of 80 voters is too small to have had any answers recorded for it at all
An 80-voter group is a much smaller sample, so its margin of error is much larger
questions.answer: An 80-voter group is a much smaller sample, so its margin of error is much larger
questions.solution: The margin of error depends on the number of people in the group, and a small group gives a much wider margin.

solve.answer: An 80-voter group is a much smaller sample, so its margin of error is much larger
solve.work: Subgroup n=80 has larger MOE (~1/sqrt80 ~ 11 points). D.

questions.skill: Margin of error and what it means
questions.stem: Poll A finds 55% in favor of a plan, with a margin of error of 2 points. Poll B finds 51% in favor, with a margin of error of 3 points. Do the polls clearly disagree?
choices: No; the intervals overlap, so both could be measuring the same true percent
Yes, because 55 and 51 are different numbers, so one of the two polls is wrong
Yes, because 57 is larger than 54, which is the top end of the other interval
No, because both polls have exactly the same margin of error as each other
questions.answer: No; the intervals overlap, so both could be measuring the same true percent
questions.solution: Poll A gives 53% to 57% and Poll B gives 48% to 54%. The two overlap from 53% to 54%.

solve.answer: No; the intervals overlap, so both could be measuring the same true percent

questions.skill: Sample size and margin of error
questions.stem: A pollster uses the rule that the margin of error, as a decimal, is about 1 divided by the square root of the sample size. How many people must she poll to have a margin of error of 0.04?

questions.skill: Sample size and margin of error
questions.stem: Using the rule that the margin of error is about 1 divided by the square root of the sample size, how many times as large is the margin of error of a poll of 100 people as that of a poll of 900 people?
questions.solution: The poll of 100 has a margin of 1/10. The poll of 900 has a margin of 1/30. The ratio is (1/10)/(1/30) = 3.

questions.stem: A student takes many random samples of the same size from a large school and finds each sample mean. Which sample size will give sample means that differ from each other the least?
choices: Samples of 4 students each
Samples of 400 students each
Samples of 40 students each
Samples of 100 students each
questions.answer: Samples of 400 students each
questions.solution: Larger random samples give sample means that are closer together, so 400 students gives the least variation.

solve.answer: Samples of 400 students each
solve.work: Largest samples vary least: 400. A.

questions.stem: Ten random samples of 20 students each are checked for left-handed students. The counts are 1, 3, 2, 4, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3 and 4. Based on the mean count, what percent of students is estimated to be left-handed?
questions.solution: The total of the counts is 25, so the mean is 2.5 per sample of 20. Then 2.5/20 = 0.125, which is 12.5%.

questions.skill: Informal inference by simulation: setting up
questions.stem: A student wants to estimate the chance that a family of 3 children has at least 2 girls. A boy and a girl are equally likely. Which simulation is valid?
choices: Flip a coin once for each of many families, and count heads as "at least 2 girls"
Flip a coin 3 times, once only, and use that single result as the chance of the event
Flip a coin 3 times for each of many families; count families with at least 2 heads
Flip a coin 3 times for each of many families and count those with exactly 2 heads
questions.answer: Flip a coin 3 times for each of many families; count families with at least 2 heads
questions.solution: Each simulated family needs 3 flips, and the event is "at least 2 heads". Many families are needed to estimate a chance.

solve.answer: Flip a coin 3 times for each of many families; count families with at least 2 heads
solve.work: Heads=girl, 3 flips per family, count at least 2 heads over many families. B.

questions.skill: Informal inference by simulation: setting up
questions.stem: A student simulates 12 people, each with a 20% chance of being left-handed. She uses digits 0 to 9 and lets the digits 0 and 1 mean left-handed. The digits for one trial are 3, 1, 8, 0, 7, 7, 2, 9, 1, 5, 6, 4. How many left-handed people are in this trial?
questions.solution: The digits 0 or 1 appear as 1, 0 and 1. That is 3 left-handed people.

solve.work: Digits 0 or 1: 1, 0, 1 -> 3.

questions.skill: Informal inference by simulation: reading the results
questions.stem: A teacher claims that 60% of students prefer online homework. In a random sample of 30 students, 12 (40%) prefer it. A simulation of 200 samples of 30 with a true percent of 60% gives 40% or lower in only 3 of the samples. What is the best conclusion?
choices: The sample proves that the true percent of all students is exactly equal to 40%
The simulation shows that the claim is true, since 3 samples is a small number
The sample is useless, since 12 students is much smaller than the claimed 60%
A result like 40% is rare if the claim is true, so it is evidence against 60%
questions.answer: A result like 40% is rare if the claim is true, so it is evidence against 60%
questions.solution: Only 3 of 200 samples (1.5%) were this low, so the result would be unusual if the claim were true.

solve.answer: A result like 40% is rare if the claim is true, so it is evidence against 60%
solve.work: 3/200 = 1.5%: rare under claim, evidence against 60%. C.

questions.skill: Informal inference by simulation: reading the results
questions.stem: In a simulation of 400 samples under a claim, 22 samples gave a result at least as extreme as the one observed. What percent of the simulated samples is this?

questions.skill: Informal inference by simulation: reading the results
questions.stem: A simulation of no effect gives differences between two group means from about -4 to 4, with the middle 95% between -3 and 3. The difference actually observed is 5. What is the best conclusion?
choices: A difference of 5 is beyond what chance usually gives, so it suggests a real difference
A difference of 5 is typical of chance alone, so there is no evidence of a real difference
A difference of 5 is impossible under chance, so the simulation was run wrongly
Any observed difference is evidence of a real difference, since chance never makes a difference
questions.answer: A difference of 5 is beyond what chance usually gives, so it suggests a real difference
questions.solution: The middle 95% runs from -3 to 3, so a difference of 5 is unusual if there is no effect. That is evidence for a real difference.

solve.answer: A difference of 5 is beyond what chance usually gives, so it suggests a real difference
solve.work: 5 lies beyond all simulated differences: suggests real difference. A.

questions.stem: A line fitted to baking data predicts the time y in minutes from the number of cookies x: $y = 8 + 0.5x$. For how many cookies does the line predict a time of 20 minutes?
questions.solution: Solve 8 + 0.5x = 20. Then 0.5x = 12, so x = 24.

questions.stem: A line fitted to the ages of teens from 10 to 17 years predicts the number of apps y on a phone from age x: $y = 15 + 2x$. A student says, "The 15 means a baby has 15 apps." What is the problem?
choices: An age of 0 is inside the ages that were studied, so the line gives 15 for sure there
An age of 0 is far outside the ages 10 to 17 studied, so the 15 has no meaning there
A baby has not yet used any apps, so the 15 must be changed to a 0 in the line itself
The line gives a prediction only for ages that are a multiple of 5, such as 15 years
questions.answer: An age of 0 is far outside the ages 10 to 17 studied, so the 15 has no meaning there
questions.solution: The line applies to ages 10 to 17. At age 0 it is extrapolating far beyond the data.

solve.answer: An age of 0 is far outside the ages 10 to 17 studied, so the 15 has no meaning there
solve.work: Intercept at age 0 is extrapolation far outside 10-17. B.

questions.stem: The line $y = 2x + 5$ is used to predict y. The data points are (2, 9), (4, 11) and (6, 20). What is the largest residual in size (the largest absolute value of actual minus predicted)?
questions.solution: Predicted values are 9, 13 and 17. The residuals are 0, -2 and 3, so the largest in size is 3.

solve.work: Predicted 9, 13, 17; residuals 0, -2, 3; largest |r| = 3.

questions.skill: When to trust a predicted value
questions.stem: A line is fitted to data for children aged 5 to 12 years, and the correlation is 0.96. A friend says the line is therefore reliable for predicting the value for a 30-year-old. What is the best reply?
choices: A high correlation guarantees that the line holds for every age, even one far outside the data
A high correlation means that the line is never reliable for any age, near the data or far
