A high correlation shows a good fit for ages studied, not a reliable guess far outside them
A high correlation is possible only when the data were collected from adults and not children
questions.answer: A high correlation shows a good fit for ages studied, not a reliable guess far outside them
questions.solution: The correlation describes how well the line fits the data in the studied range, and 30 is far outside that range.

solve.answer: A high correlation shows a good fit for ages studied, not a reliable guess far outside them
solve.work: Good fit within data; extrapolation to 30 unreliable. A.

questions.skill: When to trust a predicted value
questions.stem: The residuals for a fitted line are mostly positive for small x, mostly negative for middle x, and mostly positive for large x. What does this suggest?
choices: The line fits well, since the positive and negative residuals balance each other
The line fits perfectly, since the residuals change sign more than once
The data were recorded wrongly, since residuals should all be positive
A straight line is a poor model, since the relationship is curved
questions.answer: A straight line is a poor model, since the relationship is curved
questions.solution: Residuals with a pattern show that the data curve away from the line. A random scatter would suggest a good fit.

solve.answer: A straight line is a poor model, since the relationship is curved
solve.work: Residual pattern +,-,+ indicates curvature. C.

questions.skill: Margin of error and what it means
questions.stem: In a random sample of 400 voters, 220 support a plan. Use a margin of error of about 1 divided by the square root of the sample size. What is the lowest proportion that the resulting interval allows? Give your answer as a decimal.
questions.solution: The sample proportion is $220/400 = 0.55$. The margin of error is about $1/\sqrt{400} = 1/20 = 0.05$. The lowest value is $0.55 - 0.05 = 0.50$, so a true proportion of exactly one half is still plausible.

questions.skill: Margin of error and what it means
questions.stem: A poll shows Candidate A with 51% and Candidate B with 49%, with a margin of error of 3 percentage points. Which statement is best?
choices: The race is too close to call, since the poll cannot tell who leads
Candidate A is certain to win, because A has more than 50% of the votes
Candidate B is ahead, because the margin of error is taken away from A
The poll is biased, since the two percentages are so close together
questions.answer: The race is too close to call, since the poll cannot tell who leads
questions.solution: With a margin of error of 3 points, the true support for A could be anywhere from about 48% to 54%, so the lead of 2 points is within the margin. The poll cannot tell us who is ahead. Close results do not mean bias, and no one is certain to win.

solve.answer: The race is too close to call, since the poll cannot tell who leads
solve.work: A: 48% to 54%, B: 46% to 52%; intervals overlap heavily, so the poll cannot say who leads. Too close to call.

questions.skill: Informal inference by simulation: setting up
questions.stem: In a population, 30% of the people prefer tea. To simulate choosing one person at random, a student uses the random digits 0 to 9, each equally likely. Which rule is correct?
choices: Digits 0, 1, 2 and 3 mean the person prefers tea
Only the digit 3 means the person prefers tea
Digits 0, 1 and 2 mean the person prefers tea
Digits 0, 1 and 2 mean the person does not prefer tea
questions.answer: Digits 0, 1 and 2 mean the person prefers tea
questions.solution: Three of the ten digits make 30%, so a rule that assigns 3 digits to tea drinkers matches the population. Four digits would be 40%, one digit 10%, and the last rule would make 70% prefer tea.

solve.answer: Digits 0, 1 and 2 mean the person prefers tea
solve.work: 30% of 10 equally likely digits = 3 digits mean tea. Digits 0, 1, 2 = tea gives 3/10. B gives 40%, C gives tea 70%, D gives 10%.

questions.skill: Informal inference by simulation: reading the results
questions.stem: A simulation draws many random samples from a population in which the true proportion is 0.5. The middle 95% of the sample proportions fall between 0.42 and 0.58. About what margin of error does this suggest for samples of this size? Give your answer as a decimal.
questions.solution: The middle 95% of sample results spans from 0.42 to 0.58, which is 0.16 wide and centered at 0.50. The distance from the center to either end is $0.16 \div 2 = 0.08$. That is the margin of error.

solve.work: Middle 95% spans 0.42 to 0.58, i.e. 0.5 +/- 0.08. Margin of error about 0.08.

questions.stem: A line fitted to puppies aged 4 to 20 weeks predicts weight y (in kilograms) from age x (in weeks): $y = 2 + 0.8x$. A puppy that is 12 weeks old weighs 12.4 kilograms. By how many kilograms does its actual weight exceed its predicted weight?
questions.solution: The predicted weight at $x = 12$ is $2 + 0.8 \times 12 = 2 + 9.6 = 11.6$ kilograms. The residual is $12.4 - 11.6 = 0.8$ kilograms.

questions.stem: A line fitted to data from 20 students predicts the time y (in minutes) a student needs to finish a worksheet from the number of problems x: $y = 5 + 3x$. For how many problems does the line predict a time of 38 minutes?
questions.solution: Set $5 + 3x = 38$. Then $3x = 33$ and $x = 11$ problems.

questions.skill: When to trust a predicted value
questions.stem: A line fitted to 30 teenagers has a correlation of $r = 0.9$ between shoe size and height. A student uses it to predict one particular teenager's height. Which statement is best?
choices: It gives the exact height of that particular teenager, because $r$ is so close to 1
It is useless for predicting any one person, because $r$ is not equal to exactly 1
It gives a typical height for that shoe size, but the real height may differ
It will be within 1 inch of the real height, because $r$ is so close to 1
questions.answer: It gives a typical height for that shoe size, but the real height may differ
questions.solution: A strong correlation means the line predicts well on average, but individual teenagers scatter around it. The prediction is a reasonable estimate, not an exact value, and no particular accuracy is guaranteed. A correlation of 0.9 is far from useless.

solve.answer: It gives a typical height for that shoe size, but the real height may differ
solve.work: A strong correlation gives a good typical (predicted) height, but individuals scatter around the line; r near 1 does not guarantee exactness or a 1-inch error, nor is the line useless.

questions.skill: Limits on generalizing from a sample or an experiment
questions.stem: A random sample of 1,000 adults from a country finds that adults who exercise more report better moods. Which conclusion is justified?
choices: It applies to adults in that country, but it does not show exercise causes better mood
It shows that exercise causes better mood, and it applies to all adults in the whole world
It shows that exercise causes better mood, but only for the 1,000 adults who were surveyed
It cannot be applied beyond the 1,000 adults, and it does not show a cause of any kind
questions.answer: It applies to adults in that country, but it does not show exercise causes better mood
questions.solution: Random selection lets us generalize to the population sampled, which is the adults of that country, not the whole world. Because nobody was assigned to exercise, the study shows an association, not cause and effect.

solve.answer: It applies to adults in that country, but it does not show exercise causes better mood
solve.work: Random sample from the country lets us generalize to that country's adults; it is observational, so no causal claim. D.

questions.skill: Estimating a population value from a sample
questions.stem: In a random sample of 80 students from School A, 28 prefer online homework. In a random sample of 120 students from School B, 54 prefer it. How many percentage points higher is the sample percent at School B than the sample percent at School A?
questions.solution: School A: $28/80 = 35\%$. School B: $54/120 = 45\%$. The difference is $45 - 35 = 10$ percentage points. Whether this gap is real or just chance would need a margin of error or a simulation.

questions.skill: Informal inference by simulation: reading the results
questions.stem: A teacher claims a spinner lands on red 25% of the time. In 24 spins it lands on red 8 times. A computer simulates 100 sets of 24 spins with a 25% chance of red, and 22 of the sets have 8 or more reds. Which statement is best?
choices: The result proves that the claim is true, because 8 is close to the expected 6
The result proves that the claim is false, because 8 is more than the expected 6
The result is strong evidence that the chance of red is above 25%, since 8 is more than 6
8 reds is not unusual when the chance is 25%, so the result fits the claim
questions.answer: 8 reds is not unusual when the chance is 25%, so the result fits the claim
questions.solution: In the simulation, 22 of 100 sets (22%) had 8 or more reds, so a result like this is common under the teacher's claim. The data are consistent with the claim. That does not prove the claim true, since a different chance of red could also give such a result.

solve.answer: 8 reds is not unusual when the chance is 25%, so the result fits the claim
solve.work: 22 of 100 simulated sets under the claim had 8+ reds, so 8 reds is not unusual; the data are consistent with the claim (not proof either way). B, C, D overclaim.

questions.skill: Limits on generalizing from a sample or an experiment
questions.stem: Researcher 1 picks 100 students at random from the school's full list. Researcher 2 asks 100 students in the cafeteria. Both find that 70% like the school lunch. A report says both studies equally justify the claim for the whole school. What is the best comment?
choices: Only the first sample can speak for the whole school; the second misses students not in the cafeteria
Both samples can speak for the whole school equally well, because each of them has exactly 100 students
Only the second sample can speak for the whole school, because it asked students who really eat the lunch
Neither sample can speak for the whole school, because 100 students can never be enough for a school
questions.answer: Only the first sample can speak for the whole school; the second misses students not in the cafeteria
questions.solution: A random sample from the full list can speak for the school. A sample taken in the cafeteria leaves out students who do not eat there.

solve.answer: Only the first sample can speak for the whole school; the second misses students not in the cafeteria
solve.work: Random sample from full list is representative; cafeteria misses others. C.

questions.skill: Limits on generalizing from a sample or an experiment
questions.stem: A random sample of 50 sophomores at a school has a mean sleep time of 6.8 hours. Which statement is most precise?
choices: All students at the school sleep exactly 6.8 hours on average, with no error at all from the sampling
Sophomores average about 6.8 hours, give or take sampling error; the other grades were not studied
Students in every school in the state sleep about 6.8 hours on average, with only a small error in it
Each of the sophomores at the school sleeps exactly 6.8 hours, as this sample of 50 students has shown
questions.answer: Sophomores average about 6.8 hours, give or take sampling error; the other grades were not studied
questions.solution: The sample is of sophomores at one school, so the estimate applies to them and has sampling error.

solve.answer: Sophomores average about 6.8 hours, give or take sampling error; the other grades were not studied
solve.work: Applies to sophomores, with sampling error. C.

questions.skill: Limits on generalizing from a sample or an experiment
questions.stem: A randomized experiment on 300 volunteers shows that a tutoring method raises scores. The researcher says it will work for all students everywhere. What does the study support?
choices: The method raises the scores of all students everywhere, since the assignment was random
The method has no proven effect on anyone, since the people in the study were volunteers
The method raised scores for volunteers like these but was not shown for all students
The method may raise scores, but only the 300 volunteers can ever be said to have gained
questions.answer: The method raised scores for volunteers like these but was not shown for all students
questions.solution: Random assignment supports a cause among the volunteers. Volunteers are not a random sample of all students, so a claim for everyone goes too far.

solve.answer: The method raised scores for volunteers like these but was not shown for all students
solve.work: Randomized but volunteers; supports effect for similar volunteers. A.

questions.skill: Estimating a population value from a sample
questions.stem: A biologist tags 50 fish in a lake and releases them. A week later she catches a random sample of 100 fish, and 5 of them have tags. Assuming the sample represents the lake, about how many fish are in the lake?
questions.solution: 5 out of 100 fish in the sample are tagged, which is 5%. So the 50 tagged fish are about 5% of the lake: 50 / 0.05 = 1,000 fish.

questions.skill: Estimating a population value from a sample
questions.stem: A random sample of 60 voters from Precinct 1, which has 5,000 voters, finds that 45% favor a plan. A random sample of 40 voters from Precinct 2, which has 3,000 voters, finds that 60% favor it. Estimate the total number of voters in the two precincts who favor the plan.
questions.solution: Precinct 1: 0.45 x 5,000 = 2,250. Precinct 2: 0.6 x 3,000 = 1,800. The total is 4,050 voters.

questions.skill: Margin of error and what it means
questions.stem: A poll of 1,600 adults finds that 960 favor a plan. Use a margin of error of about 1 divided by the square root of the sample size. What is the upper end of the interval, as a decimal?
questions.solution: The sample proportion is 960/1,600 = 0.6. The margin of error is 1/40 = 0.025. The upper end is 0.6 + 0.025 = 0.625.

questions.skill: Margin of error and what it means
questions.stem: A poll reports that 54% of voters favor a plan, with a margin of error of 3 points. The mayor says, "A majority of voters favor the plan." Another speaker says, "We cannot be sure a majority favors it." Who is better supported by the poll?
choices: The other speaker, because any margin of error means a result cannot be used at all
The other speaker, because 54% is just 4 points above 50%, and 4 is more than 3
Neither speaker, because a poll can say nothing at all about whether there is a majority
The mayor, because even the lowest value in the interval, 51%, is above 50%
questions.answer: The mayor, because even the lowest value in the interval, 51%, is above 50%
questions.solution: The interval runs from 51% to 57%. All of it is above 50%, so the poll supports a majority (with the usual small chance of being wrong).

solve.answer: The mayor, because even the lowest value in the interval, 51%, is above 50%
solve.work: Interval 51% to 57%, all above 50%. D.

questions.skill: Margin of error and what it means
questions.stem: A poll with a 95% level reports a margin of error of 3 points. A news site writes, "The true value is certainly within 3 points of the poll's result." What is wrong?
choices: At the 95% level, there is still about a 5% chance the true value is outside the interval
At the 95% level, the true value is within 3 points exactly 95 times out of every 100 polls
At the 95% level, 95% of the people polled gave an answer within 3 points of the result
At the 95% level, the true value is certain to be inside the interval, so nothing is wrong
questions.answer: At the 95% level, there is still about a 5% chance the true value is outside the interval
questions.solution: A 95% level means that about 95% of polls made this way capture the true value. About 5% miss it, so "certainly" is too strong.

solve.answer: At the 95% level, there is still about a 5% chance the true value is outside the interval
solve.work: 95% confidence is not certainty; ~5% of such intervals miss. C.

questions.skill: Sample size and margin of error
questions.stem: A pollster uses the rule that the margin of error, in percentage points, is about 100 divided by the square root of the sample size. What is the smallest sample size that gives a margin of error of 2 points or less?

questions.skill: Sample size and margin of error
questions.stem: A pollster interviews 1,000 people and gets a margin of error of about 3 points. She is offered another 1,000 people at the same price. What should she expect if she doubles the sample to 2,000?
choices: The margin of error will stay the same, since the sample was random both times
The margin of error will shrink by only about a factor of 1.4, not by half
The margin of error will be cut exactly in half, to about 1.5 points
The margin of error will double, since there are twice as many answers to check
questions.answer: The margin of error will shrink by only about a factor of 1.4, not by half
questions.solution: The margin of error is proportional to 1/√n. Doubling n divides it by √2, which is about 1.4.

solve.answer: The margin of error will shrink by only about a factor of 1.4, not by half
solve.work: MOE scales as 1/sqrt(n); doubling n divides by sqrt2 ~ 1.41 (3 -> ~2.1). D.

questions.stem: The spread of sample proportions from random samples is proportional to 1 divided by the square root of the sample size. For samples of 100 people, the spread (standard deviation) of the sample proportions is 0.05. What is the spread for samples of 400 people, as a decimal?
questions.solution: Four times as many people makes the spread 1/√4 = 1/2 as large: 0.05 / 2 = 0.025.

solve.work: Spread scales 1/sqrt(n): 400 is 4x so spread halves: 0.05/2 = 0.025.

questions.stem: Which statement about the variability of sample means is true?
choices: Sample means from large random samples are usually more spread out than sample means from small ones
Sample means from a random sample are always exactly equal to the population mean
Sample means from large random samples are usually closer together than sample means from small ones
Sample means vary only when the sample was chosen in a careless or biased way
questions.answer: Sample means from large random samples are usually closer together than sample means from small ones
questions.solution: Larger random samples vary less. Even careful random samples vary, so means differ by chance.

solve.answer: Sample means from large random samples are usually closer together than sample means from small ones
solve.work: Larger samples -> less variable means. D.

questions.skill: Informal inference by simulation: setting up
questions.stem: A student flips a coin 30 times and gets 20 heads. To see how unusual 20 heads would be if the coin were fair, which simulation is appropriate?
choices: Simulate many sets of 20 flips of a fair coin and count the sets with 30 or more heads
Simulate one set of 30 flips of a coin that lands heads two thirds of the time
Simulate many sets of 30 flips of a coin that has landed heads on 20 of 30 flips
Simulate many sets of 30 flips of a fair coin and count the sets with 20 or more heads
questions.answer: Simulate many sets of 30 flips of a fair coin and count the sets with 20 or more heads
questions.solution: We assume the coin is fair, copy the real setup of 30 flips, and count how often chance alone gives 20 or more heads.

solve.answer: Simulate many sets of 30 flips of a fair coin and count the sets with 20 or more heads
solve.work: Simulate fair coin, 30 flips, count >= 20 heads. A.

questions.skill: Informal inference by simulation: setting up
questions.stem: A student simulates the chance that at least one of 3 independent people is a fan, where each person is a fan with chance 20%. She uses digits 0 to 9, with 0 and 1 meaning a fan, and 3 digits per trial. The 10 trials are (3,5,7), (1,4,9), (6,2,8), (0,0,5), (9,9,9), (4,1,3), (7,6,2), (5,5,8), (2,0,9), (8,3,6). What proportion of the trials had at least one fan?
questions.solution: The trials with a 0 or a 1 are (1,4,9), (0,0,5), (4,1,3) and (2,0,9). That is 4 of 10 trials, or 0.4.

questions.skill: Informal inference by simulation: reading the results
questions.stem: To test whether a fertilizer helps, 20 growth values were pooled and randomly split into two groups of 10, 1,000 times. In 310 of the 1,000 splits, the first group's mean was higher than the second's by at least 2.4 cm, the difference seen in the real study. What is the best conclusion?
choices: A difference of 2.4 cm happens by chance about 31% of the time, so it is not convincing evidence
A difference of 2.4 cm happens by chance only about 31% of the time, so it is convincing evidence
A difference of 2.4 cm is proof that the fertilizer does nothing, since 310 is less than half
The random splits are not valid, since the real plants were not split at random
questions.answer: A difference of 2.4 cm happens by chance about 31% of the time, so it is not convincing evidence
questions.solution: About 31% of random splits gave a difference at least as large, so chance alone often produces such a gap.

solve.answer: A difference of 2.4 cm happens by chance about 31% of the time, so it is not convincing evidence
solve.work: 310/1000 = 31%: chance often gives 2.4 cm; not convincing. A.

questions.skill: Informal inference by simulation: reading the results
questions.stem: In a simulation of 1,000 samples, 22 samples were at least as low as the observed result and 18 were at least as high as the matching high result. What percent of the simulated samples were at least as far from the center, in either direction?
questions.solution: 22 + 18 = 40 samples out of 1,000, which is 4%.

questions.skill: Informal inference by simulation: reading the results
questions.stem: A simulation shows that the middle 95% of sample proportions for samples of 100 runs from 0.40 to 0.60 when the true proportion is 0.5. A real sample gives 0.62. A friend says, "The true proportion is certainly not 0.5." What is the best response?
choices: 0.62 would be usual if the truth were 0.5, so the true proportion must be exactly 0.5
0.62 would be unusual if the truth were 0.5, but unusual samples happen, so "certainly" is too strong
0.62 would be impossible if the truth were 0.5, so the friend is entirely right about it
0.62 says nothing at all, because one sample can never be compared with a whole simulation
questions.answer: 0.62 would be unusual if the truth were 0.5, but unusual samples happen, so "certainly" is too strong
questions.solution: About 5% of samples fall outside the middle 95% even when the truth is 0.5, so we have evidence but not certainty.

solve.answer: 0.62 would be unusual if the truth were 0.5, but unusual samples happen, so "certainly" is too strong
solve.work: 0.62 outside middle 95% but unusual samples happen; "certainly" too strong. A.

questions.skill: Informal inference by simulation: reading the results
questions.stem: In a simulation under a claim, the sample proportions have a mean of 0.5 and a standard deviation of 0.04. The sample actually observed has a proportion of 0.62. How many standard deviations above 0.5 is it?
questions.solution: The difference is 0.62 - 0.5 = 0.12, and 0.12 / 0.04 = 3 standard deviations.

questions.stem: A line fitted to used-car data predicts the price y, in hundreds of dollars, from the age x in years: $y = 150 - 6x$. How many hundreds of dollars lower is the predicted price of a 7-year-old car than that of a 3-year-old car?
questions.solution: Each extra year lowers the predicted price by 6. Four more years lowers it by 6 x 4 = 24 hundred dollars.

solve.work: Slope -6 per year; 4 years -> 24 lower.

questions.stem: A line used for predictions passes through the points (2, 14) and (6, 30). What y-value does the line predict at x = 5?
questions.solution: The slope is (30 - 14)/(6 - 2) = 4. From x = 2 to x = 5 is 3 steps, so y = 14 + 4 x 3 = 26.

questions.stem: A fitted line is $y = 3 + 2x$. At x = 5, the residual of a data point is -4. What is the actual y-value of the point?
questions.solution: The predicted value is 3 + 2 x 5 = 13. Residual = actual - predicted, so actual = 13 + (-4) = 9.

solve.work: Predicted 3+10 = 13; actual = 13 + (-4) = 9.

questions.stem: Two lines are fitted to the same four data points. Line 1 has residuals 1, -1, 2 and -2. Line 2 has residuals 3, -3, 3 and -3. Which line fits better, judged by the sum of the squared residuals?
choices: Line 2, since its residuals add to 0, just as Line 1's residuals do
Neither, since the residuals of both lines add up to exactly the same total of 0
Line 1, since its squared residuals add to 10 and Line 2's add to 36
Line 2, since all of its residuals are the same size, which means a steady fit
questions.answer: Line 1, since its squared residuals add to 10 and Line 2's add to 36
questions.solution: Squared residuals: Line 1 is 1 + 1 + 4 + 4 = 10, and Line 2 is 9 + 9 + 9 + 9 = 36. The smaller sum is the better fit.

solve.answer: Line 1, since its squared residuals add to 10 and Line 2's add to 36
solve.work: Line 1: 1+1+4+4 = 10; Line 2: 9*4 = 36. Line 1 better. C.

questions.skill: When to trust a predicted value
questions.stem: A line was fitted to data from adult men aged 20 to 60. It is used to predict the value for a 40-year-old woman. What is the best comment?
choices: The age is inside the range of the data, so the prediction is as reliable as for a man
The age is outside the range of the data, since women were not included in the ages
The prediction cannot be calculated, since a line cannot be used for another person
The age is in the range, but the line was built from men only, so it may not fit women
questions.answer: The age is in the range, but the line was built from men only, so it may not fit women
questions.solution: The age 40 is within 20 to 60, but the line comes from a different group, so it may not describe women.

solve.answer: The age is in the range, but the line was built from men only, so it may not fit women
solve.work: Age in range but population differs (men only). D.

questions.stem: Researchers record what 500 adults eat and, ten years later, note who has developed heart disease. The researchers do not tell anyone what to eat. What kind of study is this?
choices: An experiment, because the researchers collected data on every adult
An experiment, because the researchers followed the adults for ten years
An experiment, because the study compared the diets of many different adults
An observational study, because the researchers did not assign the diets
questions.answer: An observational study, because the researchers did not assign the diets
questions.solution: In an experiment the researchers assign the treatments (here, the diets). These researchers only recorded what people chose to eat, so this is an observational study.

solve.answer: An observational study, because the researchers did not assign the diets
solve.work: The researchers only record diets and outcomes; they assign no treatment. That is an observational study.

questions.stem: In an experiment, what is the main purpose of randomly assigning subjects to the treatment groups?
choices: To make sure the results can be applied to the whole population of interest
To make the groups similar, so other factors do not favor one group
To make sure that every subject gets the treatment that is best for them
To make sure the groups have exactly the same number of subjects
questions.answer: To make the groups similar, so other factors do not favor one group
questions.solution: Random assignment uses chance to decide who gets which treatment, so the groups should be similar in everything else (age, health, motivation). A difference in results can then be traced to the treatment.

solve.answer: To make the groups similar, so other factors do not favor one group
solve.work: Random assignment balances other factors across groups so differences can be credited to the treatment. Generalizing to a population comes from random sampling, not assignment.

questions.stem: In summer, both ice cream sales and the number of sunburns go up. Which is the best explanation?
choices: Hot, sunny weather affects both, so neither one has to cause the other
Eating more ice cream causes people to get sunburned more often
Getting a sunburn makes people buy more ice cream
They are unrelated, because ice cream and sunburns are different things
questions.answer: Hot, sunny weather affects both, so neither one has to cause the other
questions.solution: Two things can rise together because a third factor, here hot sunny weather, affects both. An association does not show that one causes the other.

solve.answer: Hot, sunny weather affects both, so neither one has to cause the other
solve.work: A lurking variable (hot sunny weather) drives both; association does not imply either causes the other.

questions.stem: A store sold 40 items on Monday and 60 items on Tuesday. By what percent did sales increase from Monday to Tuesday? Give the number only, without the percent sign.
questions.solution: The increase is 60 - 40 = 20 items. As a percent of the starting amount, 20 / 40 = 0.5, which is 50%.

questions.skill: Critique a claim: anecdote or small sample
questions.stem: A man says, "My uncle smoked for 60 years and lived to 95, so smoking is harmless." What is the main weakness of this evidence?
choices: The uncle lived too long for the story to be believed
A single case is just as strong as a large study of many people
One person's story cannot show what happens to most people
Stories can never be true, so only numbers count
questions.answer: One person's story cannot show what happens to most people
questions.solution: A single case (an anecdote) can be an exception. To judge a claim about smoking we need data on many people, which shows what usually happens.

solve.answer: One person's story cannot show what happens to most people
solve.work: A single anecdote cannot show what happens to most people; it says nothing about the rate of harm.

questions.stem: In an experiment to test a new medicine, what does the control group provide?
choices: A comparison for the results of the group that gets the new medicine
A group chosen because its members are the healthiest people available
A guarantee that the new medicine will work for everyone who takes it
A second group that gets twice as much of the new medicine as the first
questions.answer: A comparison for the results of the group that gets the new medicine
questions.solution: The control group does not get the new medicine (it may get a placebo). Its results show what happens without the treatment, so they can be compared with the treatment group's results.

solve.answer: A comparison for the results of the group that gets the new medicine
solve.work: The control group gives a baseline for comparison with the treatment group.

questions.stem: A news story says that eating a certain snack "doubles your chance" of a rare condition. Among people who do not eat the snack, 3 in every 10,000 get the condition. If the story is right, how many in every 10,000 snack-eaters get the condition?
questions.solution: Doubling the chance of 3 in 10,000 gives 2 x 3 = 6 in 10,000. A "doubled" chance of a rare event can still be very small.

questions.stem: A randomized experiment finds that students who used a tutoring app improved more than students who did not. What kind of conclusion can this design support?
choices: Students who improve are more likely to choose the app
The app will improve the scores of every student in the world
The app caused the extra improvement in these students
No conclusion, because experiments can only show associations
questions.answer: The app caused the extra improvement in these students
questions.solution: Random assignment makes the two groups alike, so a difference in improvement can be attributed to the app. An experiment can support cause and effect, but only for subjects like those who took part.

solve.answer: The app caused the extra improvement in these students
solve.work: A randomized experiment supports a cause-and-effect conclusion for the subjects studied: the app caused the extra improvement in these students. Not every student in the world.

questions.skill: Critique a claim: source and funding
questions.stem: A study says a sugary cereal has health benefits. The study was paid for by the company that makes the cereal. What is the best way to treat the study?
choices: Ignore the study, because research paid for by a company is always false
Accept the study, because a published study is always accurate
Accept the study, because the company knows its cereal best
Check how the study was done and look for independent research
questions.answer: Check how the study was done and look for independent research
questions.solution: Funding by an interested company is a reason to look more closely at how the study was done and to compare it with independent work. It does not prove the results are false, and it does not make them reliable.

solve.answer: Check how the study was done and look for independent research
solve.work: Funding creates a possible conflict of interest: examine the methods and seek independent research, rather than accepting or dismissing it outright.

questions.skill: Interpret the results of an experiment
questions.stem: In an experiment, 30 of 100 people who took a new medicine improved, and 20 of 100 people who took a placebo improved. By how many percentage points was the improvement rate higher for the medicine group?
questions.solution: The medicine group improved at a rate of 30%, and the placebo group at 20%. The difference is 30 - 20 = 10 percentage points.

solve.work: 30/100 = 30%, 20/100 = 20%; difference 10 percentage points.

questions.stem: A school lets each of its 80 students pick either the morning or the afternoon math class. At the end of the year, a researcher compares the test scores of the two classes. What kind of study is this?
choices: An experiment, because the researcher compared two different groups of students
An experiment, because the researcher measured the test scores at the end of the year
An observational study, because the students chose their own classes
An experiment, because the two classes were compared during the same school year
questions.answer: An observational study, because the students chose their own classes
questions.solution: Nobody was assigned to a class by the researcher; the students chose. When the researcher only observes groups that formed on their own, the study is observational.

solve.answer: An observational study, because the students chose their own classes
solve.work: Students chose their own class; the researcher imposed no treatment, so it is observational.

questions.stem: A researcher flips a coin for each of 60 volunteers. Heads means the volunteer gets a new reading program, and tails means the volunteer does not. What kind of study is this?
choices: An experiment, because the researcher assigned the program to volunteers by chance
An observational study, because only volunteers took part in the study
An observational study, because the researcher did not choose the volunteers
An observational study, because a coin flip is not a kind of measurement
questions.answer: An experiment, because the researcher assigned the program to volunteers by chance
questions.solution: The researcher decided who got the program, using a coin flip. A study in which the researcher assigns the treatment is an experiment.

solve.answer: An experiment, because the researcher assigned the program to volunteers by chance
solve.work: The researcher imposes the program and assigns it by chance (coin flip): a randomized experiment.

questions.stem: In a trial of a new pain medicine, the control group gets a placebo, a pill that looks the same but has no medicine in it. What is the main reason for using a placebo?
choices: To make sure the patients in the control group get well sooner than the others
To check that all of the patients take the same number of pills every day
To keep the patients from learning how many people are in the whole trial
To separate the effect of the medicine from the effect of just taking a pill
questions.answer: To separate the effect of the medicine from the effect of just taking a pill
questions.solution: People often feel better just because they are treated. Comparing the medicine group with a placebo group separates the real effect of the medicine from that expectation effect.

solve.answer: To separate the effect of the medicine from the effect of just taking a pill
solve.work: A placebo controls for the placebo effect, separating the drug effect from the effect of taking a pill.

questions.stem: A teacher wants to assign 30 students to two groups at random. Which method does this?
choices: Put the 15 students who sit nearest the window in the first group
Put all 30 names in a hat and draw 15 of them for the first group
Put the 15 students with the highest grades in the first group
Let each student choose which of the two groups to join
questions.answer: Put all 30 names in a hat and draw 15 of them for the first group
questions.solution: Random assignment gives every student the same chance of each group, which drawing names from a hat does. The other methods let location, grades or choice decide.

solve.answer: Put all 30 names in a hat and draw 15 of them for the first group
solve.work: Drawing 15 names from a hat is random; the others use seat, grades or self-selection.

questions.stem: Among children in elementary school, those with larger shoe sizes tend to have higher reading scores. Which is the best explanation?
choices: Having larger feet makes it easier for a child to learn how to read
Older children tend to have both larger feet and more reading practice
Reading well makes a child's feet grow larger than they otherwise would
Shoe size and reading score are linked only by pure coincidence in the data
questions.answer: Older children tend to have both larger feet and more reading practice
questions.solution: Age affects both shoe size and reading score, so the two move together without either causing the other.

solve.answer: Older children tend to have both larger feet and more reading practice
solve.work: Age is a lurking variable driving both foot size and reading skill.

questions.stem: What is a confounding variable in a study?
choices: The outcome that the researchers measure at the end of the study
The group of subjects who get no treatment during the study
A mistake made when the data are typed into a computer file
A factor linked to both the groups and the outcome, which can mimic an effect
questions.answer: A factor linked to both the groups and the outcome, which can mimic an effect
questions.solution: A confounding variable is related to both the explanatory variable and the outcome, so it can make a difference look like an effect of the groups when it is not.

solve.answer: A factor linked to both the groups and the outcome, which can mimic an effect
solve.work: A confounder is associated with both the explanatory groups and the response, so it can mimic an effect.

questions.skill: Critique a claim: anecdote or small sample
questions.stem: A friend says, "I drank herbal tea when I had a cold, and I felt better in three days, so the tea cures colds." What is the biggest problem with this evidence?
choices: Colds often get better in a few days anyway, and this is only one case
Herbal teas are made from plants, so they can never help a person with a cold
A person's own report about feeling better is never worth listening to at all
Three days is far too long to wait before a cold starts getting better
questions.answer: Colds often get better in a few days anyway, and this is only one case
questions.solution: One person's story has no comparison group. Most colds clear up in a few days without any treatment, so the tea may have had nothing to do with it.

solve.answer: Colds often get better in a few days anyway, and this is only one case
solve.work: Colds resolve in days on their own, and a single anecdote has no comparison group.

questions.skill: Critique a claim: biased or nonresponse sample
questions.stem: An online store's website asks its visitors, "Do you love shopping online?" Of 2,000 visitors who answer, 90% say yes. The store claims that 90% of all adults love shopping online. What is the main problem?
choices: Two thousand people are far too few to say anything about all adults
Nine in ten is too high a percent for the results of a survey to be real
People who visit an online store are not typical of all adults
A website is not able to ask visitors a question of any kind
questions.answer: People who visit an online store are not typical of all adults
questions.solution: The visitors chose to be at an online store, so they are more likely to enjoy online shopping than adults in general. The sample is biased.

solve.answer: People who visit an online store are not typical of all adults
solve.work: Voluntary response from visitors to an online store: the sample is not representative of all adults.

questions.skill: Critique a claim: misleading graph or summary
questions.stem: A bar graph shows sales of 96 for one store and 99 for another store, but its vertical axis starts at 95 instead of 0. How does this change what the graph looks like?
choices: The two bars look exactly equal in height, which hides that the sales differ
The first bar looks taller than the second, which reverses the order of the sales
The second bar looks several times as tall as the first, although the sales are close
The bars look the same as they would if the axis started at 0
questions.answer: The second bar looks several times as tall as the first, although the sales are close
questions.solution: With the axis starting at 95, the bars are drawn 1 and 4 units tall, so the second looks four times as tall even though 99 is only a little more than 96.

solve.answer: The second bar looks several times as tall as the first, although the sales are close
solve.work: Visible heights are 96-95=1 and 99-95=4, so the second bar looks 4 times as tall though sales are close.

questions.skill: Critique a claim: counts versus rates
questions.stem: City X had 120 bicycle accidents last year and City Y had 40. A writer says bicyclists are less safe in City X. What should be known before judging this claim?
choices: How many people ride bicycles in each city, so the accidents can be compared as rates
Which of the two cities had the most recent accident, since newer accidents count more
How many streets each of the cities has, since only streets can cause accidents
Whether the accidents happened in the morning or in the afternoon in each city
questions.answer: How many people ride bicycles in each city, so the accidents can be compared as rates
questions.solution: City X may simply have far more riders. Accident counts need to be divided by the number of riders (or rides) to compare safety fairly.

solve.answer: How many people ride bicycles in each city, so the accidents can be compared as rates
solve.work: Counts must be turned into rates per rider (exposure) before comparing safety.

questions.skill: Critique a claim: source and funding
questions.stem: A poll says 70% of people support a new highway. The poll was paid for by the company that would build the highway. What is the best response?
choices: Reject the poll, because every poll paid for by a company is false
Accept the poll, because 70% is much more than a simple majority
Accept the poll, because a company would not pay for a poll that is wrong
Look at who was asked and how the questions were worded before trusting it
questions.answer: Look at who was asked and how the questions were worded before trusting it
questions.solution: Who paid is a reason to look closely, not to reject automatically. Check the sample and the wording of the questions.

solve.answer: Look at who was asked and how the questions were worded before trusting it
solve.work: Sponsorship is a reason for scrutiny, not automatic rejection: check the sample and wording.

questions.skill: Limits of inference: sampling versus assignment
questions.stem: A pollster randomly chooses 1,200 registered voters from a large city and asks them about a new park. Whose opinions can the results be used to describe?
choices: All of the voters in the whole country, because the sample was chosen at random
All of the registered voters of that city, not only the 1,200 who were asked
Only the 1,200 voters who were asked, since nobody else gave an answer
Every resident of that city, including the children who were not asked
questions.answer: All of the registered voters of that city, not only the 1,200 who were asked
questions.solution: A random sample lets the results be applied to the population it was drawn from: the registered voters of that city.

solve.answer: All of the registered voters of that city, not only the 1,200 who were asked
solve.work: A random sample of the city's registered voters generalizes to that population only.

questions.skill: Critique a claim: short-run or selective data
questions.stem: A bakery had its best sales day of the year the day after it painted its door red. The owner says, "Painting the door red boosts sales." What is the best response?
choices: The claim is proven, because the best day came right after the door was painted
One good day is not enough, because sales go up and down from day to day anyway
The claim is false, because the color of a door cannot change what people buy
The claim is proven, because the owner knows the bakery better than anyone
questions.answer: One good day is not enough, because sales go up and down from day to day anyway
questions.solution: Sales vary from day to day for many reasons. A single good day right after a change does not show the change caused it.

solve.answer: One good day is not enough, because sales go up and down from day to day anyway
solve.work: One day after the change is an anecdote; daily sales vary naturally.

questions.skill: Critique a claim: statistical versus practical significance
questions.stem: A report says a difference between two groups is "statistically significant". What does that mean?
choices: The difference is large enough to matter a great deal in everyday practice
The difference was found by a scientist, so it must be correct
The difference proves that one group's condition caused the other's
The difference is unlikely to be due to chance variation alone
questions.answer: The difference is unlikely to be due to chance variation alone
questions.solution: Statistical significance says the difference is hard to explain as luck of the draw. It does not say the difference is large or that it was caused by the groups.

solve.answer: The difference is unlikely to be due to chance variation alone
solve.work: Statistically significant = unlikely to arise from chance variation alone; says nothing about size or causation by itself.

questions.stem: A study says a vitamin lowers the chance of catching a cold in the winter from 20 out of every 100 people to 15 out of every 100 people. By how many percentage points did the chance fall?
questions.solution: 20% - 15% = 5 percentage points.

solve.work: 20% - 15% = 5 percentage points.

questions.stem: A story says that eating a certain food makes children three times as likely to have an allergy. Without that food, 4 out of every 1,000 children have the allergy. If the story is right, how many out of every 1,000 children who eat the food have the allergy?
questions.solution: Three times 4 is 12 out of every 1,000. Notice that this is still a small number of children.

questions.stem: An ad says a new battery lasts 50% longer than the old battery. The old battery lasts 8 hours. How many hours does the new battery last?
questions.solution: 50% of 8 is 4, so the new battery lasts 8 + 4 = 12 hours.

solve.work: 8 x 1.5 = 12 hours.

questions.skill: Interpret the results of an experiment
questions.stem: In a randomized experiment, 120 of 200 people given a new tutoring plan passed a test, and 80 of 200 people given the usual tutoring passed. By how many percentage points was the passing rate higher with the new plan?
questions.solution: 120/200 = 60% and 80/200 = 40%, a difference of 20 percentage points.

questions.skill: Interpret the results of an experiment
questions.stem: In the placebo group of an experiment, 36 of the 120 people reported feeling better even though they got no medicine. What percent of the placebo group felt better? Give the number only, without the percent sign.
questions.solution: 36 / 120 = 0.30, which is 30%. This shows that many people feel better without any medicine.

questions.skill: Critique a claim: counts versus rates
questions.stem: City P had 90 thefts last year and has 60,000 residents. How many thefts were there per 1,000 residents?
questions.solution: 90 / 60,000 = 0.0015 per person, which is 1.5 per 1,000 residents.

questions.stem: A researcher randomly splits 90 volunteers into three equal groups: a placebo group, a low-dose group and a high-dose group. How many volunteers get some dose of the medicine?
questions.solution: Each group has 90 / 3 = 30 volunteers. The two dose groups have 30 + 30 = 60 volunteers.

solve.work: 90/3 = 30 per group; low + high dose = 60.

questions.skill: Limits of inference: margin of error
questions.stem: A poll of a random sample finds that 52% of voters support a plan, with a margin of error of 3 percentage points. What is the lowest percent of all voters who might plausibly support the plan?
questions.solution: The plausible values run from 52 - 3 = 49 to 52 + 3 = 55 percent. The lowest is 49.

questions.skill: Critique a claim: misleading graph or summary
questions.stem: Five workers earn (in thousands of dollars per year) 30, 32, 34, 36 and 168. The boss says, "Our average pay is 60 thousand a year." What is the median pay, in thousands of dollars?
questions.solution: The five pays in order are 30, 32, 34, 36, 168, so the middle one is 34. The mean is 300 / 5 = 60, pulled up by the single large pay.

solve.work: Sorted 30, 32, 34, 36, 168; middle value 34.

questions.stem: A study finds that students who eat breakfast have higher grades. Which is the best example of a confounding variable?
choices: Grades, which are the outcome the researchers measured
Family income, which could affect both eating breakfast and grades
Eating breakfast, which is the habit the researchers compared
The school building, which is the same for all of the students
questions.answer: Family income, which could affect both eating breakfast and grades
questions.solution: A confounding variable is related to both the habit being studied and the outcome, so it can create a pattern that is not cause and effect. Family income could plausibly affect both eating breakfast and grades.

solve.answer: Family income, which could affect both eating breakfast and grades
solve.work: A confounder is related to both the explanatory variable and the response: family income could affect both breakfast and grades. The school building is constant; grades and breakfast are the variables themselves.

questions.stem: An observational study finds that adults who walk daily have lower blood pressure. A headline reads "Daily walks lower your blood pressure." What is the best critique?
choices: The headline is fair, because a study with enough adults proves cause
The study is useless, because observational studies never show any relationship
The headline is unsupported, because the study shows only an association
The headline is fair, because walking is already well known to be healthy
questions.answer: The headline is unsupported, because the study shows only an association
questions.solution: The adults chose whether to walk, so people who walk may differ in other ways (health, age, diet). An observational study can find an association, but only an experiment with random assignment can support a cause-and-effect claim.

solve.answer: The headline is unsupported, because the study shows only an association
solve.work: Observational study shows association only; the causal headline is unsupported (e.g. healthier people may walk more).

questions.stem: To test a new fertilizer, a gardener gives it to the plants on the sunny side of a greenhouse and gives none to the plants on the shady side. The plants on the sunny side grow taller. What is the main flaw?
choices: Sunlight and fertilizer are mixed up, so sunlight may explain the difference
Plants cannot be used in an experiment, because they cannot report back
Giving all the plants the fertilizer would show whether it works
Only one fertilizer was tested, so no comparison between fertilizers is possible
questions.answer: Sunlight and fertilizer are mixed up, so sunlight may explain the difference
questions.solution: The plants with the fertilizer also had more sunlight, so the two effects cannot be separated. The gardener should have assigned the fertilizer to plants at random.

solve.answer: Sunlight and fertilizer are mixed up, so sunlight may explain the difference
solve.work: Fertilizer went only to sunny plants, so sunlight and fertilizer are confounded; sunlight may explain the growth. Random assignment would fix it.

questions.stem: In a drug trial, neither the patients nor the doctors who measure their symptoms know which patients got the real drug. Why is this done?
choices: So that the two groups will end up with the same number of patients in them
So expectations cannot affect what is reported or how symptoms are judged
So that every patient receives exactly the same dose of the drug
So that the results will apply to everyone in the whole world
questions.answer: So expectations cannot affect what is reported or how symptoms are judged
questions.solution: If people know who got the real drug, their hopes can change what patients feel and report and how doctors judge them. Keeping everyone unaware (blinding) removes that effect.

solve.answer: So expectations cannot affect what is reported or how symptoms are judged
solve.work: Double-blinding prevents patients' and evaluators' expectations from affecting reported or judged outcomes.

questions.skill: Limits of inference: sampling versus assignment
questions.stem: Eighty volunteers aged 18 to 25 at one university were randomly assigned to either a new sleep routine or their usual routine. The group using the new routine reported better sleep. Which conclusion is best supported?
choices: The routine improves sleep for every person of every age in every place
The routine did not cause the improvement, because the volunteers were not randomly chosen
Nothing can be concluded, because a group of only 80 people is too small
The routine helped volunteers like these, but may not apply to other ages
questions.answer: The routine helped volunteers like these, but may not apply to other ages
questions.solution: Random assignment supports a cause-and-effect conclusion for the subjects studied. Because the subjects were young volunteers from one university, applying the result to other ages goes beyond the evidence.

solve.answer: The routine helped volunteers like these, but may not apply to other ages
solve.work: Random assignment supports causation for these volunteers; they were not randomly sampled and all aged 18-25 at one university, so generalization is limited to similar people.

questions.stem: A headline says a new drug "cuts the risk of a stroke by 25%". In the study, 8 of every 100 people on the old treatment had a stroke, and 6 of every 100 people on the new drug had a stroke. By how many percentage points did the stroke rate actually fall?
questions.solution: The stroke rate fell from 8% to 6%, which is 2 percentage points. As a share of the old rate it is 2 / 8 = 25%, which is how the headline got its number. The change per 100 people is small.

solve.work: 8% - 6% = 2 percentage points (relative fall 2/8 = 25%).

questions.stem: In a study of children ages 5 to 10, height grew about 6 centimeters per year. A writer concludes that a 30-year-old is about 150 centimeters taller than a 5-year-old. What is wrong with this conclusion?
choices: A pattern in children's heights can never be used to predict anything
The pattern is being extended far beyond the ages that were studied
The conclusion is fine, because the pattern held for every child studied
The conclusion is fine, because 6 centimeters a year is an average
questions.answer: The pattern is being extended far beyond the ages that were studied
questions.solution: A pattern found within a range of data may not hold outside it. Growth slows and stops in the teenage years, so extending the pattern to age 30 is unreliable.

solve.answer: The pattern is being extended far beyond the ages that were studied
solve.work: The rate was observed only for ages 5-10; applying it to age 30 (25 years x 6 = 150) is extrapolation, and growth stops in the late teens.

questions.skill: Critique a claim: short-run or selective data
questions.stem: A mayor says, "Crime fell 20% last month, so our new policy works!" Crime had been rising steadily for five years and fell in only that one month. What is the best response?
choices: The claim is proven, because crime really did fall 20%
The claim is false, because crime rose over the five years before
The claim is proven, because a mayor has the official numbers
The claim is unproven, because one month is too short to show a trend
questions.answer: The claim is unproven, because one month is too short to show a trend
questions.solution: A single month can fall by chance. To judge the policy we need to see whether the decrease continues over a longer time and compare it with what would have happened without the policy.

solve.answer: The claim is unproven, because one month is too short to show a trend
solve.work: One month's drop after five years of rises may be random fluctuation; a single month is too short to show the policy works. The claim is unproven, not proven or shown false.

questions.stem: A city finds that neighborhoods with more police officers also have more crime. A council member proposes cutting the number of police to reduce crime. What is the best response?
choices: The proposal is sound, because the data show that having police causes crime
The proposal is sound, because more police always means more crime in a city
The proposal is doubtful, because police may be sent to high-crime areas
Data about neighborhoods can never be used to guide any kind of policy
questions.answer: The proposal is doubtful, because police may be sent to high-crime areas
questions.solution: The cause may run the other way: high crime leads the city to send more police. The association alone does not show that police cause crime.

solve.answer: The proposal is doubtful, because police may be sent to high-crime areas
solve.work: Causation likely runs the other way: police are sent where crime is high. Cutting police is not supported.

questions.skill: Interpret the results of an experiment
questions.stem: In a randomized experiment with 150 patients in each group, 63 patients on a new treatment recovered and 45 patients on the standard treatment recovered. By how many percentage points was the recovery rate higher on the new treatment?
questions.solution: The new treatment recovery rate is 63 / 150 = 42%. The standard treatment rate is 45 / 150 = 30%. The difference is 42 - 30 = 12 percentage points.

solve.work: 63/150 = 42%; 45/150 = 30%; difference 12 percentage points.

questions.stem: A farmer wants to know whether a new fertilizer raises the yield of her corn. Which plan gives the most trustworthy answer?
choices: Divide every field into plots and use a coin flip to choose which plots get the fertilizer
Use the fertilizer on the fields with the best soil and compare them with the other fields
Use the fertilizer on all of her fields and compare this year's yield with last year's yield
Ask neighboring farmers whether they believe the fertilizer works well on their corn
questions.answer: Divide every field into plots and use a coin flip to choose which plots get the fertilizer
questions.solution: Random assignment of plots makes the fertilized and unfertilized plots alike in soil and sun, so a difference in yield can be credited to the fertilizer.

solve.answer: Divide every field into plots and use a coin flip to choose which plots get the fertilizer
solve.work: Randomly assigning plots within each field controls soil and year effects: a randomized experiment.

questions.stem: A study of 10,000 adults, who chose their own bedtimes, finds that those who go to bed late earn less on average. Which statement does the study design justify?
choices: Going to bed late causes adults to earn less than other adults earn
Earning a lower income causes adults to go to bed later in the evening
Adults who went to bed late tended to earn less than the others in this study
Going to bed late has no link with how much adults earn on average
questions.answer: Adults who went to bed late tended to earn less than the others in this study
questions.solution: The adults chose their own bedtimes, so this is an observational study. It can show an association but not which thing, if either, causes the other.

solve.answer: Adults who went to bed late tended to earn less than the others in this study
solve.work: Observational: only an association within this study is justified, not causation either way.

questions.stem: Why would a researcher test a new teaching method on 200 students instead of only 4 students?
choices: With more students, every student is sure to learn the new method well
With more students, a control group is no longer needed to make a comparison
With more students, chance differences between the groups tend to average out
With more students, the cost of teaching each student always goes down
questions.answer: With more students, chance differences between the groups tend to average out
questions.solution: In small groups a few unusual students can swing the results. With many students, such chance differences tend to cancel out, so the comparison is more reliable.

solve.answer: With more students, chance differences between the groups tend to average out
solve.work: Larger samples reduce chance variation, so random differences between groups average out.

questions.stem: To compare two brands of running shoes, each of 20 runners runs a course wearing one brand and later runs it wearing the other brand. A coin flip decides which brand each runner wears first. Why is the order chosen by a coin flip?
choices: So that tiredness or practice from the first run does not favor one brand
So that every runner is sure to wear the same brand on the first run
So that the runners are not able to tell which brand they are wearing
So that the results can be applied to all runners in the entire country
questions.answer: So that tiredness or practice from the first run does not favor one brand
questions.solution: If every runner used brand A first, the second brand might look worse because of fatigue, or better because of practice. Randomizing the order spreads those effects evenly over both brands.

solve.answer: So that tiredness or practice from the first run does not favor one brand
solve.work: Randomizing order balances fatigue/learning effects between brands.

questions.stem: A study finds that people who use sunscreen are more likely to get skin cancer than people who do not. Which is a confounding variable?
choices: Whether a person has skin cancer, which is the outcome that the study measures
Whether a person uses sunscreen, which is the habit that the study compares
The brand name of the sunscreen, which affects only the price a person pays
How much time a person spends in strong sun, which affects sunscreen use and cancer risk
questions.answer: How much time a person spends in strong sun, which affects sunscreen use and cancer risk
questions.solution: People who spend more time in strong sun are both more likely to use sunscreen and more likely to get skin cancer, so sun exposure can produce the association.

solve.answer: How much time a person spends in strong sun, which affects sunscreen use and cancer risk
solve.work: Sun exposure raises both sunscreen use and cancer risk: a confounder.

questions.stem: Counties with more hospitals have more deaths each year. A student concludes that hospitals cause deaths. What is the best critique?
choices: Hospitals are built to save lives, so they cannot be linked to any deaths
Counties with more people tend to have both more hospitals and more deaths
Deaths are rare events, so no pattern across counties can be trusted
The student should have compared the counties' sizes in square miles
questions.answer: Counties with more people tend to have both more hospitals and more deaths
questions.solution: Population size is a lurking variable: bigger counties have more hospitals and more deaths, with no need for one to cause the other.

solve.answer: Counties with more people tend to have both more hospitals and more deaths
solve.work: Population size drives both the number of hospitals and the number of deaths.

questions.skill: Critique a claim: biased or nonresponse sample
questions.stem: A school mails a survey to 3,000 parents. Only 300 return it, and most of those who do are unhappy with the lunch menu. The principal says most parents are unhappy. What is the best critique?
choices: Surveys sent by mail rarely give a true picture of what a group of people think
Parents with strong opinions are more likely to reply, so the replies may be biased
Most parents are probably happy, because only 300 of the 3,000 parents replied
The principal should count each unreturned survey as a parent who agrees
questions.answer: Parents with strong opinions are more likely to reply, so the replies may be biased
questions.solution: With only 10% responding, the replies may come mainly from people who feel strongly. This nonresponse bias means the 300 replies may not represent all 3,000 parents.

solve.answer: Parents with strong opinions are more likely to reply, so the replies may be biased
solve.work: 10% voluntary response; strong (negative) opinions more likely to reply: nonresponse/voluntary bias.

questions.skill: Critique a claim: misleading graph or summary
questions.stem: A town's report says its average household income is very high, but most families there earn modest incomes and a few households earn millions of dollars. Which measure better describes a typical household?
choices: The mean, because it uses every income in the town in its calculation
The range, because it shows how large the largest income in the town is
The mean, because large incomes show what a typical household earns
The median, because a few very large incomes do not pull it up much
questions.answer: The median, because a few very large incomes do not pull it up much
questions.solution: A few very large incomes pull the mean up but barely move the median, which is the middle household's income.

solve.answer: The median, because a few very large incomes do not pull it up much
solve.work: Right-skewed incomes: the median resists the few huge values.

questions.skill: Critique a claim: anecdote or small sample
questions.stem: Hospital A had 3 of its 4 patients recover (75%). Hospital B had 700 of its 1,000 patients recover (70%). An ad says Hospital A is better. What is the best critique?
choices: Four patients are too few for 75% to be a reliable measure of the hospital
Hospital B treated more patients, so it must have the higher recovery rate
Recovery rates cannot be compared between two different hospitals at all
Hospital A is better, because 75% is greater than 70% for a hospital
questions.answer: Four patients are too few for 75% to be a reliable measure of the hospital
questions.solution: A rate based on 4 patients can change a lot if just one patient does differently (2 of 4 is 50%). The hospital B figure rests on far more evidence.

solve.answer: Four patients are too few for 75% to be a reliable measure of the hospital
solve.work: n = 4 is far too small for a reliable rate.

questions.stem: A manager fits a line to data on advertising spending between 1,000 and 5,000 dollars a month and monthly sales. She then uses the line to predict sales for 50,000 dollars of advertising. What is the main concern?
choices: A line is not able to be used to predict sales from advertising spending
The line must pass through the point where spending and sales are both zero
The prediction goes far beyond the range of spending that the data covered
A prediction is reliable only if the spending is a round number like 50,000
questions.answer: The prediction goes far beyond the range of spending that the data covered
questions.solution: The pattern was observed only for spending from 1,000 to 5,000 dollars. Nothing shows the same line holds at ten times the highest amount, so this is risky extrapolation.

solve.answer: The prediction goes far beyond the range of spending that the data covered
solve.work: Extrapolation far beyond 1,000-5,000.

questions.skill: Interpret the results of an experiment
questions.stem: In an experiment, the treatment group improved by 8 points on average and the control group improved by 6 points. A statistician says a difference this size could easily happen by chance alone. What is the best conclusion?
choices: The treatment is proven to work, because 8 is greater than 6 points
The treatment is proven not to work, because the difference is small
The data do not give good evidence that the treatment works better
The treatment works, because the control group also improved somewhat
questions.answer: The data do not give good evidence that the treatment works better
questions.solution: If chance alone could easily produce a 2-point gap, the gap is not convincing evidence of a real effect. That does not prove the treatment is useless either.

solve.answer: The data do not give good evidence that the treatment works better
solve.work: Difference consistent with chance: no good evidence, but not proof of no effect.

questions.skill: Critique a policy proposal from data
questions.stem: A city randomly picks 40 of 80 similar schools to start a free-breakfast program. After a year, attendance is higher in the 40 program schools by far more than chance would explain. An official says the program raised attendance in schools like these. Is this claim supported?
choices: Yes, because random assignment made the two sets of schools alike apart from the program
No, because only 40 schools got the program, which is too few for any claim
No, because attendance is something that only an observational study can measure
Yes, because the program would then work in every school in the whole country
questions.answer: Yes, because random assignment made the two sets of schools alike apart from the program
questions.solution: Random assignment balances other factors, so a difference too large for chance can be credited to the program, for schools similar to these 80. It does not extend to every school.

solve.answer: Yes, because random assignment made the two sets of schools alike apart from the program
solve.work: Random assignment balances the groups, and the difference exceeds chance, so a causal claim for similar schools is supported.

questions.stem: An author studies ten of today's most successful companies and finds that all ten took big risks. The author concludes that taking big risks leads to success. What is the main weakness?
choices: Ten companies is the largest number that any author can study at once
Companies that are successful today never take any risks of any kind
Taking risks is a thing that a study of companies cannot measure at all
Companies that took big risks and then failed were left out of the study
questions.answer: Companies that took big risks and then failed were left out of the study
questions.solution: Only the survivors were studied. Many failed companies may also have taken big risks, so the risks may not explain the success.

solve.answer: Companies that took big risks and then failed were left out of the study
solve.work: Survivorship bias: failed risk-takers were never studied.

questions.stem: A drug lowers the rate of an infection from 10% of patients to 6% of patients. The rate fell by what percent of the old rate? Give the number only, without the percent sign.
questions.solution: The rate fell by 4 percentage points. As a part of the old rate of 10, that is 4 / 10 = 40%.

questions.stem: A headline says a treatment "cuts your risk in half". The risk without it was 2 in 1,000, and the risk with it was 1 in 1,000. By how many percentage points did the risk fall?
questions.solution: 2 in 1,000 is 0.2% and 1 in 1,000 is 0.1%, so the risk fell by 0.1 percentage point, a very small absolute change.

solve.work: 2/1000 = 0.2%, 1/1000 = 0.1%; fall 0.1 percentage point.

questions.skill: Critique a claim: counts versus rates
questions.stem: County X had 18 deaths from a disease last year and has 40,000 people. How many deaths per 100,000 people is that?
questions.solution: 18 / 40,000 = 0.00045 per person, which is 45 per 100,000 people.

questions.skill: Critique a claim: counts versus rates
questions.stem: Hospital A treated 200 patients and 10 of them died. Hospital B treated 50 patients and 4 of them died. By how many percentage points is Hospital B's death rate higher than Hospital A's?
questions.solution: Hospital A: 10 / 200 = 5%. Hospital B: 4 / 50 = 8%. The difference is 3 percentage points.

questions.skill: Limits of inference: margin of error
questions.stem: In a random sample of 400 voters, 220 favor a new law. The margin of error is 5 percentage points. What is the highest percent of all voters who might plausibly favor the law?
questions.solution: 220 / 400 = 55%. Adding the margin of error of 5 points gives 60%.

questions.skill: Interpret the results of an experiment
questions.stem: In a randomized experiment with 250 people in each group, 52% of the treatment group and 40% of the placebo group improved. How many more people in the treatment group than in the placebo group improved?
questions.solution: 52% of 250 is 130 and 40% of 250 is 100, so 30 more people improved.

questions.stem: The share of households with solar panels in a town rose from 5% to 8%. By what percent did the share itself increase? Give the number only, without the percent sign.
questions.solution: The share rose by 3 percentage points. Relative to the starting 5%, that is 3 / 5 = 60%.

questions.skill: Critique a claim: misleading graph or summary
questions.stem: A bar graph shows the sales of two stores, but its vertical axis starts at 90 instead of 0. One store sold 95 items and the other sold 100. As drawn, the bar for the 100-item store is how many times as tall as the bar for the 95-item store?
questions.solution: The bars are drawn from 90, so their heights are 100 - 90 = 10 and 95 - 90 = 5. The taller bar looks 2 times as tall, though 100 is only about 1.05 times 95.

questions.stem: Among people exposed to a chemical, 6% developed a rash. Among people not exposed, 4% developed a rash. The exposed group's rate is how many times the unexposed group's rate?
questions.solution: 6 / 4 = 1.5. This ratio of the two rates is called the relative risk.

questions.stem: In an observational study of 500 adults, 20 of the 200 who sleep at least 8 hours caught a cold during the winter, and 60 of the 300 who sleep less than 8 hours caught one. By how many percentage points was the cold rate lower among those who sleep at least 8 hours?
questions.solution: The rate for the 8-hour sleepers is 20/200 = 10%. The rate for the others is 60/300 = 20%. The difference is 10 percentage points. Because this is an observational study, the data show an association but cannot show that sleep caused the lower rate.

solve.work: At least 8 h: 20/200 = 10%. Less than 8 h: 60/300 = 20%. Difference 20 - 10 = 10 percentage points.

questions.skill: Critique a claim: statistical versus practical significance
questions.stem: A very large study finds that a new teaching method raises average scores by 0.2 points on a 100-point test, and the result is statistically significant. What is the best interpretation?
choices: The effect is probably real, but it may be too small to matter in practice
The effect is large, because the result is statistically significant
The effect is a mistake, because a 0.2-point change is far too small to be real
The effect applies to all students, because the study was so large
questions.answer: The effect is probably real, but it may be too small to matter in practice
questions.solution: "Statistically significant" means the difference is unlikely to be explained by chance alone. It says nothing about whether the difference is big enough to matter. With a very large study, even a tiny difference can be significant.

solve.answer: The effect is probably real, but it may be too small to matter in practice
solve.work: Statistical significance means the effect is unlikely to be chance, not that it is large; 0.2 of 100 points is practically tiny.

questions.skill: Limits of inference: sampling versus assignment
questions.stem: Researchers randomly select 1,000 adults from a country and ask each about exercise and sleep quality. They find that adults who exercise more report better sleep. Which conclusion is justified?
choices: Exercise causes better sleep among the adults of the country
The two are associated only for these 1,000 adults, not for the adults of the country
The two are associated in the country's adults, but cause is not shown
Better sleep causes adults in the country to exercise more
questions.answer: The two are associated in the country's adults, but cause is not shown
questions.solution: Random selection lets the result be generalized to adults in the country. But the adults chose how much to exercise (no random assignment), so the study shows an association, not cause and effect in either direction.

solve.answer: The two are associated in the country's adults, but cause is not shown
solve.work: Random sample from the country allows generalizing the association to the country's adults; no treatment assigned, so no causal conclusion.

questions.skill: Limits of inference: sampling versus assignment
questions.stem: Which study design could justify a cause-and-effect conclusion about all high school students in a state?
choices: Randomly choose students from the state, then randomly assign each to a sleep schedule
Randomly choose students from across the state and survey them about their sleep and grades
Ask volunteers at one school to pick the sleep schedule they prefer, then compare grades
Randomly assign volunteers from one school to sleep schedules and compare their grades
questions.answer: Randomly choose students from the state, then randomly assign each to a sleep schedule
questions.solution: Random assignment is needed for cause and effect, and random selection from the state is needed to apply the result to all the state's students. Only the first design has both. The others have only one, or neither.

solve.answer: Randomly choose students from the state, then randomly assign each to a sleep schedule
