solve.work: Cause needs random assignment; generalizing to all state students needs random selection from the state. Only the first option has both.

questions.stem: A tutor teaches a new study technique to 50 students. Their scores rose from the first test to the second, so she concludes the technique works. What is the most important thing missing from her evidence?
choices: More tests, since two tests are too few to show anything about the class
Proof that all 50 students were volunteers, since volunteers learn more
A survey asking the students whether they liked the new technique
A comparison group that did not learn it, since scores may rise anyway
questions.answer: A comparison group that did not learn it, since scores may rise anyway
questions.solution: Scores could rise because of practice, easier material or more time to study. Without a comparison group that did not learn the technique, we cannot tell how much of the rise, if any, is due to the technique.

solve.answer: A comparison group that did not learn it, since scores may rise anyway
solve.work: Without a control group, the rise could come from practice, an easier test or time; a comparison group is what is missing.

questions.stem: A headline says a vaccine "cuts the risk of infection by 40%". Without the vaccine, 5 of every 1,000 people get infected. Out of 100,000 people, how many fewer infections would be expected with the vaccine?
questions.solution: Without the vaccine, 5 / 1,000 of 100,000 people is 500 infections. A 40% cut is 0.40 x 500 = 200 fewer infections.

solve.work: Without vaccine: 5/1000 x 100,000 = 500 infections. A 40% cut: 0.4 x 500 = 200 fewer.

questions.skill: Interpret the results of an experiment
questions.stem: In a randomized experiment, 45% of the people given a treatment improved, compared with 33% of the control group. Suppose the same treatment is given to 5,000 similar people. About how many more would be expected to improve than if they had not been treated?
questions.solution: The treatment raised the improvement rate by 45 - 33 = 12 percentage points. For 5,000 similar people, that is 0.12 x 5,000 = 600 more people improving.

questions.stem: A politician says, "Unemployment rose by just 1 percent", when the unemployment rate went from 4% to 5%. By what percent did the unemployment rate itself increase? Give the number only, without the percent sign.
questions.solution: The rate rose by 1 percentage point, from 4% to 5%. As a percent of the old rate, 1 / 4 = 25%. The claim of "just 1 percent" confuses a percentage-point change with a percent change.

solve.work: (5 - 4)/4 = 0.25 = 25%. The 1 is percentage points.

questions.skill: Critique a claim: counts versus rates
questions.stem: A newspaper reports, "Town A had 30 car crashes last year and Town B had only 10, so Town B has safer drivers." Town A has 30,000 drivers and Town B has 5,000 drivers. What is the best critique?
choices: The claim is sound, because Town B had fewer crashes than Town A did
The claim is misleading, because per driver Town B has the higher crash rate
The claim is sound, because 10 crashes is much smaller than 30 crashes
The claim is false, because 30 crashes and 10 crashes are about the same
questions.answer: The claim is misleading, because per driver Town B has the higher crash rate
questions.solution: Compare rates, not counts. Town A: 30 / 30,000 = 0.1% of drivers had a crash. Town B: 10 / 5,000 = 0.2%. Town B's rate is twice Town A's, so the claim is misleading.

solve.answer: The claim is misleading, because per driver Town B has the higher crash rate
solve.work: Rates: A 30/30,000 = 1 per 1,000; B 10/5,000 = 2 per 1,000. Per driver B is higher, so the claim is misleading.

questions.skill: Critique a policy proposal from data
questions.stem: A school board reads a study finding that students in schools with a garden have higher science grades. The board proposes a garden at every school to raise grades. Which statement is the best evaluation?
choices: The plan is sound, because the study proves that gardens raise grades
The plan is unsound, because gardens cannot possibly affect science grades
The plan is sound, because the study included a great many schools
The plan is premature, because the study shows only an association
questions.answer: The plan is premature, because the study shows only an association
questions.solution: The schools chose (or could afford) gardens, so they may differ in funding, class sizes or teachers. The study does not show that adding a garden would raise grades; a randomized trial or a study that accounts for those differences would be stronger evidence.

solve.answer: The plan is premature, because the study shows only an association
solve.work: The study is observational (schools with gardens may differ in funding etc.), so it shows association only; the plan is premature.

questions.stem: A gym advertises, "Members who stay for a full year lose 15 pounds on average." Why might this claim overstate what a new member can expect?
choices: A year is too short a time to measure a change in someone's weight
Members who get no results may quit early, so only successes are counted
Averages never apply to individual people, so no average can be trusted
The gym should report the largest loss of any member, not the average
questions.answer: Members who get no results may quit early, so only successes are counted
questions.solution: The average includes only members who stayed. People who were not getting results may have dropped out, so the figure describes the survivors and overstates what a typical new member can expect.

solve.answer: Members who get no results may quit early, so only successes are counted
solve.work: Only members who stay a year are counted; those without results may quit (survivorship bias), so the average overstates what a new member can expect.

questions.skill: Critique a claim: statistical versus practical significance
questions.stem: Study 1 has 100,000 patients and finds that a drug lowers blood pressure by 1 point on average, a statistically significant result. Study 2 has 12 patients and finds a 15-point drop that is not statistically significant. Which statement is best?
choices: Study 1 shows a large effect, and study 2 proves that the drug does not work
Study 1 shows a real but tiny effect, and study 2 is inconclusive and calls for a larger study
Study 2 shows a larger effect, so study 2 gives the better evidence for the drug
Both studies show the same thing, since each one has a drop in blood pressure
questions.answer: Study 1 shows a real but tiny effect, and study 2 is inconclusive and calls for a larger study
questions.solution: With 100,000 patients even a tiny effect can be statistically significant, yet it may not matter in practice. With 12 patients a large effect may fail to be significant simply because the sample is small, so a bigger study is needed.

solve.answer: Study 1 shows a real but tiny effect, and study 2 is inconclusive and calls for a larger study
solve.work: Large n makes a 1-point effect significant but tiny; n = 12 non-significant result is inconclusive.

questions.skill: Limits of inference: sampling versus assignment
questions.stem: Researchers ran a randomized experiment using volunteers from one gym. They want their conclusion to apply to all adults in the city. What should they change?
choices: Let the volunteers pick their own groups so that more adults are willing to join
Randomly select the participants from all of the adults in the city, then randomly assign them
Use only volunteers from that gym but double the number of volunteers
Drop the random assignment and compare gym members with the city's adults
questions.answer: Randomly select the participants from all of the adults in the city, then randomly assign them
questions.solution: Random selection from the whole city lets results be generalized to the city, and random assignment keeps the cause-and-effect conclusion. More volunteers from the same gym would not fix the bias.

solve.answer: Randomly select the participants from all of the adults in the city, then randomly assign them
solve.work: Generalizing needs random selection from the target population; then randomly assign for causation.

questions.stem: A school offers two tutoring programs. Program X has a higher pass rate than Program Y among beginners, and also a higher pass rate among advanced students. Yet Program Y has the higher pass rate overall. Which is the best explanation?
choices: Program X must have had more advanced students than Program Y did
At least one of the reported pass rates must have been calculated incorrectly
A combined rate always lies below the rates of both of the subgroups
Program Y had a much larger share of advanced students, who pass more often
questions.answer: Program Y had a much larger share of advanced students, who pass more often
questions.solution: If most of Y's students were advanced (who pass more often) and most of X's were beginners, Y's overall rate can be higher even though X does better within each level. This is Simpson's paradox.

solve.answer: Program Y had a much larger share of advanced students, who pass more often
solve.work: Simpson's paradox: Y's mix is weighted toward advanced students, who pass more, lifting its overall rate.

questions.stem: An observational study finds that coffee drinkers live longer, even after adjusting for age, sex and smoking. Which statement is best?
choices: Adjusting helps, but unmeasured factors could still explain the link, so cause is not shown
Adjusting for these three factors removes every possible confounder, so cause is shown
Adjusting for factors makes the study an experiment, so cause and effect are shown
Adjusting for these factors shows that coffee has no link with how long people live
questions.answer: Adjusting helps, but unmeasured factors could still explain the link, so cause is not shown
questions.solution: Adjusting handles only the factors that were measured. Other differences between coffee drinkers and others may remain, so an observational study cannot establish cause.

solve.answer: Adjusting helps, but unmeasured factors could still explain the link, so cause is not shown
solve.work: Adjustment cannot remove unmeasured confounders; observational study cannot show causation.

questions.stem: Twenty teachers volunteer to use a new reading method, and their classes' scores are compared with the scores of classes whose teachers did not volunteer. The volunteers' classes score higher. Why is this a weak basis for saying the method works?
choices: Volunteers are always less skilled than other teachers, so the comparison is unfair
The classes of teachers who did not volunteer should have been left out entirely
Teachers who volunteer may differ in motivation or skill, so the groups differ from the start
Reading scores are an outcome that cannot be compared between different classes
questions.answer: Teachers who volunteer may differ in motivation or skill, so the groups differ from the start
questions.solution: Because the teachers chose themselves, the two groups may have differed in motivation, skill or resources before the method was used. Random assignment of teachers would avoid this.

solve.answer: Teachers who volunteer may differ in motivation or skill, so the groups differ from the start
solve.work: Self-selected volunteers may differ systematically: confounding.

questions.stem: A new drug for a serious disease is tested against the current standard drug, not against a placebo. Why might the researchers choose this design?
choices: A placebo cannot be made to look like a drug, so it cannot be used in any trial
A standard drug has no real effect, so it works the same way that a placebo does
Withholding treatment would be unethical, and the real question is whether the new drug beats the standard
Comparing two drugs removes the need to assign patients to the groups at random
questions.answer: Withholding treatment would be unethical, and the real question is whether the new drug beats the standard
questions.solution: When an effective treatment exists, giving sick patients only a placebo may be unethical, and doctors want to know whether the new drug is better than the existing one. Patients should still be randomly assigned.

solve.answer: Withholding treatment would be unethical, and the real question is whether the new drug beats the standard
solve.work: Placebo for a serious disease would withhold effective treatment; the relevant question is new vs standard.

questions.skill: Interpret the results of an experiment
questions.stem: In an experiment with 20 people in each group, 11 people on a new treatment improved and 9 people on the standard treatment improved. A headline says the treatment "boosts recovery by 22%". What is the best critique?
choices: A gap of two people in groups this small could easily be due to chance
The headline understates the effect, because 11 out of 20 people is 55%
A randomized experiment cannot report percents, so only counts may be used
The treatment must work, because more people improved on it than on the standard
questions.answer: A gap of two people in groups this small could easily be due to chance
questions.solution: 11 compared with 9 is a ratio of about 1.22, so the 22% is a relative figure, but it rests on a difference of just 2 people in groups of 20. Chance could easily produce that.

solve.answer: A gap of two people in groups this small could easily be due to chance
solve.work: 11 vs 9 of 20 (55% vs 45%) is a 2-person gap easily due to chance; 22% is the relative increase 11/9.

questions.skill: Critique a claim: short-run or selective data
questions.stem: A company's ad shows a chart of a stock's price that begins on the day the price hit its lowest point in five years. The chart shows the price nearly tripling since then. What is the best critique?
choices: Charts of stock prices can never be used as evidence about how stocks perform
The chart is fair, because the price really did nearly triple after that day
The chart is unfair, because it should end at the highest price instead
Starting at the lowest point exaggerates the rise, and a different start date would tell another story
questions.answer: Starting at the lowest point exaggerates the rise, and a different start date would tell another story
questions.solution: Picking the start date at the low point is selective: the numbers are true but the story depends on where the chart begins. A fair chart would show a longer, unselected period.

solve.answer: Starting at the lowest point exaggerates the rise, and a different start date would tell another story
solve.work: Cherry-picked start date at the low exaggerates the gain.

questions.stem: A news report says cases of a rare disease in a town "rose 300%". The town had 1 case last year and 4 cases this year. What is the best response?
choices: The report is wrong, because a rise from 1 to 4 is a rise of 400%
A rise of 3 cases is small, and a percent of a tiny base can sound dramatic
The report is right and the disease is spreading so fast that it is a serious outbreak
Percents cannot be used to describe changes in the number of cases of a disease
questions.answer: A rise of 3 cases is small, and a percent of a tiny base can sound dramatic
questions.solution: From 1 to 4 is an increase of 3, which is 300% of the starting 1, so the figure is arithmetically right. But with such a small base, the absolute change of 3 cases is the more honest measure.

solve.answer: A rise of 3 cases is small, and a percent of a tiny base can sound dramatic
solve.work: 1 to 4 is +300% but only 3 cases; small base makes percents dramatic. D is wrong (it is 300%).

questions.stem: Why are predictions from a fitted line riskier outside the range of the data than inside it?
choices: A line always becomes less steep outside the range of the data used
The relationship may change shape outside the range, and the data cannot show how
The line is calculated using only the values at the two ends of the data
Predictions inside the range are certain, so only outside ones can be wrong
questions.answer: The relationship may change shape outside the range, and the data cannot show how
questions.solution: The data only describe the pattern over the range observed. Beyond it, the relationship may curve, level off or reverse, and nothing in the data tells us.

solve.answer: The relationship may change shape outside the range, and the data cannot show how
solve.work: The pattern may change beyond observed x; data say nothing there (extrapolation).

questions.skill: Critique a claim: base rates and screening tests
questions.stem: A test for a rare disease is positive for 95% of people who have the disease and also for 5% of people who do not. The disease affects 1 in 1,000 people. A headline says, "A positive test means a 95% chance you have the disease." What is the best critique?
choices: The headline is correct, because the test is positive for 95% of the people with the disease
The headline is wrong, because the chance of having the disease is exactly 5% after a positive test
The headline is wrong, because a test is not able to be positive for a healthy person
Because the disease is so rare, most people who test positive will not actually have it
questions.answer: Because the disease is so rare, most people who test positive will not actually have it
questions.solution: Out of 100,000 people, about 100 are sick (95 test positive) and about 99,900 are healthy (about 4,995 test positive). Only about 95 of roughly 5,090 positives are sick, about 2%.

solve.answer: Because the disease is so rare, most people who test positive will not actually have it
solve.work: Per 1,000,000: 950 true positives vs 0.05 x 999,000 = 49,950 false positives; P(disease|+) ~ 1.9%.

questions.stem: A study of cities finds r = 0.05 between a city's average temperature and the number of people who visit its parks. The data show park visits are lowest in very cold and very hot cities and highest in mild ones. What is the best conclusion?
choices: The correlation measures only straight-line patterns, so a curved relationship can give r near zero
Since r is near zero, temperature has no connection with park visits
Since r is positive, warmer cities always have more park visits
Since r is small, the data must contain mistakes in how they were recorded
questions.answer: The correlation measures only straight-line patterns, so a curved relationship can give r near zero
questions.solution: The correlation coefficient measures how well data follow a straight line. A rise-then-fall (curved) relationship can be strong while r is close to zero.

solve.answer: The correlation measures only straight-line patterns, so a curved relationship can give r near zero
solve.work: r measures linear association; an inverted-U pattern can give r near 0.

questions.stem: An ad for a company's mutual funds says its funds averaged a 9% yearly return over ten years. The average includes only funds that still exist today. Why might this overstate what an investor would have earned?
choices: Ten years is too short a time to measure a yearly return, so the ad must be false
Funds that still exist today must have earned less than the ones that closed
Funds that did poorly were shut down and left out, which raises the average of the funds that remain
A yearly return can be correct only if it is exactly the same in every year
questions.answer: Funds that did poorly were shut down and left out, which raises the average of the funds that remain
questions.solution: Funds with poor results are often closed and dropped from the list. Averaging only the survivors leaves out the losers and makes the record look better than what an investor in a random fund would have seen.

solve.answer: Funds that did poorly were shut down and left out, which raises the average of the funds that remain
solve.work: Survivorship bias: closed poor performers were excluded.

questions.skill: Critique a claim: biased or nonresponse sample
questions.stem: Researchers compare 40 different foods with a certain disease, using a 5% chance cutoff for each. One food shows a "significant" link, and a headline says that food raises the risk of the disease. What is the best critique?
choices: Forty foods are too many for researchers to compare, so the study should be thrown out
A 5% cutoff means that the one significant link is 95% certain to be real
With 40 comparisons, a link or two will look significant by chance even if none are real
One food out of 40 is too few for a real link to ever be found
questions.answer: With 40 comparisons, a link or two will look significant by chance even if none are real
questions.solution: At a 5% cutoff, about 2 of 40 unrelated foods are expected to look significant by luck alone. A single hit among many tests is weak evidence and needs to be confirmed in a new study.

solve.answer: With 40 comparisons, a link or two will look significant by chance even if none are real
solve.work: Multiple comparisons: with 40 tests at 5%, about 2 false positives are expected by chance.

questions.skill: Critique a policy proposal from data
questions.stem: A bike-lane program cut bike accidents by 30% in a small, flat college town over three years. The mayor of a large, hilly city with heavy traffic says the program will cut accidents there by 30%. What is the best evaluation?
choices: The claim goes beyond the evidence, because the two cities differ in ways that may matter
The claim is sound, because a 30% drop is large enough to apply anywhere
The claim is unsound, because bike lanes cannot change how many accidents happen
The claim is sound, because three years is long enough for any city to follow
questions.answer: The claim goes beyond the evidence, because the two cities differ in ways that may matter
questions.solution: The result was found in one very different place. Whether it carries over depends on how alike the cities are, so the mayor's specific 30% promise is unsupported.

solve.answer: The claim goes beyond the evidence, because the two cities differ in ways that may matter
solve.work: Results from a small flat town may not transfer to a large hilly city: generalization beyond evidence.

questions.stem: Two treatments were used on patients with a disease. Treatment A: 9 of 10 mild cases and 27 of 90 severe cases succeeded. Treatment B: 72 of 90 mild cases and 2 of 10 severe cases succeeded. By how many percentage points is Treatment B's overall success rate higher than Treatment A's?
questions.solution: Treatment A: (9 + 27) / 100 = 36%. Treatment B: (72 + 2) / 100 = 74%. The difference is 38 points, even though A has the higher rate for mild cases (90% to 80%) and for severe cases (30% to 20%).

questions.stem: A drug is advertised as cutting the risk of a side effect by 35%. Without the drug, 0.8% of patients (80 in every 10,000) have the side effect. About how many in every 10,000 patients taking the drug are expected to have the side effect?
questions.solution: 35% of 80 is 28, so the drug leaves 80 - 28 = 52 out of every 10,000 patients with the side effect.

questions.skill: Limits of inference: margin of error
questions.stem: A pollster uses the rule that the margin of error is about 1 divided by the square root of the sample size n (as a decimal). How large must a random sample be to get a margin of error of 0.025, which is 2.5 percentage points?
questions.solution: Set 1 / sqrt(n) = 0.025. Then sqrt(n) = 1 / 0.025 = 40, so n = 40 squared = 1,600.

questions.skill: Critique a claim: base rates and screening tests
questions.stem: A disease affects 100 of every 1,000 people in a town. A test is positive for 80% of the people who have the disease and also positive for 10% of the people who do not. If all 1,000 people are tested, how many are expected to test positive?
questions.solution: Of the 100 sick people, 80% is 80 positives. Of the 900 healthy people, 10% is 90 positives. In all, 80 + 90 = 170 test positive.

solve.work: 100 diseased x 0.8 = 80; 900 healthy x 0.1 = 90; total 170.

questions.stem: A gym says, "Members who stay for a year lose 15 pounds on average." Of 1,000 people who joined, 200 stayed for the year and lost 15 pounds on average. The other 800 quit early and lost 3 pounds on average. What was the average loss, in pounds, for all 1,000 who joined?
questions.solution: Total loss: 200 x 15 + 800 x 3 = 3,000 + 2,400 = 5,400 pounds. Divided among 1,000 people, that is 5.4 pounds each.

questions.skill: Critique a claim: biased or nonresponse sample
questions.stem: A mail survey went to 2,000 residents. Only 400 replied, and 300 of those replies said yes to a proposal. What is the smallest possible percent of all 2,000 residents who would say yes? Give the number only, without the percent sign.
questions.solution: At least the 300 who replied yes would say yes, even if all 1,600 who did not reply would say no. 300 / 2,000 = 15%.

solve.work: At least the 300 yes replies: 300/2000 = 15% if every non-respondent says no.

questions.stem: A report says the risk of an illness among people who use a product is "up 150%". Without the product, 4 of every 100 people get the illness. According to the report, how many of every 100 users get the illness?
questions.solution: An increase of 150% means the new risk is 4 + 1.5 x 4 = 4 + 6 = 10 out of 100.

questions.stem: A study reports a correlation of r = 0.6 between hours studied and exam score. About what percent of the variation in exam scores is accounted for by the linear relationship with hours studied? Give the number only, without the percent sign.
questions.solution: The share of variation explained is r squared: 0.6 x 0.6 = 0.36, or 36%. It is not 60%.
